en: The Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mokṣala of Khotan during the Western Jin Dynasty,
by Imperial Decree.
Chapter One: The Emission of Light from the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra. Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats—whose outflows were exhausted, whose minds were liberated and stainless, who possessed mastery over all wisdom and had completed all their tasks; who were like great dragons, having done what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained their goal, brought an end to the three states of existence, and were fully liberated through right understanding.

Furthermore, there were five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, as well as upāsakas, upāsikās, and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had already attained the *dhāraṇī* of empty practice (*śūnyatā-caryā-samādhi*), the treasury of signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*);
who had attained equal patience (*samarpa-ksānti*) and the gate of unimpeded *dhāraṇī*; all of whom possessed the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

Their speech is gentle and supple, free from all indolence; having abandoned gain and honor, they harbor no expectations. Having attained profound *dharmakṣānti*, they have acquired the power of diligence; they have transcended the conduct of Māra and crossed over the realm of death.
Their instructions follow a sequential order, such that throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they do not forget their original practices.
Their countenances are harmonious and joyful; they are always humble and respectful, and their speech is never coarse.

Within the great assembly, his mindfulness is perfected; throughout incalculable eons, he is capable of teaching and transforming others. All that he speaks is like an illusion, a dream, an echo, a light, a shadow, a transformation, a bubble on water, a reflection in a mirror, a mirage, and the moon in water; he constantly uses these dharmas to awaken all beings.
He fully knows the inclinations and destinations of the minds of sentient beings, and with subtle wisdom, he delivers them according to their original conduct.
His mind is free from obstruction and he is endowed with the perfection of patience; his entry into truth is thorough and precise, and he vows to encompass countless and immeasurable Buddha-lands.
The samādhis practiced by immeasurable Buddhas all manifest before them;
they are able to request the Buddhas to preach the Dharma for the sake of all beings;
they are free from attachment to various views and have already sported within hundreds of thousands of samādhis for their own enjoyment.
The virtues of all these bodhisattvas were likewise thus— their names being: Bodhisattva Protector of All Bonds,
Bodhisattva Jewel-Come, Bodhisattva Guide, Bodhisattva Dragon-Giver, Bodhisattva Able-to-Speak-What-is-Received,
Bodhisattva Rain-Giver, Bodhisattva Heavenly King, Bodhisattva Worthy Protector, and Bodhisattva Sublime Intention.
Sākyamuni, there were the bodhisattvas Dhṛtimat, Vardhamānamati, Abhūtamoha, Supratiṣṭhita, Vikrāntagāmin, Nityodyukta, Anikṣiptadhura, Sūryagarbhasaṃdhārin, Akṣayamati, and Ghoṣadatta.
The Bodhisattva Ayalokeśvara, the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta, the Bodhisattva Nityotkṣiptahasta, the Bodhisattva Maitreya,
and many other hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas were all present; they were all those who occupy the position of the Honored One in his final birth before Buddhahood.
Furthermore, there were countless hundreds of thousands of millions of other bodhisattvas, as well as all the venerable sons of the elders, who had all come to the assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One personally prepared a high seat and sat upon it in the full lotus posture, entering the samādhi of right concentration.
This samādhi is named the King of Samādhis, for all samādhis enter into it.
Having attained this samādhi, he employs his divine eye to observe the world-systems.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted light from the thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of his feet, which extended from his calves up to the uṣṇīṣa on his head; from every joint and limb of his body, he emitted sixty billion hundred thousand rays of light, illuminating the entire trichiliocosm without exception.

That radiance further illuminated the eastern, western, southern, and northern directions, as well as the four intermediate points, above, and below, reaching the Buddha-lands of lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
among the various classes of sentient beings, those who beheld this light became firm in their resolve and all gave rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.

At that time, the World-Honored One again emitted light from the hairs of his body; from each and every pore, he radiated brilliant light, which further illuminated the trichiliocosm and further illuminated the countless lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.
All sentient beings who beheld this light resolved their wills to give rise to the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment.

The World-Honored One again, by means of the dharmas of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, emitted a great radiance that pervaded the entire trichiliocosm and further illuminated countless lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions;
all sentient beings who beheld this light likewise resolved their wills to generate the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his broad and long tongue, which reached throughout the trichiliocosm.
Having reached everywhere, from the root of that tongue he again emitted countless hundreds of thousands of millions of rays of light.
Each ray of light transforms into a precious lotus flower with a thousand petals, its color like gold.
Upon each flower sits a Buddha, and every one of these Buddhas expounds the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
All sentient beings who hear the Dharma being preached shall all resolve to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
Each of the lotus-flower images within the radiance of his tongue further illuminates lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions;
all sentient beings who behold that radiance and hear the Dharma being preached shall likewise resolve to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered a samādhi upon the lion throne; this samādhi is named "Lion’s Play.
He manifested his supernormal powers, causing the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system to tremble in six ways.
By the majestic power of samādhi, the ground of this trichiliocosm became soft and supple, rising and sinking.
All those in the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the class of wriggling creatures, as well as those in the eight difficult conditions, were all completely liberated.
They will be reborn in the heavens, reaching as far as the sixth heaven among the realms of humans.

As soon as they have been born in the heavens or among humans, they will all experience great joy; they will immediately recognize their past lives and come to the Buddha’s dwelling to prostrate themselves and receive the Dharma.

In this way, throughout the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions, all beings in the three evil realms and the eight difficult conditions shall likewise be freed from suffering, and those born among gods and humans shall reach as far as the sixth heaven.

Immediately upon their birth, they experienced great joy and also remembered their past lives; each went to the presence of the Buddha in their own land, prostrated themselves, and received the Dharma.

At that time, throughout the trichiliocosm, those who were blind regained their sight; those who were deaf regained their hearing; those who were mute were able to speak; those who were hunchbacked straightened themselves; those who were bound or crippled regained their hands and feet; the insane recovered their sanity; the distracted attained concentration; the sick were healed; the hungry and thirsty were fully satiated; the weak gained strength; the aged became young; and the naked obtained clothing. All sentient beings attained a single-minded purpose, regarding one another as fathers and mothers, as elder and younger brothers. They practiced the ten wholesome deeds equally and purely cultivated the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*), free from defilement and dwelling in serene happiness, like bhikṣus who have attained the third dhyāna. All sentient beings attained wisdom, becoming self-restrained and disciplined, no longer harassing other beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon the lion throne; within this trichiliocosm, his virtue was preeminent and supreme, and his radiance, physical form, and majestic power were most sublime.

Just as Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, cannot be surpassed by any other mountain, so too at that time the World-Honored One, according to the Dharma of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, used a great universal voice to pervade the Sahā world-system of three thousandfold worlds, reaching the Śuddhāvāsa deities, the Brahmās, the sixth heavenly king, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings. All the devas and sentient beings therein beheld the lion throne and heard what the Buddha spoke; each took various kinds of celestial incense and various kinds of celestial flowers and came to where the Buddha was to make offerings to the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Thereupon, the sentient beings within the trichiliocosm each took all manner of worldly famous incenses and various flowers from both land and water and came to where the Buddha was, making offerings to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the celestial incense and flowers, as well as the incense and flowers of sentient beings, which were offered and scattered over the Tathāgata, merged and transformed in mid-air into a great platform, from which various banners and streamers hung down.

The banners, streamers, and flower-canopies were a vibrant array of five colors; the radiance of the flower-canopies shone everywhere throughout the trichiliocosm, turning it entirely golden, and the same was true for the Buddha-lands of the Ganges-sands of worlds in the ten directions.
At that time, the people of Jambudvīpa thought to themselves:
"Today the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is preaching the Dharma for us alone; he is not elsewhere."
All sentient beings within the various trichiliocosm world-systems likewise thought to themselves:
"Today the Tathāgata is seated before me alone, preaching the Dharma for my sake, and not in any other land."
At that time, the World-Honored One again emitted light from his lion throne, illuminating the trichiliocosm.

Among the sentient beings therein, those who beheld the light all saw the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction, along with their assemblies of disciples; they also saw Śākyamuni Buddha and his gathered congregations here in this Sahā world-system.
It was likewise so for each of the world-systems throughout the ten directions, such that they could see one another.

To the east, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, there is a world named Ratnāvati. Its Buddha is named Ratnakāra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells there, teaching and transforming all beings through the Prajñāpāramitā.
There was a bodhisattva named Samantaprabha who, seeing the radiance, transformations, and majestic spiritual power of Śākyamuni Buddha, was moved and addressed the Tathāgata Ratnakāra, saying:
"For what reason today has there appeared such a manifestation of the Buddha’s body, with its radiance and transformations that move us so?"
The Tathāgata Ratnakāra addressed Samantaprabha, saying:
"To the far west, there is a world named Sahā; its Buddha is named Śākyamuni, who currently resides there, preaching the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of all bodhisattvas."
"This is its auspicious response.
Puming addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Indeed it is so, World-Honored One!"
I wish to go there to see Śākyamuni Buddha, to pay homage to him, and to make offerings.
In that land, all the bodhisattvas have attained dhāraṇīs and have attained various samādhis, including the Samādhi of Transcendence.
The Buddha told Puming: "Go as you wish.
Then, the Buddha Ratnakāra took a thousand-petaled golden lotus and gave it to Puming, saying:
"Take these offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha.
He addressed Puming once more:
"Go to that land; maintain your dignified deportment and do not fail in the proper ritual procedures."
"Why is this? Because the bodhisattvas in that land uphold the practice of the precepts; for this reason, they are born there.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantaraśmi, together with countless hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas, innumerable bhikṣus, and a multitude of good men and good women, came from the east—having made offerings of incense and flowers and paid homage to all the Buddhas they encountered along the way—and arrived at the Sahā world.
Having seen Śākyamuni Buddha, they prostrated themselves in worship. The Bodhisattva Puming addressed Śākyamuni Buddha, saying:
“Tathāgata Ratnakāra sends his most earnest greetings and inquiries after the World-Honored One:
‘Are you light and agile in sitting and rising? Is your physical strength as usual?’”
"I now offer these flowers as an offering to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha immediately accepted them.

Śākyamuni Buddha then scattered these flowers toward the eastern direction across buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. These flowers reached everywhere; within each flower there was a seated Buddha, all of whom preached the *prajñāpāramitā* to transform sentient beings. Those who heard this teaching all gave rise to the aspiration for unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment.

Those sons and daughters of good family who followed the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha arrived and all paid homage at the feet of Śākyamuni Buddha, bringing with them fragrances and flowers as offerings to the World-Honored One.

To the south, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a world named *Atikrama-śoka*; its Buddha is named *Aśoka-tejas* Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and he has a bodhisattva named *Vigata-śoka*.

To the west, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a world named *Pāpa-nirodha*; its Buddha is named *Ratnottama* Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and he has a bodhisattva named *Manas-caryā*.

To the north, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a world named *Jaya*; its Buddha is named *Maitrī-rāja* Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and he has a bodhisattva named *Dāna-jaya*.

Below, at a distance as many worlds away as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, there is a world named Bhadra; its Buddha is named Bhadratejas Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and he has a bodhisattva named Supuṣpa.

Above, at a distance as many worlds away as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, there is a world named Cintitārtha; its Buddha is named Cintiteśvaratejas Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and he has a bodhisattva named Cintitārthadatta.
In this way, the bodhisattvas from each of the six directions addressed their respective buddhas, saying:
"What kind of transformation is this that has appeared here?
Each of those buddhas replied to the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Far away from here, in the world-system called Sahā, there is a Buddha named Śākyamuni who is preaching the Prajñāpāramitā to the bodhisattvas; this is that auspicious omen."
Those bodhisattvas each addressed their respective Buddhas, saying:
"We wish to go to the Sahā world to see Śākyamuni Buddha, to pay homage, serve, and make offerings to him.
At that time, those Buddhas each gave them precious flowers, and together with countless hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas, bhikṣu-saṃghas, and good men and women, they all came to this place.
In all the lands they passed through, they each made offerings of incense and flowers to the various Buddhas.

Next, they proceeded to the Sahā world, where they beheld Śākyamuni Buddha; their offerings, prostrations, and inquiries were all conducted in the same manner as those of the bodhisattvas from the eastern regions.

At that time, in a single moment, the entire realm of the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system became composed entirely of jewels; all its trees, grasses, and shrubs were transformed into fragrant flowers. Banners, pennants, silken streamers, and flowered canopies were suspended everywhere, such that this Sahā world was as magnificent and wondrous as the land of the Tathāgata Samantakusuma in the Padmavati world, or the lands inhabited by Mañjuśrī, the Devaputra Susīma, and the bodhisattvas of great majestic power. All the precious wonders of this world were just like those lands.

At that time, the entire assembly—including devas, māras, and brahmās; nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas; śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; the people of the world; and all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, both those who had newly resolved their minds and those who were long-established—had all gathered together.
Knowing that the assembly was settled, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice and cultivate the Prajñāpāramitā.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If one wishes to attain knowledge of all dharmas, how should one practice the *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is never a time when they do not practice giving (*dāna*). When there is wealth, a donor, and a recipient, this constitutes the practice of the *dānapāramitā*.
To know transgressions and know blessings is to practice the *śīla-pāramitā*;
to give rise to no thoughts of anger is to practice the *kṣānti-pāramitā*;
for body and speech to be constantly diligent and the mind never indolent is to practice the *vīrya-pāramitā*.
"To find no relish in the six sense-faculties is to practice the dhyāna-pāramitā. The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñā-pāramitā, their mind remains settled and unarisen; they should fully possess the four applications of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. They should fully possess the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, and the samādhi of wishlessness; they should fully possess the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless samādhis; and they should possess the eight liberations and attain the nine successive dhyānas."
Furthermore, one should know the nine signs: the sign of fresh death;

the sign of being bound with sinews like a bundle of firewood; the sign of bluish discoloration; the sign of festering pus; the sign of blood; the sign of undigested consumption; the sign of the separation of bones and joints; the sign of long-standing bones; and the sign of being scorched and loathsome.

Having understood all marks, one should bring to mind the Buddha, resolve upon the Dharma, and resolve upon the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus; one should resolve upon giving and precepts, resolve upon ānāpāna-smṛti (mindfulness of breathing), and resolve upon the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; one should resolve upon the perception of non-delight, the perception of non-arising and non-ceasing, the perception of no-path, the perception of inexhaustibility, the perception of non-origination, the perception of goodness, and the perception of the Dharma, thereby foreknowing the intentions of all sentient beings.
This is called wisdom.

One thereby attains the samādhi of awakening, the samādhi of fearlessness, the state with perception and fear, the state without perception and fear, and the state that is neither with nor without perception and fear.
Regarding the faculty of "not yet known," one should know it as "to be known" and "already known.
One should know how to transcend the eight afflictions and eliminate the twelve decays.
One should be fully endowed with the ten powers of a Buddha, the eighteen unique dharmas, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom, and great loving-kindness and great compassion.
One who wishes to realize the wisdom of all bodhisattvas should practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to be fully endowed with *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) and to sever the habitual tendencies of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Thus it is, Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to ascend to the bodhisattva stage, who wish to transcend the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and who wish to dwell in the stage of avaivartika, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
One who wishes to abide in the six supernormal powers and know the inclinations and intentions of all people should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
One who wishes to surpass the wisdom of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to attain all the gates of dhāraṇīs and samādhis, as well as all the gates of manifold wisdoms, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

Those who wish to surpass all the merits performed by the families of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—namely, their acts of giving, observance of precepts, and various forms of encouragement and assistance—should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to know all the precepts, samādhis, wisdoms, liberations, and the knowledge and vision of liberation belonging to the families of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and wishes to surpass them, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to obtain immeasurable merit as a great reward through small amounts of giving, small amounts of ethical discipline, small amounts of patience, small amounts of diligence, and small amounts of meditative concentration—such that their practiced conduct is slight yet the reward is vast—they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to cause his kinsmen and body to be like the physical form of a Buddha, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to be fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics of a great man, to perfect the lineage of all bodhisattvas, and to attain the state of Kumārabhūta, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who constantly desires not to be separated from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and who wishes to accomplish all merits through various modes of practice toward the Buddhas, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings—wishing to provide them with food and drink, vehicles, elephants and horses, sandals, clothing and furs, incense and flowers, canopies and decorations, and bedding and furniture—and desires to satisfy whatever they seek so that all needs are fully met, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to cause all the people within buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to fully practice the six pāramitās, they should study the prajñāpāramitā."
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to practice meritorious deeds so as to reach perfect Buddhahood should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to have their meritorious deeds praised by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to, with a single resolve, transcend the Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions and reach them all, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to emit a single sound that is heard throughout all the ten directions, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to protect all the buddha-fields of the ten directions so that they are never interrupted, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to abide in internal emptiness, external emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, infinite emptiness, the emptiness of all things, essential emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of non-reliance, and the emptiness of non-existence; and if they wish to know the reality of these phenomena of emptiness, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to awaken to and know the suchness (tathatā) of all Buddhas and all dharmas, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If they wish to know the nature (svabhāva) of all dharmas, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Śāriputra, one who wishes to know the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all dharmas should study the Prajñāpāramitā. Śāriputra,
it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, should abide.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to know the number of dust motes within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system, as well as the number of all trees, growing grasses, branches, leaves, stems, and nodes, he should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to split a single hair into one hundred parts, and with one such part of hair take up the waters of the great trichiliocosm to count how many drops there are, knowing their total number without disturbing the nature of water—one who desires to achieve this should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If the fires should break out within a trichiliocosm, like those at the end of a kalpa when the world is consumed by flames, and one wishes to extinguish that great conflagration all at once, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes to be able to obstruct the force of a great wind that arises within a trichiliocosm—blowing Mount Sumeru so that it becomes like winnowed chaff—by using a single finger, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to fill the entire space of the trichiliocosm with a single paryanka cross-legged posture, and desires to attain this, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes to be able to take all the Mount Sumerus in the trichiliocosm with a single hand and place them in countless Buddha-fields in other directions, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can satisfy the Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples throughout the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions with a single bowl of food, causing them all to be fully satiated, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, one who wishes to provide offerings of precious jewels, clothing and ornaments, banners, flags, silk canopies, incense, and flowers to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, along with their assemblies of disciples, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes to cause all sentient beings within the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions to be fully endowed with precepts, samādhi, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, and to attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa up to nirvāṇa without remainder—one who desires this should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom gives a gift, he should form this thought:
'May I obtain a great fruit of retribution.'"

If one wishes to be born into the family of a venerable one, a brahmin of great lineage, or a householder; or to be born among the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the sixth heaven; or, by means of this giving, to attain the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna and the formless meditations; or, through performing such giving, to attain the Eightfold Path of the Noble Ones, reaching from the stage of Srotāpanna up to Arhat and Pratyekabuddha—one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they fulfill the six perfections through the skillful means of wisdom."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
“How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the six pāramitās through giving?
The Buddha said:

“A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the dānapāramitā should practice the dharma of non-reliance; by causing both that which is given and the recipient to fulfill all the pāramitās, this is called fulfilling the dānapāramitā.”
To neither incur sin nor merit regarding good or evil is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
To be without anger and without joy is the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
For the mind to be without indolence is the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
To give rise to no doubt regarding non-attachment is the perfection of dhyāna (dhyānapāramitā).
To be detached from all phenomena is the perfection of prajñā (prajñāpāramitā). "Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to know the dharmas of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

One who wishes to transcend conditioned and unconditioned phenomena should study the *prajñāpāramitā*. One who wishes to awaken to the suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present;

one who wishes to realize the limit of cessation (*nirodhakoṭi*) through the arising of the marks of dharmas; one who wishes to surpass the stage of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; one who wishes to serve as an attendant to all Buddhas; one who wishes to become an inner retinue of the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones; one who intends to form a great retinue; one who wishes to obtain the retinue of bodhisattvas; one who wishes to repay great generosity; one who wishes to practice signless giving (*animitta-dāna*); one who wishes not to give rise to malicious thoughts; one who wishes not to give rise to thoughts of resentment; one who wishes not to give rise to thoughts of indolence; one who wishes not to give rise to distracted thoughts; and one who wishes not to give rise to wrong wisdom—such a person should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to establish all beings in generosity, ethical discipline, and mindfulness, and to perform the work of encouraging and assisting them in their meritorious deeds, should study the Prajñāpāramitā."
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to establish the five eyes, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
What are the five eyes? They are the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the dharma eye, and the buddha eye.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to obtain the divine eye to see the Buddhas of the ten directions; wishes to hear with the divine ear the Dharma taught by the Buddhas of the ten directions; and wishes to fully know the intentions of those Buddhas, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to hear the teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions without interruption, up until the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to see the buddha-fields of the past buddhas and the present buddha-world-honored ones should study the prajñāpāramitā."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to hear the twelve divisions of the sūtras spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions, wishes to recite them, or wishes to hear that which has never been heard by the śrāvakas, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to hear all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions—both those already spoken and those yet to be spoken—and desires to fully understand them in order to teach all sentient beings everywhere, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes to hear and know all the dharmas taught by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, and having heard them, to teach them universally to all readers, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes to take up radiance and illuminate everywhere throughout all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions—vast as the sands of the Ganges—even those dark places not reached by the sun or moon, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If there are worlds throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, where sentient beings have never before heard the sound of the Buddha, the sound of the Dharma, or the sound of the Sangha, one who can establish all such beings so that they hear the sounds of the Triple Gem with right view should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to cause the sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions to gain sight if they are blind, to gain hearing if they are deaf, to regain their senses if they are insane, to obtain clothing if they are naked, and to attain satiety if they are hungry or thirsty, should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to cause the sentient beings within the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions—those who are in states of sin or in the three evil realms—to be liberated and all to attain human bodies, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes to cause all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to be fully endowed with ethical discipline, samādhi, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; from the stage of srotāpanna up to arhat, pratyekabuddha, and even up to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and the majestic deportment of all Buddhas—one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully know all matters of the Dharma and worldly affairs should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

One should study the *prajñāpāramitā* with the intention that when walking, the feet shall be four inches above the ground while wheel-marks appear; that the Four Great Kings and the Akaniṣṭha devas, together with immeasurable hosts of celestial attendants, shall surround one and proceed to the Bodhi tree; and that the gods shall provide seats of heavenly cloth, and that the places where I walk, stay, and sit upon attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* shall all become diamond (*vajra*). One should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* on the very day he goes forth into homelessness, and on that same day of going forth to turn the wheel of Dharma; to cause countless *asaṃkhyeya* beings to be cleansed of dust and free from defilement so that their Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena becomes pure; to cause countless *asaṃkhyeya* beings to have their outflows exhausted and their minds liberated; and to cause countless *asaṃkhyeya* beings to attain the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) and achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—such a bodhisattva mahāsattva should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva makes the vow that upon becoming a Buddha, he shall preach the Dharma simultaneously to an immeasurable multitude of disciples, such that those who hear it attain Arhatship while still on their seats, and those who have resolved for Bodhicitta attain the stage of Avaivartika and realize Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; and such that the immeasurable Bodhisattvas increase his lifespan to the extent of being infinite, and his radiance neither increases nor decreases according to that lifespan—he should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, if he wishes to cause his buddha-field to be free from even the names of lust, anger, and ignorance; if he wishes for all sentient beings to attain equal wisdom; if he constantly contemplates giving and constantly contemplates pure precepts; if he disciplines and restrains himself so as not to afflict other sentient beings; and if, after his parinirvāṇa, he wishes to ensure that there is no name even for the extinction of the Dharma—he should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva makes the vow that at the time he attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, all who hear his voice shall surely reach Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—one who wishes to obtain such [a result] should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

Chapter 2: On Non-Seeing The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Two: On Non-Seeing "Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom and gives rise to this thought, the Four Heavenly Kings all rejoice in their minds and think:
'We too shall present four bowls to the bodhisattva, just as the kings of old presented bowls to the Buddhas according to the royal law.'"
The King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and the King of the Sixth Heaven both thought with joy:
"When this bodhisattva attains buddhahood, we shall also serve and attend upon him, diminishing the race of the asuras and increasing the hosts of the devas."
Within the trichiliocosm, each of the Akaniṣṭha devas rejoiced and likewise thought:
"When this bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā and attains buddhahood, we too shall provide encouragement and assistance, entreating the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma."
"In this way, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they further increase and bring to fulfillment the six perfections."
Each of those good sons and good daughters will rejoice and think to themselves:
"I shall act as parents, brothers, wife and children, kinsmen, friends, or spiritual mentors for this bodhisattva."
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings and the various Akaniṣṭha devas each thought to themselves:

"We shall cause this bodhisattva to constantly practice the pure conduct (brahmacarya); from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, let him never encounter the pleasures of form and desire."
One who commits sexual misconduct loses the pure conduct (brahmacarya); how much more so for one who practices the Way?
A bodhisattva who constantly cultivates pure conduct will surely attain Buddhahood; one does not achieve the Way by committing sexual misconduct.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Must a bodhisattva necessarily have parents, a wife and children, and kinsmen?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Some Bodhisattvas have parents but no wife or children;
some Bodhisattvas, from their first generation of the aspiration for enlightenment, practice celibacy as a youth and do not take a wife until they attain Buddhahood.”

There may be bodhisattvas who, through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), manifest within the midst of the five desires the arousal of the mind for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and their departure from the household life. Śāriputra!
It is like a master illusionist skilled in the arts of illusion who conjures up the five sensory pleasures and the objects of desire, within which he indulges at will and enjoys himself with others.
What do you think? Is there anything among these creations of the illusionist that can actually be worn or eaten?
Śāriputra said: “No, World-Honored One!
An illusion has no existence.”

“In this way, Śāriputra, the bodhisattva, through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), manifests the appearance of having desire; yet within the midst of sensual desires, he nurtures all beings without being defiled by them— viewing desire as fire and like an enemy,
he speaks of the evils of desire and constantly maintains a mind of revulsion toward it.”
Although a bodhisattva manifests as being amidst the realm of desire, they constantly maintain this thought:
"If even a bodhisattva who practices skillful means maintains such an intention, how much more so should one who is newly trained and has first resolved to attain enlightenment?"
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How should a bodhisattva practice the prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive a bodhisattva, nor do they perceive the name, nor do they perceive the perfection of wisdom."
There is nothing at all to be seen, nor does one see anyone who does not practice.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva is empty, and the word [bodhisattva] is also empty.
Emptiness is the absence of the five aggregates (skandhas).
What are the five aggregates?
They are the aggregate of form, the aggregate of sensation, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
The five aggregates are emptiness, and emptiness is the five aggregates. Why is this?
It is merely words.

It is by means of words that it is called "the Path," by means of words that it is called "Bodhisattva," by means of words that it is called "emptiness," and by means of words that it is called "the five aggregates.
In reality, they neither arise nor cease, and there is neither attachment nor cessation.
When a bodhisattva practices in this manner, they neither perceive arising nor perceive cessation, and neither perceive attachment nor perceive severance. Why is this?
It is only by taking emptiness as the basis for establishing dharmas that names are provisionally designated as characters.
When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they do not perceive the characters of any dharmas; because there is nothing perceived, there is no entering.

Chapter Three: On Designations (*Prajñāpāramitā-mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Chapter on Designations) "Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* should contemplate in this way: 'Bodhisattva' is merely a designation;
'Buddha' is also merely a designation; 'prajñāpāramitā' is also merely a designation; and the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are also merely designations."

Śāriputra! All that is spoken of as "self" is merely a designation; even when one searches for a self, no self is found. There is no sentient being, no that which is born, no one who gives birth, and no self-arising. There is no person and no birth; there is no action and no agent. Furthermore, there is no one who accomplishes, no one who receives, and no one who bestows; there is neither seeing nor attaining.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are non-existent, for they are empty.
Therefore, the bodhisattva perceives nothing at all within all letter-dharmas; and within that state of non-perception, there is furthermore no perception.
When a bodhisattva practices this prajñāpāramitā in this manner, they surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—except for the Buddhas—by virtue of the emptiness of non-existence.
Why is this? Because nothing at all is seen as a place of entry. Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva is thus, they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.

For example, suppose all the trees, wild grasses, rice, hemp, sugarcane, thickets, bamboos, and reeds within a single Jambudvīpa were each like Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others—were as numerous as these, and possessed immeasurable virtue in wisdom and supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*)—yet if one wished to compare them to a bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, they could never be compared;
they would fall short by countless hundreds of thousands of millions of times, and no analogy can serve as a comparison.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is because the bodhisattva maintains wisdom in order to deliver all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
the wisdom contemplated by a bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā surpasses that of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas within a single day."
Śāriputra! Setting aside the grasses and trees within Jambudvīpa,
suppose that the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were filled with beings such as yourself, Śāriputra, and Maudgalyāyana, until it was completely full.
Setting this matter aside, suppose that throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there were beings exactly like Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana,

filling them all to capacity. Even if their number were thus incalculable, if one were to compare them to a bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, they would not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-thousand-millionth part.

When a bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā possesses this wisdom and compares it to the wisdom of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, it is not comparable even by a factor of hundreds, thousands, or tens of millions.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, as for the wisdom possessed by all the disciples—from the srotāpanna up to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and ascending to the bodhisattvas and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—all these various forms of wisdom do not contradict one another; they have no source of origination. In reality, they are all empty, without distinction, neither emerging nor arising."
In truth, emptiness possesses no distinctions of superiority or inferiority; why then does the World-Honored One say:
"The single day’s thought of a bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā surpasses that of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas"?
"Why is this so? The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The reason they surpass those above is that when a bodhisattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, even for a single day, their thought is as follows:"
"I shall, by means of the causal conditions of the Dharma, awaken all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings and deliver them.
What do you think, Śāriputra?
"Do the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas ever have such a thought? Śāriputra replied,
"Yes, World-Honored One."
“None of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas ever had such a thought.
Therefore, Śāriputra, you should know and keep this in mind:

if one were to compare the wisdom possessed by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas with the wisdom of a bodhisattva, it would not be comparable even by a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, do śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas ever think:

'I shall practice the six pāramitās, instruct sentient beings, purify buddha-fields, fulfill the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, and the four unhindered wisdoms; and having fulfilled the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, I shall attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment'?"
"Would you have any thought such as, 'I shall cause incalculable,
asaṃkhyeya numbers of people to attain nirvāṇa'? Śāriputra replied:
“No, World-Honored One!
There is no such thought.
The Buddha said:
“A bodhisattva can indeed do so.
By practicing the six pāramitās and fulfilling the eighteen dharmas, a bodhisattva shall attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) and deliver all sentient beings.”
Śāriputra, it is just as a firefly does not think:
"May my light illuminate Jambudvīpa and make it universally bright.
In this same way, Śāriputra!
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas likewise do not have such thoughts as:
"I shall practice the six pāramitās, fulfill the eighteen dharmas, attain unexcelled perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), and deliver sentient beings."
“Śāriputra! It is like the rising sun that shines everywhere upon Jambudvīpa; there is none who does not receive its light.
In the same way, when a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, fulfills the eighteen dharmas, and attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they deliver incalculable numbers of all sentient beings.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva transcend the stages of the arhat and the pratyekabuddha, attain the stage of *avaivartika*, and cultivate and adorn the stage of the Buddha-way?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“From the time a bodhisattva first resolves upon enlightenment, they constantly practice the six pāramitās, abide in the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, transcend the stages of the arhats and pratyekabuddhas, and attain the stage of avaivartika.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In what stage does a bodhisattva abide so as to serve as a field of merit for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"From the time a bodhisattva first resolves upon enlightenment until they reach the site of awakening, throughout that interval, they constantly act as protectors for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
Why is this? Śāriputra!

When there are bodhisattvas in the world, one knows that the five precepts, the ten wholesome paths of action, the eight fast-day observances, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, and even the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment all appear in the world; thus, the eighteen unique qualities and the ten powers of a Buddha, as well as the four fearlessnesses, are fully realized.

When this Dharma exists in the world, one then knows that there are the royal caste, the brahmin caste, the householder caste, and the kṣatriya caste; one then knows that there are the first Four Heavenly Kings up to the Thirty-three Heavens; and one then knows that there are the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha, up to the Buddha, all appearing in the world.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
“How does a bodhisattva fully repay the kindness of those who give?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"A Bodhisattva does not requite the merit of giving.
Why is this? Because it has already been requited from the very beginning."
The Bodhisattva constantly practices giving; what kind of giving does he maintain?
He gives all wholesome dharmas.
What are these wholesome dharmas?
The ten wholesome dharmas—

from these ten wholesome dharmas up to the dharmas of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, including the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the possession of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha— are given as this gift.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"How does a bodhisattva correspond with the prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“A bodhisattva should know that form is conjoined with emptiness; this is being in accord with the perfection of wisdom.
One should know that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are conjoined with emptiness; this is being in accord with the perfection of wisdom.”

One should know that the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are in union with emptiness; one should know that forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects are in union with emptiness. It is the same for visual consciousness, auditory consciousness, olfactory consciousness, gustatory consciousness, tactile consciousness, and the consciousness of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); this is what is meant by "correspondence."
One should know that the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—is likewise in accord with emptiness.
One should know the twelve links of dependent origination. What are these twelve?

First is ignorance, second is volitional formations, third is consciousness, fourth is name-and-form, fifth is the six sense bases, sixth is contact, seventh is feeling, eighth is craving, ninth is grasping, tenth is becoming, eleventh is birth, and twelfth is aging-and-death.
These twelve links of dependent origination are also in accord with emptiness.
One should know that all dharmas—both conditioned and unconditioned—are likewise in accord with emptiness.
One should know that intrinsic nature is likewise conjoined with emptiness;
this is what constitutes being in accord with the prajñāpāramitā. Thus it is, Śāriputra!
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows the convergence of the seven kinds of emptiness. What are the seven?
They are the aforementioned seven matters.

One who knows that these seven matters are in accord with the *prajñāpāramitā* neither perceives the conjunction of the five aggregates nor their non-conjunction; they neither perceive the dharma of the arising of the five aggregates nor the dharma of the cessation of the five aggregates.

Nor does one perceive the dharma of attachment to the five aggregates, nor does one perceive the dharma of severing the five aggregates; nor does one perceive form as conjoined with sensation, nor sensation as conjoined with perception, nor perception as conjoined with consciousness, nor consciousness as conjoined with mental formations.
Why is this? Because from the very beginning, no dharma has ever been seen to conjoin with another dharma, for their nature is fundamentally empty. Śāriputra!
Because form is empty, it is not form; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, they are not consciousness.

Because form is empty, there is nothing seen; because feeling is empty, there is nothing felt; because perception is empty, there is nothing conceptualized; because mental formations are empty, there is nothing conditioned; because consciousness is empty, consciousness is not perceived.
Why is this? Because form and emptiness are equal and without distinction. For what reason?
Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise emptiness, and emptiness is consciousness.

One does not perceive arising, nor does one perceive cessation; one does not perceive attachment, nor does one perceive severance; one does not perceive increase, nor does one perceive decrease. There is no past, future, or present; there are no five aggregates; there are no forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas; there are no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; there are no twelve links of dependent origination; and there are no four noble truths. There is nothing to be attained, nor are there stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, or pratyekabuddhas; there is no Buddha, and there is no path.
In this way, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should form this thought, should have this knowledge, and should respond in this manner.

One who practices in this manner neither perceives what is appropriate nor what is inappropriate; regarding the six pāramitās, they do not perceive them as being conjoined with the dharmas of the five aggregates, nor even with the dharmas of the body, nor do they perceive either their conjunction or their non-conjunction.

Regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and even the dharma of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), one likewise does not perceive what is appropriate or inappropriate.
Therefore, Śāriputra, you should know that a bodhisattva is conjoined with the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Śāriputra:
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not conjoin with emptiness, nor do they conjoin with signlessness or wishlessness.
Signlessness and wishlessness likewise do not conjoin with emptiness.
Why is this? Emptiness is neither seen to be conjoined nor not conjoined; the same is true for signlessness and wishlessness. This is what accords with the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, having transcended the characteristics of empty dharmas, they neither unite with the five aggregates nor do they not unite with them. They do not unite past form (*rūpa*) with past form, nor do they perceive past form; they do not unite future form with future form, nor do they perceive future form; they do not unite present form with present form, nor do they perceive present form.
It is the same for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Why is this? Because the names of the three periods of time—past, future, and present—are all empty.
To practice in such a manner is to accord with the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom and the dharma of sarvajñatā, they do not perceive it as conjoined with the past, future, or present, nor do they perceive the past, future, or present.
A bodhisattva should form this thought and respond in this way. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
omniscience (sarvajñatā) is not seen to be joined with the five aggregates, nor are the five aggregates seen to be joined with omniscience.
All-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) does not unite with the six sense-faculties, nor do the six sense-faculties unite with all-knowledge;

form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena (*dharma*) likewise do not unite with all-knowledge, nor does all-knowledge unite with form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena—yet it is also not the case that they do not unite.
This is what corresponds to the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not perceive the *dānapāramitā* as being conjoined with *sarvajñatā*; nor do they perceive the *śīlapāramitā*, *kṣāntipāramitā*, *vīryapāramitā*, *dhyānapāramitā*, and even the *prajñāpāramitā* as being conjoined with *sarvajñatā*. Furthermore, they do not perceive *sarvajñatā* as being conjoined with the six *pāramitās*.

Furthermore, one does not perceive *sarvajñatā* as conjoined with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the ten powers; nor does one perceive the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the ten powers as conjoined with *sarvajñatā*; nor does one perceive *sarvajñatā*.
This is what corresponds to the perfection of wisdom.
Śāriputra, for a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, the Buddha does not unite with omniscience (sarvajñatā), nor does omniscience unite with the Buddha.
The Path does not unite with omniscience (sarvajñatā), nor does omniscience unite with the Path. Why is this?
Because omniscience is itself the Buddha, and the Buddha is himself omniscience.
The Path is *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), and *sarvajñatā* is the Path.
This is what it means to be united with the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."
When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they know that the five aggregates do not unite with existence, nor does existence unite with the five aggregates;
furthermore, the five aggregates do not unite with suffering or pleasure, with self or non-self, and the same applies to the six sense faculties and their objects.
The five aggregates neither unite with emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, nor do they fail to unite; furthermore, one neither perceives their activity nor their non-activity.
“A bodhisattva should practice in this way and should respond in this way.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva does not,

for the sake of the perfection of wisdom, practice the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, or the perfection of meditation.”
Nor does one practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the five perfections;
nor does one teach and transform sentient beings for the sake of non-retrogression (avaivartika);
nor does one practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of purifying the buddha-fields.

Furthermore, one does not practice the perfection of wisdom by means of the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the ten powers of a Buddha, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha;

nor does one practice the perfection of wisdom by means of internal emptiness, external emptiness, the emptiness of both existence and non-existence, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, or ultimate emptiness;

nor by means of the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the bottomless emptiness, the emptiness of the characteristics of all dharmas, or the emptiness of all dharmas; nor by means of the emptiness of arising, nor the emptiness of non-arising; nor by means of true emptiness, nor false emptiness; nor by means of suchness, nor the nature of phenomena, nor the limit of reality. It is in this manner that one practices the conduct of the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive any dharma that can be destroyed. Furthermore, Śāriputra!
A bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom!
Nor does he practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the supernormal power of psychic travel, divine sight, divine hearing, knowledge of others' minds, or knowledge of his own past lives.
Why is this? One who practices the perfection of wisdom does not even perceive the perfection of wisdom, let alone perceive the various miraculous powers and activities of a bodhisattva.
This is what corresponds to the perfection of wisdom. Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not think to himself:
"I shall go to the ten directions by means of my supernormal powers to see the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones," yet he does not think:
"Whatever Dharma the Buddhas of the ten directions preach, I shall listen to and receive it."
Nor does he think: "I shall fully know the thoughts within the minds of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
Nor does he think to himself:
"I shall personally know the matters concerning my births throughout incalculable kalpas," nor does he think:
"I shall see the destinies of birth and death and the paths of good and evil to which sentient beings in the ten directions proceed."
“This bodhisattva is practicing in accordance with the perfection of wisdom.
Śāriputra, the bodhisattva reflects to himself:”
"I shall deliver incalculable, asāṃkhyeya numbers of people and lead them to parinirvāṇa"—
this is the bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā.
When a bodhisattva practices in this manner, none of the māras can find an opportunity to harm him, and all worldly affairs are brought under subjugation.
All the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, together protect this bodhisattva, ensuring that they do not fall to the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
From the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, all these devas likewise protect this bodhisattva, so that no obstacles may arise along the way.
All the various ailments within the bodies of these bodhisattvas will be cured in this present life. Why is this?
It is because they apply universal compassion toward all sentient beings.
"You should know that this is practicing in accordance with the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva who practices the *prajñāpāramitā* will swiftly attain the *dhāraṇīs*, and all the gates of *samādhi* will appear before them. In whatever place they are born, they will constantly see the Buddhas even unto the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), never being separated from the Buddhas."
This is what corresponds to the perfection of wisdom.
A bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not even conceive of dharmas as being either conjoined or unconjoined, equal or unequal.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive the conjunction of dharmas, nor does one perceive dharmas as equal.
This is what corresponds to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
A bodhisattva who practices the perfection of wisdom does not even think:
"I shall swiftly realize the nature of phenomena, nor shall I fail to realize it. Why is this?
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is that there is nothing to be realized; this is what constitutes "conformity.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any phenomenon as being distinct from the nature of phenomena, nor does he perceive a conjunction between them, nor does he think:
"The dharma-nature manifests various distinctions"—
this is that which all Bodhisattvas harmonize with. Furthermore,
they do not give rise to the thought:
"This dharma manifests within the dharma-nature, yet it does not manifest, nor does it not manifest.
Why is this? Because one initially does not see anything manifesting within the dharma-nature, you should know that this is precisely what constitutes union.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, the nature of phenomena does not unite with emptiness, nor does emptiness unite with the nature of phenomena; this is what is meant by 'union. "
The six sense organs and the eighteen elements do not unite with emptiness, nor does emptiness unite with the six sense organs and the eighteen elements.
This extends even to the dharma-nature, which does not unite with emptiness, nor does emptiness unite with the dharma-nature.
Śāriputra! Such union with emptiness is the foremost.
A bodhisattva who practices emptiness does not fall into the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha; he purifies buddha-fields, instructs sentient beings, and swiftly attains supreme buddhahood.

Śāriputra! All those things that correspond to the perfection of wisdom are without superior; they are the most honored correspondence, the foremost correspondence, and the unsurpassed. Why is this so?
This is because it is for the sake of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and unsurpassed, perfect, true, and appropriate awakening. Śāriputra,
you should know that a practitioner who acts in this way has already received a prediction [of enlightenment] and is close to the site of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).
A practitioner who acts in this way brings profound benefit to incalculable, asankhyeya beings.
Yet, the bodhisattva does not even think:
"I am in union with the prajñāpāramitā."
Nor does he think: "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, shall bestow upon me a prediction of enlightenment. Nor does he think:
"I shall receive my prediction before long and purify a Buddha-field," nor does he think:
"I shall become a Buddha and turn the wheel of Dharma."
Why is this? Because it is of one essence with the dharma-nature and possesses no distinction.
Furthermore, one does not perceive any dharma that practices the prajñāpāramitā, nor does one perceive any Buddhas who have taught anything as being *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, from the very beginning they do not perceive the mark of a sentient being arising, nor do they perceive the mark of a sentient being ceasing.
Why is this? Because all sentient beings do not initially perceive arising or ceasing.
Since all sentient beings do not see that there is birth, and do not even see the existence of arising and ceasing, how can they practice the *prajñāpāramitā*?
When a bodhisattva practices in this manner, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

They do not give rise to the mark of a sentient being, nor do they perceive the emptiness of the mark of a sentient being; they do not see the conduct of sentient beings, nor do they differentiate the conduct of sentient beings. This is the bodhisattva’s practice of the foremost practice of emptiness.
When a bodhisattva dwells within this state, they gather all things together and abide therein.

A bodhisattva who dwells in such a manner abides in great loving-kindness and great compassion; they possess no mind of envy or pride, no mind of distraction or indolence, no mind of malice or resentment, and they give rise to no mind of evil intent nor any mind of corrupt wisdom.
The Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll One;
The Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mokṣala of Khotan during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Translated by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Four: Training in the Five Eyes. From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, Chapter Four: Training in the Five Eyes. Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, from where do those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice in accordance with the *prajñāpāramitā* come before being born here?"
"Where did he go from there to be reborn?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"A bodhisattva who is in union with the *prajñāpāramitā* comes to be born here from the Tuṣita Heaven, or comes to be born here from a buddha-field in another direction, or comes to be born here from among the human realm."
Those who come down from the Tuṣita Heaven never lose the Prajñāpāramitā; all the dhāraṇīs, all the gates of samādhi, and all the gates of manifold wisdom are ever present before them.

Those who come from other Buddha-lands will swiftly accomplish the *prajñāpāramitā*; day by day they will increase in wisdom, and all profound essential dharmas will manifest before them. Thereafter, they will perfect the *prajñāpāramitā*, and wherever they are born, they will constantly see the Buddhas and never be separated from them.

Those who have come from among human beings are bodhisattvas who have not yet reached the stage of *avaivartika*; their faculties are dull and obscured, and they cannot swiftly attain the *prajñāpāramitā*.
One cannot immediately see the gateways of dhāraṇī.
Śāriputra, as for what you have asked:
"If a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, where will they ultimately be reborn after passing away from this world?

Such a bodhisattva shall be reborn in the buddha-fields of other directions, passing from one buddha-field to another, always seeing the Buddhas and never being separated from those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who lack *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) and, practicing the six *pāramitās* from within the four *dhyānas*, take the merit of these meditations to be reborn in the long-lived heavens; without exhausting their celestial lifespan, they subsequently come to be born in this world to make offerings to the Buddhas.
These bodhisattvas have dull faculties and are not particularly brilliant.

Śāriputra, furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and great loving-kindness and great compassion; while maintaining *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), their merit from dhyāna cannot detain them, and they are always born in the places where Buddhas provide instruction. They shall be born during this Bhadrakalpa as those who attain awakening, and they are never separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, by practicing the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, and through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), do not take birth according to those meditative states; rather, they are born into families of great nobility, into families of brahmins, or into families of householders (*gṛhapati*), and in whatever place they are born, they constantly teach sentient beings.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless concentrations; through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they are not detained by these meditative states, but instead take birth in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and the sixth heaven (the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven). There, they constantly instruct the devas to purify buddha-fields and teach sentient beings to serve and attend upon the Buddhas.

Furthermore, there is a bodhisattva who practices the perfection of wisdom and, through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), practices the first dhyāna, being reborn in the Brahma Heaven as one honored among the Brahmas. Having departed from the Brahma Heaven, he goes to the places in the ten directions where the Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma, and entreats those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, to turn the wheel of Dharma.

Furthermore, there arise bodhisattvas in their final birth who practice the *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). They are endowed with the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they are perfected in samādhi and do not abide in the realms of dhyāna. Constantly beholding all Buddhas and serving the World-Honored Ones, they maintain pure conduct and are reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.

In those heavens, with his life-span intact and his faculties fully perfected, he taught the Dharma while surrounded by an incalculable retinue of devas and humans; having done so, he returned to be born among the people of this world and attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

Śāriputra! Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who attain the six supernormal powers and are not born in the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm; they travel from one buddha-field to another to pay homage and serve the various buddhas.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who attain the six supernormal powers and travel through various buddha-fields; wherever they go, there is no mention of the names of the teachings of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, possessing the six supernormal powers, are born in various buddha-fields, where their lifespan is immeasurable and they are reborn in those lands.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, by means of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), travel through various worlds; arriving where there is no Buddha, they praise the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha within those lands, causing the sentient beings there to hear the merits of the Triple Gem.
Having heard this, they rejoiced and all attained rebirth in the lands of the various Buddhas.

Furthermore, there were bodhisattvas who, from their initial aspiration, attained the four dhyānas, the four purities, the four formless concentrations, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; they were not born within the three realms, but were always born in places where they could benefit sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who practice the six pāramitās; from their initial resolve, they immediately ascend to the bodhisattva stage and reach the level of *avaivartika*.

There are also bodhisattvas who, from their initial resolve, immediately attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and turn the wheel of Dharma. Having benefited countless hundreds of thousands of millions of sentient beings, they enter *parinirvāṇa* in the realm of no-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-dhātu*), and their Dharma remains for half an eon or a full eon.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, as soon as they first resolve their minds on enlightenment, become attuned to the *prajñāpāramitā*, and together with countless hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas, travel through the various buddha-fields and purify the lands of the buddhas.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who practice the six pāramitās, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, finding delight within each of them. Abiding in the four dhyānas, they arise from the fourth dhyāna and return to the meditative concentration of liberation; arising from the concentration of liberation, they enter the formless attainments. Arising from the formless attainments, they enter the concentration of liberation; arising from the concentration of liberation, they enter the dhyāna of the cessation of perception and feeling. Again arising from this, they return to the concentration of liberation, and through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they enter the *prākaraṇa* samādhi. This is called practicing the prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, by means of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, do not take the realization of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom and, through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), enter the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, so that those who have set out on the lesser path each attain deliverance.
Whatever path-wisdom is attained by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is, in fact, the patience (kṣānti) of a bodhisattva.
One who practices the Prajñāpāramitā should know that such a person is an avaivartika.
Śāriputra! Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who practice the six pāramitās and are born in the Tuṣita Heaven; you should know that these are the bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa.

Furthermore, if there is a bodhisattva who, regarding the merit of the four dhyānas up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, possesses the aspiration for the Path yet does not believe in or accept them, it should be known that this bodhisattva is one who is in his last birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha).

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who practice the six pāramitās, traveling from one buddha-field to another, establishing sentient beings so that they reach the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). One should know that such bodhisattvas, from the time they first resolved their minds [for awakening], shall only attain buddhahood after the passage of countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who practice the six pāramitās and, for the sake of sentient beings, do not speak of things that are without benefit.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who practice the six pāramitās and, for the sake of sentient beings, travel from one buddha-field to another, severing the three evil destinies.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who practice the six pāramitās and constantly bring peace and happiness to all through their generosity, freely bestowing upon those who seek them elephants, horses, carriages, clothing, wealth, grain, kingdoms, cities, and precious jewels, providing all such things to them.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who practice the prajñāpāramitā and are able to transform their own bodies into the likeness of the Buddha’s form; they enter the three evil realms and preach the Dharma to beings according to their respective languages, thereby delivering and liberating them all.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who practice the six pāramitās, manifesting bodies like those of Buddhas to reach everywhere throughout the ten directions, teaching and transforming sentient beings so as to purify buddha-lands.

Having reached the ten directions, they observe the majestic deportment and the rules of all Buddhas, as well as their various qualities—whether excellent or inferior, pure or turbid—and then they themselves give rise to superior, wondrous, most honored, and extraordinary lands, where they teach exclusively by means of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) bodhisattvas who are in their final birth before Buddhahood.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who practice the six pāramitās and thereby become endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man; their faculties are exceptionally distinguished, and among sentient beings, there are none who do not feel reverence and joy upon seeing them.
Because they are filled with joy, he delivers them by means of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles and causes them to enter parinirvāṇa. Śāriputra!
