A bodhisattva who practices the prajñāpāramitā should first train in the purity of body, speech, and mind, whereby they will attain the extraordinary excellence of the sense faculties.
Having attained such extraordinary excellence, they neither exalt themselves nor disparage others.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, from their first resolution, practice the *dāna-pāramitā* and the *śīla-pāramitā*, until they achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, never falling into the three evil realms from the very beginning.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, from their initial resolve until they reach the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika), never forget or abandon the practice of the ten wholesome paths of action.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who practice the perfections of giving (dāna) and ethical discipline (śīla), thereby attaining the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin); they transform sentient beings and establish them in the ten wholesome paths, bestowing all their wealth and treasures upon those beings.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who practice the perfections of *dāna* and *śīla*, who have become universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) hundreds of thousands of millions of times, constantly making offerings to all Buddhas and reverently receiving their teachings.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who practice the six pāramitās to illuminate the transformative teachings of the Dharma for all sentient beings; they do not cease this illumination until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. For this reason, bodhisattvas always clarify the Buddha-dharma.
This is the practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva in the perfection of wisdom.
As for the practitioner of the bodhisattva path, they constantly restrain unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, not allowing them to arise frivolously.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What is meant by a bodhisattva’s gathering together of body, speech,
and mind? The Buddha said:
“The Bodhisattva’s mind does not harbor any evil causes and conditions of body, speech, or mind to commit sinful deeds.
When the Bodhisattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they do not perceive body, speech, or mind.”

Although they possess body, speech, and mind, they never harbor envy, anger, or wrong views; they do not engage in double-tongued speech, harsh words, lying, or frivolous talk; they refrain from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; they have no thoughts of indolence or arrogance, and they never give rise to actions based on unwholesome wisdom.
If there is a bodhisattva who cannot restrain these various evil deeds, this person is not a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who practice the six pāramitās, who eliminate evil conduct of the body, eliminate evil speech of the mouth, and eliminate evil thoughts of the mind.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What is meant by a bodhisattva eliminating [the defilements of] body, speech,
and mind? The Buddha said:
“The Bodhisattva does not rely upon body, speech, or mind; therefore, he is able to eliminate them.
Since the Bodhisattva first resolved his mind [on enlightenment], he has constantly practiced the ten wholesome paths of action; for this reason, he surpasses all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.”
“A bodhisattva who practices the perfection of wisdom purifies the path of the Buddha and purifies the six perfections.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
“In what way does a bodhisattva purify the path of the Buddha?”
The Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva does not rely on body, speech, or mind; does not rely on the six pāramitās; does not rely on arhats or pratyekabuddhas; and does not rely on bodhisattvas nor on buddhas."
Why is this so? Because there is no reliance upon any phenomena;
this is the path of the bodhisattva.
“Śāriputra! Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who practice each and every pāramitā; for this reason, no one is able to subdue them.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How is it that a bodhisattva practicing the six pāramitās cannot be overcome? The Buddha said:

“A bodhisattva who practices the six pāramitās does not have thoughts regarding the five aggregates (skandhas) or the six sense faculties (indriyas); does not have thoughts regarding forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena (dharmas); does not have thoughts regarding the eighteen elements (dhātus); does not have thoughts regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma); does not have thoughts regarding the six pāramitās; does not have thoughts regarding the Buddha’s ten powers (bala), four fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma); does not have thoughts regarding the path of the śrāvaka or the pratyekabuddha; does not have thoughts regarding the path of the Buddha; and does not have thoughts regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
In this way, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, their merit increases progressively; for this reason, there is no one who can overcome them.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva dwells in the *prajñāpāramitā* and fulfills *sarvajñatā*, by means of all these wisdoms they do not fall into the evil destinies nor into poverty and low status. Their physical body has its faculties complete, such that people do not loathe them, and they are always respected and loved by the devas and asuras."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is the wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Buddha said:

"By being fully endowed with all forms of wisdom, the bodhisattva beholds all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; from these World-Honored Ones, he receives and hears their teachings, and he hears in full the dharmas of the virtues and marks of all Buddhas."

The Bodhisattva who has attained wisdom has no conception of a Buddha, nor any conception of a bodhisattva; he has no conception of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor any conception of a self, nor any conception of a person, nor any conception of the buddha-fields of the various Buddhas.

When a bodhisattva practicing wisdom practices the perfection of giving, they do not perceive the gift, nor do they perceive the perfection of wisdom; while practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, they likewise do not even hear the names of the thirty-seven factors, nor do they perceive the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.
Śāriputra! This is the wisdom of a bodhisattva.
By means of this wisdom, they are fully endowed with all dharmas, yet they do not become arrogant when perceiving any dharma.
“A bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom purifies the five eyes:
the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the dharma eye, and the buddha eye.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva purifying the fleshly eye?
The Buddha said:
"There are bodhisattvas who, with the fleshly eye, see within a range of one hundred yojanas or two hundred yojanas;"
There are bodhisattvas who, with the fleshly eye, see one Jambudvīpa, see two Jambudvīpas, and see the four continents;
there are bodhisattvas who, with the fleshly eye, see a thousand worlds, see two thousand worlds, and some see three thousand worlds.
This is called the purification of the fleshly eye of a bodhisattva.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is meant by the ‘divine eye’?
The Buddha said:
"With the divine eye, the bodhisattva sees everything belonging to the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, perceiving and knowing it all.
From the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven up to the sixth heaven, and even as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, the bodhisattva sees, perceives, and knows it all."
From the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, none of these devas recognize, know, or see what is seen by the bodhisattva’s divine eye.

The Bodhisattva’s divine eye perceives all the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions; it perceives and knows all matters regarding the birth and death, as well as the good and evil deeds, of sentient beings.
This constitutes the purity of the Bodhisattva’s divine eye.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What is meant by a bodhisattva’s purification of the wisdom-eye?
The Buddha said:
“The wisdom-eye of a bodhisattva does not form such thoughts as:
‘there are conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena; there are supramundane phenomena and mundane phenomena.
With the wisdom-eye, a bodhisattva has no phenomenon that is not seen, no phenomenon that is not heard, no phenomenon that is not known, and no phenomenon that is not realized.”
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva to have the purity of the wisdom-eye.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye?"
The Buddha said:

“By means of the Dharma-eye, a bodhisattva sees that this person possesses firm faith and dwells firmly in the Dharma. This person is established in the liberation of signlessness and wishlessness; they attain uninterrupted concentration within the five faculties, and through uninterrupted concentration, they achieve the wisdom of liberation. By means of the wisdom of liberation, they transcend the three obstacles:
the obstacle of the body, the obstacle of doubt, and the obstacle of false faith.”
Having transcended these three obstacles, one attains the stage of Srotāpanna.
Then, by cultivating mindfulness on the Path and attenuating lust, anger, and delusion, one attains the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin.
By exerting oneself diligently in the Path and eliminating lust, anger, and delusion, one attains the stage of Anāgāmin.
Thereupon, one eliminates the five types of craving:
first, craving for form; second, craving for the formless; third, craving born of delusion; fourth, craving born of resentment and hostility; and fifth, craving born of a distracted mind.
Having already transcended these, one then attains arhatship.

A bodhisattva who practices emptiness in this manner likewise attains liberation through emptiness and perfects the five faculties; swiftly approaching and not halting midway in dhyāna, they reach the path of arhatship. This person has already attained the liberation of signlessness and achieves the five powers, culminating in arhatship.
This is how a bodhisattva attains the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Whatever phenomena a bodhisattva knows to arise are phenomena that are subject to cessation; thus they attain the five faculties.
This is how a bodhisattva attains the purity of the Dharma-eye.

When a bodhisattva resolves their mind [on enlightenment], proceeding from the dāna-pāramitā to the prajñā-pāramitā, they become fully endowed with the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, and the faculty of upāya-kauśalya (skillful means). Possessing these three faculties and all such merits, they are born into the families of kings, great clans, brahmins, or kṣatriyas; or they are born among the Four Heavenly Kings up to the sixth heaven. There, they nurture and transform sentient beings according to their inclinations, purify buddha-fields, and pay homage to all Buddhas. They do not fall into the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but shall surely attain the state of a samyak-saṃbuddha.
This is what it means for a bodhisattva to attain the purity of the Dharma-eye.
With the Dharma-eye, the bodhisattva fully knows all those who have received the prediction from a Buddha and those who have not;
those who will regress and those who will not regress.
There are those who possess supernormal powers and those who do not;
there are those who, having perfected their supernormal powers, travel through various worlds to pay homage and serve the Buddhas, and those who have not yet attained this;
there are those who have attained the purity of a Buddha-field and those who have attained an impure one.
Bodhisattvas who teach and transform sentient beings and those who do not;
bodhisattvas who are praised by all Buddhas and those who are not;
bodhisattvas who draw near to the Buddhas and those who do not.
When a bodhisattva attains buddhahood, the assembly of his disciples consists of bodhisattvas whose number is either infinite or finite;
when this bodhisattva attains buddhahood, there are those who take bodhisattvas as their saṃgha and those who do not take bodhisattvas as their saṃgha;
there are bodhisattvas who attain buddhahood through arduous ascetic practices and those who attain buddhahood without arduous ascetic practices.
There are bodhisattvas who are in their final birth before Buddhahood and those who are not yet in their final birth;

there are bodhisattvas who have reached the site of enlightenment and those who have not; there are bodhisattvas who sit beneath the tree and subdue Māra and those who do not subdue Māra—he knows each and every one of these matters in detail.
"This is what it means for a bodhisattva to attain the purification of the Dharma-eye.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining the purification of the Buddha-eye?"
The Buddha said:

"Having already attained the Vajra-samādhi, one attains sarvajñā (all-knowledge), the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, practices the four immeasurable minds, the eighteen unique qualities, and great kindness and great compassion."

With this Bodhisattva-eye, all phenomena and all matters seen by him are such that there is no matter he does not see, no sound he does not hear, no object he does not protect, and no dharma he does not realize.
Śāriputra, this is how a bodhisattva attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and obtains the eye of supreme perfect enlightenment.
If a bodhisattva wishes to purify the five eyes, they should practice the six *pāramitās*.
Why is this? Because all wholesome dharmas whatsoever are entirely contained within the six pāramitās.
Among all the dharmas of the Buddhas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, as well as all other dharmas, none surpass the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
The Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of the five eyes.
A bodhisattva who studies the five eyes will swiftly attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Chapter 5: The Chapter on the Five Supernatural Powers (Abhijñā) of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

When a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they should bring to mind the fulfillment of the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). They shall attain the immeasurable spiritual faculties (*ṛddhi*) of all bodhisattvas, being able to shake heaven and earth, transform their bodies into countless forms and then merge them back into one, and possess unimpeded vision that penetrates through stone walls as if passing through empty space.

For example, like a bird flying without encountering any obstruction, one can walk upon water and tread through space, emit water and fire from the body, touch the sun and moon with the hand, and reach the Brahma Heaven.
Possessing these supernormal powers, one does not become conceited nor perceive conceit, because they are fundamentally empty.
Who is able to give rise to such psychic power?
Only one who has attained *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is able to give rise to it.
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva who trains in the prajñāpāramitā has already attained the realization of the supernormal powers; his clairaudience surpasses that of all devas and humans.

Although he attains the power of clairaudience, he remains free from arrogance; within existence and non-existence, he realizes there is nothing to be attained, and regarding both emptiness and non-emptiness, nothing arises.
When a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, he attains the realization of the supernormal power of the divine ear, enabling him to know the thoughts within the minds of others.

He knows those who possess lust, anger, and delusion, and those who are free from lust, anger, and delusion; he knows those with a mind of craving and those without a mind of craving; he knows that which exists and that which does not exist; he knows those with a distracted mind and those with an undistracted mind; he knows those who have much and those who have little; he knows those with a concentrated mind and those without a concentrated mind; he knows those who are liberated and those who are not liberated; and he knows those who are superior and those who are inferior. Although he knows these things, he does not become conceited.
Why is this? Because this mind is not a mind, and the mind is inconceivable.

By means of the supernormal power of the realization of past lives, one cognizes a single thought up to a hundred thoughts; from one day up to a hundred days, one month up to a hundred months, one year up to a hundred years, one eon up to a hundred eons, and even incalculable hundreds of eons, incalculable thousands of eons, and incalculable billions of nayutas of eons—one fully cognizes and knows their names, surnames, clans, their deeds and habits, and the length of their lifespans.

He fully recognizes all the suffering and pleasure experienced, the death here and birth there, and the transition from there to here; he is thoroughly aware of all actions performed and all modes of conduct and etiquette undergone, yet he does not become conceited on account of his supernormal powers.
When a bodhisattva trains in this way, they are training in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

By means of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they clearly know their past lives; by means of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), they see where sentient beings go after death—the paths of good and evil, and how their attainments are high or low according to their respective past actions. They see those who have committed evil with their bodies, spoken evil with their mouths, and harbored evil thoughts in their minds, who slander and revile the noble ones (*ārya*), and who believe in false and inverted views.
Due to the causes and conditions of wrong views, one destroys one's own body and, upon death, falls into hell.

As a human being, if one’s conduct is good, one’s speech and thoughts are also good, one does not slander the sages and worthies, and one practices with right view and faith, one will attain rebirth in the heavens.
He is able to see sentient beings throughout the ten directions, even those within the five realms of existence; such is his vision.

Through the virtue of this single supernormal power (*abhijñā*), he perceives all ten directions. Possessing the supernormal powers, he attains the realization of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*), yet he does not take up the paths of the *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*, nor does he hold to other dharmas. He shall surely attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and he does not become arrogant because of his supernormal powers or his realization of the exhaustion of outflows.
When a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* and fulfills the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), their merit increases further and further until they reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
There are bodhisattvas who practice the *prajñāpāramitā* and abide in the *dānapāramitā*, purifying the path to *sarvajñatā* and contemplating emptiness without doubt.

When a bodhisattva dwells in the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), they purify the track of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) and do not doubt regarding demerit or merit, because emptiness is without arising. Śāriputra!
There is a bodhisattva who, dwelling in the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), purifies the traces of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), and because of emptiness, does not give rise to anger.
A bodhisattva who dwells in the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*) purifies the traces of *sarvajñatā*, and regarding physical diligence, does not give rise to indolence.
When a bodhisattva dwells in the dhyānapāramitā, they purify the traces of sarvajñatā, and their concentrated mind does not arise [in distraction].
When a bodhisattva dwells in the prajñāpāramitā, they purify the traces of sarvajñatā, and delusion does not arise.

When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, abiding within the six perfections, they purify the traces of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge). Coming and going from emptiness, they neither doubt nor transgress; they neither harbor anger nor fail in patience; they neither strive nor are indolent; they are neither fixed nor distracted; they are neither wise nor foolish.

There is neither giving nor greed; neither observing precepts nor transgressing them; neither progress nor regression; neither patience nor anger; neither concentration nor distraction; neither wisdom nor delusion; neither slander nor praise; neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned.
In this way, Śāriputra, regarding dharmas that are unarisen, there is no one who reviles them and no one who praises them;
there is neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned.
This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom;
having attained such extraordinary virtues, they are beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Endowed with these virtues, they teach sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields.
Chapter Six: Bestowing Predictions. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Six: Bestowing Predictions. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, by giving rise to an impartial mind toward all people, and having given rise to an impartial mind toward all people, they then attain equality with respect to all dharmas.

Having attained equality toward all dharmas, one is then able to maintain an equanimous mind regarding all phenomena. Consequently, one is loved and respected by the present Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Arhats, and Pratyekabuddhas. In whatever place one is born, the eyes never behold unwholesome forms, and the mind never gives rise to evil thoughts. A Bodhisattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā never diminishes their progress toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, while the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* was being expounded, there were thirty thousand bhikṣus sitting in the assembly who offered all the robes they were wearing to the Buddha; they all resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Thereupon the Buddha smiled.
Then Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha does not smile without cause; there must surely be a reason for it."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"These thirty thousand bhikṣus shall, at the end of their lives here, be reborn in the land of the Buddha Akṣobhya.
Sixty-two kalpas hence, they shall all become buddhas, named Śrāvakaśīrṣa."
Furthermore, there were sixty thousand sons of the gods from the desire realm who were all destined to be born before Maitreya Buddha and all destined to leave the household life to become śramaṇas.

Through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, he caused those in the assembly to see a thousand Buddhas and their fourfold assemblies in the eastern direction, as well as a thousand Buddhas appearing in each of the ten directions.
At that time, the Sahā world-system was not as adorned and pure as that Buddha-land.
At that moment, there were ten thousand people in the assembly who all made this vow, saying:
"We shall all cultivate merit so that we may be born in that Pure Land."
At that time, the Buddha, knowing what the son of good family was thinking, smiled again.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
“I pray that you will tell me the reason for your smile.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you see these ten thousand people? Ānanda replied:
“Yes, World-Honored One;
I have seen it.
The Buddha said:

"When these ten thousand people have reached the end of their lives, they shall all be reborn in those buddha-fields; none shall ever be separated from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and in the future they shall become buddhas, titled Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas named King of Adornment."

Chapter Seven: The Chapter on Sublime Deliverance (Suvicāra) The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Seven: The Chapter on Sublime Deliverance. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Mahākāśyapa, and other bhikṣus of great supernormal powers, as well as other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of great supernormal powers, along with laymen (upāsakas) and laywomen (upāsikās), all addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!”

The Prajñāpāramitā is the greatest crossing, the supreme crossing, the wondrous crossing, and the unsurpassed, most honored crossing for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; indeed, O World-Honored One, there is no crossing equal to the crossing of your eloquence.

Furthermore, there is the crossing over of non-existence, the crossing over of phenomena (*dharma*), the crossing over of emptiness, the crossing over of emptiness and signlessness, the crossing over of the emptiness of all phenomena, the crossing over of the emptiness of existence and non-existence, and the crossing over of the emptiness of the perfection of all virtues.
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the prajñāpāramitā are fully endowed with all merits; none can overcome them. Indeed, World-Honored One!"
This causes this bodhisattva mahāsattva to accomplish the merit of the perfection of wisdom.
A bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom has already performed this gift that is unequaled; there is nothing that can equal it.

Fully endowed with various forms of the dānapāramitā, his physical body is such that none can equal it; having attained this peerless benefit, he practices the prajñāpāramitā and thereby personally achieves the state of an *anuttarasamyaksambuddha*.
"Indeed, World-Honored One!

The World-Honored One likewise practices the Prajñāpāramitā, turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma—the foundation of various peerless dharmas, the foundation of various peerless desires, and the benefit of various peerless five aggregates."
The Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past and the future, practice the Prajñāpāramitā in this very same way, and likewise turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Indeed, World-Honored One!
"Blessed One, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to reach the further shore of all dharmas should practice the perfection of wisdom.
"Indeed, Blessed One! [they said.]
If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the prajñāpāramitā, all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and the people of the world shall pay them homage.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly of bhikṣus and bodhisattvas:
"One should pay homage to those sons and daughters of good family who practice the Prajñāpāramitā; all devas and nāgas should likewise pay them homage."

The Buddha told Śāriputra: “When there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the world, there are then the various devas, emperors, and the people of the world; there are then the brahmins and the kṣatriya clans; there are then the wheel-turning sage-kings; there are then the Four Great Heavenly Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; there are then the path of the srotāpanna, the path of the arhat, and the path of the pratyekabuddha; there are then the bodhisattvas; and there is then the path of the Buddha.”
Once there are bodhisattvas, there will then be offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, the seven treasures, pearls, necklaces, lapis lazuli, and maṇi gems.
Śāriputra! All the articles for entertainment and physical comfort enjoyed by those in the heavens and the world exist because of the Bodhisattva. Why is this so?
Practicing the deeds of a bodhisattva, one dwells within the six pāramitās to discipline sentient beings, thereby bringing generosity to completion as the prajñāpāramitā.
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who wishes to bring peace and security to sentient beings should practice the prajñāpāramitā.

Chapter Eight: The Radiance of the Tongue-Sign The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Eight: The Radiance of the Tongue-Sign At that time, the World-Honored One extended his broad and long tongue, which completely pervaded the trichiliocosm.

From his tongue-root, he emitted hundreds of thousands of various and countless rays of light, which thoroughly illuminated ten directions, each reaching as many lands as there are sands in a Ganges River.
At that time, innumerable bodhisattvas from the eastern direction and the lands of the ten directions, seeing this radiance, each addressed their own Buddha:
"What auspicious omen is this, that such a great light appears?"
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"To the west, beyond as many worlds as there are grains of sand in one *gaṅgā* river, there is a buddha-world named Sahā; its Buddha is titled Śākyamuni."
He extended his tongue and emitted radiance, preaching the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattvas;
now this response has occurred.
Thereupon, the bodhisattvas from lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions each addressed their respective Buddhas, saying:
"We wish to go and see Śākyamuni and the various bodhisattvas, and we also wish to hear the Prajñāpāramitā.
Each of the Buddhas addressed their respective bodhisattvas,
saying, "Go as you please."

Thereupon, each of those bodhisattvas took various named flowers and incenses, as well as diverse banners, pennants, precious jewels, and flowered canopies, and set out from their respective lands to come to the Sahā world.
The Four Heavenly Kings, up to and including the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, each brought various celestial incenses and flowers and came to the place where the Buddha was.
All the devas and bodhisattvas likewise arrived; having beheld Śākyamuni Buddha, they each made offerings by scattering various named flowers.
The flowers and jewels that were scattered immediately transformed into a four-pillared platform in the air above the Buddha.
This platform was lofty and prominent, with windows facing in all four directions.

It pervaded the entire trichiliocosm; in every part, there was no one who did not see this magnificent platform. Arranged in distinct rows without obstructing one another, the platform was exquisitely beautiful, adorned with a lattice of pearls such as had never existed before.
Thereupon, the hundreds of thousands of millions of people in the assembly each rose from their seats, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O World-Honored One, we pray that in future ages we may attain the benefits of the Dharma; just as the World-Honored One now preaches the Dharma surrounded by hundreds of thousands of followers, may our manifestations and spiritual movements likewise be such."
The Buddha, perceiving that the great assembly each already possessed the capacity for the patience regarding the non-arising of all dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), smiled.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“For what cause and condition do you smile?
We pray that you will explain its meaning.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"These hundreds of thousands of millions of beings have all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas; sixty-eight million kalpas hence, in an aeon named Saṃkusumita, they shall all become buddhas, titled Buddhapuṣpa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Chapter 9: On Practice. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Nine: On Practice. Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed Subhūti, saying:
“I shall explain for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the causal conditions through which they achieve the perfection of wisdom.”
At that time, the bodhisattvas, great disciples, devas, and humans gathered there thought to themselves:
"Now, as Subhūti teaches the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattvas, does he speak by means of his own eloquence?"
"Is this the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha?
Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, the great disciples, and the devas, said to Śāriputra:
"Whatever Dharma the disciples of the Buddha preach, whatever sounds they utter, and whatever they teach—all these are the activities of the World-Honored One, the Great Being."
"What the Buddha has taught is that the practice of the Dharma does not contradict the Dharma; these sons of good family study the Dharma and take the Dharma as their realization. Śāriputra!
We shall now, relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, explain the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas; it is not within the scope of our own realization."
“Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to explain the perfection of wisdom to bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Thereupon, Śāriputra and Subhūti together addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!”
Regarding the expression "Bodhisattva, Bodhisattva," in what dharma is there such a thing as a "Bodhisattva"?

We have never before seen any dharma that is a Bodhisattva; we have never before seen a Bodhisattva, nor have we seen the word "Bodhisattva," nor have we seen the Prajñāpāramitā. For what kind of Bodhisattva, then, should one preach the Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Prajñāpāramitā, the bodhisattva, and their names likewise do not exist within, nor do they exist without, nor do they abide in between the two.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"For example, it is by means of names that sentient beings are called 'sentient beings,' and they are spoken of as 'self' and 'person,' as 'born,' as 'man,' 'gentleman,' or 'husband,' as 'doer,' 'knower,' or 'experiencer.'"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Even these so-called dharmas are merely attachments to names; they neither arise nor cease, for since time immemorial they have been nothing more than names handed down in common usage."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"That which is called 'prajñāpāramitā,' that which is called 'bodhisattva,' and the word 'bodhisattva'—these are merely attachments to the dharma of words. Since time immemorial, they have only operated within these words; they neither arise nor cease."

Subhūti! For example, all forms, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousness are merely designations for dharmas; since time immemorial, they have been reckoned as such through the convergence of causes and conditions.
All phenomena that arise from the conjunction of various causes and conditions are neither born nor extinguished.
This is likewise true for what is called *prajñāpāramitā*, what is called a "bodhisattva," and even the word "bodhisattva" itself.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"That which is called eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind has, from time immemorial, been merely attached to the phenomena of names; they neither arise nor cease."

Form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are likewise thus: they are neither internal nor external, neither arising nor ceasing; from time immemorial, they have been nothing more than attachments to the dharmas of words.
“Prajñāpāramitā, the bodhisattva, and their names likewise do not abide internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“For example, within the body there are things named ‘head,’ and those designated as ‘neck,’ ‘shoulders,’ ‘arms,’ ‘spine,’ ‘ribs,’ ‘thighs,’ ‘calves,’ ‘intestines,’ and ‘feet. These dharmas are neither produced nor extinguished; they do not abide internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.”
"The Prajñāpāramitā, the bodhisattva, and their names are also like this.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"For example, all external grasses, trees, branches, leaves, stalks, and nodes have, since time immemorial, been merely attached with names; these names neither arise nor cease, and they are neither internal nor external."
"It is the same with what are called 'prajñāpāramitā,' 'bodhisattva,' and 'name.
" The Buddha told Subhūti:
"For example, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past have, since time immemorial, resided according to names. These names neither arise nor cease; they are neither internal nor external."
Subhūti! It is as with a dream, an echo, a magical illusion, a mirage, or a transformation created by a Tathāgata—all these are merely designations for dharmas.

That which is called the *prajñāpāramitā*, that which is called a bodhisattva, and their names likewise are neither produced nor extinguished; they are neither internal, nor external, nor do they abide in between the two.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should study the dharma of syllables, the dharma of combinations, and the numerical categories of skillful means.”

When practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not perceive the characters of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as being either permanent or impermanent; nor does one perceive the characters of the five aggregates as being either suffering or pleasure; nor does one perceive the five aggregates as having a self or being selfless; nor does one perceive the five aggregates as empty, signless, or wishless; nor does one perceive the five aggregates as pure, nor as quiescent, nor as attached to, nor as annihilated;

nor does one perceive the arising of the five aggregates, nor their cessation. It is likewise for the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; for forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena; and for the eighteen elements.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not manifest the perfection of wisdom within the conditioned nature, nor does he perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the word "bodhisattva";
furthermore, he does not perceive it within the unconditioned nature either.
Why is this so? Subhūti,
it is because when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they have no conceptualization regarding any phenomena.
Practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, one dwells in the state of non-conceptual phenomena and accomplishes the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, one neither perceives the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor perceives the word "prajñāpāramitā," nor perceives the bodhisattva, nor perceives the word "bodhisattva."

While practicing the perfection of wisdom and attaining the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, one likewise does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does one perceive the word "perfection of wisdom," nor does one perceive the word "bodhisattva."
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they have already completely transcended the characteristics of all phenomena.
Having transcended them, they neither perceive nor eliminate them.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should train in knowing characters, numbers, and the conjunction of dharmas.

Having awakened to this, they do not enter into form, nor do they enter into feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor do they enter into the eye, ear, nose, [tongue, body, or mind].”
The tongue, body, and mind likewise do not enter into forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects;

they do not enter into the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), nor do they enter into the cognitions of the mental consciousness; they do not enter into suffering or pleasure, nor do they enter into that which is neither suffering nor pleasure;
they do not enter into the nature of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), nor do they enter into the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), nor do they enter into anything at all.
Dāna, śīla, kṣānti, vīrya, and dhyāna do not enter into the prajñāpāramitā; they do not enter into the marks and signs (lakṣaṇavyañjana);
they do not enter into the body of a bodhisattva; they do not enter into the five faculties (pañcendriya);

they do not enter into the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā); they do not enter into the perfection of supernatural powers (abhijñāpāramitā); they do not enter into the perfection of insight (jñānapāramitā); nor do they...
They enter into internal and external emptiness, yet they do not enter into the emptiness of existence or non-existence;
they do not enter into the transformation and guidance of sentient beings, nor do they enter into the purification of buddha-fields, nor do they enter into *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means).
"Why is this? Because one does not perceive any phenomena that can be entered.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not enter into any phenomena; thus they augment the six perfections and step into the rank of a bodhisattva."
Having stepped into the rank of a bodhisattva and transcended the stage of *avaivartika*, they become fully endowed with all supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Once endowed with these supernormal powers, they travel through the various Buddha-lands to nurture sentient beings, make offerings and pay homage to the Buddhas, purify the Buddha-fields, and behold all Buddhas. From these Buddhas, they request their vows, and they obtain everything exactly as they desire.
Having heard the Dharma from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, they attain the various dharanis and samadhi-doors, which continue without interruption until they reach Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should fully understand that these categories of phenomena are merely attached to letters.
What do you think, Subhūti? Are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness this bodhisattva?”
“Are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind the Bodhisattva?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said, "What do you think, Subhūti? Is it by means of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena that one is a bodhisattva?
Is it by means of eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness that one is a bodhisattva?"
He replied, “No, World-Honored One! The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Are earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness the bodhisattva? He replied, "No."

“Is delusion this bodhisattva? Are volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death this bodhisattva?”
"Is this a bodhisattva? He replied,
"No, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?

Is it apart from the five aggregates, the six sense-fields, the six consciousnesses, the eighteen elements, earth, water, fire, wind, and space, and apart from the twelve links of dependent origination—that one is a bodhisattva?"
He replied, “No, World-Honored One! The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“Is the suchness (tathatā) of the five aggregates and the twelve links of dependent origination the bodhisattva?
He replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
“What do you think, Subhūti? Can one be a bodhisattva apart from suchness?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"Upon what basis do you observe that the five aggregates, the six sense-bases, the twelve links of dependent origination, and suchness are not the bodhisattva, yet that the bodhisattva is also not apart from the five aggregates, the six sense-bases, the twelve links of dependent origination, and suchness?"
The Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since from the very beginning no sentient beings have been perceived, where could there be a bodhisattva?”
How is it that one takes the five aggregates, the six sense bases, and the twelve links of dependent origination as the bodhisattva?
How should one be detached from the five aggregates, the six sense bases, and the twelve links of dependent origination to be the bodhisattva?
"Suchness itself is not the bodhisattva, and apart from suchness there is no bodhisattva.
There is no such possibility.
The World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva’s training should be a training in non-seeing; one does not see sentient beings, nor does one see the prajñāpāramitā.”
What do you think, Subhūti? Is one called a bodhisattva because the five aggregates are permanent?
Is one a bodhisattva because the five aggregates are impermanent?
Is one a bodhisattva because the five aggregates belong to a self?
“Is it because of what I have done that one is called a bodhisattva?
Or is it because the five aggregates are empty, signless, and wishless that one is called a bodhisattva? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha said:
"Is it by being detached from the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of the five aggregates that one is a bodhisattva?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"What meaning do you perceive such that you say that the five aggregates being empty, signless, and wishless is not the bodhisattva, yet that the bodhisattva is also not separate from the five aggregates being empty, signless, and wishless?"
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Since one does not initially perceive the five aggregates, how can one speak of a ‘bodhisattva’ on account of the five aggregates?
Since one does not initially perceive anything permanent, how can one speak of a ‘bodhisattva’ on account of impermanence?”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since from the beginning one does not perceive any happiness, how can the suffering of the five aggregates be taken as the bodhisattva?”
Since from the outset one does not perceive a self, how can one be a bodhisattva on the basis of the five aggregates being without self?
Since from the outset one does not perceive a person, how can one speak of a bodhisattva on the basis of the five aggregates being empty?
World-Honored One!
Since from the very beginning no marks are perceived, how can one be a bodhisattva by means of the five aggregates being markless?
World-Honored One!
"If one does not perceive even the aspiration [for awakening], how can one be a bodhisattva by means of the five aggregates being without aspiration?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva training should regard the five aggregates as empty, signless, wishless, unobservable, and unattainable.
A bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should train in this manner.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Regarding what you have just said:
'I do not see any dharma that is a bodhisattva.'"
"It is truly as you have said, Subhūti!
Dharmas do not see one another."
Dharmas do not perceive the nature of dharmas, nor does the nature of dharmas perceive dharmas.
The nature of the five aggregates does not perceive the nature of dharmas, nor does the nature of dharmas perceive the nature of the five aggregates.
The nature of the six sense organs does not perceive the nature of dharmas, nor does the nature of dharmas perceive the nature of the six sense organs.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The nature of the conditioned does not perceive the nature of the unconditioned, and the nature of the unconditioned does not perceive the nature of the conditioned.
The conditioned is not separate from the unconditioned, and the unconditioned is likewise not separate from the conditioned."
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“When a bodhisattva practices this prajñāpāramitā, they do not perceive any dharmas.
Although they do not perceive any dharmas, they neither fear nor are terrified, and they neither regret nor become indolent.”

Why is this? Because one does not perceive the five aggregates, nor does one perceive the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor does one perceive forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.

One does not perceive lust, anger, or delusion; one does not perceive the twelve links of dependent origination; one does not perceive a self; one does not perceive the objects of knowledge or vision; one does not perceive the three realms; one does not perceive the minds of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; one does not perceive bodhisattvas nor the dharmas of bodhisattvas; one does not perceive Buddhas nor the dharmas of Buddhas; and one does not perceive the Path.
"One does not see any phenomena at all; one neither fears, nor is terrified, nor is cowed.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason, Subhūti, is a bodhisattva neither terrified nor afraid?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Because the mental consciousness and dharmas of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended and cannot be seen; for this reason, he is neither terrified nor afraid."
A bodhisattva should regard all dharmas as unobtainable and invisible.

When practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor do they perceive the bodhisattva, nor do they perceive the name "bodhisattva," nor do they perceive the intention of a bodhisattva; this is the training of a bodhisattva, this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Chapter Ten: On Training. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Ten: On Training. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fulfill the dāna-pāramitā should study the prajñā-pāramitā;
one who wishes to fulfill the śīla-, kṣānti-, vīrya-, and dhyāna-pāramitās should study the prajñā-pāramitā.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to know form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
One who wishes to know the six sense faculties, both internally and externally, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.

If one wishes to know the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), if one wishes to eliminate lust, anger, and ignorance, if one wishes to eliminate the notion of a self (*ātman*), one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

If one wishes to remove doubt, if one wishes to remove transgressions of the precepts and false views, if one wishes to remove lust and contention within the three realms, if one wishes to abandon the habits of the six sense-decadences (*ṣaḍāyatana*), if one wishes to eliminate the four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*), if one wishes to abandon the four floods (*ogha*), the four fetters (*saṃyojana*), and the four perversions (*viparyāsa*), and if one wishes to abandon the ten unwholesome paths of action and come to know the practice of the ten wholesome paths of action, one should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one wishes to know the four dhyānas, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four immeasurable minds, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If one wishes to attain the Samādhi of the Intention to Learn, one should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If you wish to know the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments; if you wish to obtain the lion’s stride, the lion’s spring, and the samādhis;

if you wish to obtain the various dhāraṇīs and samādhis, such as the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the Sea-Treasure Samādhi, the Moon-Banner Samādhi, the Universal Arrival of All Dharmas Samādhi, and the Seal of Contemplation Samādhi—
...the samādhi of true dharma-nature, the samādhi of the stainless banner, the vajra samādhi,
the samādhi of the entrance to all dharmas, the king of samādhis, the royal seal samādhi,
the power-purifying samādhi, the moon-banner samādhi, the samādhi of true eloquence as the entrance to all dharmas, and all dharmas...
The samādhi called Entering and Illuminating the Ten Directions; the samādhi of the Seal of the Dharanī-gate of All Dharmas;
the samādhi of Non-deceptiveness Regarding All Dharmas; the samādhi of the Universal Seal of the Collection of All Dharmas;
the samādhi of Abiding in Space; the samādhi of Purity; the samādhi of the Abode; the samādhi of Non-arising Supernatural Powers; and the samādhi of Raising the Supreme Banner.
“O Subhūti, if a bodhisattva wishes to attain these gates of samādhi as well as other samādhis,
they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fulfill the aspirations of all sentient beings should study the Prajñāpāramitā.”

If a bodhisattva wishes to fulfill all merits, and having maintained these fulfilled virtues, does not fall into states of transgression, nor is born into lowly families, nor dwells in the stages of the arhat or pratyekabuddha, nor engages in disputes with the Bodhisattvas at their summit, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "What is meant by 'the summit-contention' of a bodhisattva? Subhūti replied:

"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās without upāyakauśalya, and furthermore does not enter the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness with upāyakauśalya, they fall to the level of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas and do not conform to the bodhisattva path; this is called the 'summit-contention' of a bodhisattva."
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "For what reason is it called 'the summit-contention of a bodhisattva'? Subhūti replied:
"This is what is called 'love for the Dharma' (dharmatṛṣṇā). He asked,
"What is meant by love for the Dharma?"

Subhūti replied: "When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they enter into the five aggregates and calculate that the five aggregates are empty, signless, and wishless; this is called 'affection for the Dharma' (dharmatṛṣṇā)."

Entering into the five aggregates, one calculates and contemplates that the five aggregates are empty and still, impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; this is called a bodhisattva’s attachment to dharmas.
One further calculates, saying:
"I shall extinguish the five aggregates."

This is the realization of the unconditioned; this is non-realization; this is the attainment of the Way; this is attachment; this is abandonment; this is to be practiced; this is not to be practiced; this is the conduct of a bodhisattva; this is not the conduct of a bodhisattva; this is the Path; this is not the Path; this is the training of a bodhisattva; this is not the training of a bodhisattva; these are the six pāramitās; these are not the six pāramitās; this is skillful means (upāyakauśalya); this is not skillful means; this is a bodhisattva’s attachment to the Dharma.

Subhūti said to Śāriputra: "When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, enters into the dharmas, and engages in calculation and discrimination, this is called a bodhisattva’s attachment to dharmas."
Śāriputra said to Subhūti, "What is the bodhisattva’s conformity with the Path? Subhūti replied:
“When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not contemplate outer emptiness by means of inner emptiness, nor do they contemplate inner emptiness by means of outer emptiness;
they do not contemplate the emptiness of emptiness by means of inner-and-outer emptiness, nor do they contemplate inner-and-outer emptiness by means of the emptiness of emptiness;
furthermore, they do not perceive great emptiness by means of the emptiness of emptiness, nor do they contemplate the emptiness of emptiness by means of great emptiness.”
Nor does one perceive Great Emptiness as the foremost emptiness, nor does the foremost emptiness perceive Great Emptiness;
the foremost emptiness does not contemplate conditioned emptiness, nor does conditioned emptiness contemplate the foremost emptiness;
nor does one maintain the contemplation of conditioned emptiness regarding unconditioned emptiness, nor does one maintain the contemplation of unconditioned emptiness regarding conditioned emptiness.
Nor does one contemplate the emptiness of the unconditioned by means of the emptiness of the boundless;
nor does one contemplate the emptiness of the conditioned by means of the emptiness of the boundless.

Furthermore, while contemplating the emptiness of the conditioned, one does not contemplate the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and while contemplating the emptiness of intrinsic nature, one does not contemplate the emptiness of the conditioned.
When practicing emptiness, one does not contemplate self-emptiness;
one does not contemplate the emptiness of intrinsic nature by means of self-emptiness;
nor does one contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena by means of self-emptiness, nor maintain the contemplation of the emptiness of all phenomena to observe self-emptiness.
The emptiness of all phenomena does not observe the emptiness of non-existence, nor does the emptiness of non-existence observe the emptiness of all phenomena;
the emptiness of all phenomena does not observe the emptiness of existence,
nor does the emptiness of existence observe the emptiness of non-existence.
One does not contemplate emptiness as having existence, nor does one contemplate emptiness as being non-existent.
Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, they progress upward and thereby accord with the path of a bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva trains in this manner in the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not dwell upon the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) nor become conceited; they do not dwell upon the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; they do not dwell upon forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena (*dharmas*); and they do not dwell upon the six *pāramitās* up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), nor do they become conceited."
When practicing this study of the Prajñāpāramitā, one does not even conceive of the thought of enlightenment as being subtle and peerless, nor does one conceive of it with pride. Why is this?
"This mind is neither mind nor non-mind, because the nature of the mind is vast and pure.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "In what way is the nature of the mind vast and pure?"

Subhūti replied: "With respect to desire and delusion, it neither unites nor disperses; it neither unites with nor disperses from the afflictions (*kleśa*); it neither unites with nor disperses from evil conduct and the sixty-two views; nor does it unite with or disperse from the mentalities of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
This is what is meant by the bodhisattva’s mental nature being vast and pure."
Śāriputra asked again: "Does the mind exist?
You say that this mind is not the mind."
Subhūti replied: "When the mind is without any thought, can that which has intention or that which lacks intention be obtained, seen, or known?"
Śāriputra replied: "Indeed, Subhūti!
It cannot be apprehended, it cannot be seen, and it cannot be known."
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
“When the mind is without thought, one neither perceives the existence of mind nor the non-existence of mind; it is neither obtainable nor visible. Therefore, it is pure.”
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "What is meant by 'the intention that is no intention'? He replied:
"To have no volitional activity and no conceptualization regarding all phenomena—this is what is meant by 'the mind that is without mind.
Śāriputra asked again: "Is it also the case that the unconditioned and the uncreated are the mind?"
"Is it also the mind that [perceives] the five aggregates as unconditioned and uncreated? And even up to the Path, is it also the mind that [perceives it] as unconditioned and uncreated?
Subhūti replied, "So it is, so it is!"
"It is as you have asked.
At that time, Śāriputra praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

Subhūti, as you are a son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha, and born through transformation by the Dharma, your giving is a gift of the Dharma rather than a gift of desire; you preach the Dharma according to what you have realized. Truly, as the Buddha has described you, you are foremost among those who delight in the practice of emptiness and tranquility.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom in this manner; they will then become irreversible and shall never again be separated from the perfection of wisdom.
If a bodhisattva wishes to study and know the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā; they should read, practice, and uphold it.
If they wish to study the bodhisattva stages, they should study the Prajñāpāramitā; they should read, study, uphold, and practice it.

Why is this? Because within the Prajñāpāramitā, the teachings of the three vehicles are extensively expounded; both bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas should likewise study and achieve accomplishment therein.
Chapter Eleven: On Original Non-existence. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
Just as when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), I do not perceive a bodhisattva, nor do I see a bodhisattva.
For what kind of bodhisattva, then, should I teach the perfection of wisdom?
Whom should one teach?
Since one does not perceive the beginning or end of all phenomena, how could one assign a name to a bodhisattva and say, "This is a bodhisattva"?
World-Honored One!
This word neither abides nor does it not abide. Why is this?
Because this word is neither seen nor can it be apprehended.
World-Honored One!
I do not perceive a beginning or an end to the five aggregates; how, then, could I bestow a name upon a bodhisattva?
For this reason, World-Honored One, [I cannot do so].
This word neither abides nor does it not abide.
World-Honored One!
I do not perceive the beginning or end of the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and the six objects of decay (*ṣaḍdhātu*). How then could I designate a name for a bodhisattva?
This word neither abides nor does it not abide. Why is this?
Because this word is neither visible nor knowable.
What is the establishment of the syllables of a bodhisattva?
These syllables are neither visible nor knowable; these syllables do not abide, nor do they not abide.
World-Honored One!
I do not perceive the eighteen elements, nor do I perceive the beginning or end of the twelve links of dependent origination.
World-Honored One!

I do not perceive the root of the arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination; nor do I perceive the beginning or end of lust, anger, and delusion; nor do I perceive the sixty-two views; nor do I perceive the beginning or end of the six *pāramitās*; nor do I perceive a self, a person, a life-soul, or a living being, nor their beginning or end; nor do I perceive the beginning or end of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, or the aspirations for the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, morality, giving, heaven, *ānāpāna*, or death—all these are likewise unfindable and cannot be perceived.
I also do not perceive the beginning or end of the Buddha’s eighteen unique qualities.
World-Honored One!

The five aggregates are like a dream, like an echo, like a light, like a shadow, like an illusion, like a mirage, and like a transformation; their beginning and end cannot be apprehended. They are quiescent, neither arising nor ceasing in terms of beginning and end, and they are neither attached to nor severed from beginning and end.
Furthermore, the beginning and end of the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of dharmas that accord with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) are all unobservable.
World-Honored One!

I likewise do not see the beginning and end of wholesome or unwholesome dharmas; I also do not see the beginning and end of the conditioned (saṃskṛta) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), or the outflowing (sāsrava) and the non-outflowing (anāsrava).
World-Honored One!
I do not perceive the beginning or end of the future, the past, or the present; nor do I perceive the beginning or end of dharmas that are neither future, nor past, nor present.

I do not perceive the beginning or end of the World-Honored One; nor do I perceive the beginning or end of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, along with their assemblies of disciples and bodhisattvas, in the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.
World-Honored One!
Since the beginning and end of all phenomena cannot be apprehended and cannot be seen, which bodhisattva should be instructed?
For whom should the Prajñāpāramitā be taught?
The syllable is neither abiding nor non-abiding; this syllable cannot be known.
It cannot be apprehended and it cannot be seen; therefore, the syllable neither abides nor does it not abide. Why then would one apply a name to a bodhisattva?
Why is this? World-Honored One, all dharmas consisting of syllables are invisible and cannot be apprehended.
A bodhisattva is a designation formed by the combination of numerical characters, yet there is no one who creates this designation for them.

The five aggregates, the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha likewise have no one who creates their designations.
World-Honored One!
It is like a dream, a letter, an echo, a light, a shadow, a mirage, a transformation, or empty space.
World-Honored One!
For example, when one speaks of earth, water, fire, wind, and space, there is likewise no one who creates these words.
When one speaks of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, there is likewise no one who creates these words.
Regarding the terms *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, *arhat*, and *pratyekabuddha*, these words likewise have no one who creates them as names.
To speak of "bodhisattva" or "the Way," to speak of "Buddha" or "Buddha-dharma"—the characters for these have no creator.

To speak of "good" and "evil," to speak of "permanence" and "impermanence," "suffering" and "pleasure," or "self"; to speak of "quiescence" and "tranquility," or "existence" and "non-existence"—the characters for these have no creator.
For this reason, I am filled with doubt. Why is this?
Because the beginning and end of all phenomena cannot be perceived, yet you bestow the title of "bodhisattva" upon them.
World-Honored One!
These words also do not abide within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Why is this?
These syllables are non-existent and unattainable; therefore, these syllables neither abide nor do they not abide.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, does not grieve or regret, is not lax or indolent, and is neither terrified nor afraid, one should know that this bodhisattva truly dwells in the stage of *avaivartika*, dwelling in non-dwelling.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, when a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they should not abide within form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; they should not abide within the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; they should not abide within forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas; they should not abide within the six consciousnesses; they should not abide within the six bases; they should not abide within the six contacts; they should not abide within earth, water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness; and they should not abide within the twelve links of dependent origination."
Why is this? Because form,
sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty,
World-Honored One.
If the five aggregates are empty, they are not [separate from] the five aggregates; the five aggregates do not depart from emptiness, nor does emptiness depart from the five aggregates.
Emptiness is the five aggregates, and the five aggregates are emptiness.
Therefore, World-Honored One,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell within the five aggregates, nor should they dwell within anything up to and including the twelve links of dependent origination.
Why is this? Because the twelve links of dependent origination are empty.
The twelve links of dependent origination are themselves emptiness, and emptiness is itself the twelve links of dependent origination.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, he should not dwell within the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; nor should he be separated from emptiness regarding these eighteen qualities of a buddha. Emptiness is the eighteen qualities, and the eighteen qualities are emptiness. Therefore, he should not dwell within them."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell within the six perfections. Why is this?
Because the six pāramitās are empty, abiding in them is not the six pāramitās.
The six pāramitās are not separate from emptiness, and emptiness is also not separate from the six pāramitās.
Therefore, World-Honored One,
a bodhisattva should not dwell within the six pāramitās.
Furthermore, World-Honored One:
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should not abide within the enumeration of syllables.
Whether the enumeration of syllables is many or few, they should not abide therein.
Why is this? Because the enumeration of syllables is empty.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!"
A bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should likewise not dwell within the supernormal powers. Why is this?
Because the supernormal powers are emptiness, and emptiness is the supernormal powers.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should not dwell within [the notion that] form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent."
Why is this? Because impermanence is empty.
If impermanence were not empty, it would not be impermanent; yet emptiness is likewise not separate from impermanence.
That which is impermanent is empty, and that which is empty is impermanent; therefore, a bodhisattva should not dwell therein.

One should not dwell in the suffering of the five aggregates, nor should one dwell in the selflessness of the five aggregates; one should not dwell in the emptiness of the five aggregates, nor should one dwell in the tranquility of the five aggregates.

"Furthermore, World-Honored One, a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should not abide within it; they should not abide within phenomena (dharma) or the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); they should not abide within the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they should not abide within the various gates of samādhi or the gates of dhāraṇī."
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva lacks upāyakauśalya (skillful means), conceives the notion of a self, and becomes attached to the five aggregates, even if they receive the prajñāpāramitā while still possessing the five aggregates, they will not accord with the prajñāpāramitā and will not fulfill the prajñāpāramitā; consequently, they will be unable to give birth to sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).”
"Furthermore, World-Honored One, when a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*,

if they become attached to the notion of a self (*ātman*), abide in the various *dhāraṇī* and *samādhi* gates, and seek those *dhāraṇī* and *samādhi* gates through conceptualization and cognition, yet still receive the *prajñāpāramitā*, they will neither be in accord with the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor will they fulfill the *prajñāpāramitā*, and they will be unable to give birth to *sarvajñatā*."
Why is this? Because one does not grasp at form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Since one does not grasp at the five aggregates, they are no longer the five aggregates.
Why is this? Because their nature is empty.
The various *dhāraṇī*s and gates of *samādhi* do not receive [anything]; that which does not receive is not a *dhāraṇī* or a gate of *samādhi*, because its nature is empty.
Even up to the perfection of wisdom, one likewise does not grasp it, because its intrinsic nature is empty.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should contemplate the dharma of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Although one contemplates all phenomena, one should not allow anything to be grasped; this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s samādhi of non-appropriation.
It accumulates vast and limitless efficacy, which no Arhat or Pratyekabuddha can equal.
Even *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is not grasped, and even internal and external emptiness, as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence, are not grasped. Why?
Because it cannot be practiced by means of signs.
Why is this so? Because the practice of signs (nimitta) is defiled.
What are these signs?
The characteristics of the five aggregates and the characteristics of samādhi are called the characteristics of defilement.
One should receive [this teaching] in this way and contemplate it in this way.
Otherwise, the non-Buddhist practitioner Śreṇika would never have gained faith in the wisdom of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).

What is faith? It is faith in the Prajñāpāramitā; one does not believe by means of signs while understanding, receiving, upholding, and contemplating what is appropriate, nor by means of signs, nor by means of signlessness.

Having cultivated this mark of non-reception, Śreṇika attained the understanding and faith of the essential principle; he immediately attained the wisdom that transcends the nature of emptiness and no longer received [the aggregates of] sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Why was this so?
This is because one perceives the dharma of the mark of emptiness. Why is this?
One does not perceive wisdom within, nor does one perceive wisdom without, nor does one perceive wisdom apart from internal and external phenomena.

Why is this? Because one does not perceive any dharma that can be known; nor does one perceive wisdom within the five internal aggregates, nor does one perceive wisdom within the five external aggregates, nor does one perceive wisdom apart from the five aggregates.
By these causes and conditions, Śreṇika attained liberation.
Having attained liberation, he then gained faith in *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).
This is called taking the equal faith in all phenomena as one's witness, yet not perceiving those phenomena.
Once Śreṇika had attained this liberation, he was no longer receptive to any phenomena, because he neither conceptualized nor dwelt upon them.
These phenomena are such that there is no one who attains them, no one who receives them, and no one who understands them.
This Dharma is neither received, nor maintained, nor can it be obtained, nor is there any mindfulness, because all dharmas are devoid of mindfulness.
World-Honored One!
Why is it that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, through their mastery of the Prajñāpāramitā, come and go between this shore and the other?
It is because they do not grasp at any phenomena.
One who does not grasp at form, sensation, perception, formations, or consciousness does so because they have no grasping toward any phenomena (*dharma*).

This extends even to the gates of samādhi and dhāraṇī, for which there is no grasping; likewise, they have no grasping toward any phenomena. Without having fully perfected the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Buddha, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they never enter parinirvāṇa midway.

Why is this? Because the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are not thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are not eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
These dharmas are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas; this is the practice of the prajñāpāramitā by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp the five aggregates.
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should contemplate in this way:
"In what sense can one speak of 'the perfection of wisdom'?"
"To whom does this Prajñāpāramitā belong? Who possesses this Prajñāpāramitā?
When a bodhisattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they should further reflect in this way:
"An unobtainable dharma and an invisible dharma are not the Prajñāpāramitā.
Thereupon, Śāriputra asked the Venerable Subhūti: "Worthy one!..."
"What dharmas are unobtainable and invisible?
Subhūti replied, "The Prajñāpāramitā is unobtainable and invisible."
Dhyāna, vīrya, kṣānti, śīla, and dāna-pāramitā are likewise unobtainable and invisible, because of outer emptiness, inner emptiness, and the emptiness of existence and non-existence.

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are likewise unapprehendable; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are also non-existent and unapprehendable.

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the Buddha’s omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) likewise neither exist nor can they be perceived, because both the internal and external are empty, and existence and non-existence are all empty.

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, if they engage in such contemplation and maintain such reflection, with a mind that is neither weary nor disheartened, and neither terrified nor afraid, you should know that this bodhisattva never departs from the prajñāpāramitā.
Śāriputra asked the Venerable Subhūti:
"How should one know that a bodhisattva does not depart from the prajñāpāramitā? Subhūti replied:

"Just as the characteristic marks of form are separate from form; as the characteristic marks of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are separate from sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; as the characteristic marks of the *dānapāramitā* are separate from the *dānapāramitā*, and so on up to the characteristic marks of the *prajñāpāramitā* being separate from the *prajñāpāramitā*; and so on, even up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it is likewise."
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "What is the nature of the five aggregates?
What is the nature of the six perfections and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?"
"What are the characteristics of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), suchness (tathatā), and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)? Subhūti replied:

"The characteristics of the five aggregates are non-existent; likewise, the characteristics of the six perfections, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the limit of reality are also non-existent."
Their category is not the category of things. Śāriputra!

Therefore, one should understand that just as the characteristics of the five aggregates are detached from the five aggregates, and the characteristics of the six pāramitās are detached from the six pāramitās, even so it is with the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).

“The five aggregates are devoid of the characteristics of the five aggregates; even the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is devoid of its own characteristics, and characteristics are also devoid of that limit of reality.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: “Does the bodhisattva mahāsattva, within this, give birth to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)?”
He replied: "It is exactly as you have asked, without any difference. Why is this?"
"All dharmas have no emergence and no arising.
Śāriputra asked again,
"For what reason do all dharmas have neither arising nor emergence?"
Subhūti replied: “The five aggregates are empty; neither their emergence nor their arising is perceived.
