From its fundamental state of non-attachment and indestructibility up to the emptiness of the three realms—this is the emptiness of the conditioned.
What is the emptiness of the unconditioned?
Neither arising nor ceasing, it abides in non-differentiation; from non-attachment and indestructibility, it is entirely empty.
Why is this? Because it is fundamentally empty.
This is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of the ultimate (*atyanta-śūnyatā*)? That which has no perceivable limit is the emptiness of the ultimate.
What is the emptiness of the unoriginated (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*)?
All things that may come have no known place from which they originate, because there is no locus; this is called the emptiness of the unoriginated.
What is the emptiness of non-action?
To have nothing to discard among all phenomena—this is the emptiness of non-action.
What is the emptiness of nature?

The intrinsic nature of all phenomena, as well as their conditioned and unconditioned natures, is not something produced by arhats, pratyekabuddhas, or the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; this is what is meant by the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*)?

"All phenomena" refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*), conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); these are called all phenomena.
From non-attachment and non-destruction up to the nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*), this is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*)?

The characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristic of what is perceived; the characteristic of that which is sustained, the characteristic of perception (*saṃjñā*), and the characteristic of what belongs to it, as well as the characteristic of that which is cognized—this is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Up to and including the characteristics of the conditioned and the unconditioned—from the characteristics of the conditioned and the unconditioned to all phenomena being entirely empty—this is called the emptiness of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*)?
From non-attachment and non-destruction up to the dharma of non-apprehension, there is likewise no apprehension; this is called the emptiness of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*)?
That within which nothing is perceived—this is called the emptiness of non-existence.
What is the emptiness of existence (bhāva-śūnyatā)?
All phenomena lack a counterpart; within all combinations and associations, there is nothing substantial. This is called the emptiness of existence.
What is the emptiness of non-existence (abhāva-śūnyatā)?
Even within all assemblies there is no reality; this is the emptiness of existence and non-existence.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, existence is empty of existence, non-existence is empty of non-existence, and difference is empty of difference."
What is existence? Existence refers to the nature of the five aggregates; that this nature is empty of nature is called the emptiness of existence.
What is non-existence?
Because it is empty of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there is nothing to be accomplished; that which is not accomplished is itself emptiness.
This emptiness cannot be produced by knowledge, nor can it be produced by vision.
What, then, is the emptiness of other things?
Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, the dharma-nature of dharmas is quiescent and such-like, abiding as suchness and the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi).
Because it is distinct from [mere] emptiness, this is called the "emptiness of other things" (parabhāva-śūnyatā), Subhūti!
This is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Subhūti, furthermore, there is another Mahāyāna.
What is the Mahāyāna?
It consists of one hundred and seven samādhis, each having its own name.
What is the samādhi named Śūraṅgama-samādhi?
What is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi?
All the gateways of samādhi converge and enter into it; therefore, it is named Śūraṅgama.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named Jewel Seal (Ratnamudrā). What is the Jewel Seal Samādhi?
It seals all the seals belonging to every samādhi.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named Lion’s Play (*siṃhavikrīḍita*). What is Lion’s Play?
One who dwells in this samādhi plays freely within all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Moon Samādhi; one who abides in this samādhi is able to illuminate all samādhis with light.
Furthermore, there is the Moon Banner Samādhi; one who abides in this samādhi upholds all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called "Abiding Above All Dharmas"; one who dwells in this samādhi has all samādhis emerge from within it.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called "Illuminating the Crown"; one who dwells in this samādhi is able to illuminate the tops of all samādhis with light.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called "Dharma-nature Completion," by abiding in which one can decisively comprehend all dharmas.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called "Mandatory Victory Banner," by abiding in which one necessarily upholds a firm victory banner among all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Vajra Samādhi; for one who abides in this samādhi, no other samādhis dare to confront it.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-entrance-Seal Samādhi; for one who abides in this samādhi, they are in accord with the seals of all dharmas.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of Abiding; one who dwells in this samādhi is able to abide in all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of Emitting Radiance; one who dwells in this samādhi is able to universally illumine all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of powerful progress; one who abides in this samādhi can teach all samādhis by means of its power and force.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of equal stride; one who abides in this samādhi can practice all samādhis with equanimity.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of entering the teaching of eloquence; one who dwells in this samādhi is able to analyze and explain all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of immeasurable sound; one who dwells in this samādhi attains entry into the samādhi of immeasurable names.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called "Illuminating All Places"; one who dwells in this samādhi is able to illuminate all directions within all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called "Seal of Dhāraṇī"; one who dwells in this samādhi is able to maintain the seal of all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of non-forgetfulness; one who dwells in this samādhi does not forget any of the samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of the ocean that gathers all dharmas; one who dwells in this samādhi is able to cause all samādhis to function equally.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Universal Space; one who dwells in this samādhi is able to fully satisfy all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Vajra Family Samādhi; one who dwells in this samādhi maintains the families of all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Jewel-Victory Samādhi; one who abides in this samādhi subdues all defilements and turbidities.
Furthermore, there is the Blazing Flame Samādhi; one who abides in this samādhi is able to universally illuminate all samādhis with its radiant flames.
Furthermore, there is the wishless samādhi; one who dwells in this samādhi does not grasp at any phenomena.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of dwelling in scrutiny; one who dwells in this samādhi does not perceive any place of abiding for phenomena.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Selection; one who dwells in this samādhi has no mental ideation regarding any samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of the Stainless Lamp; one who dwells in this samādhi acts as a lamp for all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Infinite Light; one who dwells in this samādhi finds no limit among all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Producing Radiance; one who dwells in this samādhi is able to illuminate all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Universal Illumination; for one who abides in this samādhi, all samādhis appear before their eyes.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Pure Essentiality; for one who abides in this samādhi, they attain the Samādhi of Equal Purity.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Stainless Light; one who dwells in this samādhi disperses the defilements of all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Creating Joy; one who dwells in this samādhi experiences the bliss of all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Electric Radiance; one who abides in this samādhi acts as a lamp for all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Inexhaustibility; one who abides in this samādhi perceives neither exhaustion nor non-exhaustion.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Supreme Majesty; one who dwells in this samādhi possesses a majesty that stands alone among all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Total Exhaustion; one who dwells in this samādhi perceives all samādhis as being completely exhausted, such that they are as if not seen at all.
Furthermore, there is the immovable samādhi; one who abides in this samādhi causes all samādhis to be immovable, non-conceptual, and non-discursive.
Furthermore, there is the non-differentiated samādhi.
One who dwells in this samādhi does not perceive separation.
Furthermore, there is the Sun-Lamp Samādhi; one who dwells in this samādhi illuminates all gates of samādhi.
Furthermore, there is the Moon-Stainless Samādhi.
One who dwells in this samādhi is able to dispel the darkness of all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Pure Radiance; one who dwells in this samādhi distinguishes the four unhindered wisdoms within all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Producing Illumination; one who dwells in this samādhi produces illumination for the gates of all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Creation; one who dwells in this samādhi brings all samādhis to ultimate completion.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of All Wisdom; one who dwells in this samādhi perceives the wisdom of all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Vajra Samādhi; one who dwells in this samādhi decisively cuts through all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of abiding in the mind; one who dwells in this samādhi is unmoving, unshakable, without fear, without terror, and free from mental ideation.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of manifesting light; one who dwells in this samādhi perceives light pervading all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of establishment; one who dwells in this samādhi is well-situated within all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the jewel-accumulation samādhi; one who dwells in this samādhi universally beholds the jewels of all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of the Dharma-Seal; one who dwells in this samādhi seals all samādhis, whether they are sealed or unsealed.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Equality; one who dwells in this samādhi does not perceive any dharma as having equality or liberation.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of abandoning pleasure; one who dwells in this samādhi completely abandons all pleasures.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of transcending dharmas; one who dwells in this samādhi extinguishes the darkness of all dharmas and stands above all other samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called Dispelling Knots; one who dwells in this samādhi is able to disperse the applications of all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called Resolving the Phrases of All Dharmas; one who dwells in this samādhi is able to resolve all samādhis as well as the phrases of all dharmas.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Equal Letters; one who dwells in this samādhi attains all equal letters.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of the Letter Pi; one who dwells in this samādhi does not see a single letter.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of severing causal conditions; one who dwells in this samādhi severs all causal conditions.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of signlessness; one who dwells in this samādhi does not perceive the signs of any phenomena.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of non-action; one who dwells in this samādhi does not perceive the activity of any dharmas.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of non-nesting activity; one who dwells in this samādhi does not perceive any nesting or dwelling-place activity within any samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called "Exhausting the Aggregates" (*skandhakṣaya*); one who dwells in this samādhi is able to purify all the aggregates.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called "Mastery over Practice" (*caryādhipati*); one who dwells in this samādhi perceives the practices of all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of non-arising; one who dwells in this samādhi does not perceive the arising of any samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of transcending realms; one who dwells in this samādhi passes beyond all realms.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called "Accumulating All Virtues"; one who dwells in this samādhi is able to accumulate all dharmas and all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called "Cessation and Selection"; one who dwells in this samādhi does not fall away from their intention.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Pure Flowers; one who abides in this samādhi attains the pure flowers of all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Mastering Awakening; one who abides in this samādhi possesses the seven factors of awakening within all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of infinite eloquence; one who dwells in this samādhi attains immeasurable eloquence.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of the peerless and equal; one who dwells in this samādhi immediately attains that which is peerless and equal.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi that transcends all dharmas; one who dwells in this samādhi transcends the three realms.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of decisive resolution; one who dwells in this samādhi is able to see all dharmas and see the matters of decisive resolution regarding all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Dispelling All Doubts; one who abides in this samādhi attains the Samādhi of Dispelling All Dharmas.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Non-abiding; one who abides in this samādhi does not perceive any location for dharmas.
Furthermore, there is the One-Practice Samādhi; one who dwells in this samādhi does not perceive any phenomena as being dual.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Entering Sentient Beings; one who dwells in this samādhi perceives neither sentient beings nor that which is entered.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of "one matter"; one who abides in this samādhi does not perceive the matters of any samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of "disgust for all matters"; one who abides in this samādhi does not perceive any distinction.

Furthermore, there is the samādhi called "Scattering All Toil and Enmity of Birth and Death. One who dwells in this samādhi attains the wisdom of all samādhis of detachment and enters the sphere of non-perception.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called "Entry into the Sounds of All Practices"; one who dwells in this samādhi finds all the sounds of various practices following after them.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called "Liberation from All Sounds and Syllables"; one who dwells in this samādhi perceives all samādhis as being liberated from sounds and syllables.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of the Blazing Torch; one who dwells in this samādhi possesses a majesty and brilliance that alone outshines all other samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Pure Characteristics; one who dwells in this samādhi is able to purify the characteristics of all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of no standard; one who dwells in this samādhi perceives no standard among all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of being fully endowed with all matters; one who dwells in this samādhi attains full endowment in all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of not desiring suffering or pleasure; one who dwells in this samādhi does not perceive any suffering or pleasure in any samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of non-diminution of phenomena; one who dwells in this samādhi does not perceive any exhaustion in any samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called Holding the Trace; one who dwells in this samādhi thoroughly examines all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called Gathering of the Deviant and the Right; one who dwells in this samādhi perceives neither deviance nor correctness within any samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called "extinguishing anger and strife"; one who dwells in this samādhi perceives no anger or strife within any samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called "absence of anger"; one who dwells in this samādhi perceives neither anger nor the absence of anger regarding any phenomena or any samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Stainless Light; one who dwells in this samādhi perceives neither light nor stain within any samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Essentiality; one who dwells in this samādhi does not perceive a lack of essentiality within any samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called "The Radiance of the Stainless Full Moon. One who dwells in this samādhi can cause all samādhis to be fully perfected, like the moon on the fifteenth day.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Great Adornment; one who dwells in this samādhi can cause all samādhis to be beautifully adorned.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Creating Radiance for the World; one who dwells in this samādhi causes radiance to universally illuminate the ten directions as well as all dharmas.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Equality of Samādhis"; one who dwells in this samādhi perceives neither disorder nor stability among all phenomena.
Furthermore, there is the "Non-anger" samādhi; one who dwells in this samādhi is able to cause all samādhis to be free from anger.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of non-reliance, no lair, and no delight; one who dwells in this samādhi perceives no nesting place among all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of ultimate suchness; one who dwells in this samādhi does not deviate from suchness within all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Physical Remains" (*śarīra*); one who dwells in this samādhi does not perceive the intrinsic nature of this samādhi.

Furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Severing Verbal Activity and Unifying with Emptiness" (*vāk-karma-ccheda-śūnyatā-samavasaraṇa*); one who dwells in this samādhi does not perceive any verbal expression within all samādhis.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Innately Liberated Space Without Form. One who dwells in this samādhi attains the fundamental emptiness of all dharmas.
Subhūti, this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā.
20. The Chapter on Dhāraṇīs. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā, Chapter Twenty: The Chapter on Dhāraṇīs. "Furthermore, Subhūti, there is another Mahāyāna."
What is meant by the "Great Vehicle" (Mahāyāna)?
It refers to the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni).
What are the four foundations of mindfulness?
The Bodhisattva observes his own body, observes the bodies of others, and having observed the internal and external body, is without the perception of a body and has no dependence.
Whether in motion or at rest, he constantly reflects that the world arises from ignorance and is subject to affliction.

One contemplates internal feelings, mental formations, and phenomena; one contemplates external feelings, mental formations, and phenomena; and one contemplates both internal and external feelings, mental formations, and phenomena—whether in motion or at rest—constantly mindful of the delusion and ignorance of the world.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva contemplate the activities of the internal body?

The bodhisattva knows for himself: when it is time to walk, he knows he is walking; when it is time to stand, he knows he is standing; when it is time to sit, he knows he is sitting; when it is time to lie down, he knows he is lying down. He is able to know for himself all the movements of his body as they occur.
This is how a bodhisattva observes his own bodily conduct: whether moving or at rest, he constantly keeps in mind the suffering and afflictions of the world.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva enters or exits, advances or halts, he is composed and mindful; whether sitting or lying down, turning to the left or right, he remains always composed, wearing the three dharma-robes without losing his dignified demeanor.
A bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom observes the activities of the body internally and externally in this way, remaining without any dependence.
The bodhisattva constantly observes the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, knowing when the breath is long and knowing when it is short.
It is like a potter’s wheel, which regulates its speed;
the Bodhisattva’s mindfulness of breathing is such that the mind and the breath move together, both exiting and entering.
This is the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the activities of the internal body—whether in motion or at rest—constantly mindful of the suffering, affliction, and peril of worldly delusion.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, by practicing this prajñāpāramitā, one should constantly contemplate the body and analyze it into its four components:
earth, water, fire, and wind."
It is like a butcher who divides an ox into four parts;
the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the body as being analyzable into these four matters—from its origin to its end—is likewise so.
This is the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the internal and external body, wherein there is no dependence whatsoever.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva contemplates the body from head to foot as consisting only of impurities: what is there to be craved in the thirty-six components, such as hair, body hair, nails, teeth, sinews, bones, and the five internal organs?
For example, it is like a farmer’s vessel filled with the five grains; a person with sight, upon opening the vessel, sees all the seeds and crops and distinguishes them with full knowledge.
When a Bodhisattva contemplates the body, everything within the body is likewise so.

This is how a bodhisattva contemplates his own internal body, whether in motion or at rest, constantly mindful that the delusion, craving, and suffering of the world are likewise without any basis of reliance. "Furthermore, Subhūti!

The Bodhisattva contemplates human beings from the day of death until the fifth day: the body becomes bloated, putrid, and foul-smelling; it decays and fluids flow out, drenching one another so that no part remains clean. Sometimes it is devoured by flying birds or running beasts; sometimes half-eaten, it is a mass of loathsome impurities. Some corpses have their skeletons bound together by sinews with blood still dripping over them; some have their flesh and blood entirely consumed, leaving only the sinews and bones entangled. Among these, there are skeletons whose joints have already come apart, with each bone separated from its place. One may see long-dead skeletons that are bluish-white in color, or those that are rotted and decayed, or those that have become the same color as the earth and soil.
The Bodhisattva performs this contemplation in its entirety; having performed this contemplation, he further reflects:
"My own body has not yet escaped nor separated itself from these phenomena; it too shall likewise be so."

This is how a bodhisattva contemplates the phenomena of their own body and contemplates the bodies of others without attachment; whether moving or at rest, they constantly keep in mind the delusion, suffering, and calamities of the world.

One contemplates the mental states of one’s own awakening and also contemplates the mental states of others’ awakening; through discernment and reflection, one severs the mind of delusion and confusion.
Subhūti! This is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti! Furthermore, there is the Mahāyāna, which gradually masters the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). What are these four?
When unwholesome states of mind have not yet arisen, one takes delight in restraining them, practicing diligence, and collecting the mind so that they do not arise.
When unwholesome states of mind have already arisen, one likewise takes delight in restraining them, practicing diligence, and collecting the mind through practice so that they are abandoned.
Regarding wholesome dharmas not yet arisen, one maintains joyful intent and diligence to practice so that they may arise.

Regarding wholesome dharmas already arisen, one maintains mindfulness and aspiration, fully and extensively manifesting them with desire so that they are not forgotten; furthermore, one joyfully practices diligence, gathering and controlling the mind to bring them to fulfillment.
This is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Subhūti, furthermore,
there is another Mahāyāna, namely the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda).
What are the four? They are:

the basis for supernormal power that, having attained concentration through pleasure, eliminates all conditioned activities; the basis for supernormal power that, through concentration through diligence, eliminates all conditioned activities; the basis for supernormal power that, through concentration through mental volition, eliminates all conditioned activities; and the basis for supernormal power that, through concentration through investigation, eliminates all conditioned activities.
This is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti, furthermore, there is the Mahāyāna, which refers to the five faculties.
What are the five faculties?
They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of resolve, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
These constitute the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Subhūti! Furthermore, there is the Mahāyāna, which refers to the five powers (pañcabala). What are these five?
The power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of resolve, the power of concentration,
and the power of wisdom— these, Subhūti, constitute the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, there is the Mahāyāna, which refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). What are these seven? They are:

the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of dharma-discrimination, the factor of enlightenment of vigor, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
This is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Subhūti, furthermore, there is another Mahāyāna, namely: the Noble Eightfold Path.
What are these eight?
Right view, right mindfulness, right speech, right conduct, right action, right effort, right intention, and right concentration.
These constitute the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, which likewise has no point of reliance.
Subhūti! Furthermore, there is the Mahāyāna, which refers to the three samādhis. What are these three?
The samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, and the samādhi of wishlessness—
this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Furthermore, there is another Mahāyāna, namely, all matters of wisdom.

The wisdom of suffering, the wisdom of its origin, the wisdom of its cessation, the wisdom of the path, the wisdom of elimination, the wisdom of non-arising, the wisdom of phenomena, the wisdom of illumination, the wisdom that individually knows the thoughts of others, and true wisdom.
What is the wisdom regarding suffering?
The non-arising of suffering is the wisdom regarding suffering.
What is the wisdom regarding the origin [of suffering]?
The complete eradication of the origin [of suffering] is the wisdom of the origin.
What is the wisdom of cessation?
The extinguishing of all matters of suffering is the wisdom of cessation.
What is the wisdom of the path?
The noble eightfold path is the wisdom of the path.
What is the wisdom of elimination?
The exhaustion of greed, lust, hatred, and delusion constitutes the wisdom of elimination.
What is the wisdom of non-arising?
Not taking up birth-and-death is the wisdom of non-arising.
What is the wisdom of phenomena?
To clearly understand and sever the five aggregates is the wisdom of phenomena.
What is the wisdom of clarity?
That the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are impermanent, and that forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are likewise impermanent—this is called clear wisdom.
What is the wisdom that knows the thoughts of others individually?

To know all that is thought and all that arises within the minds of all sentient beings in their various forms is what constitutes the wisdom of knowing the thoughts of others individually. What is true wisdom?
That which is called the Tathāgata’s omniscient wisdom (sarvajñājñāna) is true insight, and it is likewise without any dependence. Subhūti,
this is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, there is the Mahāyāna, which refers to the three faculties (*indriya*).
What are these three faculties?
They are the five faculties of the seeker (*śaikṣa*), from the white-robed layperson up to the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), which are "the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown.'"
From the Sakṛdāgāmin to the Anāgāmin, there are likewise five faculties: the faculty of "I shall come to know" and the faculty of "knowing.
From the Arhat, Pratyekabuddha, and Bodhisattva up to the Buddha, there are also five faculties, namely: the faculty of "having known" and the faculty of "no more to learn."
You should know that this is the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
Subhūti, furthermore, there is the Mahāyāna, namely, the three samādhis.
What are the three?
First, with vitarka and vicāra; second, without vitarka but with vicāra; third, without vitarka and without vicāra.
What is meant by "with vitarka and vicāra"?
That is to say, the first dhyāna is characterized by both applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra).
What is characterized by sustained thought without applied thought?
It refers to that which lies between the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna; this is characterized by sustained thought without applied thought.
What is the absence of applied thought and sustained thought?
From the second dhyāna up to the dhyāna of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is the absence of applied thought and sustained thought.
This is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti! Furthermore, there is the Mahāyāna, which refers to the ten recollections. These are:

recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṃgha, recollection of ethical discipline, recollection of generosity, recollection of the devas, recollection of cessation, recollection of mindfulness of breathing, recollection of the body’s suffering, and recollection of death. These, too, are without any point of reliance; this is the Mahāyāna.

Subhūti! Furthermore, there is the Mahāyāna, namely: the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the ten powers of a Buddha, and the four fearlessnesses.

As for the ten powers: first, the Buddha manifests his physical body with its marks and signs, and through supernatural powers and transformations, moves and inspires the various heterodox ones, turning them toward and causing them to enter the正道 (the Right Path);
this is the first power.
Second, that which is spoken from his mouth surpasses all worldly wisdom; he is able to transform doubts and fetters, opening them so that they may attain liberation.
This is the second power.

When the mind enters the samādhi of emptiness, it becomes clear and bright, penetrating all six directions; even if malevolent spirits cause disturbances, the resolve for the Way remains unshaken—this is the third power.

Silently severing conceptualization through the supernormal power of the divine foot (*ṛddhipāda*) and remaining unconditioned, one moves the suns and moons of the trichiliocosm without causing alarm among men;
this is the fourth power.

With the wisdom of the aspiration for enlightenment, one expounds the Dharma and spreads its transformation, so that it flows abundantly throughout the ten directions, each attaining their proper place.
This is the fifth power.
To know the intentions of the multitude in advance and understand the inclinations of people’s conduct—whether they are bound or liberated—and to be able to resolve them all;
this is the sixth power.
Regarding the karmic retributions for the merits and misfortunes created throughout the three periods of time, before they have yet been received, Mahāmati knows them all without any obstruction;
this is the seventh power.
He fully awakens to the fundamental origins and the causal conditions from which all the various and distinct roots of action of all people arise, as well as their differing modes of embodiment.
This is the eighth power.
With the purified eye of wisdom, his observation is boundless; he perceives all births and deaths, the comings and goings, and the states into which beings fall.
This is the ninth power.

Mahāmati has already perfected his skillful means and completed his preparations; birth and death have been severed, attachments and habitual tendencies have been exhausted, and what was to be done has been accomplished so that he will no longer undergo rebirth. Being spontaneously enlightened without a teacher, he is called the All-Knowing One;
this is what is meant by the Ten Powers.

Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*): as the Buddha has attained perfect enlightenment, there may be śramaṇas, brahmins, Māras, devas, Brahmās, or any other beings who might come to challenge or interrogate me; yet the Buddha perceives no one capable of giving rise to such an intention. Because he is thus certified, the Buddha proceeds with ease and attains fearlessness—this is the first fearlessness.

Having attained the stage of supreme mastery through diligent practice, he stands among the multitude and utters the lion’s roar, able to turn the Brahma-wheel, which no other śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, or followers of any other doctrine can turn—only a Buddha can turn it;
this is the second fearlessness.
The Buddha’s outflows are exhausted; among all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or even gods, Māras, and Brahmās, none dare to say that his outflows are not yet exhausted.
This is the third fearlessness.

As the Buddha has spoken, his words are true; there is no evasion of the retribution for good and evil, and what one has practiced shall not go unrewarded. Among all other beings—whether gods, Māras, or Brahmās—none are seen who dare to contravene the Buddha’s words.
As the Buddha has taught, by practicing the Noble Eightfold Path one attains the Way and achieves deliverance from all sufferings.
Among all other beings—whether gods, Māras, Brahmās, or humans—none are able to contradict this teaching, nor does the Buddha perceive anyone who could do so;
this is the fourth fearlessness.
This is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, which is likewise without any dependence.
Subhūti, furthermore,
there is the Mahāyāna, namely the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom.
What are the four? His wisdom is unimpeded in knowing the phenomena of all dharmas;
his wisdom is unimpeded in understanding the meanings of all phrases.
The wisdom of analytical eloquence is unimpeded;
the wisdom that brings what is explained to clear understanding is unimpeded.
This is the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Subhūti! Furthermore, there is the Mahāyāna, namely the eighteen dharmas of a Buddha.
What are these eighteen dharmas?
First, it means that from the time he attained Buddhahood until now, the Buddha has never had a moment of error;
second, from the time he attained Buddhahood until now, his speech has been free from coarseness and devoid of lapses;
third, he possesses no loss of mindfulness.
Fourth, there is no perception of diversity;
fifth, the mind is never at any time undisciplined;
sixth, from the very beginning, there is no other-directed contemplation.
Seventh, mastery does not diminish;
eighth, diligence does not diminish;
ninth, mindfulness and intention do not diminish.
Tenth, there is no diminution of wisdom;
eleventh, there is no diminution of liberation;
twelfth, there is no diminution of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Thirteenth, wisdom precedes all actions of the body;
fourteenth, wisdom precedes all matters spoken by the mouth;
fifteenth, wisdom precedes all actions performed by the mind.
Sixteenth, his wisdom is unimpeded when seeing past events;
seventeenth, his wisdom is unimpeded when seeing future events;
eighteenth, his wisdom is unimpeded when seeing present events.
This is the Mahāyāna, which likewise has no point of reliance. Subhūti,
there is further the Mahāyāna, namely the *dhāraṇīmukha*.
What is the *dhāraṇīmukha*?
It is that which is equal to syllables and equal to words; it is the gateway through which syllables enter.
What is the "syllable-gateway" (*akṣaramukha*)?
First is "A. "A" means that although all phenomena come and enter [into consciousness], one does not perceive any arising.
Second is "Ra. "Ra" means that regarding the appearance of defilement, there is no dust within all phenomena.
Third is *pā*, and *pā* refers to the foremost teaching among all dharmas for crossing over to *nirvāṇa*.
Fourth is *ccha*, and *ccha* refers to not perceiving the existence of birth and death within all dharmas.
Fifth is *na*: *na* means that regarding all dharmas, once the syllables have been exhausted, the intrinsic nature of those syllables is neither attained nor lost.
Sixth is *ra*: *ra* means that having attained transcendence from worldly craving, the various causes and conditions have each been extinguished.
Seventh is *ḍha*; *ḍha* means that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are like [space], without interruption.
Eighth is *pha*; *pha* means that all phenomena have already departed from hell.
Ninth is *ta*; *ta* means that the defilements of all phenomena have been exhausted.
Tenth is *sa*; *sa* means that all dharmas are without obstruction.
Eleventh is *ha*; *ha* means that for all dharmas, speech and action have been severed.
Twelfth is *ta*; *ta* means that all dharmas are as they are.
The thirteenth is *dong* (動); "night" (*ye*) means that all dharmas are truly without arising.
The fourteenth is *zha* (吒); "zha" means that the heavy defilements of all dharmas cannot be seen.
Fifteenth is *ka*: as for *ka*, even the agent who creates all phenomena cannot be perceived.
Sixteenth is *sa*: as for *sa*, since all phenomena cannot be apprehended, they cannot be turned back.
Seventeenth is *ma*; *ma* means that among all phenomena (*dharmas*), a self (*ātman*) cannot be perceived.
Eighteenth is *ga*; *ga* means that one who receives and upholds all phenomena cannot be perceived.
Nineteenth is *ta*: "other. Regarding "other," the locus of all phenomena (*dharmas*) is unobtainable.
Twentieth is *ja*: regarding "birth," the birth of all phenomena is likewise unobtainable.
Twenty-first is *śiva*; "śiva" means that all phenomena (*dharma*) are unattainable as being good.
Twenty-second is "Great" (*mahat*); "Great" means that the nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is unattainable.
The twenty-third is *śa*. "Śa" means that all phenomena are quiescent and unobtainable.
The twenty-fourth is *kha*. "Kha" means that all phenomena are empty and unobtainable.
Twenty-fifth is *cha*; *cha* means that all phenomena are extinguished and cannot be apprehended.
Twenty-sixth is *che*; *che* means that all phenomena each abide in their own place and cannot be shaken.
Twenty-seventh: "If," "if" means that the wisdom of all phenomena is unattainable.
Twenty-eighth: "Ita," "ita" means that the meaning of all phenomena is unattainable.
Twenty-ninth is "Proliferation" (*prapañca*); "proliferation" means that among all phenomena there is no time of rest.
Thirtieth is "Chariot" (*ratha*); "chariot" means that among all phenomena there is nothing to be discarded.
Thirty-first is "Māra"; "Māra" means that among all phenomena there are no graves or tombs.
The thirty-second is *pha*; *pha* means that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are indivisible.
The thirty-third is *tsa*; *tsa* means that death and extinction cannot be found among all phenomena.
Thirty-fourth is Ā: Ā signifies that all dharmas have no factions or partisan attachments.
Thirty-fifth is Ṭha: Ṭha signifies that all dharmas each have their distinct differences, yet there is nowhere they do not exist.
Thirty-sixth is *na*. *Na* means that all phenomena neither come nor go; they do not abide, do not sit, do not lie down, and do not depart.
Thirty-seventh is *pha*. *Pha* means that all phenomena are unstable within the three realms.
Thirty-eighth is *ga*; "ga" means that the nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*) is unattainable.
Thirty-ninth is *ca*; "ca" means that all phenomena are not to be found as permanent.
Fortieth is *ca*, *ca* meaning that the various dharmas are abandoned through analysis and cannot be apprehended.
Forty-first is *ṭa*, *ṭa* meaning that among all dharmas there is no one who crosses over.
Forty-second is *cha*. *Cha* is the limit and the ultimate end of all phenomena; therein there is neither birth nor death.
Among all syllables and numerical designations, none surpasses *cha*.
Why is this? These syllables have no number, nor do they think:
"These syllables are deficient."
"It is neither visible nor can it be spoken; it cannot be written down, nor does it manifest.
Subhūti, you should know that all dharmas are like space; that which is entered through these letters and teachings is entirely the gateway of the dhāraṇī."
If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who thoroughly understand the reality of these syllables, they do not dwell in verbal enumeration and thereby come to know the wisdom of verbal enumeration.

If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who hear these seals of the phrases entered by the forty-two syllables, and who uphold, recite, or further explain their meaning to others, doing so without seeking any reward for their recitation, they shall obtain twenty merits.
What are the twenty? First, one attains the power of strong mindfulness and recollection.
Second, one attains the power of shame, remorse, and modesty.
Third, attaining the power of firm conduct;
fourth, attaining the power of awakening and awareness;
fifth, attaining the power of eloquence and skillful discourse.
Sixth, they attain the power of dhāraṇī without difficulty.
Seventh, in their speech, they do not discuss matters that are not urgent.
Eighth, they never harbor doubt regarding the sūtras.
Ninth, he does not rejoice upon hearing of good nor feel sorrow upon hearing of evil.
Tenth, he neither exalts himself nor disparages himself.
Eleventh, his movements and halts are composed and serene, never losing his dignified deportment.
Twelfth, he thoroughly understands the five aggregates and the six sense-bases.
Thirteenth, he is skilled in the matters of the four truths and the twelve links of dependent origination.
Fourteenth, he is skilled in the matters of the causes and conditions of spiritual friends.
Fifteenth, he is skilled in the wisdom of the Dharma and is able to fulfill and perfect all the sense faculties.
Sixteenth, he knows the thoughts of others and understands the retribution of auspicious and inauspicious deeds.
Seventeenth, he is skilled in the divine ear for hearing through all things and possesses the knowledge of his own past lives.
Eighteenth, he well knows the births of sentient beings.
Nineteenth, he is able to eliminate all outflows (*āsrava*).
Twentieth, he is skillful in coming and going, providing instruction everywhere.
Subhūti! This is the gateway of dhāraṇī;
this is the gateway of syllables; this is the gateway of entry; this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva; this is the Mahāyāna.
Chapter 21: The Stage of Cultivation (*Bhūmi-parikarma*) The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-one: The Stage of Cultivation. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:

"Regarding what you have asked concerning the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s great armor (*mahā-saṃnāha-saṃnaddha*) and his arrival at the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna-samprasthita*): when a Bodhisattva practices the six *pāramitās*, he transcends from one stage (*bhūmi*) to the next."
How does a bodhisattva transcend from one stage to another?
Because all dharmas are not something to be transcended; dharmas neither come nor go, and there is neither transcending nor non-transcending.

All dharmas are likewise without destruction; they are neither arrogant nor do they give rise to thought. One merely attends to the tasks of purifying the stages (*bhūmi*), yet does not perceive those stages.
What is the bodhisattva’s task of purifying the stages?
From the time one first dwells in the First Ground, one should practice ten matters. What are these ten?
First, one should first purify the three defilements and remain without any dependence.

Second, whatever they give in charity is not for their own sake; their thoughts are free from attachment as they purify the four immeasurable minds for the sake of all sentient beings, yet they do not perceive the existence of sentient beings.
Third, one practices giving without there being anything given, nor anyone who receives.
Fourth, one should attend upon virtuous friends without being conceited.
Fifth, one desires to attain the Dharma without clinging to any dharmas whatsoever.
Sixth, one desires to leave the household life and be free from craving and desire.
Seventh, one desires to attain the body of a Buddha and not merely the marks and signs of excellence.
Eighth, one desires to disseminate the teachings of the Dharma so that they are never destroyed.
Ninth, they constantly desire to extinguish reliance on external things and self-will that lacks the wealth of the Dharma.
Tenth, they desire to speak with truthfulness because they possess no [fixed] verbal teachings. Subhūti!
These are the ten matters for which a bodhisattva on the stage of purification should strive. Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, while in the second stage, should constantly keep eight dharmas in mind and should also accomplish them.
What are the eight?
First, one should purify one's precepts.
Second, one should constantly bear in mind the repayment of kindness.
Third, abiding in patience;
fourth, attaining a joyful mind;
fifth, not abandoning anything.
Sixth, taking great compassion as the starting point.
Seventh, being reverent toward teachers, honoring them with sincere faith.
Eighth, regarding all the pāramitās as if serving the World-Honored One, constantly desiring to cultivate and practice them.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should fulfill these eight dharmas within the second bhūmi. Furthermore, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva should abide in five dharmas within the third stage. What are these five?
First, being insatiable in extensive learning.
Second, not entering into the dharma of letters, and distributing the gift of Dharma without arrogance.
Third, purifying the Buddha-fields.
Fourth, bestowing the roots of goodness without arrogance.
Fifth, they abide in the ground of shame and modesty.
Subhūti, these are the five dharmas in which a bodhisattva abides within the third bhūmi.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva, while in the fourth stage, should not abandon the practice of ten dharmas.
First, not abandoning solitary meditation (*pratisaṃlayana*).
Second, having few desires;
third, being content;
fourth, not abandoning the twelve ascetic practices of a śramaṇa.
Fifth, not abandoning the precepts;
sixth, viewing sensual desires as defiled and impure;
seventh, regarding the arising of the mind as being like nirvāṇa.
Eighth, not being sparing of one's own body or possessions;
ninth, being free from indolence and pride;
tenth, not longing for anything that belongs to oneself.
Subhūti! These are the ten matters that a bodhisattva should practice and not abandon while on the fourth stage. Subhūti!
In the fifth stage, a bodhisattva should abandon eight things. What are these eight?
First, one should distance oneself from domestic affairs.
Second, one should keep far away from bhikṣuṇīs.
Third, being skilled in merit, one should remain free from envy.
Fourth, one should distance oneself from worldly assemblies.
Fifth, he remains far removed from anger and contention.
Sixth, he remains far removed from strife and litigation.
Seventh, he remains far removed from dwelling in arrogance.
Eighth, to remain far removed from despising others. Subhūti,
these are the eight things from which a bodhisattva dwelling in the fifth stage remains far removed.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva, in the sixth stage of abiding, should fully possess six dharmas. What are these six?
These are the so-called six pāramitās.
Furthermore, there are six things that one should not do. What are these six?
First, not having the intention of a śrāvaka;
second, not having the intention of a pratyekabuddha;
third, not having a narrow-minded intention.
Fourth, when seeing those who seek something, one remains far removed from any sense of weariness or lack of satisfaction.
Fifth, after giving away all that is good, one remains far removed from any sense of regret.
Sixth, one should remain far removed from the notion of a self. Subhūti,
these are the six matters that a bodhisattva should fulfill and the six matters from which they should remain far removed while abiding in the sixth stage.
Subhūti! There are twenty things that a bodhisattva should not do while on the seventh stage.
What are these twenty?

There is the notion of a self, a sentient being, a life-span, and a vital principle; there is the notion of annihilation, the notion of permanence, and the notion of recollection; there is the notion of seeds; one enters into the aggregates, the elements, and the sense-bases, desiring birth within the triple world. One does not enter into reliance on the vision of the Buddha, does not enter into reliance on the vision of the Dharma, does not enter into reliance on the vision of the Saṃgha; one does not enter into reliance on the precepts, nor into emptiness, nor into signlessness, nor into wishlessness, nor into the Path.
These are the twenty matters that one ought not to do.
One should further fulfill another twenty matters. What are these twenty?

Awakening to emptiness and signlessness, realizing the wisdom of wishlessness, purifying body, speech, and mind, feeling compassion for all sentient beings while not conceiving of them as "sentient beings," and viewing all phenomena with equanimity.

Although he thus enters nothing, he desires to guide and lead others without arrogance; he possesses the patience of non-arising, teaching and transforming through the single path, severing all discrimination, and turning away from conceptualization, views, and the vision of defiled extinction. His wisdom-ground naturally harmonizes his mind; his wisdom is unimpeded, and he is untainted by the affairs of desire.
Subhūti! These are the twenty dharmas that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should fully possess while dwelling on the stage of the seven practices. Furthermore, Subhūti!
Furthermore, a bodhisattva in the eighth stage must be fully endowed with four dharmas.
What are these four? They are:
to employ supernormal powers as a means of observation, thereby entering into the minds of sentient beings.
One shall go to the lands of all Buddhas to observe their wonders;
one shall adorn one's own Buddha-land;
one shall go to see, pay homage to, and make offerings to all Buddhas, observing the body of the Buddha as it truly is.
"One should be fully endowed with these four dharmas. Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the eighth stage should further be fully endowed with four dharmas."
What are these four dharmas? They are:

to purify buddha-fields through the perfection of wisdom; to constantly dwell in the illusion-like samādhi; to know the merits originally performed by sentient beings; and to bring each being to fulfillment according to what they ought to attain.
"Subhūti! A bodhisattva, in the eighth stage, fulfills four dharmas. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
A bodhisattva mahāsattva in the ninth stage should fulfill twelve dharmas.
What are these twelve? They are:
maintaining vast vows that reach infinite realms, and bestowing the appropriate realization upon each according to their needs.
Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas are all fully present. Knowing their languages,
he teaches them through his eloquence according to their respective causes,
thereby bringing the womb-birth to fulfillment.
Accomplishment in the household life;
accomplishment in one's parents;
accomplishment in one's lineage.
The accomplishment of kinsmen;
the accomplishment of birth;
the accomplishment of renunciation.
Subhūti, the adornment of the Buddha-tree is accomplished;
all virtuous merits are accomplished. Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva in the ninth stage should accomplish twelve dharmas.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva in the tenth stage should be designated as a Tathāgata.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what constitutes a bodhisattva’s purification of all that they possess?”
The Buddha said:
“To direct all the various good deeds toward the mind of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience) is for a bodhisattva to purify that which belongs to them.
[The interlocutor asked: “What is it for a bodhisattva to be equal toward sentient beings?”
The Buddha said:
"Purify the four immeasurable minds and be equal toward all sentient beings.
[The interlocutor asked: "What constitutes a bodhisattva’s giving of all that they possess?"
The Buddha said:
"One bestows gifts upon sentient beings without making distinctions.
[The interlocutor asked: "What is it for a bodhisattva to attend upon a virtuous friend?"
The Buddha said:

“To teach others to enter into sarvajñā (all-knowledge), to diligently cultivate and encourage them in its practice, and to engage in the same activities as such persons while revering and receiving their instruction—
this is what constitutes a bodhisattva’s good spiritual friend.”
“What is meant by ‘desiring to attain for the sake of the Dharma’?
The Buddha said:
“It is when one practices the Dharma solely seeking the dharma of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), and does not fall into the stages of the arhat or pratyekabuddha.”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva who always desires to leave the household life for the sake of the Way?
The Buddha said:

“In whatever place they are born, they always desire to become a śramaṇa; no one can create obstacles along the way, and from the beginning they never forget the matter of leaving the household life.”
“What is meant by ‘the mental aspiration for the physical marks of a Buddha’s body’?
The Buddha said:
“If one beholds the image of the Buddha, the mind remains constantly upon the Buddha until the attainment of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), never being separated from it.”
“What is meant by ‘the dissemination of the Dharma-transformation’?
The Buddha said:

“Whether the Buddha is in the world or after his parinirvāṇa, if a bodhisattva upholds and teaches the twelve divisions of the scriptures—such that the introductory teaching is true, the intermediate teaching is true, and the concluding teaching is true, with the explanations of the meaning from beginning to end being complete and pure.”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva who is not a slave to self-will?
The Buddha said:
“Since the extinction of anger and resentment, he has never again fallen into a lowly or base state.”
“What is meant by the ‘truthfulness of what a bodhisattva speaks’?
The Buddha said:
“It is when one’s speech accords with one’s actions.”
"These are the ten dharmas of the bodhisattva’s practice.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What constitutes the pure precepts of a bodhisattva?"
The Buddha said:
"Not to harbor thoughts of arhats or pratyekabuddhas, nor to hold other evil precepts or slander the Path—this is pure precept.
What is the bodhisattva’s way of repaying kindness and being mindful of kindness?"
The Buddha said:
"One who practices the bodhisattva path does not forget even a small kindness, let alone a great one;
this is what it means to be mindful of kindness."
“How does a bodhisattva establish the power of patience?
The Buddha said:
“To have no aggression or malice toward any sentient being—this is the power of patience.”
“How does a bodhisattva attain the joy of rapture?
The Buddha said:
“To instruct sentient beings is what constitutes this joy.”
“How does a bodhisattva not abandon sentient beings?
The Buddha said:
“Because they wish to rescue all.”
“How does a bodhisattva possess great compassion?
The Buddha said:
“The bodhisattva thinks to himself:”

"For the sake of each and every sentient being, I shall endure the hardships of suffering in the hells for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, so that each and every sentient being may attain the Way of the Buddha and enter parinirvāṇa."
"Encouraging and gladdening others in this way constitutes great compassion.
"How does a bodhisattva accord with their masters and teachers through faith and reverence?
The Buddha said:
"One should regard one's teacher as one regards the World-Honored One.
[The Bodhisattva asked: "How does a bodhisattva desire to practice the various pāramitās?
The Buddha said:
“Distant from all other matters and seeking only the various pāramitās. [The interlocutor asked:
“What is meant by a bodhisattva’s insatiability in extensive learning?
The Buddha said:
"One should receive and uphold all that is taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions; this is called being insatiable.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s distribution of the gift of Dharma through upholding the teaching of no expectation?"
The Buddha said:
"One who upholds the Dharma they have received does not even hope for the Path, let alone anything else.
[The interlocutor asked: "What is meant by a bodhisattva purifying a buddha-field?"
The Buddha said:
“For the sake of various roots of goodness and manifold merits, one takes these merits to purify a buddha-field.
“What is meant by saying that a bodhisattva does not regard immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of birth and death as a limit?”
The Buddha said:

"By means of the full equipment of all merits, one sustains and nurtures sentient beings and purifies the buddha-field, until the perfection of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is attained, without weariness or indolence."
“What is meant by a bodhisattva being established in shame and remorse?
The Buddha said:
“It is to feel shame regarding the mental states of arhats and pratyekabuddhas.”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva not abandoning meditative seclusion?
The Buddha said:
“That which no arhat or pratyekabuddha can equal—this is what is meant by a bodhisattva not abandoning meditative seclusion.”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva having few desires?
The Buddha said:
“A bodhisattva does not even desire the path of a bodhisattva, let alone other desires.”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva knowing contentment?
The Buddha said,
“Attaining *samyaksambodhi* (perfect enlightenment) is what constitutes contentment.”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva not abandoning the ascetic dhūta virtues of a śramaṇa?
The Buddha said: “It is the entry into the profound patience regarding dharmas (gambhīradharmanidhyānakṣānti).”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva not abandoning the precepts?
The Buddha said:
“When a bodhisattva no longer makes use of the precepts, this is what is meant by not abandoning the precepts.”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva’s defilement regarding form and desire?
The Buddha said:
“To give rise to nothing at all in the face of lust and envy.”
“What is meant by ‘the mind of a bodhisattva being equal to nirvāṇa’?
The Buddha said:
“A bodhisattva does not possess any dharmas whatsoever.”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva relinquishing all that they possess?
The Buddha said:
“Not grasping at anything internal or external—this is relinquishment.”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva being neither weary nor indolent?
The Buddha said,
“To not give rise to dualistic consciousness is what is meant by being without weariness.”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva having no longing for anything that exists?
The Buddha said:
“Because they have no conceptualization regarding any objects.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What constitutes a bodhisattva’s dwelling in seclusion?
The Buddha said:
"To travel through the lands of all Buddhas and wherever one is born, always shaving off hair and beard and donning the *kāṣāya*, this is what it means to distance oneself from household affairs.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva distancing themselves from the community of bhikṣuṇīs?"
The Buddha said:

"To not dwell together with them for even the duration of a finger-snap, and to not give rise to [unwholesome] thoughts for even the duration of a finger-snap—this is what it means for a bodhisattva to distance himself from bhikṣuṇīs."
“What is meant by a bodhisattva being free from envy and jealousy?
The Buddha said:
“A bodhisattva should form this thought:”
"I should bring peace and security to sentient beings; it is not fitting for me to give rise to envy.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva being detached from social gatherings?
The Buddha said:
"In the assemblies where Bodhisattvas dwell, if there are those with the mindset of Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, one should always remain far removed from them.
"What is meant by a Bodhisattva remaining far removed from ill-will?"
The Buddha said:
"One does not allow anger, malice, or strife to find an opportunity.
"How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from self-exaltation?"
The Buddha said:
“Because internal phenomena cannot be perceived. [The interlocutor asked:
“How does a bodhisattva remain far removed from disparaging others?”
The Buddha said:
"It is because one does not perceive external dharmas either.
[The interlocutor asked: "What is meant by a bodhisattva remaining far removed from the ten unwholesome actions?"
The Buddha said:
"These ten unwholesome deeds constantly seek to destroy the path of the worthy and noble; how much more so the path of the Buddha?
Therefore, one should distance oneself from these ten evils."
“What is meant by a bodhisattva being far removed from stubbornness?
The Buddha said:
“Not perceiving any dharma that can be used for arrogance—this is what it means to be free from stubbornness.”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva remaining far removed from self-conceit?
The Buddha said:
“Since one does not even perceive the existence of form, how could one act with self-conceit in any place?”
“What is meant by a bodhisattva’s distancing from inversion?
The Buddha said,
“Because form cannot be perceived.”
“How does a bodhisattva become free from lust, anger, and delusion?
The Buddha said,
“Because they no longer perceive the forms of lust, anger, and delusion.”
“How does a bodhisattva, while abiding in the six stages, fulfill the six pāramitās?
The Buddha said:

“Abiding in the six pāramitās—that which the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, have used to cross to the other shore—this is what it means for a bodhisattva to fulfill the six pāramitās.”
“How is it that a bodhisattva does not have the intention of a śrāvaka?
The Buddha said,
“Because the affairs of a śrāvaka are not the path of equality.”
One does not act with a narrow-minded intent. Why?
Because it is also not the path of equality.
What is meant by "not being weary"?
Being weary is not the path of equanimity.
To relinquish without regret—regret is not the path of equanimity.
One who has first resolved their mind toward awakening should immediately practice giving and should not be stingy.
Why should a bodhisattva not form the notion of a self?
Because from the very beginning, it has been unobservable.
Even until sentient beings possess the notion of a life-span, [such a thing] has likewise been invisible from the very beginning.
Why is it that a bodhisattva does not sever the view of arising?
Because all phenomena are without interruption; from the very beginning of existence, there is nothing that arises.
How is it that a bodhisattva does not hold the view of permanence?
Because even those phenomena that are unarisen do not possess permanence.
How is it that a bodhisattva does not form conceptualizations?
Because there is no defilement.
How does a bodhisattva not produce the signs of seeds?
Because all views cannot be apprehended as objects of vision.
How does a bodhisattva not enter name-and-form?
Because they do not perceive any form.
How does a bodhisattva not enter the five aggregates, nor enter their nature, nor enter their decay? Because in reality, these cannot be apprehended or seen.
How does a bodhisattva not enter the triple world?
Because the triple world is likewise without reality.
How does a bodhisattva not make a dwelling place, nor establish a pact with empty space, having nothing upon which to rely?
Why is this? Because there is no physical form or image.
How does a bodhisattva not enter into the view of a Buddha?
Because one does not perceive the Buddha by means of a basis.
How is it that a bodhisattva does not dispute with emptiness?
All phenomena are empty, and emptiness does not dispute with emptiness.
How does a bodhisattva become fully endowed with emptiness?
To desire to be fully endowed with its characteristics is itself to be fully endowed with emptiness.
How does a bodhisattva attain the realization of signlessness?
Because they do not dwell upon any signs.
How does a bodhisattva attain the wisdom of wishlessness?
Because they do not cling to the three realms.
How does a bodhisattva purify the three matters?
By fulfilling the ten wholesome paths of action.
How does a bodhisattva, through wisdom, fully possess compassionate concern for sentient beings?
Because they benefit others through great compassion.
Why is it that Bodhisattvas have no sentient beings?
Because they intend to purify the Buddha-land.
How does a bodhisattva equally contemplate all phenomena?
By not regarding phenomena as high or low.
How does a bodhisattva attain awakening to the Path?
Because they deliver beings according to the realization of all phenomena.
How does a bodhisattva attain the patience of non-arising?
It is because they attain the non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena, and thus have nothing further to endure.
How does a bodhisattva attain the wisdom of non-arising?
By knowing that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) do not arise.
How does a bodhisattva attain the teaching of the single path?
Because there are no two teachings.
How does a bodhisattva extinguish all conceptual discriminations?
By not making any divisions among phenomena.
How does a bodhisattva not cultivate the transformation of views?
By not transforming the aspiration for the state of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha.
How does a bodhisattva transform defilement?
Because it extinguishes all habitual outflows (*āsrava*).
How does a bodhisattva attain the extinction of all defilements and achieve purity?
It is what is called the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
How does a bodhisattva discipline his own mind?
By not being weary of the triple world.
How does a bodhisattva attain the cessation of the mind?
Because they have brought the six sense faculties under control.
How is it that a bodhisattva’s wisdom is unimpeded?
It is because they have attained the Buddha-eye.
How does a bodhisattva know that desire and craving are not solid?
By observing the six sense-bases (ṣaḍāyatana).
How is a bodhisattva able to enter into the minds of sentient beings?
Because they maintain a single-mindedness that fully knows the thoughts of all sentient beings.
How does a bodhisattva travel through the supernormal powers from one buddha-field to another?
Because they have no initial conception of a "buddha-field."
How does a bodhisattva attain the contemplation of the Buddha-lands?
It is by dwelling in such a land while seeing all Buddha-lands everywhere, yet without the notion of "Buddha-land.
How does a bodhisattva, according to what they perceive, cause the various Buddha-lands to become their own land, and dwell upon the ground of a Cakravartin?
Because they travel through all the trichiliocosm world-systems.
How does a bodhisattva reverently behold the Buddhas?
By seeing the Dharma; this is what it means to see the Buddha.
How does a bodhisattva truly see the Buddha-body?
Because they have attained the dharma-nature (dharmatā), this is called true seeing.
How does a bodhisattva possess the power of perfected wisdom?
Having already established oneself in the stage of the World-Honored One’s ten powers, one is then able to be fully endowed with the power of sentient beings.
How does a bodhisattva purify a buddha-field?
By being able to purify sentient beings.
What is the bodhisattva’s illusion-like samādhi?
It is because whatever is performed is done according to what is appropriate, without any wavering or shifting.
What is the bodhisattva’s ever-abiding samādhi?
Because they have already attained retribution,
how does a bodhisattva enter into all merits?
It is because they deliver beings according to their respective paths and dharmas.
Why is it that a bodhisattva no longer engages in conceptual deliberation?
Because they are able to establish themselves and provide instruction to all beings.
Why is it that a bodhisattva’s aspirations are fulfilled?
Because they are fully endowed with the practice of the six pāramitās, they are thus harmonious and perfect.
How does a bodhisattva know what the devas, nāgas, and spirits know and say?
It is because, through the wisdom of eloquence (*pratibhāna*), there is nothing they do not understand.
How does a bodhisattva achieve perfection of the womb?
Because wherever they are born, they are always born by transformation.
How does a bodhisattva achieve perfection of the household life?
Because he is born into a family of noble and high status.
What is the perfection of a bodhisattva’s parents?
It is because he is born into a family of kṣatriyas or brahmins.
What is the accomplishment of a bodhisattva’s lineage?
It is because they have succeeded to the lineage of all past bodhisattvas.
What is the accomplishment of a bodhisattva’s kinsmen?
Because they have a multitude of bodhisattvas as their retinue.
How does a bodhisattva achieve the perfection of birth?
At the time of birth, light pervades immeasurable lands and immeasurable lands are shaken.
What is the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of renunciation?
When a bodhisattva renounces the world, they establish countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, fulfilling and perfecting their aspirations for the three vehicles.
How does a bodhisattva adorn the Buddha-tree?

Taking gold for the trunk and the seven treasures for the branches and leaves, the radiance of those branches and leaves shines everywhere throughout the countless lands of the ten directions; this is the perfection of the Buddha-tree.
How does a bodhisattva accomplish all virtuous merits?
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva purifies buddha-fields and purifies sentient beings, this is called accomplishing the purification of all merits.
Why is it that a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage is called a Tathāgata?

Because they are fully endowed with the six pāramitās, have exhausted all residual habits and tendencies, have attained the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and are complete in the wisdom of sarvajñatā.
"Subhūti! For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has attained the ten stages is called a Tathāgata.
"In what way has the bodhisattva already dwelled in the ten stages?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“A bodhisattva mahāsattva, through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and practices the eighteen dharmas; he transcends the stage of purity, the stage of lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of vision, the stage of refinement, the stage where lust, anger, and delusion are extinguished, the stage of having completed what was to be done, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, and the stage of the bodhisattva.”
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva has transcended these nine stages, he abides in the stage of a Buddha. Subhūti!
These are the ten stages of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva; you should know that these constitute the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s Mahāyāna *samāpatti*. Chapter 22:

Inquiry on the Departure from the Vehicle (*Yāna-niryāṇa-parivarta*) The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-two: Inquiry on the Departure from the Vehicle. The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "Regarding what you have asked: [the nature of the departure from the vehicle]..."
As for the question, "From what Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) do Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas emerge,
and in what should they abide?"—
this shall now be explained.
The Buddha said:
"One should transcend the triple world and abide in sarvajñā (all-knowledge), without relying on anything. Why is this?"

The Mahāyāna and the *sarvajñatā* (omniscience) are equal in these dharmas; they are neither distinct nor identical, neither have form nor are they visible, and they are not characterized by the single mark of obstruction. This "single mark" is called the markless.
Why is this? Subhūti, the dharma of signlessness neither emerges nor does it not emerge.
Subhūti! If dharmas without marks were to arise, then the nature of dharmas (dharmatā) would also have to arise.
If dharmas without marks were to arise, then suchness (tathatā) would also have to arise.
One who wishes to give rise to the signless dharma wishes to give rise to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
If one wishes to give rise to the signless dharma, one further wishes to give rise to the inconceivable nature.
One who wishes to give rise to the signless dharma further wishes to give rise to the nature of peace and security.
One who wishes to give rise to the signless dharma wishes to give rise to cessation.
One who wishes to give rise to the signless dharma wishes to give rise to the essence of cessation.
One who wishes to give rise to the signless dharma wishes to give rise to the emptiness of form, and the emptiness of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Why is this? That which is the emptiness of form neither emerges from the triple world nor abides in sarvajñā;
the same applies to the emptiness of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Why is this? Subhūti!
Form is empty of form itself; sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are each empty of consciousness itself.
One who wishes to give rise to the dharma of signlessness does so because they wish to give rise to the emptiness of the eye, and they wish to give rise to the emptiness of the mind.

One who wishes to give rise to the dharma of signlessness does so because they wish to give rise to the emptiness of the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
Why is this? That which is empty of the six sense-bases neither emerges from the triple world nor abides in *sarvajñatā*.
To wish to bring forth the signless dharma is to wish to bring forth dreams, illusions, mirages, echoes, optical illusions, and shadows.
One who wishes to bring forth the signless dharma wishes to bring forth that which is manifested by the Tathāgata. Why is this?
Because dreams, illusions, mirages, echoes, light, reflections, and the manifestations of the Tathāgata neither emerge from the triple world nor abide in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

Why is this? Because a dream is empty of the phenomena of a dream; the phenomena of a mirage, an illusion, an echo, a reflection, and even the phenomena of those emanated by a Tathāgata are all themselves empty.
One who wishes to give birth to the dharma of signlessness wishes to give birth to the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

One who wishes to give birth to the dharma of signlessness wishes to give birth to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*), the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), and the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*).
One who wishes to give rise to the dharma of signlessness wishes to give rise to the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Subhūti!
The matters of the six pāramitās neither emerge from the triple world nor abide in sarvajñatā. Why is this?
Because the six pāramitās are empty of the six pāramitās.
One who wishes to give rise to the signless dharma wishes to give rise to internal and external emptiness.
One who wishes to give rise to the signless dharma wishes to give rise to the emptiness of existence and the emptiness of non-existence.

Why is this? Subhūti, from the phenomena of internal and external emptiness up to the phenomena of the emptiness of non-existence and existence, they are themselves empty; they neither emerge from the triple world nor do they abide in *sarvajñatā*.
Why is this? Because it is the emptiness of the internal and external, up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence.

One who wishes to bring forth the signless dharma wishes to bring forth the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
One who wishes to give rise to the signless dharma wishes to give rise to the eighteen dharmas.
One who wishes to give rise to the signless dharma wishes to give rise to the arhats and pratyekabuddhas, up to and including the Tathāgatas, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Why is this? From the deeds of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas up to those of the Buddhas, they neither exit the triple world nor abide in sarvajñatā (all-knowledge). Why is this?
Arhats are empty of the activities of arhats; pratyekabuddhas are empty of the activities of pratyekabuddhas; Buddhas are empty of the activities of Buddhas.

To wish to give birth to the dharma of signlessness is to wish to give birth to the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, the fruit of pratyekabuddha, and the fruit of buddhahood.
One who wishes to give rise to the signless dharma wishes to give rise to sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
One who wishes to give rise to the signless dharma wishes to give rise to names and signs.
For one who wishes to bring forth practice, it is for the sake of bringing forth the establishment of dharmas and the enumeration of teachings.
Why is this? Subhūti!
It is called "emptiness of emptiness" and the practice of teaching the dharma through emptiness. Why?
Because it is the emptiness of emptiness.
