One who wishes to give rise to the signless dharma wishes to give rise to that which is neither produced nor extinguished, neither attached to nor abandoned, and which is non-existent.
For this reason, Subhūti,
the Mahāyāna emerges from the triple world and abides in the immovable state of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge). Subhūti!
Regarding your question,
"In what does the Mahāyāna abide?
the Buddha said that the Mahāyāna abides nowhere.
Why is this? Just as all phenomena have no place of abiding, so too the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) has no place of abiding.

For example, just as the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) neither abides nor does not abide, so too the Great Vehicle neither abides nor does not abide; it is unarisen, and neither abides nor does not abide.
Neither arising nor ceasing, neither clinging nor abandoning, it is non-existent; it neither abides nor does it not abide.
The Mahāyāna is also like this. Why is that?
The phenomena of the dharma-nature neither abide nor do they not abide, because the phenomena of the dharma-nature are themselves empty.
This extends even to non-existence; non-existence itself is also empty.
Subhūti! The Great Vehicle has no place of abiding. Why is this?
All dharmas abide nowhere yet abide, remaining unmoving.
As Subhūti has asked: "Who will emerge in the Mahāyāna?"
"There is no one who emerges from the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna).
Why is this? Subhūti!"
That which has already emerged, as well as that which is currently emerging or yet to emerge, likewise does not exist and cannot be seen.
Since all dharmas also cannot be seen, from what dharma could they possibly emerge?
Why is this? Because the self (*ātman*) cannot be seen.

This extends even to the matters of life-span and knowledge-and-vision; from the beginning to the ultimate end they are pure. From the notions of self and person up to knowledge-and-vision and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they cannot be seen; their suchness (*tathatā*) also cannot be seen, and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) likewise cannot be seen, being ultimately pure.
The inconceivable, its nature, the aggregates (*skandha*), and the bases (*āyatana*) are invisible; the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are also invisible, being ultimately pure.
From internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), they are also invisible, being ultimately pure.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are also invisible, being ultimately pure.
From the stage of stream-enterer up to arhat, pratyekabuddha, and finally up to the Buddha, these too are invisible, being ultimately pure.

From the path of the *srotāpanna* up to the paths of the *arhat* and *pratyekabuddha*, and ascending further to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, these too are ultimately pure and thus unobservable; they are neither arising nor ceasing, neither attached to nor severed, and being non-existent, they are ultimately pure and thus unobservable.
The past, future, and present are likewise non-existent and ultimately pure.
Departing, abiding, and proceeding from here to there are likewise non-existent and ultimately pure.
Increase and decrease are likewise unobservable, up to and including ultimate purity.
What is it that is unborn and thus unobservable?
It is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which is unborn and unobservable.

Why is this? The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is neither visible nor invisible; as it is invisible and there is nothing to be seen, so too from emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they are non-existent and invisible.
From internal and external emptiness up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence, there is nothing seen and nothing that can be seen.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are non-existent and cannot be seen.
From the stage of a srotāpanna up to the Buddha, there is nothing that exists and nothing that can be perceived.

From the path of a srotāpanna up to the path of a Buddha and the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is nothing that exists and nothing that can be perceived; there is nothing produced and nothing that can be perceived.
Reaching the state of non-existence, from that non-existence, non-existence cannot be seen.
Why is this? Subhūti!
That which is non-existent is invisible;
the first stage of abiding is also invisible.
Up to the tenth stage of abiding, that which is non-existent remains invisible.
It is non-existent and invisible, ultimately and eternally pure.

What are the stages? They are the stage of cessation and purity, the stage of the spiritual lineage, the eighth stage, the stage of vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of removing defilements, the stage where what was to be done has been done, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, the stage of the bodhisattva, and the stage of the buddha; even within internal and external emptiness, these are not perceived.
The first stage is invisible; from the emptiness of the internal and external up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence and the emptiness of non-attainability, it is thus.

The second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and even the tenth stages of abiding—from the emptiness of the internal and external up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence—up to the tenth stage of abiding, they too are invisible.
Why is this? Subhūti!
From the first stage to the tenth stage, they likewise do not exist and cannot be perceived; they are ultimately pure.
From the emptiness of the internal and external up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence, the purity of sentient beings is non-existent and ultimately pure.
From the emptiness of the internal and external up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence, the purity of the Buddha-land is non-existent and ultimately pure.
The emptiness of the internal and external, and the emptiness of existence and non-existence, as well as the five eyes, are non-existent and ultimately pure. Subhūti,
it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of non-reliance, causes all dharmas to emerge into omniscience (sarvajñatā) through the Mahāyāna.
The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Four;
The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Five.

Chapter 23: Praising the Vaipulya. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā, Chapter Twenty-three: Praising the Vaipulya. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Yes, World-Honored One!"
Mahāyāna, Mahāyāna—this Great Vehicle transcends all devas, worldly humans, and asuras.
This vehicle is equal to emptiness, like space itself; it provides protection and refuge for immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings. For this reason, World-Honored One!
It is for the sake of the Mahāyāna.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva likewise does not perceive a time of coming, nor a time of going, nor a place of abiding;
the Mahāyāna is thus, such that one does not perceive a beginning or an end, nor a middle.
“World-Honored One!
For this reason, the Mahāyāna is called that which has no equal and is without peer; therefore it is named ‘Mahāyāna.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is, so it is, Subhūti! The Mahāyāna is precisely these six pāramitās."

Furthermore, there is the Mahāyāna, namely the various gates of dhāraṇī and the various gates of samādhi, from the Śūraṅgama-samādhi up to the space-limit liberation and the non-attached samādhi; this is the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Subhūti! Furthermore, there is the Mahāyāna: from internal and external emptiness up to the emptiness of non-existence; this is the Mahāyāna, and furthermore, there is the Mahāyāna.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha constitute the Mahāyāna of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
As Subhūti has said, the Mahāyāna transcends all devas, asuras, and the people of the world.
Subhūti! Suppose that everything contained within the desire realm were truly existent, not different from reality, not inverted, permanent, solid, and unchanging—not being empty phenomena.
If that were the case, the Mahāyāna would likewise be unable to surpass the gods, nāgas, asuras, and the people of the world. Subhūti!

One should know that when the kalpa of the desire realm is consumed by fire at its end, all things therein are utterly exhausted; they are impermanent, lacking strength, and devoid of any solid essence.
For this reason, the Mahāyāna transcends the world of humans, devas, and asuras.
If the realm of form (rūpadhātu) were also eternal and possessed of permanent solidity, then even the Mahāyāna could not surpass it.
Because the realm of form is empty and impermanent, its solidity must likewise perish and it cannot endure for long; therefore, the Mahāyāna transcends it.
It is likewise for the formless realm, wherein all things shall be extinguished.
Subhūti, if form were serene,
solid, permanent, true, and non-erroneous— were it a solid dharma— then the Mahāyāna would likewise be unable to surpass the gods, the asuras, and the people of the world.
Because form is impermanent, lacks strength and solidity, is not real, and is inverted, the Mahāyāna transcends it.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all likewise impermanent.

If the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena; and the twelve links of dependent origination were all tranquil, permanent, solid, firm, true, non-erroneous, and eternally secure, then the Mahāyāna could not surpass them.

However, because these dharmas and the twelve links of dependent origination are impermanent, without solidity, without strength, without firmness, without stability, untrue, and erroneous—being like the conflagration at the end of an eon and not being secure dharmas—the merit of the Mahāyāna surpasses that of all devas, nāgas, spirits, and the people of the world.
Subhūti! If there were anything existing within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), it would not be the Mahāyāna;
because the nature of phenomena is non-existent, it is the Mahāyāna.
If suchness, the limit of reality, and the inconceivable possessed an intrinsic nature or any substantial existence, they would not constitute the Mahāyāna;
because suchness, the limit of reality, and the inconceivable have no intrinsic nature and no substantial existence, they constitute the Mahāyāna.
Subhūti! If the six pāramitās possessed any intrinsic existence, they would not constitute the Mahāyāna;
because the six pāramitās are without intrinsic existence, they constitute the Mahāyāna, transcending all devas, nāgas, asuras, and the people of the world.
If the emptiness of the internal and external, as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence, possessed any substantiality, they would not constitute the Mahāyāna;

because the emptiness of the internal and external, as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence, are without any substantiality, they constitute the Mahāyāna, surpassing all devas, asuras, and the people of the world.
If the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha possessed any intrinsic existence, they would not constitute the Mahāyāna;

because the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen qualities of a Buddha are without intrinsic existence, they constitute the Mahāyāna, surpassing all devas, asuras, and the people of the world.

Subhūti! If the dharmas of the eight ranks—the dharma of the srotāpanna, the dharma of the sakṛdāgāmin, the dharma of the anāgāmin, the dharma of the arhat, the dharma of the pratyekabuddha, the dharma of the avaivartika bodhisattva, and the dharma of the Buddha—possessed any intrinsic existence, they would not constitute the Mahāyāna.

Because these dharmas of the eight ranks, from the srotāpanna up to the Buddha-dharma, are without intrinsic existence, they constitute the Mahāyāna, which transcends all devas, asuras, and the people of the world.

Subhūti! If the eight ranks—from the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, and the avaivartika bodhisattva, up to the Buddha—possessed anything whatsoever, it would not be the Mahāyāna.
Because these lineages, from the srotāpanna up to the Buddha, are without anything whatsoever, they constitute the Mahāyāna, which transcends all devas, asuras, and the people of the world.
Subhūti! If the devas, asuras, and the people of the world possessed anything, it would not be the Mahāyāna;
because the devas, asuras, and the people of the world possess nothing, it is the Mahāyāna that transcends them all.

Subhūti! If there were any Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, from the first production of the thought of awakening until sitting at the seat of Buddhahood, possessed anything whatsoever among all the things they might do during that interval, it would not be the Mahāyāna.

Because the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, from the first production of the thought of awakening until sitting at the seat of Buddhahood, possess nothing whatsoever, it is the Mahāyāna; it transcends all devas, asuras, and the people of the world.

Subhūti! If the vajra-wisdom of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva possessed any objective referent, the bodhisattva would not awaken to the traces of habitual tendencies and would not achieve sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).

Because vajra-wisdom is without objective referent, the bodhisattva awakens to the traces of habitual tendencies and achieves sarvajñatā; for this reason, they transcend all devas, asuras, and the people of the world.

Subhūti! If the thirty-two marks of a great man possessed by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha were substantial entities, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha would not be able to transcend all devas, asuras, and the people of the world; he would lack this majestic virtue, spiritual radiance, and towering brilliance.

Because these thirty-two marks are without substantiality, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses majestic virtue, spiritual radiance, and towering brilliance that surpasses all devas, asuras, and the people of the world.

Subhūti! If the light of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, possessed any substantiality, the light of the Tathāgata would not be able to pervade the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions.
Subhūti! Because light is non-existent, it is able to universally illuminate lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Subhūti!
If the eight kinds of sound possessed any inherent existence, the voice of the Tathāgata would be unable to pervade the infinite lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

If the Buddha’s Wheel of Dharma possessed any inherent existence, the Tathāgata would be unable to turn that wheel—the wheel which no śramaṇas, brahmins, worldly people, devas, ghosts, spirits, nāgas, māras, or Brahmās have ever been able to turn.

Subhūti! If sentient beings possessed any inherent existence, the Tathāgata would be able to turn the wheel of Dharma for them, causing all sentient beings to attain parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder.

However, because sentient beings are not substantial entities and possess no inherent existence, it is for this reason that the Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma to enable them to attain nirvana; likewise, those who will come in the future shall also attain parinirvāṇa.
Chapter 24: The Chapter on the Great Vehicle Being Equal to Emptiness. In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Twenty-Four: The Great Vehicle Being Equal to Emptiness. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
"As you have said, the Great Vehicle is equal to emptiness."
So it is, so it is! Reality is equal to emptiness.
It is like space, which cannot be known as east, nor known as west, nor known as south, nor known as north, nor known as the four intermediate directions or above and below.
Subhūti! This Great Vehicle of the Tathāgata likewise has no east, west, south, or north, nor does it have the four intermediate directions, above, or below. Subhūti!
For example, space is neither long nor short, neither square nor round;
the Mahāyāna of the Tathāgata is likewise.
For example, space is neither blue nor yellow, neither red nor white, nor is it crimson or pale green.
The Mahāyāna of the Tathāgata is also like this. Therefore, Subhūti,
because the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness, it is called the Mahāyāna.
For example, space does not belong to the past, nor will it belong to the future, nor does it exist in the present;
the Mahāyāna of the Tathāgata is likewise: the Mahāyāna is equal to space.
For example, space is neither long nor large, neither increasing nor decreasing.
The Mahāyāna of the Tathāgata is also like this; therefore, the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
Subhūti, it is, for example, like space, which neither clings nor is severed.
The Mahāyāna of the Tathāgata is also like this.
It is, for example, like space: neither arising nor ceasing, neither abiding nor differing; therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna, which is equal to space.
For example, just as space is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and neither speaks nor utters words;
so too is the Mahāyāna—neither speaking nor characterized by wholesome or unwholesome evil. Therefore, the Mahāyāna is equal to space.
Subhūti! For example, just as space is neither seen nor heard, neither exists nor is cognized;
so too the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) is neither heard nor seen, neither exists nor is cognized. Therefore, the Great Vehicle is equal to space.
Subhūti! For example, space does not think, nor does it perceive; it does not realize, nor does it abandon, nor does it recollect.
The Great Vehicle is also like this.
For example, just as space is neither a dharma of lust nor a dharma of non-lust, so too is the Mahāyāna, Subhūti.
For example, just as space belongs neither to the realm of desire, nor to the realm of form, nor to the formless realm;
so too is the Mahāyāna: it does not belong to the three realms. Therefore, the Mahāyāna is equal to space.
For example, just as space neither initiates the first thought [of awakening], nor possesses the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, or tenth thought of dwelling;
so too is the Mahāyāna: it lacks even the thought of the ten dwellings. Therefore, the Mahāyāna is equal to space.
For example, in empty space there is neither the path of a srotāpanna, nor the path of a sakṛdāgāmin, nor the path of an anāgāmin, nor the path of an arhat;
the Mahāyāna is likewise thus. Therefore, the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
Subhūti! For example, just as space is neither the stage of a śrāvaka, nor the stage of a pratyekabuddha, nor the stage of an anuttarasamyaksambuddha;
so too is the Mahāyāna. Therefore, the Mahāyāna is equal to space.
For example, space is neither form nor color, yet it is not non-form and non-color; it is neither obstructive, yet it is not non-obstructive; it is neither responsive, yet it is not non-responsive.
The Mahāyāna is likewise: therefore, the Mahāyāna is equal to space.
Subhūti! For example, just as space is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither suffering nor happiness, neither self nor non-self;
so too is the Mahāyāna. Therefore, the Mahāyāna is equal to space.
For example, space is neither empty nor non-empty, neither characterized by marks nor non-characterized by marks, and neither a wish nor non-wish;
the Mahāyāna is likewise. Therefore, the Mahāyāna is equal to space.
Subhūti! For example, just as space is neither extinguished nor purified, neither non-extinguished nor non-purified, neither quiescent nor non-quiescent;
so too is the Mahāyāna. Therefore, the Mahāyāna is equal to space.
Subhūti, just as space is neither bright nor dark,
so too is the Mahāyāna. Subhūti!
For example, just as space is neither visible nor invisible, so too is the Mahāyāna;
therefore, the Mahāyāna is equal to space.
For example, just as space neither moves nor does not move, so too is the Mahāyāna.
The *vaipulya* is also like this; therefore, the *vaipulya* is equal to emptiness.
For this reason, Subhūti, the Mahāyāna is equal to emptiness.
As Subhūti has said, just as empty space covers and protects incalculable asaṃkhyeya beings,
so too is the Mahāyāna, Subhūti!
Sentient beings have no beginning; space also has no beginning.
Since space has no beginning, the Mahāyāna likewise has no beginning.
One should form this thought and one should know this.
Subhūti! For this reason, incalculable and asaṃkhyeya people look up to the Mahāyāna. Why is that?
Subhūti! Because sentient beings, the Mahāyāna, and empty space are all equally non-existent.
Sentient beings have no limit, empty space has no limit, and the Mahāyāna is likewise immeasurable.
Therefore, Subhūti, immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings aspire to the Mahāyāna. Subhūti!
Space, the Mahāyāna, and sentient beings are all equally unobservable. Subhūti,
just as sentient beings are limitless, so too is space limitless.
One should know this: the Mahāyāna is likewise without limit.
Sentient beings have no beginning, and the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) likewise has no beginning;
as the nature of phenomena has no beginning, so too space has no beginning.
Just as space has no beginning, the Mahāyāna also has no beginning;
just as the Mahāyāna has no beginning, the immeasurable and the limitless likewise have no beginning.
Just as the infinite has no beginning, so too the incalculable has no beginning.
For this reason, Subhūti, one cannot calculate the number of sentient beings who aspire to the Mahāyāna.

Why is this? Because sentient beings, the nature of phenomena, space, the Mahāyāna, the incalculable (asaṃkhyeya), the immeasurable (apramāṇa), and the uncountable (agaṇeya) are all ultimately unapprehendable.
Subhūti! Just as sentient beings have no beginning, you should know that the Tathāgata likewise has no beginning;
just as the Buddha has no beginning, empty space likewise has no beginning.
Just as space has no beginning, one should know that the Mahāyāna also has no beginning;
just as the Mahāyāna has no beginning, the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) has no beginning;
just as the incalculable has no beginning, one should know that the immeasurable and the limitless also have no beginning.
Just as the infinite has no beginning, one should know that all sentient beings likewise have no beginning. Thus, Subhūti,
incalculable asaṃkhyeya persons all rely upon the Mahāyāna.

Why is this? Because sentient beings, Buddhas, empty space, the Mahāyāna, the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*), and the limitless—all phenomena (*sarvadharma*)—are entirely invisible.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! From the series of the self up to the series of knowledge and vision, and the series of the limit of reality—just as with the series of the limit of reality, so should one understand the series of all phenomena."
Therefore, Subhūti, countless asaṃkhyeya people all look up to the Mahāyāna. Why is this?
Sentient beings and all phenomena are both invisible.

Subhūti! Just as the self, sentient beings, lineages, knowledge, and vision are inconceivable in essence, one should know that the lineages of the five aggregates and the lineages of all phenomena are likewise inconceivable.
Subhūti! Incalculable asaṃkhyeya people aspire to the Mahāyāna. Why is this?
This is because what is called "self" and all phenomena are all unobservable.
Subhūti! Just as there is no continuity to the self and no continuity to knowledge and vision, so too the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind have no continuity.
Just as the six sense faculties have no beginning, one should know that all dharmas likewise have no beginning. Thus, Subhūti,
incalculable asaṃkhyeya beings all rely upon the Mahāyāna.
Why is this? Because both the self and all phenomena are ultimately unobservable. Subhūti!
Just as the self has no continuity and knowledge and vision likewise have no continuity, one should understand that the six pāramitās also have no continuity.
Just as the prajñāpāramitā has no continuity, one should know that all dharmas likewise have no continuity.
Subhūti! For this reason, countless asaṃkhyeya people all look up to the Mahāyāna. Why is that?
"Subhūti, both the self and all phenomena are invisible.
Because the self has no basis, it is empty internally and externally; and because it is without basis, even the emptiness of existence and non-existence is likewise without basis."
Just as existence and non-existence are empty and without beginning, so too are all phenomena without beginning.
For this reason, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings all look toward the Mahāyāna.
Why is this? Because both the self and all phenomena are unobservable. Subhūti!
The self, sentient beings, and knowledge and vision have no beginning; likewise, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha also have no beginning.
Subhūti, just as the eighteen unique qualities have no beginning, so it is with these.
Therefore, one cannot calculate the number of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) persons who aspire to the Mahāyāna. Why is this?
Because neither the self nor any phenomena (*dharma*) can be perceived.
Subhūti! The self has no beginning;
since the spiritual lineage has already been discerned and all dharmas have no beginning, one cannot calculate the number of sentient beings who aspire to the Mahāyāna.
Why is this? Subhūti, both the self and all phenomena are entirely invisible.

The stream-enterer has no beginning; likewise, the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, the pratyekabuddha, and so on up to the Buddha’s omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and all dharmas, have no beginning.
For this reason, all sentient beings look toward the Mahāyāna. Why is this?
Because neither the self nor any phenomena can be perceived.
Just as the nature of nirvāṇa provides protection for all sentient beings, so too does the Mahāyāna provide protection for all sentient beings.
Subhūti! That which is called the Mahāyāna is neither seen to come, nor is it seen to go, nor is it seen to abide. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are immovable;
all dharmas neither go nor come, nor do they have any place of abiding. Why is this?

The nature of the five aggregates, the characteristics of the five aggregates, the entities of the five aggregates, and the suchness of the five aggregates neither come, nor go, nor have they any place of abiding.

The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and form, sound, smell, taste, tangibles, mental objects, their natures, their suchness, their entities, and their characteristics—these also neither come, nor go, nor have they any place of abiding.

The four great elements—nature, suchness, substance, and characteristic—are empty of the nature of consciousness; their suchness, substance, and characteristics neither come, nor go, nor have they any place of abiding.
Suchness, the limit of reality, and the inconceivable nature likewise neither come, nor go, nor have any place of abiding.
The nature, suchness, substance, and characteristics of the six perfections likewise neither come, nor go, nor have any place of abiding.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen dharmas—whether by way of their nature, suchness, activity, or characteristics—neither come nor go, nor do they have any place of abiding.
The Way and the Buddha—whether in their nature, suchness, substance, or characteristics—neither come nor go, nor do they have a place of abiding.
Whether conditioned or unconditioned—whether in their nature, suchness, substance, or characteristics—they neither come nor go, nor do they have a place of abiding.

Subhūti! As you have said, because the Mahāyāna is not seen in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, or above and below, it is called equal to the three periods of time; for this reason, it is the Mahāyāna.
Subhūti! What you have said is precise and without error. Why is this?

The past world is empty of being a world; the future world is empty of being a world; the present world is empty of being a world. The equality of the three worlds is emptiness; the Mahāyāna is empty of itself; the Bodhisattva is empty of himself.
Subhūti! Emptiness is neither a number, nor is it many, nor is it few.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and the Mahāyāna are equal to the three periods of time; they are neither paired nor solitary. They are without lust, anger, and delusion, yet they are not separate from lust, anger, and delusion. They are neither resentful nor visible; good and evil are also invisible. Permanence and impermanence, as well as the self (*ātman*), are also invisible. Suffering and happiness, self and non-self, are also invisible. The triple world (*traidhātuka*) is also invisible, and the transcendence of the triple world is also invisible.
Why is this? Because its form and activities cannot be perceived.
Past form is empty of past form; future form is empty of future form; present form is empty of present form. The same applies to sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

The emptiness of form in the past is invisible; the emptiness of that emptiness in the past is invisible. Even the emptiness of form within the five aggregates of the present is still invisible; how much more so could the emptiness of the five aggregates of the past or the future ever be seen?
Emptiness does not perceive the five aggregates, nor do the five aggregates perceive emptiness.
If emptiness were able to perceive the five aggregates, then the five aggregates would likewise perceive emptiness.
Subhūti! The six pāramitās of the past are not perceived; the six pāramitās of the future are not perceived; and the six pāramitās of the present are also not perceived.

In the equality of the three periods of time, one does not perceive the six *pāramitās*, nor does one perceive that equality; furthermore, one does not perceive the equality of the equality of the three periods of time.

Because equality does not perceive equality, the three periods of time are not perceived; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of the past, future, and present are also not perceived, and the equality of the three periods of time is likewise not perceived.
Subhūti! Even these are not perceived;

the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are likewise not seen in the past, future, or present. They cannot be seen within the three periods of time, nor can the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities be seen within those three periods. How much less could they be seen as something existing equally throughout the three periods?

"Furthermore, Subhūti, ordinary persons of the past, ordinary persons of the future, and ordinary persons of the present are likewise unobservable; even ordinary persons as equal across the three times are unobservable."
Why is this? Because sentient beings are fundamentally unobservable.

Disciples, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present are likewise unobservable; for disciples, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas of the three times, as well as sentient beings, are fundamentally unobservable.
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells within the perfection of wisdom, they shall comprehend the matters of the three periods of time and shall fulfill all-knowledge (sarvajñatā).
This is the Mahāyāna training in the equality of the three periods of time for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have already established themselves therein, they transcend all devas, asuras, and the people of the world, and emerge into sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “Excellent, excellent,
World-Honored One!”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas train in the Mahāyāna and thereby personally attain the fulfillment of sarvajñā-jñāna (all-knowing wisdom).

All bodhisattvas of the ten directions in the past attained and reached sarvajñā-jñāna through this Mahāyāna; all bodhisattvas of the ten directions in the future shall likewise train in this Mahāyāna and attain and reach sarvajñā-jñāna; and all the innumerable and incalculable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the ten directions in the present also attain the fulfillment of sarvajñā-jñāna through this Mahāyāna.
For this reason, it is called the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s Mahāyāna.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is! Subhūti!”
All Buddhas of the past, future, and present shall all achieve *sarvajñā* by training within this Mahāyāna.
Those who have already attained it, those who have not yet attained it, and those who are about to attain it—all shall fully perfect the wisdom of *sarvajñā* by training within this Mahāyāna.
Chapter 25: The Chapter on the Compendium of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā. At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!”
“World-Honored One, why does the World-Honored One cause Subhūti to speak the Prajñāpāramitā, and thereby expound the Mahāyāna teaching?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Yes, World-Honored One!”
“Subhūti, in teaching the Mahāyāna, will he not be departing from the Prajñāpāramitā? The Buddha said, “No.”
Subhūti! What you have spoken regarding the teaching of the Mahāyāna conforms to, does not contradict, and does not deviate from the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?

Subhūti! All the various wholesome dharmas that exist, including those of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, up to and including the Buddha-dharma, are all collectively gathered within the Prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One,
how is it that wholesome dharmas, as well as the dharmas of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas, are all collectively contained within the Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“Subhūti, that which is called the six pāramitās, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, the noble eightfold path, the three gates of liberation, the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom, great loving-kindness and great compassion, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities—these are dharmas free from expectation, practiced with constant equanimity.”
These are the wholesome dharmas.

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the dharmas of the śrāvakas, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, and the dharmas of the buddhas—all these are gathered together within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Subhūti! That which is called the Mahāyāna consists of the six pāramitās, the five aggregates (skandhas), the twelve bases (āyatanas),

the eighteen elements (dhātus), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the three gates of liberation, and wholesome dharmas with outflows (sāsrava).
The Dharma; conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena; the phenomena of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;
the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm; internal emptiness, external emptiness, the emptiness of all things, and the emptiness of non-existence;
the various gates of samādhi and the gates of dhāraṇī; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—such as these are the [teachings] of the Tathāgata.
In teaching the Dharma and the Vinaya, he speaks of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the inconceivable nature, and *nirvāṇa*.
All phenomena are neither joined nor dispersed; they have no form and are invisible;
they possess no resistance and are of a single characteristic. This "single characteristic" is what is called the absence of characteristics.
For this reason, Subhūti, what you have taught regarding the Mahāyāna doctrine is in accord with the Prajñāpāramitā; their meanings are consistent and do not contradict one another.

Why is this? Because the Mahāyāna is neither distinct nor different from the Prajñāpāramitā; likewise, the Mahāyāna is not distinct from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to the eighteen unique attributes of a Buddha.
The Mahāyāna is the Buddha-dharma, and the Buddha-dharma is the Mahāyāna; these two things are one and not two, nor are they mutually contradictory. Subhūti!
"For this reason, it is said that to teach the Mahāyāna is to teach the Prajñāpāramitā.

Chapter 26: The Non-apprehensibility of the Three Periods of Time The Mahāprajñāpāramitā, Chapter Twenty-Six: The Non-apprehensibility of the Three Periods of Time Thereupon, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have no beginning, no end, and no bottom; likewise, form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have no beginning and no end."
One should know that it is the same for the bodhisattva.
If one asks whether form is the bodhisattva,
the answer is no.
"Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness the Bodhisattva? "No. Subhūti said:
“Bhagavān! Throughout all time, I do not see any bodhisattva at all; for whom, then, should I speak the Prajñāpāramitā?
To whom should I teach it?”
Subhūti said: "That which is called 'bodhisattva,' O World-Honored One, is merely a name."
For example, it is like saying:
"I. Phenomena that exist or do not exist do not arise.
"How is it that form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not arise?
World-Honored One!
That which does not arise is neither form, nor sensation, perception, mental formations, nor consciousness."
Since there is ultimately nothing that arises, for whom should one preach the Prajñāpāramitā?

Yet, without departing from the locus of arising, when one sees a bodhisattva practicing the path and making such a statement, if the bodhisattva hears this and is neither afraid nor terrified, neither regretful nor cowed, this is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "If it is the case that the prior limit,
the posterior limit, and the middle limit of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended,
for what reason is this so?"
Form and the bodhisattva are both without limit.
How can it be that form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not the bodhisattva?
Why do you say that nowhere at all is a bodhisattva to be seen, and for whom, then, should the *prajñāpāramitā* be taught?
For what reason is it said that a bodhisattva is merely a name?
For what reason is it said that the dharma of existence and non-existence does not arise, yet the five aggregates do arise?
For what reason is it said that that which does not arise is not the five aggregates?
If all things are unarisen, whom should one teach when speaking of the *prajñāpāramitā*?
Why do you say that no one is seen who departs from birth to practice the bodhisattva path?
For what reason do you say that for a bodhisattva to hear this without fear or terror constitutes practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*?
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
“Because the beginning, end, and intermediate stages of sentient beings cannot be apprehended, the prior, subsequent, and middle limits of a bodhisattva cannot be seen.”
Śāriputra! Because sentient beings are empty, the initial point of the bodhisattva cannot be perceived.
Because sentient beings are quiescent, the initial point of the bodhisattva cannot be perceived.

Because the five aggregates are without limit, because the five aggregates are empty, because the five aggregates are quiescent, and because the five aggregates are not real, the starting point of the bodhisattva cannot be perceived; this is because the six pāramitās are bottomless and without limit.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
Emptiness, the five aggregates, and the bodhisattva are without distinction; these three things are one, and there are not two.
Therefore, Śāriputra, the starting point of a bodhisattva cannot be perceived.
Because the six pāramitās are empty, quiescent, and not real, the starting point of a bodhisattva cannot be perceived.

Why is this? Śāriputra, the original limit of emptiness cannot be seen; its final limit cannot be seen; its middle limit cannot be seen; and emptiness together with the bodhisattva cannot be seen either.
Śāriputra! Emptiness and the starting point of the bodhisattva are one and the same; there are not two. Therefore, the starting point of the bodhisattva cannot be seen.
The limits of internal emptiness, external emptiness, and the emptiness of existence and non-existence cannot be seen; therefore, the starting point of the bodhisattva cannot be perceived.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are all without beginning or end; the Buddha-dharma is empty, the Buddha-dharma is quiescent, and the Buddha-dharma is not real. For this reason, the beginning or end of a bodhisattva cannot be perceived."

From the six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, all are without beginning or end, all are empty, all are quiescent, and all are unreal; therefore, the beginning or end of a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended nor seen.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, all the gates of samādhi and the gates of dhāraṇī are entirely without beginning, entirely empty, entirely quiescent, and entirely unreal; therefore, the beginning of a bodhisattva cannot be perceived."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), suchness (tathatā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), and the inconceivable nature are all without beginning or end; they are empty, quiescent, and not real. For this reason, the beginning or end of a bodhisattva cannot be perceived."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and tathāgatas are all without beginning, all empty, all quiescent, and all unreal; therefore, the beginning of a bodhisattva cannot be perceived."
The Path and *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) are both without beginning, all empty, all quiescent, and all unreal; therefore, the beginning of a bodhisattva cannot be perceived.
Why is this? Śāriputra, because the beginning,
end, commencement, middle, and extremity of emptiness are all unobservable, the bodhisattva is likewise unobservable.
Śāriputra! Emptiness, the five aggregates, and the bodhisattva—these three things are all one; there are no two distinct dharmas. Therefore, the starting point of the bodhisattva cannot be seen.
"As Śāriputra has asked, because the five aggregates have no bottom, one should know that the bodhisattva likewise has no bottom. Subhūti said:
"The five aggregates are like space; space is also boundless, limitless, immeasurable, and without bottom—it is merely designated by the name 'space'."
Śāriputra! Form is empty and has no limit; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty and have no limit, nor can they be perceived. Therefore, Śāriputra!
The bottom of space, the bottom of the five aggregates, and the bottom of the bodhisattva cannot be perceived.

The twelve bases, the twelve links of dependent origination, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—all these dharmas, as well as the very source of the bodhisattva—cannot be perceived, for they all lack any limit or boundary.
Subhūti said, “Śāriputra, regarding what you have asked:
are the five aggregates the bodhisattva?”
It cannot be seen; it is neither bounded nor limited, it is immeasurable and bottomless, existing as space only by way of name.
Śāriputra! Form is empty and has no limit; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty and have no limit, nor can they be perceived. Therefore, Śāriputra!
The bottom of space, the bottom of the five aggregates, and the bottom of the bodhisattva cannot be perceived.

The twelve bases, the twelve links of dependent origination, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—all these dharmas, as well as the starting point of the bodhisattva—cannot be perceived, for they are all without limit.
Subhūti said: "Regarding what Śāriputra has asked—whether the five aggregates are the bodhisattva—they cannot be apprehended;
therefore, both the five aggregates and the bodhisattva are unapprehendable."

Śāriputra! The six pāramitās are empty of the six pāramitās themselves; internal and external emptiness is empty of internal and external emptiness itself; and so on, up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence, which is empty of the emptiness of existence and non-existence itself. The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are empty of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment themselves; and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, which are empty of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha themselves. Suchness, the limit of reality, the inconceivable nature, the dhāraṇīs, the gates of samādhi, omniscience (sarvajñatā), the matters of the Path, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the meaning of a Buddha—all these are each and every one empty of themselves.
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata’s five aggregates are empty; they neither exist nor can they be seen.
For this reason, Śāriputra, the bodhisattva’s five aggregates cannot be apprehended or seen.
As Śāriputra has asked: for what reason is the bodhisattva invisible and unobtainable; and for whom, then, should the Prajñāpāramitā be taught?
Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
“Form does not perceive form;
form also does not perceive sensation, and sensation also does not perceive form.”
Feeling is not seen in formations, nor are formations seen in feeling;
feeling is not seen in perception, nor is perception seen in feeling;
perception is not seen in consciousness, nor is consciousness seen in perception.
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
The eye is neither existent nor visible; this continues up to the mind, which is neither existent nor visible.

Eye-consciousness and mind-consciousness are also neither existent nor visible. From the eye-fetter up to the mind-fetter, and from the conditions of dependent origination, they are also neither existent nor visible.
Even the six pāramitās neither exist nor can they be seen.

From internal emptiness and external emptiness up to the emptiness of all things and the emptiness of non-existence, as well as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, these too neither exist nor can they be seen;
the various gates of samādhi and the gates of dhāraṇī likewise neither exist nor can they be perceived.
From the dharma of the *srotāpanna* up to the dharma of the *arhat*, they neither exist nor can they be perceived;
the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) also neither exist nor can they be perceived;
the dharmas of the Path and the dharma of *sarvajñatā* likewise neither exist nor can they be perceived.
From the stream-enterer up to the arhat, pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha—these do not exist and cannot be seen;
even the teachings of the Dharma do not exist and cannot be seen.
Śāriputra! Because all dharmas are non-existent and invisible, the bodhisattva is invisible.
For this reason, there is nothing to be taught.
Subhūti said to Śāriputra: "Regarding what you have asked, as to why one is called a 'bodhisattva' by means of a mere designation:
the dharma of designation is merely a provisional name and a conventional appellation for a bodhisattva; for this reason, one is called a 'bodhisattva' by means of a mere designation."

Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise merely provisional designations and names; those things that have names are themselves devoid of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Why is this? Because emptiness has no true name.
If that which is empty were not the bodhisattva, then it would be said that the bodhisattva exists merely as a name.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the six pāramitās are merely names; the six pāramitās are not the names, nor are the names the six pāramitās."
Why is this? Because the name, the bodhisattva, and the various pāramitās are all equal and cannot be perceived.
Therefore, a bodhisattva possesses only a provisional designation as a name.
Śāriputra! Inner and outer emptiness, as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence, are likewise merely attachments to names.
Names are not empty, and emptiness is not a name.
Why is this? Because letters are empty, and from internal and external emptiness up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence, none of them can be perceived. Śāriputra!
Therefore, it is merely by means of words that one is called a "bodhisattva. Śāriputra,
from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, these too are merely provisional names and designations.
The various gates of samādhi and the gates of dhāraṇī are likewise so;
even up to sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), it is universally thus and thus.
As for what Śāriputra asked—why is it called "self" when, from its very root, there is nothing that arises?
From the very beginning until the point of the "self," it cannot be perceived; how then could it arise?
From birth and life up to cognition and vision, these are constantly imperceptible; how then could they arise?
Since the beginning of having names, the five aggregates have been invisible and unknowable; how then could they arise?
From the six sense bases up to the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination, these likewise cannot be seen.
How much more so for that which has arisen?
Even the six *pāramitās* cannot be seen; how much more so for that which has arisen?
From inner and outer emptiness up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence, they are eternally unseeable; how much more so for that which has arisen?
Since the time of "having a name," the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen dharmas are also invisible; from what, then, could they arise?
Since the time of "having a name," the various gates of samādhi and the gates of dhāraṇī are also invisible; from what, then, could they arise?
Since the beginning of designation, even śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas cannot be perceived; from what, then, could they arise? Śāriputra!
For this reason, it is called "self," because all dharmas are non-arising.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, regarding the matter of whether all phenomena exist or do not exist as you have asked,
there is no agent. Śāriputra then asked Subhūti:
“What is it that has no agent? Subhūti replied: “The five aggregates have no agent.”
From the six sense-faculties and their internal and external objects up to all that exists within the twelve links of dependent origination, there is likewise no agent;
and as for all that exists within the six pāramitās, there is likewise no agent.
For this reason, Śāriputra, all dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent. Furthermore, Śāriputra:
"All dharmas are entirely impermanent; there is nothing that can destroy them.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "Which dharmas are such that they have no permanence and nothing can destroy them?"
He replied: "The five aggregates have no permanence, yet there is nothing that can destroy them. Why is this?
Because they are impermanent, non-existent, and subject to exhaustion; therefore, all phenomena are impermanent, and there is nothing that can destroy them."

Even conditioned phenomena, unconditioned phenomena, tainted phenomena, untainted phenomena, determined phenomena, and undetermined phenomena are impermanent, and there is nothing capable of destroying them.
Śāriputra! Impermanence is non-existent and subject to exhaustion; for this reason, all phenomena are impermanent, and there is nothing capable of destroying them. Śāriputra!
"All dharmas are neither gathered nor dispersed.
Śāriputra asked, "What is it that is not gathered? What is it that is not dispersed?"
Subhūti said: “The five aggregates neither aggregate nor disperse. Why is this?”
Its nature is thus.
Even so, wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, and outflowing and non-outflowing dharmas neither aggregate nor disperse.
Why is this? Because their nature is such.
For this reason, all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent.
Śāriputra! Regarding your question as to why the five aggregates are unarisen: it is because the five aggregates and the six sense-fields have no creator, for one does not perceive a creator.
All dharmas are devoid of an agent; for this reason, there is nothing that arises.

Śāriputra, as to your question regarding that which is unarisen being other than the five aggregates: because the nature of the five aggregates is itself empty, they neither arise, nor do they cease, nor do they abide.
Even up to the point that conditioned phenomena are empty of their own nature—since their nature is itself empty—they neither arise, nor cease, nor abide.
Therefore, there is nothing produced that is not the five aggregates.
Śāriputra! Regarding your question as to for whom the one who is unarisen (*anutpanna*) might preach the *prajñāpāramitā*: if there were no one who is unarisen, it would not be the *prajñāpāramitā*;
yet the *prajñāpāramitā* is also not something that is unarisen.
Non-arising and the Prajñāpāramitā are one dharma; there are not two. Therefore, it is asked: for whom should the Prajñāpāramitā be taught?

Śāriputra, as to what you have asked—namely, those who do not depart from the five aggregates while practicing the bodhisattva path—for them, non-arising is the Prajñāpāramitā, and the Prajñāpāramitā is non-arising.
That which is non-arising is the five aggregates; the five aggregates are non-arising. These dharmas are not distinct and are not dual.
Śāriputra, for this reason, one does not practice the bodhisattva path apart from arising.
Śāriputra! Regarding your question as to why one who hears this is neither terrified nor frightened is a practitioner of the *prajñāpāramitā*:

it is because the bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives all dharmas as empty—like a dream, like an illusion, like a mirage, like an echo, like a shadow, and like a magical transformation. For this reason, when the bodhisattva hears this teaching, they are neither terrified nor frightened.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“When a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* and performs this contemplation, at that time they do not perceive form (*rūpa*), nor do they enter into form, nor do they give rise to form, nor do they abide in form, nor do they say, ‘This is form.

Regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vijñāna*), they likewise do not perceive consciousness, nor do they enter into consciousness, nor do they give rise to consciousness, nor do they abide in consciousness, nor do they say, ‘This is consciousness.’”
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are neither seen, nor entered, nor produced, nor abiding, nor can they be said to be "mine."
The six pāramitās are neither seen, nor entered, nor produced, nor abided in, nor claimed as "mine.
From internal and external emptiness up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence, they are likewise neither seen, nor entered, nor produced, nor abided in, nor claimed as "mine."
“World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, they neither perceive them, nor enter them, nor give rise to them, nor abide in them, nor claim them as 'mine'.”
Regarding the various gates of samādhi and the gates of dhāraṇī, one neither perceives them, nor enters them, nor gives rise to them, nor dwells within them, nor claims them as "mine."
Why is this? When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive form, nor do they perceive anything up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
World-Honored One!

That which is not produced as form is non-form; likewise, that which is not produced as sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is non-consciousness; that which is not produced as the six sense-bases is non-six-sense-bases; and that which is not produced as the six perfections is non-six-perfections.
From the six pāramitās up to non-arising, there is but a single dharma without duality.

Non-arising is not "emptiness of the internal and external," for it is not emptiness; non-arising is not "emptiness of existence and non-existence," for it is not emptiness. Emptiness of existence and non-existence, as well as non-arising, are but a single dharma without duality.
World-Honored One!

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, being non-arising, are not [inherently] the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, being non-arising, are not [inherently] the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
That which is non-arising and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are a single dharma without duality.
World-Honored One!

There is not even a single dharma that arises; there are not two, nor three, nor four, nor five, nor any number at all. Therefore, the Buddha-dharma and the dharma of non-arising are a single dharma without duality.
"Bhagavan! If suchness and the inconceivable nature are non-arising, would they not then be non-suchness and non-inconceivable nature?

If the Path is non-arising, it would not be the Path; if omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is non-arising, it would not be omniscience. Yet there is no arising, and omniscience is a single dharma without duality."
World-Honored One!
That which is unarisen is neither one nor manifold.
Therefore, that which does not arise as *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is not *sarvajñatā*, and that which extinguishes form is not form.
The cessation of form is a single dharma and has no duality.
World-Honored One!
Cessation is one; it has no duality.

Therefore, that which extinguishes form is non-form; that which extinguishes sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is non-consciousness. Thus, that which gives rise to consciousness is non-consciousness.

This applies likewise to internal emptiness, external emptiness, up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence, as well as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
“World-Honored One!
This is cessation; it is not manifold.
From consciousness up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), it is likewise so—this is practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*.”
Chapter 27: Inquiry into Contemplation. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Seven: Inquiry into Contemplation. Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the *prajñāpāramitā* while contemplating all dharmas?"
What is a bodhisattva?
What is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?
And what is contemplation?
The Venerable Subhūti said to Śāriputra:
"Regarding what you have asked, 'What is a bodhisattva?
a bodhisattva is one who is a seeker of the Way; therefore, he is called a bodhisattva."
"By means of the Way, one knows the affairs of all dharmas yet has no point of entry.
He asked: "What kind of affairs of all dharmas does one know?"

He replied: "One knows the matter of form, yet does not enter into form; one knows the matters of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, yet does not enter into consciousness; one fully knows the matters of the eighteen dharmas of a Buddha, yet does not enter into those eighteen dharmas."
Śāriputra asked: "What constitutes the affairs of all phenomena? Subhūti replied:

"That which can be named is the appearance of all phenomena: forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects; internal phenomena and external phenomena; conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena—their characteristics and appearances.
That which can be named constitutes the affairs of all phenomena."
Śāriputra! As to your question regarding what constitutes the prajñāpāramitā:
the prajñāpāramitā is called "detachment."
He asked: "For what reason is it called 'separation'? Subhūti replied:

"To be detached from the five aggregates, detached from the eighteen elements, detached from the six sense bases, detached from the *dānapāramitā* up to the *dhyānapāramitā*, detached from internal and external emptiness up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence, and detached from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to the eighteen unique qualities—this is called detachment."
"Venerable Śāriputra, it is because one is detached from omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and detached from the objects of omniscience that it is called 'detachment from the Prajñāpāramitā.'"
Śāriputra! Regarding your question as to what constitutes the practice of the Prajñāpāramitā:

a bodhisattva does not contemplate the five aggregates as being either permanent or impermanent; nor do they contemplate the five aggregates as being suffering or pleasure; nor do they contemplate the five aggregates as being self or non-self. They do not contemplate them as empty or non-empty, as characterized or non-characterized, as wishful or non-wishful, as extinguished or non-extinguished, or as tranquil or non-tranquil. This absence of such contemplations extends to the six pāramitās.
From the emptiness of the internal and external up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence, and likewise regarding the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, it is also thus.

Regarding the various gates of samādhi and dhāraṇī, up to sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), and even to cessation and non-cessation, one does not form the contemplation of them as being either permanent or impermanent.
“Śāriputra, a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should contemplate in this way.
Śāriputra then asked the Venerable Subhūti:
"For what reason, Venerable One, do you say:
'The five aggregates, being unarisen, are not the five aggregates; and so on, up to omniscience (sarvajñatā), being unarisen, is not omniscience'?"
Subhūti replied: “The five aggregates are empty;
emptiness is not the five aggregates. Therefore, that which is unarisen within the five aggregates is not the five aggregates.”

The six pāramitās are empty; emptiness is neither the six pāramitās nor something produced. Therefore, because the six pāramitās have nothing that is produced, they are not [inherently] the six pāramitās.
From the emptiness of the internal and external up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence, it is likewise;
from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, it is likewise;
and so too is *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).
For this reason, the five aggregates, being without anything produced, are not the five aggregates.
The five aggregates are likewise not produced, and so on up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), which is also without anything produced.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"For what reason do you say that 'the five aggregates are non-dual and thus not five aggregates,' and so on, up to 'omniscience (sarvajñatā) is non-dual and thus not omniscience'?"
Subhūti replied: “The five aggregates are non-dual;

they neither unite nor disperse. They have no form, are invisible, and possess a single characteristic. That which has a single characteristic is itself without characteristics. Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is also like this.”
"For this reason, the five aggregates have no duality, yet they are not 'not-five-aggregates'; omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) has no duality, yet it is not 'not-omniscience. Śāriputra asked:
"For what reason are the five aggregates reckoned as having no duality, and even up to omniscience being reckoned as having no duality?"
Subhūti said: “There is no duality between that which is unproduced and the five aggregates.
The five aggregates are themselves the unproduced, and the unproduced is itself the five aggregates.”
"For this reason, the five aggregates have no duality; they are merely designated as such by number.
Even up to *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), there is no duality; it is merely designated as such by number.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When a bodhisattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā and contemplates these dharmas, they see that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are unarisen and eternally pure;
they see that the self (*ātman*) is also unarisen and eternally pure; and they see that from the dānapāramitā up to the prajñāpāramitā, they too are unarisen and eternally pure;
they see [the emptinesses] from internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of existence..."
Because emptiness is unborn and eternally pure; because one sees that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are also unborn and eternally pure;
because one sees that all *dhāraṇīs* and gates of *samādhi* are also unborn and eternally pure;
because one sees that *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is unborn from anywhere and eternally pure; and because one sees ordinary persons as ordinary...
Because persons and dharmas are likewise unarisen and eternally pure, one perceives the srotāpanna and the dharma of the srotāpanna;
the sakṛdāgāmin and the dharma of the sakṛdāgāmin; the anāgāmin and the dharma of the anāgāmin; the arhat and the dharma of the arhat;
the pratyekabuddha and the dharma of the pratyekabuddha; one perceives the bodhisattva and the dharma of the bodhisattva; and one perceives the Buddha.
"The Buddha-dharma is entirely without arising, for it is eternally pure. Śāriputra asked:

"As I have heard from Subhūti, the five aggregates are without arising; even the Path is without arising, and the Buddha-dharma is likewise without arising, such that there is nothing to be attained."
From the srotāpanna up to the arhat and pratyekabuddha, there is likewise nothing attained; the bodhisattva has nothing to attain, and even sarvajñatā has nothing to be attained.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not grasp at anything as being "all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā), it is for the sake of destroying the five destinies; this is what is meant by a Bodhisattva not attaining the Way within the five destinies.

Śāriputra said: "If all dharmas are such that nothing is produced, how is it that a srotāpanna attains realization by contemplating the extinction of the three fetters; a sakṛdāgāmin attains realization by contemplating the thinning of the three impurities; an anāgāmin attains realization by contemplating the extinction of the five lower fetters; an arhat attains realization by contemplating the extinction of the five higher acquisitions; and a pratyekabuddha attains realization by contemplating the awakening through causes and conditions?"
For what reason do Bodhisattvas perform arduous practices and undergo toil on behalf of sentient beings?
For what purpose does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the one who has attained equal and perfect enlightenment, turn the wheel of Dharma?
Subhūti said: "Śāriputra!

I do not cause unarisen dharmas to be attained; nor do I cause the unarisen to attain the path of a srotāpanna, a sakṛdāgāmin, an anāgāmin, an arhat, or the path of a pratyekabuddha; nor do I cause a bodhisattva to engage in arduous practices, for in the practice of a bodhisattva there is no perception of arduousness."
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva likewise does not perceive the notion of suffering. Why is this?
Śāriputra! One cannot, by means of the perception of suffering, serve as a foundation for incalculable, asaṃkhyeya sentient beings.

For a bodhisattva toward sentient beings, there is no such thing as the perception of them as a father, the perception of them as a mother, the perception of them as a child, or the perception of them as one's own body.
Regarding internal and external phenomena, a bodhisattva should form this perception and maintain this reflection:
"That which is called 'self' and 'all sentient beings' neither exists nor can be perceived."
Regarding internal and external phenomena, one should form this reflection and maintain this contemplation without giving rise to thoughts of exertion or hardship.
Why is this? Because all things are non-existent.

The Blessed One is unarisen, and it is not within my power to cause him to arise; likewise, the Tathāgata’s *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is unarisen, and the Tathāgata does not turn the wheel of Dharma by means of that which is unarisen.
Śāriputra asked the Venerable Subhūti:
"Do you wish for them to attain it from that which is unarisen,
or do you wish for them to attain it from that which is arisen?"
Subhūti said: “I do not cause anyone to attain [enlightenment] from that which is unarisen, nor do I cause them to attain it from that which is arisen. Śāriputra said:
“As you have said, is it that there is nothing attained and nothing obtained? Subhūti replied:

“There is something attained and something obtained; yet there is no attainment or obtaining through dualistic worldly matters. It is only by means of worldly conventions that there are those who are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas.”
Regarding the discourse on the most supreme, there is no reaching and no attaining; from the stage of *srotāpanna* up to the Buddha, there is likewise neither reaching nor attaining.
“Subhūti, how is it? Is it only through worldly matters that there is attainment and acquisition?
Is it likewise for one who destroys the five destinies?”
Subhūti said: "It is by way of worldly convention that there is attainment and acquisition; it is by way of worldly convention that there is the teaching of the five destinies. Why is this?"
“Śāriputra! The foremost Dharma is without birth and death, without the retribution of good or evil, and is neither severed nor attached. Śāriputra said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is there anything produced from that which is unproduced?
Or is there anything produced from that which is produced?"
Subhūti replied: "I do not cause that which is unarisen to arise, nor do I cause that which is already arisen to arise."
Śāriputra said: "For what purpose would one wish for that which is a non-arisen dharma to have an arising? Subhūti replied:
“I do not cause the five aggregates to arise through existence, non-existence, or emptiness; nor do I cause even the Path to arise through existence, non-existence, or emptiness.
Śāriputra asked: “Is non-arising itself arising?”
"Is arising arising? Subhūti replied,
"Arising is not arising, and non-arising is also not arising."

Why is this? All that can arise and all that does not arise are one and the same; they are not distinct, nor do they have form. They are invisible, ungraspable, and possess a single characteristic. That which is a single characteristic is the very nature of non-existence.
"Therefore, Śāriputra, that which has arisen does not arise, and that which has not arisen also does not arise. Śāriputra said:
"When you speak of the non-arising of that which is unarisen, and speak of the arising and non-arising of that which has arisen,
I wish to hear it. Subhūti said:
"Do as you please. Why is this? Śāriputra!..."
Regarding the dharmas that are non-arisen and the dharmas that are arisen, there is nothing to be delighted in.

That which is asked about—non-arising and the absence of arising—is such that all these dharmas neither conjoin nor disperse; they are formless, invisible, ungraspable, and of a single characteristic. This single characteristic is, in fact, the absence of characteristics.

Śāriputra said: "That which is produced is likewise non-produced; that which is delighted in is likewise non-produced; dharmas are likewise non-produced; and that which is retributed is likewise non-produced."
"So it is, so it is! Śāriputra, all dharmas are entirely without arising."

Why is this? The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are unproduced; the six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are also unproduced. The six elements—earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness (*ṣaddhātu*)—these six elements are also unproduced. The activities of body, speech, and mind are also unproduced, up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), which is also unproduced.
Therefore, Śāriputra, that which is reported is also a dharma that is unarisen;
all that is heard through causes and conditions is likewise unarisen.
Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti is the foremost among these Dharma-preachers. Why is this?"
He is able to provide answers to whatever questions are asked. Why is this?
Because he has no dependence upon any phenomena.
Śāriputra asked the Elder Subhūti:
"In what way are all dharmas without support? He replied:
“Śāriputra, the nature of form is empty; it does not rely on the internal, nor does it rely on the external, nor does it rely on that which is between the two.

The natures of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty; they do not rely on the internal, nor do they rely on the external, nor do they rely on that which is between the two.”
The six sense-faculties and the eighteen elements are empty of intrinsic nature, and they do not rely upon the internal, the external, or that which is between them.
The six perfections are empty of intrinsic nature, and they likewise do not rely upon the internal, the external, or that which is between them.
From internal and external emptiness up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence, they do not rely on the internal, the external, or the intermediate.

From the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, their nature is empty, and they likewise do not rely on the internal, the external, or the intermediate.
Śāriputra, that the nature of all phenomena is empty does not rely upon the internal, the external, or that which is between them;
therefore, it has no basis.
"Therefore, a bodhisattva practicing the six pāramitās is able to purify the five aggregates up to the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñatā). Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"How does a bodhisattva practicing the six pāramitās purify the bodhisattva path?"

He replied: "Śāriputra, there is both the supramundane dānapāramitā and the mundane dānapāramitā; this continues up to the prajñāpāramitā, which likewise has both a supramundane and a mundane aspect."
He asked again:
"What is the mundane perfection of giving (dānapāramitā)?
What is the supramundane perfection of giving?"

He replied: "A bodhisattva abides in generosity; if there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, or those who are poor, sick, or physically impaired, he gives them whatever they seek—be it a city or kingdom, precious jewels, clothing and bedding, food and drink, wife and children, kinsmen and retainers, or even his own head, eyes, flesh, muscles, marrow, brain, bones, and blood—giving all that he possesses."
Regarding those with whom one gives, there is a sense of dependence, and one forms this thought:
"I am the giver and they are the recipients; I do not envy others for their giving. It says:
"I am a donor," he said, "I give everything."
He said: "I follow the Buddha's teaching. He said:
"I am practicing the dānapāramitā.

Although he makes such a gift, he still has a basis for attachment; yet, he shares the merit of this practice toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* with all sentient beings, desiring by means of this giving to lead all sentient beings to enter parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Although one practices giving, there are three obstructive mentalities.
What are these three? They are:
the notion of a self, the notion of another, and the notion of giving.
These are the three hindrances.
This is mundane generosity. Why is it called mundane generosity?
Because it cannot transcend the mundane and does not go beyond mundane affairs, this is called mundane giving (*laukika-dāna*).
What is the giving of the Path (*mārga-dāna*)?
It is that which is purified by three factors.
What are these three?
When a bodhisattva practices giving, they do not perceive themselves as the giver, nor do they perceive a recipient, and they do not look for a reward;
this is the bodhisattva’s purity regarding these three matters.

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva practices giving and bestows it upon sentient beings, they do not rely on sentient beings for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor do they perceive any sign of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is the perfection of dāna-pāramitā of the Way.
For what reason is it called the *dāna-pāramitā* of the Path?
Because the *dāna-pāramitā* of the Path excels and surpasses that of the world.
From the *dāna-pāramitā* up to the *prajñā-pāramitā*, the mundane has something upon which it relies; the Path has nothing upon which it relies.
Subhūti said: "This is how a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās to purify the bodhisattva path. Śāriputra asked Subhūti:
"What is the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva? He replied: "The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva;

the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; internal and external emptiness up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence; the various gates of samādhi and the gates of dhāraṇī; the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom, and great loving-kindness and great compassion—these constitute the path of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva."
Śāriputra said: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"
“What is the power of the merit of which pāramitā?
Subhūti replied, “It is the power of the merit of the prajñāpāramitā.”
Why is this? The Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all wholesome dharmas and merits.
The Prajñāpāramitā fully sustains the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
All the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the past, practiced the Prajñāpāramitā and thereby attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi);
all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the future, will likewise practice the Prajñāpāramitā and thereby attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;

and all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones currently residing in the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, also practice the Prajñāpāramitā and thereby attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Subhūti said: "If, upon hearing the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not doubt or fear, it should be known that this bodhisattva is able to practice the bodhisattva path without abandoning sentient beings, is able to act as a protector for all sentient beings, and remains without attachment, never departing from this thought—namely, the thought of great loving-kindness and great compassion."
Śāriputra further [said], "Sentient beings will never be separated from this thought.
Subhūti praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent!"
Śāriputra! I have already become aware of the source from which this censure comes; I shall accept it.
Just as sentient beings do not exist, so too mindfulness does not exist; even existence and non-existence do not exist.
Just as sentient beings are quiescent, so too is mindfulness quiescent.
As sentient beings are empty, so too is mindfulness empty.
As sentient beings have nothing to perceive, so too does mindfulness have nothing to perceive.
As the five aggregates are non-existent, so too is mindfulness non-existent.
