Just as the five aggregates have no reality, just as the five aggregates are empty, just as the five aggregates are quiescent, and just as the five aggregates are without anything to be perceived, one should know that mindfulness likewise has nothing to be perceived.

The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena; earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are likewise empty. The six pāramitās are empty;

from internal and external emptiness up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; the gates of dhāraṇī and the various gates of samādhi; as well as omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and the activities of omniscience, down to the path and mindfulness—all these are non-existent.
Just as the Path has nothing to be awakened to, so too mindfulness has nothing to be awakened to.
Śāriputra, I desire that the bodhisattva not be separated from this practice of mindfulness.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!

To explain the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, it should be exactly as Subhūti has spoken. Just as Subhūti has expounded the *prajñāpāramitā* by receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, so too should the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas act in accordance with what Subhūti has said."

When Subhūti spoke this chapter on the Prajñāpāramitā, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways: it sank in the front and surged in the back; it surged in the front and sank in the back; and so it was throughout the eight directions, above, and below.
Because of this matter, the Buddha smiled.
At that time, Subhūti joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“For what reason do you smile?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Now as I speak this Prajñāpāramitā, immeasurable Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction are likewise speaking this Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of the bodhisattvas.”
The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions likewise teach the Prajñāpāramitā to the bodhisattvas in this very same way.
When Subhūti spoke this Prajñāpāramitā, twelve nayuta koṭis of devas, humans, and asuras all attained the patient endurance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
When the Buddhas of the ten directions preach the Prajñāpāramitā, incalculable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings all resolve to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
*The Sutra of the Radiant Prajñāpāramitā*, Fascicle Five;
*The Sutra of the Radiant Prajñā*, Fascicle Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Wu-luo-cha of Khotan during the Western Jin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Twenty-Eight: Non-Abiding. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, Chapter Twenty-Eight: Non-Abiding. At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings of the trichiliocosm, together with incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of devaputras, all came and assembled there.
Śakra-devānām-indra and countless hundreds of thousands of millions of devas all came together for this assembly;
from Suyāma-devaputra up to the Śuddhāvāsa devas, the various devas therein, each accompanied by countless hundreds of thousands of millions of devaputras, all came together for this assembly.
From the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens, the merit and radiance of all these devas are magnificent;
yet even so, they do not equal the radiance of the World-Honored One’s lowest light by a factor of hundreds of thousands of millions, billions, and trillions.
The radiance of the various devas and the brilliance of Jāmbūnada gold were both rendered invisible.
Standing beside the Buddha, the bodies and radiance of the devas appeared like burnt wicks; therefore, the light of the devas no longer manifested.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Venerable Subhūti:

"Now, the Four Heavenly Kings and the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa realm throughout this trichiliocosm wish to hear Subhūti expound the Prajñāpāramitā, teaching how a bodhisattva should abide in the Prajñāpāramitā."
"What is the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva?
How should one practice the prajñāpāramitā?
Subhūti replied to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:

“Kauśika! Now, relying upon the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, I shall expound the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of all bodhisattvas; I shall explain it to the bodhisattvas according to how they should abide.”
Those sons of the gods who have not yet resolved their minds should now resolve upon the mind of a bodhisattva.
Those who are already established in the restraints of the Path lack the power to give rise to the thought of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because they create obstructions and barriers within the realm of birth and death.
Even if such individuals were able to resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I would likewise rejoice on their behalf.
Ascending ever higher in honor, I shall never interrupt their merit midway.
Kauśika! What is the Prajñāpāramitā?

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should maintain a mind corresponding to sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) and should contemplate that form is impermanent, suffering, empty, and not-self; that it is a collection of aging, sickness, grief, affliction, and fetters; that it is subject to transformation and decay, fearful, contentious, and cannot be relied upon.
A bodhisattva should contemplate that these, too, are without any basis for reliance.
Regarding sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as the six sense organs and the six sense objects, one should contemplate them all as suffering.
Even regarding purity, one should remain without any basis for reliance.
One should contemplate the purity of the five aggregates; one should contemplate the purity and quiescence of the six sense organs and the six consciousnesses.

With the mind of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), one should know that from ignorance arises the habituation of craving, yet the twelve links of dependent origination are likewise without any basis for reliance.

Furthermore, one should contemplate the cessation of ignorance and craving, whereby the twelve links of dependent origination are extinguished, and all sufferings are likewise without any basis for reliance.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, with the mind of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), should contemplate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment without relying on them, and should likewise contemplate even up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha without relying on them."
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva, with the mind of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), practices the dānapāramitā, śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, and dhyānapāramitā, yet remains without any dependence."
Thus it is, Kauśika!
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they perform this contemplation so that phenomena succeed one another and phenomena attain one another, bringing them all to full completion.
The Bodhisattva is likewise without a self even in mindfulness; if one forms a divergent thought, it does not accord with the mindfulness of the Way.
Kausika! Because of an uneven state of mind, the Way cannot be seen and cannot be attained.
The Way has no intentionality; even the thought of intentionality cannot be apprehended nor can it be seen. Kauśika!
A bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā should contemplate in this way: there is nothing to be apprehended among all dharmas.
Śakra Devānām-indra said:
"Venerable Subhūti! In what way is the mind of recollection not identical with the mind of the Path?"
"How is it that the mind of the path is not identical to the mind of recollection?
How is it that both the mind of the path and the mind of recollection are unobtainable and cannot be perceived? Subhūti replied:

“Kauśika! That which is conceived by the mind does not constitute the mind; the mind of the Way (*mārga-citta*) is likewise neither mind nor constituted of mind, for it does not maintain what is non-mind.
To conceive of non-mind is for the mind to be non-mind, and non-mind is likewise the mind.”
"This is the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Thereupon, the Buddha praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
“Such is the intention with which you teach and encourage the bodhisattvas in the Prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Yes, World-Honored One!”
I must repay their kindness; I cannot fail to repay it.
I shall repay the kindness of the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as well as that of their disciples who exhorted, assisted, and established all the Bodhisattvas.
World-Honored One, at that time you also studied the six *pāramitās* and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
World-Honored One,
we too shall likewise exhort and assist all bodhisattvas to study the six *pāramitās*, and we shall also cause them to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti said: "Kauśika!
Listen as I explain how a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the suchness of the prajñāpāramitā: he dwells, yet he does not dwell."

The five aggregates are empty of the five aggregates; the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva. The emptiness of the five aggregates and the emptiness of the bodhisattva are one and the same emptiness;
there are not two.
Kauśika, a bodhisattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner.

Kauśika! The six sense-faculties are empty of the six sense-faculties; the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva. The emptiness of the six sense-faculties and the emptiness of the bodhisattva are equal and without distinction.
The six natures are empty of the six natures; the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva. The emptiness of the six natures and the emptiness of the bodhisattva are equal and without distinction.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should act in this way and should abide in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) in this manner.

Furthermore, Kauśika, the twelve links of dependent origination are empty of the twelve links of dependent origination; the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination is empty of the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination; and the bodhisattva is empty of the bodhisattva. The twelve links of dependent origination, the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination, emptiness, and the bodhisattva who is empty—all these are one single emptiness, without duality.
Kauśika! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in the perfection of wisdom in this manner:

the six perfections are empty of the six perfections; likewise are internal and external emptiness, the emptiness of existence and non-existence, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, the various gates of samādhi and dhāraṇī, as well as the vehicle of the śrāvaka and the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha.
It is the same for the bodhisattva, the Tathāgata, and sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
The emptiness of the bodhisattva and the emptiness of sarvajñatā are one single emptiness, not two;
thus should the bodhisattva abide in the prajñāpāramitā.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said: "How is it,
Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not dwell within the perfection of wisdom?"
Subhūti said: "Kauśika!
A bodhisattva does not abide in the five aggregates with any dependence, nor does he abide in the six sense-faculties with any dependence."
They do not abide in or rely upon the six sense-faculties; from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), they do not abide in or rely upon anything.
From the *srotāpanna* up to the *arhat*, the *pratyekabuddha*, and up to the Buddha, they all do not abide in or rely upon anything.
From the five aggregates up to *sarvajñatā*, these are non-abiding and without reliance.
From the *srotāpanna* up to the Buddha, they likewise do not abide and have no reliance.

One should not dwell upon the five aggregates as impermanent; one should not dwell upon the five aggregates as permanent; one should not dwell upon the five aggregates as suffering or pleasure; one should not dwell upon them as pure or impure; one should not dwell upon them as self or non-self; one should not dwell upon them as empty or non-empty; one should not dwell upon them as ceasing or non-ceasing; and one should not dwell upon them as tranquil or non-tranquil, for such dwelling involves reliance.
Because the stage of *srotāpanna* is incomplete, one should not dwell therein; up to and including the stage of a Buddha, because it is incomplete, one should not dwell therein.

Because all the virtues, powers, and merits of a *srotāpanna* are not fully perfected, one should not dwell therein; up to and including the virtues, powers, and merits of a Buddha being fully perfected, one should not dwell therein.
"Furthermore, Kauśika,
a bodhisattva should not abide in the first stage, nor should they abide in any stage up to the tenth, for [such abiding] involves a point of attachment."
From the first stage, one should say: "I shall fulfill the dāna-pāramitā, but I should not dwell therein";
likewise, regarding the śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā, one should not dwell therein or rely upon them.
"I shall fully accomplish the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, yet I should not dwell upon them with any attachment.
I should not dwell within the path of a bodhisattva.
From the path of a bodhisattva, I shall proceed to the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), yet I should not dwell therein."
When a bodhisattva is endowed with the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), they should not dwell within them nor rely upon them.

Once a bodhisattva has attained these supernormal powers, they may say, "I shall travel to immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* buddha-fields, see the various Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and listen to and receive their teachings; having done so, I shall in turn instruct all sentient beings. Yet, they should likewise not dwell within this nor rely upon it.
One should say: "I too shall manifest transformations to be exactly like all those possessed by the worlds of the Buddhas, Tathāgatas;
yet I should not dwell therein, nor rely upon anything. One should not dwell in or rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā."
I shall instruct sentient beings in the ultimate path, yet I should not dwell therein.

I shall make offerings to countless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) Buddhas, with banners, streamers, incense, flowers, silk canopies, and countless billions of hundreds of thousands of layers of fine cloth; yet I should not dwell therein.
I shall bring to fulfillment countless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings, causing them to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I should not dwell therein.
"I shall fulfill the five eyes— the fleshly eye,
the divine eye, the Dharma-eye, the wisdom-eye, and the Buddha-eye— and yet I should not dwell therein.
I shall give rise to all samādhis, and yet I should not dwell therein."
Furthermore, one should not form the wish, "When I attain this samādhi, I shall sport within it," nor should one dwell therein.
One should fully master the gates of dhāraṇī, yet not dwell therein.
I shall fulfill the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom, the four fearlessnesses, the ten powers of a Buddha, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, yet I should not dwell within them.
I shall fulfill the four immeasurable minds and great kindness and compassion, yet I should not dwell therein.
I shall fulfill the thirty-two marks of a Great Being and the eighty minor characteristics, yet I should not dwell therein or rely upon them.
One who abides in the matters of the eight classes of noble ones and has accomplished the essential Dharma of faith should not abide therein;
from the stage of stream-enterer up to the seventh [fruit], one should not abide therein.
One should not dwell in the state of a once-returner;
one should not dwell in the equality of the Path;
one should not dwell in the exhaustion of defilements at the end of life.
The srotāpanna attains parinirvāṇa on the middle path; one should not dwell therein.
The sakṛdāgāmin has not yet severed the root of all suffering; one should not dwell therein.
Having attained the realization of the path of the Anāgāmin, one should not abide therein.
Passing into parinirvāṇa midway through the stage of the Anāgāmin, one should not abide therein.
Having attained the realization of arhatship and become an arhat, one should not dwell therein while entering parinirvāṇa into the nirvana without remainder from this state.
One should not dwell within the stage of a pratyekabuddha.
One should not dwell within the stages from those who have surpassed the arhat and pratyekabuddha up to the bodhisattva stage.
One should not dwell within the wisdom of the path’s affairs, for that would involve dependence.
One should not abide in the thought that one will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through various deeds;
nor should one abide in the thought that all subsequent defilements have been extinguished;
nor should one abide in the thought that, having become a Tathāgata, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, and one who is unattached, one shall turn the wheel of Dharma.
"I shall perform the work of a Buddha and deliver all immeasurable sentient beings; I should not dwell therein.
By means of the four bases of power, I shall abide in samādhi for lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; I should not dwell therein."
May my lifespan be immeasurable; I should not dwell therein.
Regarding the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, each mark is perfected through a hundred merits; I should not dwell therein.
May my single Buddha-field be as vast as the Buddha-fields of the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, yet I shall not abide therein.
May this trichiliocosm be made entirely of vajra, yet I shall not abide therein.

May fragrances emerge from the Bodhi tree of my Buddha-field, such that all sentient beings who smell them shall be free from the three poisons and shall not give rise to the thoughts of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

May those who smell this fragrance have both physical and mental illnesses completely healed. May the sounds of the five aggregates—form, sensation, perception, formations, and consciousness—and the six perfections not be heard within my Buddha-field, nor should one dwell therein.

May my Buddha-land not hear of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment or the eighteen unique qualities; may it not hear the sounds of those from the stage of srotāpanna up to that of a Buddha—I should not abide therein.
Why is this? Because when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha attained unexcelled perfect enlightenment, he likewise found nothing to be apprehended among all dharmas.
Thus it is, Kauśika!
"A bodhisattva does not rely upon or dwell in the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra thought to himself:
"In what manner, then, should a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwell?"
Subhūti, knowing what was in Śāriputra’s mind, asked Śāriputra:
“What do you think? In what do the Buddhas abide?”
Śāriputra replied: “The Buddhas have no abode. They do not abide with the mind fixed upon anything;

nor do they abide in the five aggregates, nor in accomplishment, nor in non-accomplishment, nor in the conditioned or the unconditioned. They do not abide in the eighteen dhātus, nor in sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).”
Subhūti said: "A bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in the perfection of wisdom should dwell as the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas dwell—dwelling in non-dwelling."
“A Bodhisattva should abide in this way: abiding in non-abiding.
Thereupon, a son of heaven in the assembly had this thought:
“The speech and discourse of all the yakṣas can be fully understood, but the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā spoken by the Venerable Subhūti is utterly incomprehensible.”
Subhūti, knowing what the sons of the gods were thinking, said to them:
"Do you not understand? Do you not know?
The sons of the gods replied:
"Indeed, Subhūti! You truly do not understand and do not know.
Subhūti then spoke to the devaputras, saying:
"In what I have taught, not a single word has ever been seen; likewise, there is no one who hears the teaching.
Why is this? For the Prajñāpāramitā is not composed of letters, nor is it something that can be heard."
For what reason?
O sons of the gods!
The path of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas is likewise without letters.
"O sons of the gods!
It is as if a Tathāgata were to manifest a transformed Buddha and create fourfold assemblies of disciples.
Having created these transformations, he would then preach the teaching that all phenomena are transformations."
"What do you think, sons of the gods? Is there any teaching, any exposition, or indeed any recipient?
The sons of the gods replied, "Yes, Subhūti!"
"This is non-existent.
Subhūti said: "All dharmas are like a magical transformation; there is neither one who speaks, nor one who receives, nor one who knows."
“Suppose, for example, a man were to see a Buddha in a dream, and that Buddha were to preach the Dharma to him.
What do you think? Is there one who speaks and one who receives?
The sons of the gods replied:
“There is no speaking and no receiving. Subhūti said:
“All phenomena are like illusions; there is no speaking and no receiving, nor is there anything at all.”
Suppose there are two people standing on opposite sides of a deep ravine, both uttering sounds to praise the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus.
Would the echoes of their voices ever reach one another?
The devaputras said, “An echo has no cognition. [The Buddha asked,] “Is it not like something that has been severed?”
The devaputras replied,
"In truth, there is nothing at all.
The devaputras then thought again:
"Now, Subhūti, as you expound the Prajñāpāramitā, its matter is exceedingly profound; what you teach becomes ever more profound, and what you speak becomes ever more sublime.
Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"Form (rūpa) is neither profound nor subtle; it is not because of the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) that it is subtle."

The six sense-faculties are empty from the perspective of internal emptiness and the emptiness of existence and non-existence; this applies even unto the six pāramitās and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
All the gates of samādhi and the gates of dhāraṇī, up to and including sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), are neither deep nor subtle; it is not because of sarvajñatā that they are deep and subtle.

The sons of the gods thought to themselves: "What is spoken here does not speak of the five aggregates (skandhas) or the six sense bases (āyatanas); it does not speak of the six perfections (pāramitās), nor does it speak of internal and external emptiness (śūnyatā) or the emptiness of existence and non-existence; it does not speak of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma) or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma); it does not speak of the path of the stream-enterer (srotāpanna), nor does it speak of the paths of the arhat or the pratyekabuddha; nor does it speak of written characters."
"What do you think of this matter? Subhūti replied, "So it is, so it is!"
O sons of the gods!

The path of all Tathāgatas is entirely without anything to be attained and without anything to be expounded. Therefore, among all dharmas, there is neither one who speaks nor one who hears; there is neither one who receives nor one who attains.
Subhūti said: "O sons of the gods!

Those who wish to abide in the path of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) or take the realization of a stream-enterer; or those who wish to abide as arhats, pratyekabuddhas, up to and including Buddhas, and wish to take their respective realizations—if they establish themselves in such a way, they will ultimately never attain this patience (kṣānti)."
"From the time a bodhisattva first resolves upon enlightenment, there is nothing to be spoken and nothing to be heard; they should abide in this manner.
Chapter 29: Like an Illusion (*Māyopama*) from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. At that time, the sons of the gods thought to themselves:
"How shall we listen to and receive the teaching from Subhūti?"
The Venerable Subhūti, knowing what the sons of the gods were thinking, addressed them, saying:
"Now, let those gathered here listen to what I say as if they were phantom figures created by magic; they should receive it without anything being received, see nothing, and realize nothing."
The devaputras asked:
"How is it, Subhūti? Are sentient beings like illusions and transformations?"
"Are those who have come to this assembly also like an illusion or a transformation? Subhūti replied, "So it is, so it is!"

Sentient beings are like illusions; those who assemble are likewise like illusions; even the self is like an illusion and like a dream. The five aggregates are like illusions and like transformations;

the six sense organs and the seeds of consciousness are like illusions and like transformations. Internal and external emptiness, as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence, are like illusions and like dreams. The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are like illusions and like transformations; the stage of the srotāpanna up to the Buddha, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is likewise like an illusion.
At that time, the sons of the gods asked Subhūti:
"In what way is it that even a Buddha is like an illusion and like a dream? Subhūti replied:
“I say that even the attainment of Buddhahood is likewise like an illusion.
If there were any dharma superior to *nirvāṇa*, I would also say that it is like an illusion.
O sons of the gods!
“Dreams, illusions, and transformations are one; they are non-dual and not two.

At that time, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, Mahākātyāyana, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Mahākāśyapa, and others, together with immeasurable bodhisattvas—this entire great assembly—asked Subhūti:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is extremely profound and extremely vast; it is difficult to comprehend, difficult to understand, difficult to see, and difficult to explain.”
"Who is able to obstruct or suppress this?
At that time, Ānanda spoke to the assembly of disciples and the various bodhisattvas, saying:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is a profound and subtle Dharma; it is exceedingly vast, difficult to see, difficult to understand, difficult to comprehend, and inconceivable."

Only those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are *avaivartika*, those arhats who have fully realized the truths, and those sons or daughters of good family who possess great wisdom—having cultivated merit under countless Buddhas in previous lives and having associated with virtuous friends—it is only such persons as these who, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, are able to believe and rejoice in it, and can never be deterred from doing so.
One does not differentiate the five aggregates by means of emptiness, nor does one differentiate emptiness by means of the five aggregates;
likewise, one does not differentiate signlessness or wishlessness by means of the five aggregates, nor does one differentiate the five aggregates by means of signlessness or wishlessness.
Nor does one differentiate the five aggregates by means of non-arising and non-ceasing, nor does one differentiate non-arising and non-ceasing by means of the five aggregates;
nor does one differentiate the five aggregates by means of quiescent purity, nor does one differentiate quiescent purity by means of the five aggregates.
It is likewise for the six sense faculties and all dependent origination.

It is likewise from the *dānapāramitā* through to the *prajñāpāramitā*. It is likewise from internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) through to the emptiness of existence and non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*). It is likewise from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) through to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharmāḥ*).

The various gates of samādhi and the gates of dhāraṇī do not differentiate the five aggregates, nor do they differentiate the gates of samādhi and the gates of dhāraṇī by means of the five aggregates.
From the stage of Srotāpanna up to Arhat, Pratyekabuddha, and even to Sarvajñā, one does not differentiate emptiness, nor does one differentiate Sarvajñā by means of emptiness;
nor does one differentiate Sarvajñā by means of signlessness or wishlessness, nor does one differentiate signlessness and wishlessness by means of Sarvajñā.
One does not discriminate emptiness by means of the nature of being complete or incomplete, nor does one discriminate the nature of being complete or incomplete by means of emptiness;
this is likewise for signlessness and wishlessness.
"One does not differentiate quiescent purity by means of non-arising or non-ceasing, nor does one differentiate the five aggregates by means of quiescent purity.
Subhūti said to the devaputras:
"This profound Prajñāpāramitā cannot be obstructed even by those of supreme wisdom."
Why is this? Because dharmas have neither sorrow nor grief.
If sentient beings are without sorrow and without grief, there is likewise no one who can obstruct or cut them off.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

“The Prajñāpāramitā extensively expounds the teachings of the three vehicles and the teachings on the bodhisattva’s dhāraṇīs; from the initial generation of the mind up to the stages of the ten dwellings, it includes the teachings on the six pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha—all these are the teachings on the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s total retention (dhāraṇī). This is what constitutes the birth by transformation through a bodhisattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā.”

Without exhausting their supernormal powers, they travel to the buddha-fields; according to their wishes, they perform the roots of goodness and make offerings to the Buddhas, thereby attaining their aspirations.
From those World-Honored Ones, they hear and receive the Dharma, which continues without interruption until they reach sarvajñā (all-knowledge).

Never departing from samādhi, he shall possess unimpeded eloquence, uninterrupted eloquence, appropriate eloquence, sharp eloquence, eloquence regarding meaning, and the most supreme of all eloquences.
Subhūti said: "So it is, so it is!

Just as Śāriputra has spoken, regarding the extensive exposition of the three vehicles and the bodhisattva vehicle—the supreme eloquence attained by the Mahāyāna bodhisattva mahāsattvas is likewise without reliance and does not rely."

One does not rely on the self, knowledge and vision, life span, or the five aggregates; one does not rely on anything from the dāna-pāramitā up to the prajñā-pāramitā; one does not rely on anything from internal and external emptiness and the emptiness of existence and non-existence; and one does not rely on anything from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha up to the wisdom of sarvajñatā.
Śāriputra said: "For what reason?
Because within the Prajñāpāramitā, the teachings of the three vehicles are expounded without any dependence."
"For what reason is it said that a bodhisattva possesses dhāraṇī?
For what reason does one attain the most sublime eloquence without any dependence? Subhūti replied:
"From internal emptiness up to the Three Vehicles, all emerge from the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, yet they have no basis upon which to rely.
From external emptiness up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence, the extensive exposition of the teachings of the Three Vehicles likewise has no basis upon which to rely."
From the teaching on internal and external emptiness up to the bodhisattva, the summary exposition of all the most wondrous eloquence in the world is likewise without dependence.
From the emptiness of existence and non-existence up to the bodhisattva, one protects the foremost eloquence in all the world while remaining without dependence.
Chapter 30: Raining Down the Rain of Dharma. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Thirty: Raining Down the Rain of Dharma. At that time, Śakra Devānām-Indra thought to himself:
"The Dharma taught by the Venerable Subhūti is a raining down of the rain of Dharma."
Throughout the trichiliocosm, from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, each thought to themselves:

"Now that Subhūti is preaching this rain of Dharma, we should surely create flowers and scatter them over the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the bodhisattvas, the great disciples, and upon Subhūti himself."

At that time, the Śakras, Indras, and the various Cāturmahārājas throughout the trichiliocosm each manifested flowers, scattering them over the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, and the community of bhikṣus, as well as over Subhūti, thereby making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā.

The devas scattered flowers, which at that moment pervaded the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system without leaving any empty space on the ground, as if they had been spread out as seats.
Those flowers in the air that had not yet fallen to the ground were, at that very moment, transformed into exquisite flower-canopied pavilions of interlaced blossoms, most wonderfully adorned.
At that time, Subhūti thought to himself:
"I have frequently ascended to the heavens, yet I have never before seen flowers such as these.
These flowers scattered by the sons of the gods do not grow from trees; they are merely emanated flowers."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Subhūti:
"These flowers are not born flowers, nor are they flowers from the trees of the mind. Subhūti replied:
"What Kauśika has said is true: these flowers are neither born flowers nor flowers from a mental tree.
Kauśika! That which is unborn is not a flower."
Śakra Devānām Indra said to Subhūti:
"Is it only these flowers that are non-arisen?
Or are the five aggregates also not arisen?"
Subhūti said: "These flowers and the five aggregates are both equally unproduced; if they are not produced, they are not the five aggregates.
The six sense faculties are also unproduced; if they are not produced, they are not the six sense faculties."
The six pāramitās are likewise unarisen; if they were not unarisen, they would not be the six pāramitās.

From internal and external emptiness up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence, they are also unarisen; if they were not unarisen, they would not be the emptiness of existence and non-existence.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are also non-arising; if they are non-arising, they are not the eighteen unique qualities.
Up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), these too are non-arising; if they are non-arising, they are not omniscience.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:
"How profound and subtle is Subhūti’s eloquence!
In accordance with what is appropriate, he preaches the Dharma without any contradiction."
The Buddha told Śakra-devānām-indra:
“So it is, so it is! Kauśika!”
“Subhūti is truly one who has deeply entered [the Dharma] and is foremost in eloquence; he preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate, without any error.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Yes, World-Honored One!”
"How is it, Subhūti, that you preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each person without error?
The Buddha told Kuyì:
"The five aggregates and the six sense-faculties are merely designations."
Because the five aggregates and the six sense bases exist merely as numerical designations, what Subhūti has said is without error.
Why is this? That which is in accordance with the Dharma neither contradicts nor is it joined together.
Because there is no discordance and no error, what Subhūti has spoken is without error.

This applies to the six pāramitās, from internal and external emptiness up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence, as well as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; all are likewise so.
From the path of the *srotāpanna* up to the path of the *pratyekabuddha*, and up to *sarvajñatā*—the matter of *sarvajñatā* is also like this.
From the *srotāpanna*, the *arhat*, and the *pratyekabuddha*, up to the Buddha, the *Tathāgata*, the *Arhat*, the *Samyaksaṃbuddha*, O Kauśika!
This, too, is merely a designation among the categories of dharmas.
What Subhūti has spoken is likewise a designation among the categories of dharmas; therefore, what he has said contains no contradiction.
Why is this? Kauśika!
That which is in accordance with the Dharma is neither in discord nor erroneous.
"Because it is neither discordant nor erroneous, Subhūti preaches the Dharma in this way, according to what is appropriate, without any contradiction or mistake. Subhūti said: "So it is, so it is!"

Kauśika! Just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, bestows the teachings of all dharmas, so too should one know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, all dharmas are likewise merely the bestowal of numerical designations.
Kauśika! A bodhisattva who trains in this way does not train in form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he perceive the five aggregates as something to be trained in.
One who trains in this manner does not train in the six pāramitās.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive the six pāramitās as something to be learned.
One who trains in this manner does not train in internal and external emptiness, nor in the emptiness of existence and non-existence.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive any dharma of emptiness that is to be learned.

One who trains in this manner does not train in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; they do not train in the path of the *srotāpanna*, nor in the paths of the *arhat* or *pratyekabuddha*, nor in the path of *sarvajñatā*.
"Why is this? Because one does not perceive that which is to be learned in sarvajñatā.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed Subhūti, saying:
"For what reason is it that the five aggregates are not seen?
Is it also that up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) they are not seen? Subhūti replied:
"Therefore, Kauśika! The five aggregates are empty of the five aggregates themselves; omniscience (sarvajñatā) is empty of omniscience itself. Why is this so?"
One should not study the emptiness of form by means of the emptiness of form; one should not study the emptiness of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) by means of the emptiness of *sarvajñatā*.
Not practicing the study of emptiness is itself the study of emptiness.
One does not train by means of duality; one trains in this way.
One does not train in the emptiness of the five aggregates by means of two things, nor does one train in the emptiness of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) by means of two things. Kausika!
To train in the emptiness of the five aggregates without employing duality is to train in the six pāramitās.
To train in the emptiness of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) without employing duality is to train in the six pāramitās;
it is to train in the emptiness of the internal and external up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence.
One trains in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
one trains in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
One does not train in these two matters separately, but trains for the sake of [attaining] the stage of a srotāpanna up to that of an arhat or pratyekabuddha.
One does not train in two things for the sake of training in the Samyaksaṃbuddhas;
nor does one train in two things for the sake of training in Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) or training in the Buddha.
To train in Sarvajñā is to train in the incalculable, asaṃkhyeya dharmas of all Buddhas.

One who studies the various Buddha-dharmas does not study the increasing of the five aggregates, nor does he study their decreasing; likewise, he does not study the increasing of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), nor does he study its decreasing.

In this way, one who trains without increasing or decreasing does not grasp at the five aggregates, nor does he train by extinguishing the five aggregates midway; likewise, until reaching *sarvajñatā*, he does not grasp at training, nor does he extinguish *sarvajñatā* midway.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: "When a bodhisattva trains in this way, does he not also train in sarvajñatā, and yet not midway extinguish his training in sarvajñatā?"
Subhūti replied: “So it is, so it is! Śāriputra asked again:
"Why is it that one neither undergoes training from the five aggregates up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*),
nor does one extinguish the training for the knowledge of all modes midway? He replied:
"Form itself is without reception, nor is there anyone who receives form.
Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) itself is without reception, nor is there anyone who receives Sarvajñā.
From internal and external emptiness up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence, these too are themselves without reception, nor is there anyone who receives emptiness."
"In this way, Śāriputra, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has no apprehension of any dharmas; therefore, they are born within sarvajñatā. Śāriputra said:
“If a bodhisattva trains in the *prajñāpāramitā* and does not grasp at any phenomena, is this for the sake of giving birth to *sarvajñatā*? Subhūti replied, “So it is, so it is!”
Śāriputra asked again:
“If a bodhisattva trains in this way, not apprehending any dharmas, neither training in their apprehension nor training in their cessation, how does he give rise to sarvajñatā?”

Subhūti replied: “When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not perceive the arising of form, nor do they perceive its cessation; they neither accept it nor reject it, neither cling to it nor abandon it, and neither increase it nor decrease it.”
Why is this? Śāriputra, it does not exist by way of the five aggregates;
nor is its arising seen, nor its cessation; nor is its appropriation seen, nor its non-appropriation; nor is its attachment seen, nor its severance; nor is its increase seen, nor its decrease.

Why is this? Śāriputra, one does not perceive the five aggregates as having anything up to and including sarvajñatā; nor does one perceive arising or ceasing, nor does one perceive receiving, nor does one perceive attachment or abandonment, nor does one perceive increase or decrease.
Why is this? Because omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is empty, there is nothing to be attained.

Therefore, regarding all phenomena, the bodhisattva has neither arising nor ceasing, neither apprehension nor attachment, neither severance nor non-severance, and neither increase nor decrease. Training in the *prajñāpāramitā* to emerge into omniscience, they should form this thought: "There is nothing to be learned, and there is nothing to be emerged from."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Śāriputra:
"From where should a bodhisattva seek the prajñāpāramitā? Śāriputra replied:
"Kauśika! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should seek it from the chapter turned by Subhūti.
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"By the power of Subhūti’s causes, conditions, and kindness, Śāriputra said:
'The Prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva should be sought within the chapter on the Turning of the Dharma by Subhūti.'"
Subhūti replied: "Kauśika!"
"It is not through my causal conditions or the power of my grace. Śakra Devānām Indra said,
"By whose grace and power does this abide?"
Subhūti said: "This is due to the power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority.
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"All dharmas are without location; how then can it be said that this is the place where the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power resides?
The Tathāgata does not perceive a Buddha apart from the dharma of non-location, nor does he perceive one apart from suchness."
Subhūti said: "It is so, Kauśika! The Tathāgata is not seen apart from suchness, nor is he seen as something other than suchness."
Nor does one regard the Tathāgata as suchness, nor suchness as the Tathāgata;
nor does one regard the suchness of the five aggregates as the Tathāgata, nor the Tathāgata as the suchness of the five aggregates;
nor does one regard the dharmas of the five aggregates as the Tathāgata, nor the Tathāgata as the dharmas of the five aggregates.
Nor does one take the suchness of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) as the Tathāgata, nor does one take the Tathāgata as the suchness of sarvajñā;
nor does one take the dharmas of sarvajñā as the Tathāgata, nor does one take the Tathāgata as the dharmas of sarvajñā.

Kauśika! If the Buddha is neither conjoined with the dharmas of the five aggregates nor non-conjoined with them, yet there is no conjoining or non-conjoining apart from the dharmas of the five aggregates, nor is there conjoining or non-conjoining as if existing apart from the five aggregates;

and so on, up to the *sarvajñā* and the suchness (*tathatā*) of the *sarvajñā* dharmas, which are neither conjoined nor non-conjoined, and there is no conjoining or non-conjoining apart from the *sarvajñā* and the suchness of the *sarvajñā* dharmas.
Kauśika! Because these dharmas abide in the power of being neither conjoined nor dispersed, this is the practice of the non-abiding.
Regarding what you have just asked, Kauśika—where should one seek the *prajñāpāramitā*?
Nor is it sought within the five aggregates, nor is it sought apart from the five aggregates.
Why is this? O Kauśika!

The Prajñāpāramitā and the five aggregates—these dharmas are neither identical nor different; they have no form and are invisible; they are without obstruction and possess a single mark, and that which is a single mark is markless.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks the prajñāpāramitā, he neither seeks it apart from sarvajñatā, nor does he seek it within sarvajñatā."
Why is this? Because the *prajñāpāramitā*, the *sarvajñatā*, and that which is sought are neither identical nor different; they are formless and invisible.
Nor does it obstruct the single characteristic; the so-called "single characteristic" is the absence of characteristics.

Why is this? Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is neither the five aggregates nor is it separate from the five aggregates; the *prajñāpāramitā* is neither *sarvajñatā* nor is it separate from *sarvajñatā*.
The suchness of the five aggregates is not the Prajñāpāramitā, nor is the Prajñāpāramitā separate from the suchness of the five aggregates;

the Prajñāpāramitā is neither the dharmas of the five aggregates nor is it separate from the dharmas of the five aggregates; the Prajñāpāramitā is neither the dharma of sarvajñatā nor is it separate from the dharma of sarvajñatā.
Why is this? Kauśika! These dharmas neither exist nor can they be apprehended.

Because all dharmas are unattainable, the five aggregates are not the *prajñāpāramitā*, yet the *prajñāpāramitā* is not separate from the five aggregates. The *prajñāpāramitā* is neither the dharma of the five aggregates nor is it separate from the dharma of the five aggregates; the *prajñāpāramitā* is neither the suchness (*tathatā*) of the five aggregates nor is it separate from the suchness of the five aggregates.

The *prajñāpāramitā* is neither omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) nor is it separate from omniscience; it is neither the suchness of omniscience nor is it separate from the suchness of omniscience; it is neither the dharma of omniscience nor is it separate from the dharma of omniscience.
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
“The Great Perfection (mahāpāramitā) is the great crossing-over of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas; this perfection is the immeasurable and limitless great crossing-over of all bodhisattvas.”

Within this [Dharma], one attains the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, *arhat*, and *pratyekabuddha*; within this, one becomes a bodhisattva, purifies buddha-fields, transforms and teaches sentient beings, and achieves *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti said: “Kauśika! So it is, so it is!”

It is no different from what Śakra Devānām-indra has said: those who have already attained and those who are yet to attain shall all achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through the *prajñāpāramitā*; because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are great, the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise vast.
Kauśika! The five aggregates have neither beginning nor end, neither middle nor limit;
it is the same even up to sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
Kauśika! This is the great crossing of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Because the five aggregates are immeasurable, the crossing of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise immeasurable.
Why is this? Because the five aggregates are immeasurable.
Just as space cannot be measured, so too the five aggregates cannot be measured.
Just as space cannot be measured, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) also cannot be measured.
Because the five aggregates cannot be measured, the *prajñāpāramitā* also cannot be measured;
and because even *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is immeasurable, the bodhisattva’s crossing over by means of the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise immeasurable.
Why is this? Kauśika!
Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is likewise immeasurable, just as space cannot be measured.
Because omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is immeasurable, space is immeasurable.
Because space is immeasurable, the *prajñāpāramitā* is also immeasurable.
For this reason, Kauśika,
the prajñāpāramitā of the bodhisattva mahāsattva cannot be measured, and emptiness likewise cannot be measured.
Because the five aggregates have no bottom, the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā also has no bottom. Why is this?
Because the limit or boundary of the five aggregates cannot be perceived.
Even up to *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), there is no bottom; the *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva likewise has no bottom.
Why is this so, Kauśika?
Because *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is neither fathomable nor has it any limit,
the *prajñāpāramitā* of the bodhisattva is likewise without depth.
From the five aggregates being bottomless, up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*),
it is likewise bottomless. "Furthermore, Kauśika,
because causes and conditions are bottomless, the bodhisattva’s *prajñāpāramitā* is also bottomless."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"Venerable Subhūti, by what cause and condition is the bodhisattva’s *prajñāpāramitā* bottomless, given that [all phenomena] are bottomless?"
He replied: "Because the causal conditions for sarvajñā (all-knowledge) are bottomless, the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā is bottomless.
Because the causal conditions of dharmas are bottomless, the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā is therefore bottomless."
He asked again:
"In what way are the causal conditions of dharmas bottomless, and how is the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā bottomless? He replied:
“Kauśika! Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is bottomless, the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā is bottomless.
Just as conditions (pratyaya) are bottomless, the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā is bottomless.”
He asked again:
"In what way are the causal conditions bottomless, such that the Bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā is bottomless? He replied:
"As suchness is bottomless, and as the conditions and causes are bottomless, because the conditions and causes are bottomless, the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā is bottomless.
Because sentient beings are bottomless, the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā is bottomless."
He asked again:
"In what way are sentient beings bottomless, and how is the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā bottomless? He replied:
"What do you think, Kauśika? Is there any dharma that can be called 'bodhisattva'?
"It is neither by way of a dharma nor by way of a non-dharma that it is so called; it is merely a provisional name and a designation."

"This is called that which is designated, yet it has no form; the name by which it is designated has no causes or conditions, and the designation itself, as well as sentient beings, have no causes or conditions.
"What do you think, Kauśika? Does the Prajñāpāramitā ever speak of there being a creator of sentient beings?"
“Indeed, Subhūti! There is none. “Kauśika!”
If there were no one to speak of beings as being created, what basis would there be for the existence of beings? Kauśika!
Suppose a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha were to remain for a lifespan as long as the sands of the Ganges; he would say that beings are born and beings perish.
"What do you think, Kauśika? Is there any sentient being who is born or who undergoes extinction? He replied, "No."
Subhūti! Why is this?
Because sentient beings are pure, and because that which is non-existent is pure.
"For this reason, Kauśika, you should know that sentient beings are bottomless; likewise, the Prajñāpāramitā is also bottomless and has no limit."

Chapter 31: Praise (Stuti-parivarta). The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Thirty-one: Praise. At that time, the various Brahma kings together with the Brahma devas were present in the assembly; Śakra-devendra, along with his retinue and the host of celestial maidens, was also present in the assembly. Each of these sons of the Śakras and Brahmās uttered these words of praise:
"How wonderful, how wonderful! The Dharma taught by Subhūti is truly marvelous!"
It is solely through the causal power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority that this teaching can be expounded and disseminated.

If there are those who do not distance themselves from the practice of this Prajñāpāramitā, we should regard such Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as being like the Tathāgata himself. Furthermore, there is no one who can perceive this Dharma, nor is there anyone who can perceive form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Up to the stage of the triple vehicle’s teaching of Sarvajñā, even Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha told the devaputras: "So it is, so it is!

Just as you have said, dharmas are neither obtainable nor visible. From form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), all are neither obtainable nor visible; there are only the teachings of the three vehicles, and these teachings of the three vehicles are likewise neither obtainable nor visible."
Those who practice this prajñāpāramitā without relying on anything should be regarded as Tathāgatas.
Why is this? Because within the prajñāpāramitā, the teachings of the three vehicles are extensively expounded.

Furthermore, one does not become a Buddha apart from the six pāramitās; nor does one become a Buddha apart from internal and external emptiness and the emptiness of existence and non-existence; nor does one become a Buddha apart from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; nor does one become a Buddha apart from sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
"O sons of the gods!
A bodhisattva must fully learn to know all dharmas, from the dānapāramitā up to sarvajñatā.
For this reason, you should know that such a bodhisattva is just like a Tathāgata."
The Buddha told the sons of the gods:

"In the past, since I was under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in the land of Kusumavati, I have never been apart from the six pāramitās; from internal and external emptiness up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the various gates of samādhi, the gates of dhāraṇī, the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom, great kindness and great compassion, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and all other countless supreme dharmas of the Buddhas—I have never been apart from these dharmas, nor have I ever relied upon them."
At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara made this prediction concerning me:
"In a future age, after an incalculable number of kalpas, you shall become a Buddha, named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, and Dharmasvāmī."
Thereupon, the devaputras addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
This is most marvelous and extraordinary."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they neither grasp nor relinquish omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and they likewise neither grasp nor relinquish the dharmas of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

At that time, the Buddha, having observed that the fourfold assembly of disciples—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—as well as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and all the devas from the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, were settled in their places, addressed Śakra Devānām Indra: “Kauśika!

If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as devas and devīs, who receive and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, recite and read it, and further disseminate it to others, causing them to recite, study, and keep it in mind, never departing from the intention of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), then Māra and the sons of Māra will be unable to find an opportunity against them.

Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family dwell in the practice of the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of the five aggregates; thus, no one can find an opportunity to exploit their emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness.

This extends even to the practice of the emptiness of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), wherein no one can find an opportunity to exploit that emptiness of *sarvajñatā*, for they do not perceive any such thing that could provide an opening for exploitation.
Kauśika! Non-human beings cannot find an opportunity to harm these good men and good women. Why is this?
These sons and daughters of good family possess great kindness and great compassion, for they bestow the four immeasurable minds upon all sentient beings.
Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family shall never err throughout the course of their lives.
Why is this so? It is because when these sons and daughters of good family practice the *dānapāramitā*, they do so equally for the sake of all sentient beings.
For this reason, their lifespan does not err.

Kauśika! Among all the Cāturmahārājika devas, Trāyastriṃśa devas, Yāma devas, Tuṣita devas, Nirmāṇarati devas, Paranirmitavaśavartin devas, Brahmakāyika devas, Abhāsvara devas, Śubhakṛtsna devas, and Bṛhatphala devas within this trichiliocosm, those sons of gods who have resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—if there are among these sons of gods any who have not yet heard the Prajñāpāramitā, nor recited, read, or upheld it—they shall all practice the Prajñāpāramitā, recite, read, and uphold it, so that their minds are never separated from *sarvajñatā*.

Kauśika! If these sons or daughters of good family practice the Prajñāpāramitā—whether they uphold, recite, read, or explain it, or cultivate, contemplate, and maintain its practice without departing from the mind of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge)—then these sons or daughters of good family, whether they have gone far into a secluded place, sit in the open air, or remain at home, shall never be afraid and shall never be terrified.

"Why is this so? It is because these sons and daughters of good family are clear regarding internal and external emptiness as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence, and thus have no basis for attachment.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings of the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system, up to the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, all addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!

We shall protect these good men and good women who practice, recite, read, explain, study, and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā; we shall provide them with guardianship so that they do not depart from sarvajñatā.”

Why is this? Because through the causes and conditions of the Bodhisattva’s coming and going, he cuts off the three evil destinies, cuts off the poverty of gods and humans, cuts off the poverty among human beings, cuts off such calamities and transformations for these classes of beings, and cuts off all famines and the high prices of grain.

Because of the coming and going of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the ten wholesome deeds manifest in the world; thus one comes to know the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the six pāramitās, from internal and external emptiness up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence; and thus one comes to know the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, up to sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).

Because of the coming and going of bodhisattvas, the world comes to know that there are kṣatriya and householder lineages; it comes to know that there are brahmin great clans; it comes to know that there are wheel-turning sage-kings; and it comes to know that there are the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

Because of the causes and conditions of the Bodhisattva’s coming and going, one comes to know that there are the paths of the Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, Arhat, and Pratyekabuddha; one comes to know that there is the instruction of sentient beings; and one comes to know that there is the purification of Buddha-fields.

Because of the coming and going of Bodhisattvas, one comes to know that there is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha; one comes to know that there is the turning of the Wheel of Dharma; and one comes to know that there are the Three Jewels.
"For this reason, the devas, asuras, and all people of the world shall all protect these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The Buddha told Śakra Devānām Indra: "It is so, Kauśika!"
Because of the causes and conditions of the Bodhisattva’s coming and going, the three evil realms are severed and the Three Jewels of the Buddha arise.
For this reason, all devas and people of the world should together revere and serve these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, provide them with what they require, and constantly protect them.
Kauśika! One who makes offerings to and serves this bodhisattva mahāsattva should do so with the same reverence and service as one would offer to me.
You should know it thus: it is no different from making offerings to a Tathāgata.
Therefore, Kauśika! All the devas and the people of the world should show him such reverence. Kauśika!
Suppose the great trichiliocosm were filled with sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, rice, hemp, and groves, and all these were śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, numbering as many as that.
If there were sons or daughters of good family who provided all manner of offerings, service, and attendance to [the Buddhas],
it would not equal that of these sons or daughters of good family who provide offerings and service to a bodhisattva who has resolved their mind on awakening and practices the six pāramitās.
Why is this so? Kauśika!
It is not because there are arhats and pratyekabuddhas that one knows there are bodhisattvas, tathāgatas, arhats, samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Because there is the causal condition of the bodhisattva, one comes to know of the arhat, the pratyekabuddha,
and the samyaksambuddha. Therefore, Kauśika,
all devas and people of the world should respectfully serve these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and should protect them.
Chapter 32: Subduing Sentient Beings. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Thirty-two: Subduing Sentient Beings. At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O World-Honored One!
Most marvelous and extraordinary!
Those who receive, uphold, recite, study, practice, and maintain mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā* shall obtain merits in the present life,
instruct sentient beings, and purify all Buddha-fields, traveling from one Buddha-field to another.
Having seen the Buddhas in those lands, he desires to make offerings; according to his wishes, he immediately obtains the means to offer them, thereby perfecting the roots of goodness.
Whatever Dharma he hears from the Buddhas he encounters, he never forgets until he attains *samyaksambuddhatva*.
Thus, he achieves the perfection of family, the perfection of parents, and the perfection of birth.
Furthermore, they attain the perfection of retinue, the perfection of marks, the perfection of radiance, the perfection of the eyes, the perfection of the ears, the perfection of samādhi,
and the perfection of dhāraṇī; through skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), they manifest bodies like those of a Buddha, traveling from one land to another.
Upon reaching places where there is no Buddha, having arrived, they immediately extol the merits of the six pāramitās;

they extol internal and external emptiness as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence; they extol the merits of all these: the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments.

Furthermore, he extols the merits of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; employing skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), he preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings and subdues them through the three vehicles.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How wonderful, World-Honored One!
How truly marvelous and extraordinary!”

How does one uphold the Prajñāpāramitā so as to encompass the five pāramitās, and likewise encompass the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and likewise encompass the teachings of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; and likewise encompass omniscience (sarvajñatā) and the activities of omniscience?
The Buddha told Śakra-devānām-indra: "It is so, Kauśika!

One who upholds the Prajñāpāramitā has already upheld all the pāramitās; they have already upheld the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—all matters pertaining to sarvajñatā (omniscience) have been fully upheld."
Furthermore, Kauśika!
Listen, listen attentively to the merits that correspond to those who uphold, maintain, recite, and contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā.
"I shall now explain to you the merit obtained by these good sons and good daughters.
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"Yes, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said:

"If there are heterodox practitioners or outsiders, or Māra and his followers, or stubborn and perverse people who intend to destroy it, or those who intend to cause discord, or those who harbor evil intentions and come to ruin it—all such wishes shall not be fulfilled, and they shall perish midway."
Why is this? Kauśika!

Because these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have practiced the six pāramitās for a long night; and because sentient beings are greedy and contend over wealth, the bodhisattvas completely relinquish all internal and external dharmas they possess, establishing sentient beings [in the Dharma] as they practice the dāna-pāramitā.
Because sentient beings practice unwholesome precepts, the bodhisattva relinquishes internal and external phenomena and establishes sentient beings in the *śīlapāramitā*.

Because sentient beings have long been engaged in strife, litigation, resentment, and anger throughout the long night, the bodhisattva relinquishes internal and external phenomena and establishes sentient beings in the *kṣāntipāramitā*.
Because sentient beings are indolent, the Bodhisattva relinquishes internal and external phenomena and establishes sentient beings so that they may practice the *vīrya-pāramitā*.

Because sentient beings are constantly distracted in mind, the Bodhisattva relinquishes internal and external phenomena and establishes sentient beings so that they may practice the *dhyāna-pāramitā*.

Because sentient beings are addicted to unwholesome knowledge, the Bodhisattva relinquishes both internal and external phenomena, establishing sentient beings so that they may practice the Prajñāpāramitā.

Because sentient beings dwell within the cycle of birth and death due to their bonds of affection, the Bodhisattva’s *pāramitā* and *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) extract them from those bonds of affection and from birth and death, establishing them in the four *dhyānas*, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. He encourages and establishes them therein; he encourages and establishes sentient beings so that they attain the stage of *srotāpanna* up to *arhat*; he encourages and establishes sentient beings so that they become *pratyekabuddhas*; and he encourages and establishes sentient beings so that they practice as Bodhisattvas and attain Buddhahood.
Kauśika! To practice the conduct of a bodhisattva is to attain extraordinary virtues in the present life;

in future lives, one shall then attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and turn the wheel of Dharma, delivering and liberating sentient beings according to their needs—this is the extraordinary virtue of a bodhisattva in future lives.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives and upholds the *prajñāpāramitā*, and if they recite, chant, read, study, and practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, then as for that place, Māra and his celestial hosts, heterodox teachers and outsiders, or those who are stubborn and perverse—should they wish to cause disruption, or wish to cut short their progress midway, or should they harbor malicious intentions toward them through strife and contention—they shall ultimately never be able to give rise to such thoughts."
The merit of this bodhisattva’s practice becomes increasingly sublime, distinguished, and peerless; none can equal it.
By means of the sound of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they bring forth the three vehicles and thereby attain liberation.
For example, Kauśika!
There is a medicine named Maṅgī.
Suppose there is a hungry viper wandering about, seeking insects with which it wishes to feed.
The insect saw the snake from afar and ran toward the place where the medicine was.
The snake wished to go there as well, but because of the scent of the medicine, it could not advance. Why was this?
"By the majestic power of this medicine, the snake was made to turn back midway.
O Kauśika! Such is the majestic power of this Maṅgī medicine."

If there are sons or daughters of good family who practice the Prajñāpāramitā, whether by reciting, reading, studying, upholding, or maintaining it, and if there should be those who wish to cause disturbance, or who wish to interrupt, destroy, or provoke conflict toward them—by the power of the majesty of the Prajñāpāramitā, wherever they may go, those disturbances shall naturally vanish and perish right there.
Why is this so? Because the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is the definitive nature of all phenomena, not the contention among phenomena.
What are these phenomena?

That is to say: lust, anger, and delusion; the twelve links of dependent origination arising from a lack of wisdom; the mind having attachments; the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, the view of annihilation, the view of permanence, the view of purity, the view of non-existence, various false views, the view of envy and evil precepts, the view of malice, indolence and a distracted mind, and the constant view of evil wisdom; the perception of pleasure, the perception of purity, the perception of self, and the practice of affectionate attachment; receiving form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; receiving the six *pāramitās*; receiving internal and external emptiness; receiving the emptiness of existence and non-existence; receiving the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; receiving the eighteen unique qualities; receiving *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge); and receiving *nirvāṇa* while augmenting the five faculties—this is the emptiness of all dharmas.

The Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra-devānām-indra, and the Brahmās throughout the trichiliocosm, up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven—all these devas and humans shall protect those sons and daughters of good family who practice the Prajñāpāramitā, who recite, read, explain, study, uphold, and maintain it.

All the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions collectively protect these good men and good women who practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, those who recite, read, explain, study, uphold, and maintain it; all evils are completely eliminated and all virtues are increased. They further increase their progress in the six *pāramitās* without any dependence;
they likewise increase their realization of internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) without any dependence;

and regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the various gates of *samādhi*, the gates of *dhāraṇī*, and the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*), they all further increase their progress without any dependence.
Whatever they say, all people believe and trust.
They act as friends to all sentient beings, and their speech is never in error.
They are ultimately free from anger, never act out of self-interest, and are likewise without envy.
He himself abstains from taking life and teaches others to practice loving-kindness; he extols the virtue of non-killing for the sake of sentient beings and constantly praises those who do not kill.
He himself always remains far removed from taking what is not given and teaches others not to steal; he also constantly extols the virtue of non-stealing.
One purifies oneself and teaches others not to engage in sexual misconduct, while also praising the virtue of abstaining from sexual misconduct.

One personally distances oneself from false speech, harsh words, abusive language, and frivolous chatter; one also constantly distances oneself from envy, malice, and wrong views, teaches others right view, and likewise praises the virtue of right view.
They personally practice the six pāramitās, constantly exhort and assist others to practice the six pāramitās, and always proclaim the great merit of practicing the six pāramitās.
They personally practice internal and external emptiness, encourage others to practice emptiness, and likewise praise the virtues of practicing emptiness;
the same applies to the emptiness of existence and non-existence.
They personally practice the various dharanis and samadhi gates, teach others to uphold and study these various samadhis, and extol the virtues of the dharanis and samadhis.
He himself practices the four dhyānas, teaches others to practice dhyāna, and speaks in praise of the virtues of practicing meditative concentration.
He himself practices the four immeasurables, teaches others to practice the four immeasurables, and likewise speaks in praise of the merits of loving-kindness and compassion.
One practices the four formless concentrations oneself and teaches others to practice them, praising the merit of the formless concentrations.
One practices the faculties, the powers, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment oneself and teaches others to practice them, likewise praising the merit of the factors of the path.

They themselves practice the three samādhis, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditations, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom, great loving-kindness and great compassion, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*); they teach others to practice the wisdom of omniscience and praise and extol the merits of the wisdom of omniscience.
Constantly practicing the six pāramitās, whatever they give in charity, they share with all sentient beings for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, without relying on anything whatsoever.

The acts of giving, maintaining the precepts, diligence, patience, single-minded concentration, and wisdom that they perform are solely for the sake of all classes of sentient beings, so that they may attain liberation through *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and yet they remain without any dependence.
When good sons or good daughters practice the six pāramitās in this manner, they give rise to this thought:

"If I do not practice giving, I may be born into a poor or lowly family; then I would be unable to instruct sentient beings, nor would I be able to purify a buddha-field, nor would I be able to attain sarvajñatā."

If I do not maintain the precepts, I may be reborn in the three evil realms and fail to obtain a human body; consequently, I would be unable to instruct sentient beings, purify Buddha-fields, nor attain *sarvajñatā*.

If I were not to practice patience, I would destroy my sense faculties; I would not obtain the mark of a tongue that can cover the face, my physical form would not be perfected, and I would not attain the body of a Bodhisattva endowed with all practices. Consequently, I would be unable to instruct sentient beings, purify Buddha-fields, nor achieve *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).

If I am not diligent and possess indolence, I may be reborn in an evil realm with an obscure body; furthermore, I will be unable to instruct sentient beings, purify Buddha-fields, or achieve sarvajñā (all-knowledge).

If I do not practice dhyāna and my mind is not concentrated, I will likewise be unable to attain the wisdom of the various samādhis, to instruct sentient beings, to purify the Buddha-fields, or to achieve sarvajñatā.

If I were to practice evil wisdom, I would be unable to attain the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of an Arhat or the stage of a Pratyekabuddha; nor could I instruct sentient beings, purify a Buddha-field, or achieve omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
“Good sons and good daughters should form this thought: ‘I must not, following a mind of greed and envy, fail to fully practice the dāna-pāramitā;

I must not, because of evil precepts, fail to fully practice the śīla-pāramitā; I must not, because of anger, fail to fully practice the kṣānti-pāramitā; I must not, because of indolence, fail to fully practice the vīrya-pāramitā; I must not, because of a distracted mind, fail to fully practice the dhyāna-pāramitā; and I must not, because of false wisdom, fail to fully practice the prajñā-pāramitā.’”
"If I do not fully practice the six pāramitās, I shall never give birth to sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).

Those sons and daughters of good family who receive, uphold, recite, and practice the prajñāpāramitā shall obtain merits in both the present life and future lives, and their minds shall never depart from the intention for sarvajñatā.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
This is most marvelous and extraordinary.”
"How wonderful!
This Prajñāpāramitā is such that it serves as the guide for the deeds of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The Buddha said:
“Kauśika! How does the perfection of wisdom act as a giver and a guide for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Regarding all worldly acts of giving that lack *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means)—whether given to Buddhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or to the poor and beggars—if one lacks *upāyakauśalya*, one falls into arrogance and says: 'I am fully practicing the perfection of dāna, the perfection of śīla, the perfection of kṣānti, and the perfection of dhyāna.'"
If one says,
"I have fully attained and practiced the Prajñāpāramitā," they will consequently fall into arrogance regarding worldly pāramitās.
He says:
