Furthermore, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the future and the present shall also attain unexcelled perfect enlightenment by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and their assemblies of disciples shall likewise each attain their respective stages from *srotāpanna* up to *arhat* and *pratyekabuddha*."
Why is this? Because these vehicles of the Three Vehicles all emerge from within the Prajñāpāramitā.

Although they emerge as the Three Vehicles, they are without that which is produced, without marks or conceptions, without attachment, without cessation, and without anything existing. They are neither appropriate nor inappropriate; they neither move nor do not move; they neither grasp nor abandon. This is merely according to conventional enumeration, not according to the ultimate reality.

Why is this? The Prajñāpāramitā is neither here nor there; it does not flow midway, nor does it stay near the shore; it is neither paired nor solitary; it is neither with marks nor without marks; it is neither the Path nor the mundane; it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned; it is neither good nor evil; and it is neither of the past, the future, nor the present.
Why is this? Kauśika!
The Prajñāpāramitā does not uphold the Buddha-dharma, nor does it uphold the dharma of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, nor does it abandon the dharma of ordinary persons.
Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One! The Prajñāpāramitā is the great deliverance among all deliverances.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā, they fully know the intentions of all sentient beings, yet there is neither a sentient being nor a locus for such knowledge and vision. They do not perceive the five aggregates (*skandha*), nor do they perceive the six sense faculties (*indriya*). There are no six sense objects (*āyatana*), nor is there dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). There are no thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) nor the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*). They do not perceive the Path, nor is there any dharma of the Path. They do not perceive a Buddha, nor is there any dharma of a Buddha.”
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā likewise does not abide by relying upon anything. Why is this?
"The Prajñāpāramitā has no form and cannot be seen; how much less could one see anything upon which it might depend?
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"As you have said, Kauśika, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā throughout the long night, they do not even perceive a path, let alone the dharmas practiced by a bodhisattva."
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice only the prajñāpāramitā and not the other pāramitās?”
The Buddha told Śakra-devānām-indra:
“A bodhisattva practices all six pāramitās without relying on anything.

There is no giver, no recipient, and no gift; there is neither precept nor transgression; there is neither patience nor anger; there is neither diligence nor laziness; there is neither dhyāna nor distracted mind; and there is neither wisdom nor folly.”

The perfection of wisdom is the foremost practice of a bodhisattva; within the perfection of wisdom, there are generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and single-minded concentration, because one desires to fulfill the five perfections.

When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, desiring to contemplate all phenomena as being without dependence, they proceed from the five aggregates up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); this is what is meant by all phenomena being without dependence.

For example, in Jambudvīpa there are various kinds of excellent trees, with many varieties of colors, many varieties of leaves, many varieties of flowers, and many varieties of fruits, each of which has a distinct color;
yet, regarding their various trunks, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, their shade is no different and possesses no distinction.
Kauśika! The Prajñāpāramitā encompasses the five pāramitās up to sarvajñatā; it is not manifold, without distinction, and without dependence.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is fully complete in all meritorious qualities.”
World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is fully endowed with countless and immeasurable merits.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā contains and sustains all dharmas, being fully endowed with all merits.
World-Honored One!

If there are good men or good women who receive and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā—copying its scrolls and making offerings of famous flowers, powdered incense, silken canopies, banners, and pennants, and practicing the matters therein.
Furthermore, if there is someone who writes out the Prajñāpāramitā as a scroll and gives it to others,
which of these two would have the greater merit?
The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām-indra, saying:
"I shall now question you; answer me as you see fit.
Suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to make offerings to the relics of the entire body; [how would their merit compare?]"
"If one were to take even as much as a mustard seed and give it to another person to offer in worship,
which of these would produce greater merit?
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
According to what I have heard from the Buddha regarding the matters within the Dharma, if a son or daughter of good family makes offerings to the śarīra,
and furthermore divides and holds even as much as a mustard seed to give to others, their merit will be exceedingly great.”
World-Honored One!
As I further examine its meaning,

when a Tathāgata abides in the Vajra-samādhi and spontaneously dissolves his own body, leaving behind śarīra relics as small as mustard seeds, those who make offerings to them receive boundless merit and bring an end to all suffering.
The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying:
"It is so, Kauśika! If there is someone who makes offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā by copying and upholding its scrolls;

Furthermore, Kauśika, if one were to take up the Prajñāpāramitā and further teach it to others, explaining its wisdom and analyzing each matter in detail, the merit thereof would be exceedingly great, exceedingly great.
The merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family exceeds that of those who previously made offerings.

One should know that the person from whom one hears this Prajñāpāramitā is more venerable than all other noble and holy ones; one should regard such a person as no different from the World-Honored One himself.
Why is this? One who perceives the Prajñāpāramitā has already perceived the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One is the Prajñāpāramitā, and the Prajñāpāramitā is the World-Honored One.

Why is this? Because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present have all emerged from within the Prajñāpāramitā and thereby attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

All the noble sages and wise ones, as well as all the bodhisattvas who are irreversible (avaivartika), have emerged from this Prajñāpāramitā and attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
The śrāvakas likewise all attain the state of arhat or pratyekabuddha from within it, each obtaining their respective goal.
Those who resolve upon the bodhisattva path likewise all obtain the various virtues of bodhisattvas from this.
Therefore, Kauśika!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to see the Buddhas of the present, serve them, and make offerings to them, they should make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha said:
"By upholding and making offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā in this manner, I have personally attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), becoming the most honored among all."
Who else could there be worthy of honor, to be revered and supported?
From the heavens down to the world, beyond the three realms, there is no one more venerable.
Reflect deeply within yourself:
"I originally attained the state of a Samyaksaṃbuddha through the Prajñāpāramitā; the Prajñāpāramitā is that which I revere.
Therefore, I should now make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā and pay it due honor."
"Therefore, Kauśika! I myself have made offerings to and served this Prajñāpāramitā, never being apart from it for a moment.
Whatever I have done, I have performed entirely by means of the Prajñāpāramitā."
If good sons or good daughters wish to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, receive and uphold it, and practice it faithfully.
Why is this? Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are born from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are born from the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

Therefore, Kauśika! If sons of good family or daughters of good family practice the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, they should all make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā; they should likewise transcribe, uphold, receive, and study it.
The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Seven;
The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mokṣala of Khotan during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Translated by Imperial Decree.
Chapter 39: On Merit. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, Chapter Thirty-nine: On Merit. The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra:

“If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who taught all the sentient beings within a single Jambudvīpa, causing them to establish themselves in the ten wholesome paths of action;”
"What do you think, Kauśika? Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied to the Buddha, "It would be very great, very great!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!”

It is not as meritorious for a son of good family or a daughter of good family to merely uphold this volume of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra themselves; rather, it is far more meritorious to bestow it upon others, enabling them to copy, uphold, recite, and understand its contents. The merit they thereby obtain is many times greater.

Why is this? Because within this Prajñāpāramitā, the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) are extensively expounded, enabling all sons and daughters of good family to obtain and study them; those who will come in the future shall likewise obtain and study them, attaining equality with the Way.
Those who seek the path of Arhat or Pratyekabuddha all obtain it herein, and those who will seek it in the future shall likewise obtain it herein.
Those who seek the path of a bodhisattva all attain it therein; those who are just beginning to seek it shall all likewise attain it therein.
Those who have already attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* all attained it therein; those who are just beginning to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* shall also attain it therein.
Kauśika! What are the dharmas without outflows?

They are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, emptiness and the three gates of liberation, the four truths, internal and external emptiness as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence, and the ten powers of a Buddha—these immeasurable Buddha-dharmas enable good sons and good daughters to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
One who has just begun their quest shall also attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Kausika!
To instruct all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa so that they are established in the ten wholesome paths of action is not as good as enabling a single person to attain the stage of *srotāpanna*.
Why is this? Although one might teach the sentient beings of a single Jambudvīpa to practice the ten wholesome paths of action, they would not yet be liberated from the three evil realms;
whereas by teaching a single person to attain the stage of Srotāpanna, that person has already departed from the three evil realms.

Kauśika! If one were to teach all the sentient beings within a single Jambudvīpa to practice the ten wholesome deeds so that they all attained the stage of Srotāpanna, it would not equal the merit gained by teaching a single person to attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha; the latter yields far more merit.

Kauśika! Even if one were to instruct all the people of Jambudvīpa to abide in the ten wholesome paths of action, causing them all to attain the stages of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, or pratyekabuddha, it would not equal the merit of instructing a single person to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; the latter's virtue is far greater.

Why is this? It is because if even a single person gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it serves to continue the lineage of the Buddhas; for thus the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed. O Kauśika!
From the stream-enterer up to the pratyekabuddha and the Buddha, all are born from the bodhisattva.
Therefore, one should know that if a good man or a good woman takes up a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and bestows it upon another, the merit they obtain is exceedingly great.
Why is this? Because all vast dharmas enter into the *prajñāpāramitā*. It is because of this that one comes to know of the *kṣatriyas*, *brahmins*, and great clans of householders;

it is because of this that one knows of the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; it is because of this that one knows of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge); and it is because of this that one knows of the *srotāpanna* up to the *samyaksambuddha*.

Kauśika! Setting aside the sentient beings of this single Jambudvīpa, and those of the four continents up to the small thousand-world system, the medium thousand-world system, and the great trichiliocosm, as well as the sentient beings filling as many worlds as there are grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges—if one were to teach them all and establish them in the ten wholesome paths of action.

It is not equal to the merit gained by a son or daughter of good family who writes down and upholds the Prajñāpāramitā, and teaches others to write down, uphold, recite, and explain this sūtra; their merit is far, far greater.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son or daughter of good family were to instruct all the sentient beings filling the entirety of Jambudvīpa, causing them to establish themselves in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, and to obtain the five supernormal powers—would that person gain much merit?"
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Very much, very much,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:

"Therefore, it is not as meritorious as when a son or daughter of good family writes down and upholds this Prajñāpāramitā and bestows it upon others, enabling them to write, uphold, recite, and explain the sutra; the latter shall obtain far more merit."
For what reason, Kauśika?
It is because that which is taught as the Prajñāpāramitā is exceedingly vast and far-reaching.

Kauśika! Setting aside this single Jambudvīpa, and even the four continents, the small thousandfold world system, the medium thousandfold world system, the great trichiliocosm, and all the sentient beings filling as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges throughout the ten directions—if you were to teach them all so that they attain the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions, and cause them to obtain the five supernormal powers, would their merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Very many, very many,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:

"Therefore, it is not as good as for a son of good family or a daughter of good family to write down and uphold this Prajñāpāramitā and bestow it upon others, causing them to write it down, uphold it, recite it, and explain its contents; the merit they obtain is far, far greater."
"Furthermore, Kauśika! One who upholds the Prajñāpāramitā does so neither by means of duality nor by non-duality;
one who practices the five pāramitās likewise does so neither by means of two paths nor by non-duality."
Nor does one contemplate internal and external emptiness, as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence, by means of two things;
nor does one practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment on the path by means of two things;
nor does one practice *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) on the path by means of two things.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, by means of countless skillful means,
upholds the Prajñāpāramitā and teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them to study, receive, uphold, recite, explain, and extensively expound its meaning..."
One contemplates the *prajñāpāramitā* through two aspects: neither by means of signs nor by means of signlessness;
neither conjoined nor dispersed; neither appropriate nor inappropriate;
neither raised nor lowered; neither attached nor severed; neither arising nor ceasing; and neither maintained nor not maintained.
It is not maintained, nor does it abide, nor does it not abide; it is neither real nor unreal,
neither defiled nor pure, neither faithful nor faithless, neither dharma nor non-dharma,
neither suchness nor non-suchness, and neither the reality-limit nor non-reality-limit.
Thus it is, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives and upholds the Prajñāpāramitā, and imparts it to others so that they may recite and study it, explaining its meaning, chapters, and phrases clearly in every detail, the merit obtained by teaching others in this way surpasses that of one who merely recites and practices it oneself.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family personally studies the Prajñāpāramitā, recites it, explains it, and makes offerings to it themselves; and furthermore, teaches others to recite, study, and understand its meaning, causing them to distinguish its wisdom with clarity and completeness—then the merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family is most exceptionally and abundantly increased.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Those sons and daughters of good family who receive and study the Prajñāpāramitā should fully receive and understand the meaning of its phrases.”
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is! Kausika!”
Sons and daughters of good family who receive and study the Prajñāpāramitā should fully receive and understand its phrases and meanings.
Those sons and daughters of good family who study in this manner will attain the merit of countless and incalculable roots of goodness.
If there were good sons or good daughters who, for as long as their lives lasted, made offerings to all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions according to their every desire,
would the merit planted by such a person not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra said,
“Very much, very much! The Buddha said:

Therefore, it is not as meritorious for a son of good family or a daughter of good family to do so, as it is for them to uphold the *prajñāpāramitā* through innumerable skillful means and bestow it upon others, enabling them to study, maintain, and practice it, and to fully realize wisdom and understand its words and meanings; the merit and blessings obtained by the latter are far more abundant.

Why is this? Because all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, when they originally practiced the bodhisattva path, all studied within the Prajñāpāramitā and thereby attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
those who study it now shall likewise attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to practice the perfection of giving for incalculable eons, it would not equal the merit of this son of good family or daughter of good family who upholds the Perfection of Wisdom, extensively teaches sentient beings, and remains free from all attachments."
Kauśika! If a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) has any dependence, and gives rise to the thought:
"I am giving this to that person; I am acting in such a way."
To dwell upon giving constitutes a failure to fulfill the dāna-pāramitā.
To say, "I maintain the precepts; these are my precepts," is likewise so.
Thus, he abides in the precepts but does not fulfill the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
He says:
"I practice patience; it is for this reason that I am patient."
Thus, he abides in patience, yet this does not constitute the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
He says:
"I am diligent; I advance for the sake of what is to be accomplished."
He then dwells in diligence, yet this does not constitute the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
He says:
"I practice meditation; I have a purpose for my meditation."
He then dwells in dhyāna, yet this does not constitute the perfection of dhyāna (dhyānapāramitā).
He says:
"I practice wisdom (prajñā), and thus I dwell upon wisdom."
"Because by abiding in wisdom, one fails to accomplish the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Kauśika! A son of good family or a daughter of good family who practices in this manner does not accomplish the six *pāramitās*."
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What practices must a bodhisattva mahāsattva perform in order to fulfill the six pāramitās?
The Buddha told Śakra Devānām Indra:

“When a bodhisattva practices giving, they do not regard it as their own, nor do they regard there being anything given, nor do they regard there being a recipient; this is the practice of the perfection of dāna.”
Even up to the *prajñāpāramitā*, it neither exists nor can it be apprehended; this is what constitutes a bodhisattva’s complete practice of the six *pāramitās*.
Kauśika! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family practices the six *pāramitās* and their interpretive understanding, they should know it in this way.

Why is this? In future ages, there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family who resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and abide in the *prajñāpāramitā*, yet who do not fully hear the *prajñāpāramitā* nor its explanatory meaning, and thus may fail to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, one should provide these people with a complete exposition of the wisdom within the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying,
“For what kind of person should one explain the Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha told Śakra Devānām Indra:
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who teach the Prajñāpāramitā, having taught it, they shall teach it again.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way do sons or daughters of good family teach the Prajñāpāramitā, having taught it, so that they shall teach it again?"
The Buddha said to Śakra-devānām-indra:
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who have newly entered the Prajñāpāramitā, you should explain the Prajñāpāramitā to them."
Having already explained it for them, one should explain it again.
For those who have newly entered [the path], one should explain that form is impermanent, and should speak to them in this way:
"One who practices in this manner is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)."
"To speak in this way is to keep in mind that the five aggregates are impermanent.
When good sons and good daughters speak thus of the impermanence of the five aggregates, they are desiring to initially set out to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*;
when they speak of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) as impermanent, suffering, and empty, they are practicing the six *pāramitās*.
To preach that the eighteen elements are impermanent, suffering, and empty, while practicing the six pāramitās;
to preach that the five aggregates are suffering, empty, and so forth, while practicing the six pāramitās;
and to preach that the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions are impermanent, suffering, and empty, while practicing the six pāramitās.
To teach the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eighteen dharmas, up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and to teach the doctrine of impermanence—

that all things are impermanent, suffering, and empty— and to speak and explain in this manner, is what constitutes teaching those who have newly resolved their minds to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Kauśika! Those who have newly begun their training and first resolved their minds should practice in this way. Furthermore, Kauśika!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has deeply entered the study speaks the *prajñāpāramitā*, they should say to those who are newly trained and have recently resolved their minds:
"You should receive and keep the six *pāramitās* in mind; having received them, you should abide in the first bodhisattva stage, proceeding from the first to the second, up to the tenth stage."
"Forming such a thought, having a thought of attachment and a thought of dependence, one conceives of this as the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Kausika! This is how those who have newly resolved to practice the *prajñāpāramitā* act."
"Furthermore, Kauśika! These sons and daughters of good family further give this instruction, saying:
'You should form this thought regarding the Prajñāpāramitā; having formed this thought, you will transcend the level of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas.'"
"This is the practice for those who have newly resolved their minds.
Furthermore, Kauśika, there are those who practice the bodhisattva path and should say to those who are newly learning: "
"You should receive this Prajñāpāramitā; you shall attain the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

Having attained this patience, you will abide in the supernormal powers (abhijñā) and travel from one Buddha-field to another Buddha-field to pay homage, serve, and revere the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."
"Furthermore, Kauśika! Those who have deeply entered this study should instruct those who are newly trained and have first resolved their minds, saying:
'Good sons and good daughters, you should receive and train in the Prajñāpāramitā in this manner, and you should maintain mindfulness of it in this manner.'"
"Once you have formed this thought, you shall immediately attain immeasurable and incalculable merit, virtue, and blessings.
This is the instruction for those who have newly resolved their minds [on enlightenment].
"Furthermore, Kauśika! A student who has deeply entered the path should instruct a novice student, saying:

'Good son, you should study the roots of goodness and the merits performed by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present; you should maintain single-minded mindfulness until you attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
"This is the instruction for training those who are newly learned.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Having given such instructions and explanations, how should one further instruct those who are newly learned?"
The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying:
"One who has deeply entered the study should further instruct a novice, saying:
'O son of good family!'"
One should practice mindfulness of the Prajñāpāramitā.
When practicing mindfulness of the Prajñāpāramitā, one should not contemplate the five aggregates as impermanent. Why is this?
The five aggregates are empty of their own inherent nature; that which constitutes the five aggregates is non-existent, and that which is non-existent is not the five aggregates.

Within the Prajñāpāramitā, the five aggregates possess neither permanence nor impermanence; since within the Prajñāpāramitā one does not even perceive the five aggregates, how much less could there be permanence or impermanence?
"Kauśika! If a son or daughter of good family speaks in this way, they are not instructing those who have newly begun their training.
One should instead instruct those who have newly begun their training as follows:"
"You should receive and maintain mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
In maintaining mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā*, do not allow it to transcend any phenomena, nor do you dwell in any phenomena."
Why is this? Because in the Prajñāpāramitā, there is no dharma that can transcend it, nor is there any that abides within it. Why is this?
Dharmas are empty by their very nature.
That which is "empty" is non-existent; that which is non-existent is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Within the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is no dharma that can be either appropriate or inappropriate, nor is there any dharma of arising or non-arising.
“Good sons and good daughters who speak in this manner are not teaching those who are newly trained and attached. Kauśika!
Good sons and good daughters should explain the meaning within the Prajñāpāramitā in this way.”
Good sons and good daughters who provide such instruction shall obtain merit far greater than the former.
Furthermore, Kauśika, if a good son or good daughter instructs all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa and causes them to attain the stage of Srotāpanna.
"Would that merit not be great?
Śakra-devānām-indra replied,
"It would be very great, indeed very great!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“It is not as good as this son or daughter of good family who, by means of the Prajñāpāramitā, bestows it upon others, causing them to study, copy, uphold, and explain its meaning.”
The merit obtained by this is exceedingly great, indeed very great.
One teaches this *prajñāpāramitā* to these good sons and good daughters, and they follow that teaching to practice, study, and maintain it.
Why is this? Because all those who follow the path of the srotāpanna are born from the prajñāpāramitā. "Furthermore, Kauśika!
Setting aside this Jambudvīpa, the various four continents, and the trichiliocosm,

suppose there were sentient beings filling as many lands in the eastern direction as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and you were to teach them all until they attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
"Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied,
"It would be very great, indeed very great!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“It is not as great as when a son of good family or a daughter of good family bestows the Prajñāpāramitā upon others, causing them to study, write, uphold, recite, practice, and explain its wisdom; the merit they obtain is exceedingly, exceedingly great.”
Why is this? Because the path of the srotāpanna is born entirely from the prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!"
If all the sentient beings filling Jambudvīpa were taught and led to attain the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat,
would their merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Very many, very many,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:

"It is not as great as when a son of good family or a daughter of good family bestows this Prajñāpāramitā upon others, causing them to study, write it down, uphold it, recite it, and practice it according to its teachings, and explaining the meaning of wisdom therein; the merit obtained from this is far, far greater."
Why is this? Because the path of the srotāpanna up to that of the arhat are all born from the prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

Setting aside this Jambudvīpa and the trichiliocosm, suppose there were sentient beings filling as many lands as there are grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges; and suppose one were to teach them all so that they attained the stage of srotāpanna up to arhatship.
"Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It would be very great, very great!"
The Buddha said:

"It is not as [meritorious] as when a son or daughter of good family bestows the Prajñāpāramitā upon others, causing them to study, write it down, uphold it, recite it, and practice it, and explaining its meaning and wisdom according to its teachings; the merit they obtain is exceedingly great, exceedingly great."
"Furthermore, Kauśika! Suppose all the sentient beings filling a single Jambudvīpa were taught and led to attain the path of a Pratyekabuddha.
Would their merit be great?"
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
“Very much, very much,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:

"It is not as [meritorious] as when a son or daughter of good family bestows the Prajñāpāramitā upon others, causing them to study, write it down, uphold it, recite it, and practice it, and explaining its meaning with wisdom according to its teachings; the merit they obtain is exceedingly great, exceedingly great."
Why is this? Because all pratyekabuddhas are born from the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). "Furthermore, Kauśika!
Setting aside this Jambudvīpa and the trichiliocosm,
suppose all sentient beings in as many lands as there are grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges were taught and led to attain the path of a pratyekabuddha.
"Is the merit not great?
Śakra Devānām-indra replied,
"It is very great, indeed it is very great!"
“World-Honored One!

The Buddha said, “It is not as great as when a son or daughter of good family bestows the Prajñāpāramitā upon others, causing them to study, write, uphold, recite, and practice it, and explaining its wisdom and meaning according to its teachings; the merit they obtain is exceedingly great, exceedingly great.”
Why is this? Because all pratyekabuddhas are born from within the Prajñāpāramitā. "Furthermore, Kauśika!

If there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who instructs all sentient beings filling a single Jambudvīpa and as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, exhorting and assisting them to resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

It is not as meritorious as when these good sons and good daughters bestow the Prajñāpāramitā upon others, instructing them to copy, uphold, recite, and practice it, and explaining its wisdom and meaning for them; the virtue of this is far greater.
He said to that person:
"Receive this Prajñāpāramitā and you should follow its instructions.
Having followed these instructions, you shall attain the benefit of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge)."
Having attained this benefit, you will then fulfill the *prajñāpāramitā*, and you shall thereby realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
"Because all bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds are born from the Prajñāpāramitā. "Furthermore, Kauśika,

if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who were to instruct all the sentient beings filling a single Jambudvīpa and as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and cause them to be established in the state of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression)..."
"Would that merit not be great?
Śakra Devānām Indra replied,
"It would be very great, very great!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Kauśika!”

It is not as good as this: if a son or daughter of good family takes up a scroll of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and bestows it upon another, explaining its central matters and its wisdom of meaning so that they may proclaim and practice it.
He says to that person:

"If you receive and uphold this volume of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra and practice and carry out all as instructed above, you shall then obtain the benefits of all dharmas, up to the attainment of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Why is this? Because the stages of the irreversible Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas all emerge from the Prajñāpāramitā. “Furthermore, Kauśika!
Suppose all sentient beings within a single Jambudvīpa were to become irreversible from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to preach the Prajñāpāramitā and explain its meaning for the sake of such people;
If there were a person who said,

"I wish to quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," and if a son or daughter of good family were to explain the Prajñāpāramitā to that one person, fully providing its meaning and analyzing it for them, their merit would be the greatest.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is intent on attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he must diligently instruct this bodhisattva to practice the six pāramitās; he must instruct him in internal and external emptiness as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha.”
One should instruct these people with this Dharma and provide them with whatever they require, such as clothing and all manner of offerings.
By means of these two matters of Dharma, one should make offerings to these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
“World-Honored One!
The merit obtained by these good sons and good daughters is most supreme, surpassing that which was previously performed. Why is this so?”

"Bhagavān! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should instruct others to practice the six pāramitās in this manner; they should also instruct others to practice internal and external emptiness, the emptiness of existence and non-existence, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and so on up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, in this very same way."
Subhūti said to Śakra Devānām Indra: "Excellent, excellent, Kauśika!"
Thus you have encouraged and assisted these good men and good women who seek the bodhisattva path to such an extent.

According to the dharma of being a worthy disciple of the Buddha as you are, you ought to further benefit the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas by providing them with the gift of Dharma and the gift of offerings, thereby nurturing the bodhisattvas and encouraging them to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples arise from these two kinds of giving.
If a bodhisattva does not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, that bodhisattva will ultimately be unable to study the six *pāramitās* and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

If a bodhisattva does not train in the six pāramitās and the eighteen dharmas of a buddha, they will ultimately never attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor will they know of the existence of arhats or pratyekabuddhas.
Because the Bodhisattva studies the six *pāramitās* and the eighteen *dharmas* of a Buddha, he attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;

the three evil realms are thereby severed. The world then comes to know of the great clans of the *kṣatriyas*, *brahmins*, and householders; it knows of the Four Heavenly Kings and the Heaven of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception; it knows of the six *pāramitās*, from internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) through the emptiness of existence and non-existence (*bhāva-abhāva-śūnyatā*); the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmas*) and the eighteen *dharmas* of a Buddha; and the world then knows of the vehicles of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
Chapter 40: Encouragement and Assistance The Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra, Chapter Forty: Encouragement and Assistance At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya said to Subhūti:

"The likeness of the merit resulting from the encouragement and assistance performed by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is shared with all sentient beings for the sake of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; being free from any expectation of reward, it surpasses [the merit of] all sentient beings."
Regarding the merit and blessings generated by all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they surpass those of all sentient beings.

This includes the likeness of the merit from giving practiced by those who have set out upon the vehicle of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, as well as the likeness of the merit from maintaining the precepts and self-restraint with single-minded concentration.

It is not equal to the merit of this bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, together with all sentient beings, encourages and assists them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; that merit is most honored and foremost, fully perfected and unsurpassed, for all acts of encouragement and assistance are performed so that sentient beings may achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Why is this? The merit of the giving, upholding of precepts, and self-restraint practiced by Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas is intended only for their own discipline, only for their own purification, and only for their own deliverance.
They practice mindfulness of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and mindfulness of the three gates of liberation, seeking only to discipline themselves and attain deliverance for themselves.

The Bodhisattva, however, desires only to discipline sentient beings, to purify sentient beings, and to deliver sentient beings; he exhorts and assists sentient beings toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya:

"Regarding these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, throughout the countless Buddha-fields in the eastern direction, from the time when the countless Buddhas first resolved their minds until their parinirvāṇa as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and further until the complete extinction of the Dharma following their parinirvāṇa—during all that interval, they have performed roots of goodness corresponding to the six *pāramitās*."

Furthermore, it includes the merit of the giving, the observance of precepts, and self-restraint practiced by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; the various untainted precepts; the roots of goodness from the precepts of practice up to the state of no-precepts; and even the blessings of the pure precepts of all Buddhas, the blessings of samādhi, the blessings of wisdom, the blessings of liberation, and the blessings of the knowledge and vision of liberation, as well as great loving-kindness and great compassion, and the teachings spoken by immeasurable asaṃkhyeya Buddhas.

Regarding those who hear and receive [the teaching] from within that Dharma—whether they attain the stage of Srotāpanna up to Arhat, Pratyekabuddha, or even Bodhisattva and all Buddhas who have entered Parinirvāṇa—if one were to calculate and sum together all the merits they have performed, the merit of exhorting and assisting them is the most honored, the most unsurpassed, and the most complete.

I also take up these merits; such merit and blessings from providing encouragement and assistance constitute encouragement and assistance toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and this is precisely what brings about the accomplishment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
These sons and daughters of good family who practice the path of the bodhisattva may form this thought:

"May I obtain such an intention as that which was formed by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past; may I give rise to such an intention and practice; may I attain such a state of mindfulness."
Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Subhūti:

“Good sons and good daughters who have resolved their minds toward bodhicitta do not, by means of these causes and conditions, nor by these marks, nor by forming such conceptions, [seek] anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
Subhūti said to Maitreya Bodhisattva:

"If it is not by means of this attainment, nor by means of these causes and conditions, for what reason do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, from the Buddhas of the ten directions, from their first production of the thought of enlightenment until the exhaustion of the Dharma—taking all roots of goodness, including those who have set out in the vehicle of the śrāvakas, and all my own merits from the precepts up to non-precepts—calculate and aggregate them all together to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"

One should be without conceptualization, lest one give rise to perverted conceptualizations: taking the impermanent to be permanent through perversion of thought, perversion of intention, and perversion of view; taking the impure to be pure; speaking of suffering as pleasure; and taking the non-self to be self.

Using inverted perception, inverted intention, and inverted views, their affairs are like space, their causes and conditions are also like that, the mind of the Way is likewise, the six *pāramitās* are likewise, and even the eighteen *dharmas* are likewise.

If things are thus, then so too is the mind set on enlightenment (bodhicitta), the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā), and likewise the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) and the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana). So too are internal and external emptiness (adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā) and the emptiness of existence and non-existence (abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma), the ten powers (daśabala), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma). What is the thing? What is the causal condition (pratyaya)? What is the path (mārga)? What are the roots of all goodness (kuśalamūla)? What is the intention of encouragement and assistance? And what is the intention of encouragement and assistance in response—to that which seeks anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Subhūti:
"If there is a bodhisattva who practices the six pāramitās, beholds the buddhas of the past, makes offerings to and serves those buddhas, and associates with spiritual friends."

If they have already trained themselves in the emptiness of the body, such persons do not seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of phenomena or appearances, nor by means of these causes and conditions, nor by means of the marks of the Buddha’s roots of goodness, nor by means of the merit of encouragement and assistance, nor by means of the performance of these various blessings.

Furthermore, one should again cultivate this intention: to seek so as not to fall into duality, nor yet into non-duality; neither by means of perception nor by means of non-perception; neither by relying on anything nor by not relying; neither by attachment nor by severance; and neither by arising nor by cessation.

If a bodhisattva does not train in the six pāramitās, does not serve and honor the Buddhas, lacks the roots of all wholesome dharmas, does not encounter spiritual friends, and does not personally study emptiness, yet still seeks anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of these matters, these causes and conditions, these meritorious aids, and these various activities while giving rise to conceptual notions regarding them.
Therefore, Subhūti, one should not speak of the six pāramitās,
nor of internal and external emptiness, the emptiness of existence and non-existence, and the emptiness of all dharmas, before bodhisattvas who have only recently resolved to attain awakening;
one should not explain these to newly trained bodhisattvas.
Why is this? If those who are newly trained should lose their faith or lose their joy, all their reverence will be utterly lost, and they will thereby destroy the roots of all goodness;
therefore, this should be taught for the sake of the *avaivartika* bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
If one has long associated with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), one may also speak to them.
For those who have cultivated merit under various Buddhas in the past, one should preach the Dharma of the characteristic of emptiness (śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa) to such persons.
When this person hears this, they will not be startled, nor terrified, nor fearful.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should provide such encouragement and assistance; yet the intention by which one provides such encouragement, and the intention by which one seeks anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—these intentions have already been extinguished and are no longer present.
The actions that were performed and the merits produced through various causes and conditions are likewise extinguished.

What is the intention of encouragement? What are the manifold activities? What are the causes and conditions? And what are the roots of goodness and merits by which one seeks *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—does one maintain an intention that has something to seek?
The mind has no duality; according to the nature of the mind, it seeks nothing.
If there is a bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā, even the six pāramitās are non-existent; even the five aggregates are non-existent; even the Way is non-existent.

If there are bodhisattvas seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should understand it in this way, seek it in this way, provide assistance in this way, and cultivate the roots of goodness in this way.
"Seeking in this way is to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said to the Elder Subhūti:
"If newly initiated bodhisattvas hear this, will they not become terrified?"
How should one cultivate the roots of goodness and merits with a specific aspiration?
And how should one encourage others and uphold these various merits for the sake of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Subhūti said to Maitreya Bodhisattva:

“A newly initiated bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* and upholding the six *pāramitās* should do so without relying on or grasping anything, and without conceptualization. They should understand internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence (*bhāvābhāva-śūnyatā*). They should understand the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharmāḥ*). They should always associate with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), attain the six *pāramitās* and their underlying meanings, and be instructed so as not to depart from the six *pāramitās*, until they reach the path of a bodhisattva without departing from the Buddha-dharma.
They should be taught about the deeds of Māra; having heard of these deeds of Māra, they should neither increase nor decrease [in their practice].”

Why is this? Upon attaining the bodhisattva path, one constantly contemplates all dharmas and does not depart from the Buddhas; therein one performs meritorious deeds and upholds the tenets of the bodhisattvas, so that until the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one never departs from these merits.

When a newly initiated bodhisattva encourages and assists all the merits performed by the countless Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and their disciples throughout the ten directions; as well as the merits performed by those of the Kṣatriya and Brāhmaṇa castes of great lineage, and the merits performed by the Four Heavenly Kings and the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa realm—he takes these merits of encouragement and assistance and seeks anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi through them. These merits are supreme and unsurpassed.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Subhūti:

"If there is a newly initiated bodhisattva who contemplates all the meritorious virtues of the encouragement and assistance provided by the Buddhas and their disciples, and who, upholding these unsurpassed, incomparable, and immeasurable merits of encouragement and assistance, seeks anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they will not fall into error regarding perceptions, conceptions, or views."

Subhūti said: "Although one brings to mind the Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples, therein there is no perception of a Buddha, nor any perception of an assembly of disciples, nor any perception of the roots of goodness; even when the mind has something to seek, there is no perception of that seeking."
When a bodhisattva seeks in this manner, they are not inverted in perception, not inverted in mindfulness, and not inverted in view.

If a bodhisattva, while recollecting the merits of the Buddhas and the Sangha, and recollecting the roots of goodness they have performed, maintains such perceptions while seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this constitutes a bodhisattva’s inversion of perception, inversion of mindfulness, and inversion of view.

Although a bodhisattva has these thoughts—recalling the Buddha and the assembly, and recalling all roots of goodness—one should know that although these thoughts exist, they are ultimately extinguished and non-existent.

That which can be exhausted is without anything to be sought; if the mind has something it seeks, that is the nature of the mind, and the dharma that is sought is likewise its nature. Although one makes such a seeking, this constitutes right seeking and not perverse seeking.
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should seek in this manner: namely, the merit performed by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as their disciples;
down to the merit performed by ordinary worldlings and the teachings they have heard and received; and those performed by devas, asuras, gandharvas, and mahoragas.
The merit performed by [himself], as well as the merit performed by the kṣatriyas, brahmins, great clans, and elders;
the merit and the teachings received by the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Śuddhāvāsa devas;
and all the resolve generated to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—taking all these together and combining them into one mass...
To plan for it, to praise it, and to regard it as such— thereby encouraging and assisting all the merit one has performed—
and to rely upon this merit of encouragement and assistance to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If one should know that these dharmas have already ended and ceased, such that there is no further dharma to be sought and they are likewise exhausted and empty—
if one makes this kind of seeking, it is for the sake of seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
One should understand it thus: phenomena do not seek phenomena. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are inherently empty.
One who seeks in this manner seeks for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
When a bodhisattva practices the six *pāramitās* in this way, they are unerring regarding perceptions and unerring regarding mindfulness and views.
Why is this? Because they do not enter into that which is sought.
Since they do not perceive any place where the roots of goodness and the aspiration for the Way (bodhicitta) could enter, this constitutes the unsurpassed seeking of a bodhisattva.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is quiescent and without production regarding all merits; he is likewise quiescent and without production regarding the five aggregates, the eighteen elements, the six sense bases, and up to the six perfections; and he is quiescent and without cognitive apprehension regarding internal and external emptiness, the emptiness of existence and non-existence, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
When a bodhisattva thus knows that quiescence is without anything to be attained, this is what constitutes seeking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva knows that the merit of exhortation and assistance is quiescent and unarisen; that the Buddha is quiescent and the Buddha’s activities are quiescent; that all fundamental wholesome practices are quiescent and those fundamental wholesome practices are quiescent; that all matters of the path-mind are quiescent and those matters of the path-mind are quiescent; that all matters of seeking are quiescent and those matters of seeking are quiescent; that all matters of the bodhisattvas are quiescent and those matters of the bodhisattvas are quiescent; that the matters of the six *pāramitās* are quiescent and those matters of the six *pāramitās* are quiescent; and even up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha being quiescent and those eighteen qualities of a buddha being quiescent.
In this way, a bodhisattva should practice the pure and tranquil conduct of the *prajñāpāramitā*; this is what it means for a bodhisattva to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.

All the roots of goodness cultivated by the Buddhas of the past, and whatever they sought, have all entered *parinirvāṇa*; a bodhisattva mahāsattva should likewise seek in this manner, such that the roots of goodness he cultivates and that which he seeks are like *nirvāṇa*.

When the intention that seeks and the intention that is sought are exactly equal and no different, seeking in this manner and knowing in this manner—this is what it means to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
One who seeks in this manner possesses no perversion in perception, no perversion in mindfulness, and no perversion in view.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* through conceptualization and uses such conceptualization to recollect the merits of the Buddhas, this constitutes not seeking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The Buddhas of the past were neither possessed of thought nor devoid of thought. If one again forms a recollection or again forms a thought, this constitutes not seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; it is a perversion of thought, a perversion of recollection, and a perversion of view.

Furthermore, if one does not dwell upon the roots of goodness of all Buddhas, and regarding all instances of generating the resolve [for enlightenment], neither forms a cognition nor forms a conceptualization, this is indeed seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is the non-perverted conceptualization of a bodhisattva, and the non-perverted mindfulness and vision.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Subhūti:
"In what way does a bodhisattva have a seeking yet remain without conceptualization? Subhūti replied:
"A bodhisattva who wishes to attain *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one does not seek the *prajñāpāramitā*, one will ultimately never obtain the merits that are the roots of all goodness."

Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not manifest within the Prajñāpāramitā; nor are the roots of goodness seen as manifold phenomena, nor is there any mind perceived that can achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What has been done is extinguished, and all activities are also extinguished; I merely give rise to these various conceptions, these various wholesome merits, and these various resolves by myself.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, likewise have no conceptual seeking, no such encouragement or assistance, and no such cognition.
Why is this? Because one seeks through conceptualization that which cannot be obtained.
If conceptualization were something that could be obtained, then the conceptualizations constructed by myself and all the Buddhas would indeed have something to be obtained.
Therefore, regarding the merits of a bodhisattva and whatever a bodhisattva seeks, one should neither form conceptualizations nor rely upon anything.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not praise those who seek while relying on conceptualization.
Why is this? For those who seek through conceptualization, it is like poison mixed [with food].
It is, for example, like pure and delicious food that has come into contact with poison; although its color and fragrance are exquisite, it is nonetheless poisoned.
If there is a foolish person who wishes to eat it, although they may crave its fine color, fragrance, and delicious taste at the time, it will later prove detrimental to their body.

Receiving [the teachings] in such a manner, they do not contemplate them with clarity nor know them with clarity; they do not understand how to recite them, they misinterpret their inner meaning, and being unable to understand it themselves, they speak to others, saying:
"O son of good family!..."

This teaching comprises all the merits performed by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present—from the time they first resolved their minds until they attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, from their remaining in *sa-upādi-śeṣa-nirvāṇa* to their entry into *an-upādi-śeṣa-nirvāṇa*, and even until the exhaustion of the Dharma—including the practice of the *prajñā-pāramitā* and the six *pāramitās* during that interval; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four *dhyānas*, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; the ten powers and the eighteen unique qualities through which roots of goodness were produced; as well as the purification of Buddha-fields and the instruction of sentient beings.

The merit made among the śrāvakas regarding the Buddhas’ categories of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), the quality of non-forgetfulness, and constant equanimity;

as well as the merit made by those whom the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have prophesied as pratyekabuddhas, and by the devas, nāgas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas—all these merits taken together and gathered into one, he maintains them to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"To rely on conceptual thought while seeking the Samyaksambuddha is like food mixed with poison.
One who possesses such reliance on conceptual thought will ultimately achieve nothing. Why is this?"

To have reliance, to have conceptualization, and to have a formal appearance while seeking that which is mixed with poison is to slander the Tathāgata; such a person neither accepts the teaching of the Tathāgata nor accepts the Dharma.
"Good sons and good daughters who practice the bodhisattva path should form this thought:
'Regarding all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present—from the time they first resolved their minds until they attained Buddhahood—what was it that they sought to accomplish?'"

And as for the deeds performed by the various disciples within the sphere of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), the case above is also like this: how should one perform deeds in order to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
“Good sons and good daughters who seek the bodhisattva path and do not wish to be superior or inferior to the Tathāgatas should make this aspiration:

‘Just as that which is known by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—namely, the characteristics of eloquence, wisdom, and all roots of goodness that accord with the Dharma—I uphold and assist these; whatever Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi I seek is entirely what is known by the Buddhas.’”
"Good sons and good daughters who seek the bodhisattva path do not rely upon the merits of various roots of goodness to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
One who seeks in this manner does not treat the Tathāgata with partiality; such a person is a bodhisattva who has faith in the Buddha and faith in the Dharma.
One who practices in this manner is untainted by poison, and that which they seek shall likewise be free from poison.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family seeks the bodhisattva path and practices the perfection of wisdom, they should seek their merit in this manner.

One does not cling to the five aggregates; one does not cling to the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm. One does not cling to the six *pāramitās* of the past, future, or present; one does not cling to the three realms. One does not cling to the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of existence and non-existence, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Buddha, or the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). One does not cling to the three realms. One does not cling to the suchness (*tathatā*) of the past, future, or present; nor to the nature of phenomena as they arise, the nature of phenomena as they cease, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the inconceivable nature, morality, patience, wisdom, liberation, the vision and knowledge of liberation, omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the state of no-losing, or the constant and equal practice.
One who is unattached to the three realms does not exist in the past, future, or present. Why is this?
Because there is nothing into which they enter.

Those who have something to seek do not enter into anything; the dharmas that are sought likewise have no attachment, and these persons also have no attachment. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, likewise have no attachment; all other roots of goodness have no attachment; and even the roots of goodness of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have no attachment.
Those who are thus unattached do not belong to the past, future, or present.

If there is a bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā, they know that the five aggregates are not to be clung to, and that the three realms are neither past, future, nor present; furthermore, they must not rely on conceptualization or have anything to seek.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive anything that arises.

That which has no arising also has no existence; that which has no existence cannot perform any action. Thus, one does not even become attached to the six pāramitās, nor to the practice of non-extinction, permanence, and so forth.
The three realms are likewise neither past, future, nor present; that which is neither past, future, nor present cannot be grasped through conceptual thought or purposeful action. Why is this?
Because that which is produced is unattainable.
All that is produced is non-existent, and that which is non-existent cannot perform any action;
this is the bodhisattva’s seeking free from poison.

If a son or daughter of good family seeks the bodhisattva path with a mind of attachment, it is a perverted seeking; if they seek the roots of goodness they have performed with a mind of attachment, it is a perverted seeking.
Those who seek through wrong means are not praised by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Those whom the Buddhas do not praise are those who have not fully perfected the six pāramitās.

One who is not fully endowed with the six pāramitās is then not fully endowed with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; they are then not fully endowed with internal and external emptiness, nor with the emptiness of existence and non-existence; and they are then not fully endowed with the ten powers of a Buddha and the eighteen unique dharmas.
One who is not endowed with these eighteen dharmas cannot purify a buddha-field, cannot instruct sentient beings, and will ultimately fail to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Because there is a pursuit mixed with poison.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should form this thought:

"Just as the Buddhas seek the dharmas of the roots of goodness and merit that they know, and just as they seek them for the sake of seeking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I too shall seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of these same dharmas."
At that time, the Buddha praised Subhūti, saying: “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”
He then performed the deeds of a World-Honored One, being able to expound for all bodhisattvas the Dharma regarding what is to be practiced and what is to be sought.

It is without conceptualization, without dependence, and without emergence; neither severed nor attached, neither existent nor non-existent; it accords with the mark of emptiness, accords with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and accords with suchness.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Suppose all sentient beings within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were to obtain the benefits of the ten wholesome paths of action, and were to fully attain the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, and the five supernormal powers—should they all obtain such benefits."
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is the merit obtained by these sentient beings great or not?
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is very great, very great!"
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“It is not as [great] as when these good sons and good daughters, regarding all roots of goodness, give rise to nothing and cling to nothing, taking this as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This merit is the most honored transformation, the unsurpassed, truly correct transformation, and the complete transformation.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose all sentient beings within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were to attain the stage of srotāpanna, up to arhat and pratyekabuddha."

If there are good men or good women who, for the duration of their entire lives, provide offerings to these types of arhats and pratyekabuddhas—providing whatever they require of food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites for illness—and honor and sustain them with all that they possess.
"What do you think, Subhūti? Would that merit be great?
Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, very great!"
The Buddha said:

"It is not as good as this son or daughter of good family who dwells in non-arising and non-attachment, seeking nothing from the virtues of the roots of goodness; their merit is most honored and supreme."
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose all the sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to set their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Then, suppose every single one of those sentient beings throughout as many world-systems as there are sands in the Ganges in the ten directions were to provide offerings to this bodhisattva for as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges—providing whatever food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine they required, while attending to, honoring, and serving them with reverence."
"What do you think, Subhūti? Would that merit be great?
Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, very great!"
"World-Honored One!
That merit is so vast it is incalculable and beyond counting!"
"It cannot be compared by means of analogy.
If merit were to have a physical form, even the empty space of the ten directions would not be able to contain it.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Though one were to perform such merit, it would not equal the roots of goodness performed by these sons and daughters of good family, who give rise to nothing and cling to nothing, and who seek nothing from the virtue of those roots of goodness."
The merit of these sons and daughters of good family is the most honored, the most supreme, incomparable, and unsurpassed transformation.
This merit, which is unarisen and unattached, cannot be compared to the previous merit even by a hundred thousand million times.

Why is this? Because these good men and good women possess reliance and conceptualization; they fully possess the ten wholesome deeds, as well as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, and the five supernormal powers.
Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family provide offerings to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, up to and including the bodhisattvas, by means of conceptual attachment.
At that time, twenty thousand devaputras from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings all joined their palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) employed by the bodhisattva in his giving is most excellent and truly marvelous!”

Having performed these deeds, one should be without dependence and without attachment; one should be empty and signless. The roots of goodness from such giving are for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and such giving constitutes the entrance into non-duality.

At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra, together with innumerable Trāyastriṃśa devas and their sons, carrying celestial mixed flowers, powdered incense, liquid perfumes, silk banners, flower canopies, celestial robes, celestial curtains, and multicolored flags and pennants, and playing celestial music, came to where the Buddha was. They made offerings by scattering them over the Buddha and all praised him, saying:
"The practice of giving performed by the Bodhisattva is skillful means (upāyakauśalya); how excellent and wonderful it is!"

Having performed what was to be done, one should be without dependence and without attachment; one should dwell in emptiness and signlessness, dedicating the roots of goodness from all giving toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and practicing giving as the entrance into non-duality.

Upwards to the Brahmakāyika devas, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads, they likewise praised the bodhisattva’s *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), all of them doing so in this same manner.
The Akaniṣṭha devas, together with immeasurable billions of hundreds of thousands of devas, came to where the Buddha was, paid homage to him, and in unison raised their voices, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
How truly marvelous and great!
The roots of goodness produced by practicing skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) within the *prajñāpāramitā* surpass the merits achieved by those sons and daughters of good family in the past.
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed the Four Heavenly Kings and the various devaputras of Akaniṣṭha, saying:
"Suppose all sentient beings within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were to become *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
and further, were to take the place of all Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present..."
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, rejoices on their behalf;

he rejoices on behalf of the assembly of disciples—from their first resolution until their parinirvāṇa, and even until the exhaustion of the Dharma—for all the roots of goodness they have cultivated during that interval;
he rejoices on behalf of the roots of goodness cultivated by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; and furthermore...
He rejoices on behalf of all the roots of goodness performed by sentient beings, from the practice of the *dāna-pāramitā* up to the *prajñā-pāramitā*;

he rejoices on behalf of all the categories of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the vision and knowledge of liberation possessed by the noble ones; and likewise for all other immeasurable qualities of the Buddha-dharma.
Calculating and summing them all together, one should rejoice on behalf of all these aforementioned merits;
relying upon the merit of this rejoicing on behalf of others, one should [direct it] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, if there are good sons or good daughters who wish to set forth toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and who, on behalf of all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas—from the initial resolution until the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—rejoice in their practice of the six *pāramitās* during that interval, as well as in their other countless Buddha-dharma merits, doing so without expectation and entering into non-duality; having already conformed to the signless (*animitta*), conformed to non-attachment (*asaṅga*), and conformed to emptiness (*śūnyatā*)—this is the foremost and primary rejoicing on their behalf, the unsurpassed rejoicing on their behalf.

If one takes these merits of sympathetic joy and, for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, remains without any attachment, then the merit and blessings of this surpass those performed by the aforementioned good men and good women who practice sympathetic joy; compared to their merit, it is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even hundreds of billions of times greater. This is the supreme practice of sympathetic joy performed by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the World-Honored One has said, if one were to collect the merits of these sons and daughters of good family, among all such merits, none surpasses that of sympathetic joy."
"There is no virtue of sympathetic joy that surpasses this virtue. Subhūti said:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the most supreme? What is the most venerable?
The Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying:

"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, regarding the dharmas of the future, past, and present, neither grasps nor rejects them; neither becomes arrogant nor non-arrogant; neither relies upon anything nor does not rely upon anything; and regarding these dharmas, there is neither arising nor ceasing, neither attachment nor severance; and within these dharmas, they see neither increase nor decrease, neither going nor returning, neither the path nor the mundane—just as it is with the dharmas of the past, future, and present, and likewise with the dharmas that are thus, the dharmas that abide, and the dharmas that cease—I too shall rejoice on their behalf. Taking this merit of rejoicing, I dedicate it toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and bestow it upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas."
To rejoice on behalf of one who performs such acts of giving is the foremost; there is nothing that surpasses this rejoicing on their behalf. Subhūti!

This merit of rejoicing on behalf of others, compared to other merits of rejoicing, is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, even a hundred millionfold greater; it cannot be matched by those other forms of rejoicing.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

A son of good family or a daughter of good family who practices the bodhisattva path, wishing to take upon themselves the roots of goodness performed by all Buddhas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas of the past, future, and present—from their first resolution until their attainment of buddhahood, including all the roots of goodness they cultivated during that interval, such as the practice of the six pāramitās and other countless roots of goodness of the Buddha-dharma."

If one wishes to rejoice on behalf of others, and further wishes to rejoice on behalf of all sentient beings for the roots of goodness they have performed, one should practice this rejoicing in such a manner; this rejoicing is the most supreme.
The six pāramitās are equal to liberation;
liberation is equal to the five aggregates;
and the reality of that liberation is equal to internal and external emptiness.
The matter of liberation is equal to existence, non-existence, emptiness, and so forth;
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are equal to liberation;
and the ten powers are equal to liberation.
Liberation is equal to the wisdom that perceives liberation;
the dharmas of the past, future, and present are equal to liberation;
and liberation is itself the liberation of the past, future, and present, just as it is enacted by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Liberation is like the disciples of the Buddhas;
the disciples of the Buddhas are also like liberation;
liberation is equal to the *nirvāṇa* of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
The matter of liberation is equal to the Dharma of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
liberation is also like that of the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas;
liberation is likewise like the Dharma of all dharmas.

Regarding these dharmas that are neither bound nor liberated, these dharmas that are unattached, as if non-existent, undefiled, and pure; regarding these dharmas that are neither produced nor non-produced, neither extinguished nor non-extinguished—I perform my acts for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in accordance with these aforementioned dharmas: dharmas that are not bound, not defeated, and not destroyed.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This is the unsurpassed sympathetic joy of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, which is the most supreme.
The Buddha said:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva fully practices such sympathetic joy on behalf of others, they will swiftly attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).”
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who practice the bodhisattva path, and throughout their entire lives they make offerings to the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions, along with their assemblies of disciples, providing them with whatever food, clothing, bedding, and medicine they require for the full duration of those Buddhas' lives.
