After those Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, they continue to serve their relics day and night, making offerings of banners, streamers, flowers, canopies, and music. Yet, while constantly mindful of practicing the six pāramitās, they still harbor a basis for attachment."

Furthermore, there are good men and good women who wish to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, practicing the six *pāramitās* with *upāya-kauśalya* while remaining without attachment, and maintaining these merits without harboring any expectations regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Compared to the merit of those roots of goodness, this merit of joy in this present life is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a myriad of billions of times greater; it is the most honored and supreme. Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six pāramitās, by means of skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) and merit that is without dependence, they do so for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, remaining without dependence.
The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Eight.
The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mokṣala of Khotan during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Translated by Imperial Decree.
Chapter 41: Illumination. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Forty-one: Illumination. Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Is this the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said, "It is."
"Śāriputra! Śāriputra replied,
"World-Honored One!"
World-Honored One, the perfection of wisdom acts as illumination;
World-Honored One,
the perfection of wisdom is ultimately pure.
"Bhagavān! Prajñāpāramitā has a name. Bhagavān!"
"O World-Honored One, the Prajñāpāramitā is unstained by the three realms;
the Prajñāpāramitā eliminates all defilements and darkness."
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is the most supreme among the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
World-Honored One!
“O Bhagavān, the Prajñāpāramitā brings peace to all calamities and terrors; O Bhagavān,
the Prajñāpāramitā acts as a light for those obscured by the five kinds of deluded views.”
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā acts as the correct guide for boundless sentient beings who have entered upon deviant paths.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is the Sarvajña; it is able to eliminate all residual habitual tendencies.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of the Bodhisattvas, for she gives birth to all Buddha-dharmas.
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is neither born nor destroyed, because it proceeds from having a name to ultimate emptiness.
World-Honored One!”
The Prajñāpāramitā is detached from birth and death, yet it does not bring about their cessation, for it does not act as their basis.
World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā receives those who are solitary and destitute, acting as a gift of precious jewels for them.
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is fully perfected; from the very beginning, there has been nothing capable of subduing it.
World-Honored One!”
The Prajñāpāramitā turns the wheel of Dharma through the three turnings and twelve aspects; yet there is no one who can turn it, for that which is turned never moves or returns.
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is able to manifest the root of all various things, as well as the emptiness of both existence and non-existence.
World-Honored One, how should one dwell in the Prajñāpāramitā?”
The World-Honored One replied:
"Śāriputra, you should dwell as the World-Honored One dwells."
One should pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā as one would pay homage to the World-Honored One. Why is this?
Because the Prajñāpāramitā is the World-Honored One; there is no distinction between the World-Honored One and the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Prajñāpāramitā is the Bhagavān, and the Bhagavān is the Prajñāpāramitā.

It is because of the Prajñāpāramitā that the Buddhas, the Bhagavāns, receive their names; likewise, from Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, down to Srotāpannas, all receive their names because of the Prajñāpāramitā.

The ten wholesome paths of action, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, the five supernormal powers, internal and external emptiness as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Buddha and the eighteen unique qualities, up to and including sarvajñatā—all these are born from the prajñāpāramitā.
Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra thought to himself:
"For what reason has the Venerable Śāriputra raised this question?
Śakra Devānām Indra then asked Śāriputra:
“Venerable sir!
For what reason have you raised this question?
On account of what matter is there this question?”
Śāriputra replied: "Kauśika!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) and being sustained by the *prajñāpāramitā*, as well as by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present—from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until the end of the Dharma—takes all the roots of goodness cultivated during that interval and dedicates them entirely to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)."
Kauśika! For this reason, the bodhisattva mahāsattva who upholds the prajñāpāramitā surpasses the other five pāramitās. Kauśika!

It is like a person born blind, whether there be a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand such people, who wish to go somewhere or enter a city; without a guide, they will ultimately be unable to reach their destination.

Kauśika! These five pāramitās are like those who are blind; separated from the prajñāpāramitā, they are like blind people without a guide. They cannot fulfill the path to enlightenment, nor can they achieve sarvajñatā.
The five pāramitās are protected by the prajñāpāramitā, like those who are blind obtaining eyes.
The prajñāpāramitā protects the five pāramitās, enabling each of the five pāramitās to obtain its respective name.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to Śāriputra:
"If it is as you say—that the five perfections receive their names because of the perfection of wisdom—then do the five perfections exist only as names and lack actual crossing-over?"
Śāriputra said: "It is so, Kauśika!
The five pāramitās receive their names because of the prajñāpāramitā; the five pāramitās have only a name, but they do not possess the quality of crossing over."

For a bodhisattva who dwells in the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the five perfections are already fully accomplished; therefore, among the five perfections, the perfection of wisdom is the supreme transformation, the sublime transformation, and the peerless transformation.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should one enter into the Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said:
“Just as one enters the five aggregates, so should one enter the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Just as one enters the five perfections, so should one enter the perfection of wisdom.”

Just as one enters into internal and external emptiness and the emptiness of existence and non-existence; just as one enters into the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Buddha, and the eighteen unique qualities; just as one enters into omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and all phenomena (*dharmas*), so should one enter into the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Śāriputra said: “World-Honored One,
how does one enter the five aggregates in the same manner as entering the Prajñāpāramitā?”
"How does one enter the Prajñāpāramitā by entering into all dharmas?
The Buddha said:
"One should enter the Prajñāpāramitā by regarding the five aggregates as neither produced nor obtained, neither grasped nor relinquished, and neither destroyed."
"In all phenomena there is no arising and nothing to be obtained; there is no grasping, no relinquishing, and nothing to be destroyed—this is the entry into the Prajñāpāramitā.
Śāriputra said: "If one enters the Prajñāpāramitā in this manner, with what dharma does one coincide?"
The Buddha said:
“That which reaches nothing among all dharmas is the very designation for Prajñāpāramitā.
[Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!”
"What dharma does he not attain?

The Buddha said, "He does not attain wholesome dharmas, nor does he attain unwholesome dharmas; he does not attain dharmas of the Path, nor does he attain worldly dharmas; he does not attain outflowing or non-outflowing dharmas, nor does he attain conditioned or unconditioned dharmas."
Why is this? The arising of the *prajñāpāramitā* does not arise from any aspiration.
For this reason, it reaches nothing among all phenomena and attains nothing.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it, World-Honored One?
Does this Prajñāpāramitā not reach sarvajñatā?"
The Buddha said:
"It is so, Kauśika! The Prajñāpāramitā does not reach sarvajñatā; it neither reaches it nor exists."
“World-Honored One!
How is it that there is neither attainment nor existence?
The Buddha said:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is neither by means of letters, nor by means of conceptualization, nor by means of birth and death.
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
“World-Honored One!”
"Furthermore, it is not by means of letters, nor by means of conceptualization, nor by means of birth and death; how then can there be 'attainment'?
The Buddha said:
"It is like not entering, neither accepting, nor rejecting, nor abiding; thus one acts as if reaching, yet as if not reaching."
"Kauśika! Thus does the Prajñāpāramitā attain the suchness of all dharmas, yet there is nothing attained.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The arising of the Prajñāpāramitā is most marvelous and extraordinary!
Regarding all dharmas, it is without production, without existence, without dependence, and without destruction.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, does he attain all dharmas?
Or does he not attain all dharmas?"
When a bodhisattva hears this, they may become fearful or terrified, and thus depart from the prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha said: "It is so;
when a bodhisattva hears this, they may indeed become afraid."
If there is a bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā who should think thus:
"The prajñāpāramitā is empty; the prajñāpāramitā has no solidity; the prajñāpāramitā deceives people."
One who forms such a thought is able to distance themselves from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
By this cause and condition, the bodhisattva then distances themselves from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"One who has faith in the Prajñāpāramitā—of what dharmas would they have no faith?
The Buddha said:

"To have faith in the *prajñāpāramitā* is to have no faith in form (*rūpa*), to have no faith in sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*); it is to have no faith in the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), no faith in forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects (*dharmas*); it is to have no faith in the eighteen elements (*dhātus*) and the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), nor even the five *pāramitās*; it is also not to have faith in internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) or the emptiness of existence and non-existence (*bhāva-abhāva-śūnyatā*); it is not to have faith in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmas*) or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharmas*), nor the ten powers of a Buddha (*daśa-tathāgatabalāni*); it is not to have faith in the stages from the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) up to the arhat or the pratyekabuddha; it is not to have faith in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor is it to have faith in *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge)."
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If the five aggregates and sarvajñatā do not exist, this constitutes a lack of faith in the prajñāpāramitā.
For this reason, Subhūti!"
One who has faith in the Prajñāpāramitā does not have faith in the five aggregates, all dharmas, or sarvajñatā.
If the five aggregates and all dharmas do not exist, one does not have faith in the Prajñāpāramitā;
one who has faith in the Prajñāpāramitā does not have faith in any dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is a great deliverance.”
The Buddha said:
"What do you think? By what means do you know that the Prajñāpāramitā is the great vehicle? Subhūti replied:

“Prajñāpāramitā does not cause the five aggregates to be large, nor does it cause the five aggregates to be small; it does not cause the five pāramitās to be large, nor does it cause the five pāramitās to be small.”
From the emptiness of the internal and external up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence, they cause neither enlargement nor diminution.
Regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, they likewise cause neither enlargement nor diminution.
The ultimate Way and the Buddha-dharma are neither made great nor made small.
They do not aggregate the five aggregates nor disperse the five aggregates; even the Buddha-dharma is neither aggregated nor dispersed.

Furthermore, the five aggregates are neither characterized by inequality nor characterized by non-inequality; even the Buddha-dharma is neither characterized by inequality nor characterized by non-inequality.
Moreover, the five aggregates are neither broad nor narrow; even the Buddha-dharma is neither broad nor narrow.
Nor does one cause the five aggregates to be strong, nor does one cause them to be weak; even up to the Buddha-dharma, one causes it neither to be strong nor to be weak.
World-Honored One!
For this reason!
The Prajñāpāramitā is the great vehicle of the bodhisattva.
World-Honored One,

if a newly resolved bodhisattva who has not yet practiced the six pāramitās hears that these five aggregates and the six pāramitās neither increase nor decrease, and possess neither expansion nor contraction.
Those who hear these words might fail to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*. Why is this?

It is not because of the *prajñāpāramitā* that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and the Buddha-dharmas have greatness or smallness; it is not because of the *prajñāpāramitā* that the five aggregates and the Buddha-dharmas have strength or weakness.
World-Honored One!

To practice the perfection of wisdom while seeking the five aggregates in their great or small aspects, or desiring the strength or weakness of the Buddha-dharma, constitutes a great burden. Why is this?
The Way is from the beginning free from any thought of defilement. Why is this?
Because sentient beings are unarisen and the Prajñāpāramitā is unarisen; one should view it thus and know it thus.
One should contemplate that the five aggregates are unarisen and that the Buddha-dharma is also unarisen;
one should contemplate all that exists in the prajñāpāramitā as one contemplates all that exists in sentient beings.
One should contemplate the existence of the prajñāpāramitā as one contemplates the existence of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha).
One should contemplate the existence of the Buddha as one contemplates the existence of the prajñāpāramitā.
To contemplate that the *prajñāpāramitā* is non-existent is like contemplating that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are non-existent.
To contemplate that the *prajñāpāramitā* is non-existent is like contemplating that the Buddha is non-existent.
One contemplates that the prajñāpāramitā is non-existent, just as one contemplates that sentient beings are also non-existent.
One contemplates that the prajñāpāramitā is quiescent, and one contemplates that sentient beings are also quiescent.
One contemplates that the *prajñāpāramitā* is quiescent, and one contemplates that the Buddha-dharmas are also quiescent.
One contemplates that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are quiescent, and one contemplates that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also quiescent.
Since the *prajñāpāramitā* has no beginning, one should know that sentient beings likewise have no beginning.
The five aggregates and the Buddha-dharmas likewise have no beginning; the Prajñāpāramitā also has no beginning.
The Prajñāpāramitā is inconceivable; one should know that sentient beings are also inconceivable, the five aggregates are also inconceivable, and the Buddha-dharmas are also inconceivable.
Since sentient beings are not subject to destruction, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also not subject to destruction.

Since sentient beings do not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* also does not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; one should know that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) also do not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and even the Buddha does not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If the power of sentient beings is incomplete, one should know that the power of the *prajñāpāramitā* is incomplete, the power of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) is incomplete, and the power of the Buddha is likewise incomplete.
"For this reason, World-Honored One, the Great Deliverer is the Prajñāpāramitā of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. 42.
The Chapter on Niraya. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā, Chapter Forty-Two, the Chapter on Niraya. Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
From where does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva who understands the *prajñāpāramitā* come to be born in this world?
And for how long has he set out for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
How many Tathāgatas have you further seen and made offerings to?
For how long have you practiced the six pāramitās?
And how do you understand the profound meaning of the introduction to the Prajñāpāramitā?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have made offerings to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions, and have come from there to be born in this world.”
Since this bodhisattva first resolved [on enlightenment], incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed, and his practice of the six pāramitās has likewise been incalculable.
Having come to this realm, the time since then is again beyond calculation; he has constantly made offerings to all Buddhas and has now been born here.
When these bodhisattvas see the Prajñāpāramitā, it is no different from seeing the World-Honored One.
When they hear the Prajñāpāramitā, it is no different from hearing what the World-Honored One has spoken.

This bodhisattva mahāsattva understands the profound meaning of the entrance into the perfection of wisdom; they do not enter by means of conceptualization, nor do they enter by means of duality, remaining without any dependence.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
can the Prajñāpāramitā be seen or heard?"
The Buddha said:
"It cannot be seen or heard. Why is this?"
Subhūti, the Prajñāpāramitā is neither a matter of seeing nor a matter of hearing.
The Prajñāpāramitā is neither heard nor seen, because all dharmas are deaf.
As for the five perfections, they are neither seen nor heard, because all dharmas are deaf.
Internal and external emptiness, as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence, are neither heard nor seen, because all dharmas are deaf.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the eighteen unique qualities, there is nothing seen and nothing heard, because all dharmas are deaf. Subhūti!
"The Path and the Buddha are likewise neither seen nor heard, for they are like the dharma of the deaf.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For how long must a bodhisattva mahāsattva study the prajñāpāramitā before he should be considered to be in accord with the prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti: “This matter should be analyzed, Subhūti!”

There are causes and conditions by which a bodhisattva, as soon as they first resolve their mind [on enlightenment], should correspond with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*; through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they do not perceive any hope for the glory of dharmas, never slandering them, never departing from the six *pāramitās*, and never departing from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Furthermore, if one wishes to establish the foundation for all roots of goodness and to make offerings to and serve the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, then according to one's wish, one shall go from one Buddha-land to another Buddha-land; one shall never again undergo birth from a mother’s womb, shall never be separated from the five supernormal powers, shall not associate with various defilements, nor shall one associate with the mentalities of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, while teaching and transforming sentient beings and purifying the Buddha-lands.
A bodhisattva who practices in this manner accords with the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

Subhūti, furthermore, there are sons of good family and daughters of good family practicing the bodhisattva path who have seen countless, incalculable, and asankhyeya Buddhas; yet, while practicing the six *pāramitās*, they harbor attachments, and upon hearing the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they immediately abandon it and depart.
In this way, such bodhisattvas give rise to conceited thoughts; they then become separated from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and consequently fail to hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Those who do not delight in hearing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* are also sitting here in this assembly."
Why is this? Because when these sons and daughters of good family practice the bodhisattva path, having heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā* from the beginning, they do not delight in abandoning it.

For this reason, upon hearing this profound Prajñāpāramitā now, they do not rejoice but instead wish to abandon it; their body, speech, and mind are not in harmony with it, thereby accumulating the karmic offenses of lack of wisdom.
Because this offense is so grave, one rejects and opposes the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
To reject and oppose the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is to reject and oppose the *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Because they have committed the offense of opposing omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they sever omniscience.

Due to the offense of severing omniscience, they shall enter the hells and be boiled for countless hundreds of thousands of years; emerging from one hell, they go to another, until at the time of the conflagration at the end of the kalpa, they must again go to the great hells of other directions.

When that other world-system reaches the end of the kalpa, he shall again go from one niraya in another world-system to yet another niraya in a different world-system, thus traversing all the nirayas of those other world-systems.

Because of this sin of abandoning the Dharma, one shall again come to be born in this intermediate niraya, where one must undergo the severe pains of that hell; until the end of the kalpa, one shall fall into the realm of animals in other directions.
In this manner, they will successively fall into the various realms of animals throughout the ten directions.
Emerging from the animal realm, they shall be born in the Yama world, assuming the form of a preta and undergoing extreme and intense suffering.
After such a long time, they may finally obtain human form;

yet wherever they are born, they will always be born into families of the congenitally blind, or into families of executioners, or into families of fishermen, hunters, and butchers, or into families of low-caste beggars. They will be either blind, or deaf, or lacking hands and feet, or mute and unable to speak.
Having undergone these punishments, they shall further be reborn in borderlands where there is no Buddha, no Dharma, and no disciples.
Those who commit such acts of destroying the Dharma must all fully undergo these supreme offenses.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"One who severs these dharmas shall fall into the five immediate offenses.
The Buddha said:
"The offense of thus rejecting the Dharma cannot be fully described.
While this Prajñāpāramitā is being taught, if one rejects it by saying of others:
'This is not the Vinaya; this is not the teaching of the Honored One; this is not the teaching of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.'"
Not practicing and training oneself, one further cuts others off and causes them to distance themselves from it;
losing one’s own resolve, one further loses the resolve of others;
poisoning one’s own mind, one further poisons the minds of others.
Having lost it for themselves, they cause others to lose it as well;
not understanding the profound *prajñāpāramitā* themselves, they abandon it and further teach others to distance themselves from it.
Śāriputra! Such people as these should not even hear their voices, let alone associate with them or sit and rise together with them. Why is this?
You should know that such people are a great calamity within the Dharma; you should know that such people have fallen into the darkness of decline.
If there are those who, upon hearing what these people say, believe and accept it, they too shall incur immeasurable sin.
“Śāriputra! You should know that one who rejects the Prajñāpāramitā commits what is the greatest illness among all dharmas. Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One!
In whatever place such a person who slanders the Dharma is born, may it be said what kind of physical form they will receive?
The Buddha said:
"Set aside for now the physical forms received by those who slander the Dharma. Why is this?

Should such a person happen to hear [this teaching], hot blood will gush from their mouths; they will be filled with grief and anxiety, or fall ill, or die, or become emaciated and jaundiced, suffering the agony of being ground to death."
If there were no such individuals with such offenses, the World-Honored One would never have caused Śāriputra to pose this question.
Because those who experience such agony possess such physical forms, the Tathāgata did not speak of it for Śāriputra’s sake.
Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One!
You should now describe the physical form received by such a person who has severed the Dharma."
"What the World-Honored One has spoken shall serve as a great illumination for future generations.
The Buddha said:

"Regarding the offenses one incurs by slandering and severing the Dharma as I have taught, the number of kalpas spent wandering through the hells, the number of kalpas spent receiving the bodies of animals or the forms of hungry ghosts, and the manner in which one receives a human body only to be blind, deaf, mute, low-born, or a beggar—these very things shall serve as a great illumination for future generations."
"Having heard this teaching, they will not dare to again sever the Dharma or slander it. Śāriputra said,
"World-Honored One!"
Good sons and good daughters should each reflect within themselves:
"Upon hearing these words, my heart is filled with terror.
I shall never dare to commit such deeds; for as long as this life lasts, I shall never dare to sever the Dharma or slander it as they have done."
"If I were to slander it, I might fall into an evil realm and undergo such diligent suffering.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Good sons and good daughters should always restrain the actions of body, speech, and mind, and their thoughts should be as follows:

"We must not incur the sin of destroying the Dharma, nor fail to see the Tathāgata, nor fail to see the Dharma, nor fail to see the Saṅgha; nor should we be born in a place where there is no Buddha, nor fall into a poor household, nor be born in a remote, desolate place where the Dharma is not heard."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
does one incur the grave and heavy sin of destroying the Dharma merely because of verbal actions?”
The Buddha said, "It is so!
It is because of verbal transgressions!"
They will thus incur the grave sin of destroying the Dharma. Subhūti!
In future ages, there may be foolish people who, having become śramaṇas for me within the teachings of the wholesome Dharma, instead slander and distance themselves from the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
Those who slander and distance themselves from the profound *prajñāpāramitā* have already slandered the path of all Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, which is free from attachment.
One who has slandered the path of the Tathāgata has thereby slandered the *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
One who has slandered *sarvajñatā* has thereby abandoned the Dharma.
One who has already distanced themselves from the Dharma distances themselves from the Saṃgha.

One who has already distanced themselves from the Saṃgha distances themselves from the right view of the world. One who has already distanced themselves from right view distances themselves from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and sarvajñā (all-knowledge). One who has distanced themselves from sarvajñā shall receive a body of sin for incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
"To receive such a body of sin is to undergo immeasurable, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of sorrow, lamentation, suffering,
and affliction. Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying, "World-Honored One!"
“How many factors cause a foolish person to distance themselves from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha said, “There are four.”
What are the four? First, being instigated by Māra;
second, lacking faith and understanding in the profound Dharma, and neither loving nor delighting in it.
Third, associating with evil friends and failing to practice correctly so as to enter into the five aggregates—by these three matters, one distances oneself from the profound Dharma;
fourth, such deluded people frequently give rise to anger, delighting in self-exaltation and disparaging others.
"Because of these four matters, foolish people distance themselves from the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"The profound *prajñāpāramitā* is difficult to comprehend."
"Why is this? Because their understanding does not accord with the truth, they do not cultivate the roots of goodness, and they associate with evil friends.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, Subhūti! It is as you have said.
Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Why is the profound *prajñāpāramitā* so difficult to comprehend and so difficult to know?
The Buddha replied:
“Subhūti! The five aggregates are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?

Form has its own intrinsic nature; feeling has its own intrinsic nature; perception has its own intrinsic nature; mental formations have their own intrinsic nature; and consciousness has its own intrinsic nature.
The six pāramitās are neither bound nor liberated.
Why? Because that which constitutes the six pāramitās is non-existent.
Internal emptiness, external emptiness, and the emptiness of existence and non-existence are neither bound nor liberated.
Why? Because internal and external emptiness are likewise non-existent.

Subhūti! From the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and even unto omniscience (*sarvajñā*) and the objects of omniscience, there is neither bondage nor liberation.
Why is this? Because that which exists is entirely non-existent.
The five aggregates of the past are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the past of the aggregates is empty; it is empty of the past. Subhūti!
Even up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), that which is past is neither bound nor liberated. Why?
Because the past of omniscience is empty.
Subhūti, the five aggregates of the future are neither bound nor liberated. Why is this?
Because the five aggregates of the future are empty;
and so it is likewise even for *sarvajñatā*.
The five aggregates of the present are neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because the five aggregates of the present are empty;
and so it is, even up to and including sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!

Those who do not accord with understanding, who lack roots of goodness, who associate with evil friends, who are indolent, who lack wisdom and diligence, and who delight in a distracted mind—such persons as these cannot understand the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.”
The Buddha said: "As you have said, such persons as these will not be able to explain the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Subhūti!"
When the five aggregates are pure, the Path is also pure; because the Path is pure, the fruit attained is pure.
Subhūti, through the purity of the five aggregates, the Prajñāpāramitā is pure; through the purity of the Prajñāpāramitā, the five aggregates are pure.
Because the five aggregates are pure, all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is pure; because all-knowledge is pure, the five aggregates are pure.
The five aggregates and all-knowledge are thus one and not two; they are neither broken nor destroyed.
Subhūti! The five aggregates have no dual purity; omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) likewise has no dual purity. There is no duality in a single dharma.
Sentient beings, their knowledge and vision, and their life-span are also pure.
Sentient beings are pure, and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is pure; this single purity is non-dual. Subhūti!
The self is pure, omniscience is pure, and knowledge, vision, and the life-span are pure.
The five aggregates and *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) are one purity without duality; they are neither severed nor destroyed. Subhūti!
Lust, anger, and delusion; the five aggregates; and the purity of *sarvajñatā*—these are one purity, not two.
Subhūti! When delusion is pure, because delusion is pure, then volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are pure.
When conduct is purified, consciousness is purified;
when consciousness is purified, name-and-form are purified;
when name-and-form are purified, the six sense bases are purified.
When the six sense bases are purified, then the latent tendencies are purified;
when the latent tendencies are purified, then feeling is purified;
when feeling is purified, then craving is purified.
When craving is purified, grasping is purified;
when grasping is purified, existence is purified;
when existence is purified, birth is purified.
When birth is purified, death is purified;
when death is purified, the six pāramitās are purified;
when the six pāramitās are purified, internal and external emptiness as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence are purified.
When non-existence, emptiness, and purity are established, then the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are pure;
when the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are pure, then all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is pure.
This purity of all-knowledge is a single purity without duality; it is neither broken nor severed.
Subhūti! The purity of the prajñāpāramitā, the purity of the five aggregates, and the purity of sarvajñatā are one purity, not two purities.
The purity of the five pāramitās is the purity of sarvajñatā.
The purity of internal and external emptiness and the purity of the emptiness of existence and non-existence is the purity of *sarvajñatā*;
the purity of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is the purity of *sarvajñatā*;
the purity of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is the purity of *sarvajñatā*.
Subhūti! The purity of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) up to the purity of the prajñāpāramitā are equal and without distinction. Subhūti!
Conditioned purity and unconditioned purity are a single purity;
there are not two. Subhūti!

Past purity, future purity, and present purity—purity of the past, future, and present—is a single purity; there are not two. It is neither destroyed nor interrupted; for this reason, it is called purity.
Chapter 43: On Clarity and Purity. In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Forty-three, "On Clarity and Purity," Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Purity is profound.
The Buddha said,
"It is eternally pure."
Śāriputra said: “World-Honored One!
For what reason is it eternally pure?”
The Buddha said:
“Because the five aggregates are pure, they are eternally pure, Śāriputra.”

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, and the eighteen unique qualities; the purity of the path, the purity of the Buddha, and the purity of omniscience (*sarvajñā*) and the objects of omniscience—therefore, this purity is profoundly deep.
Śāriputra said: “It is clear and pure,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said,
“Because it is eternally pure. Śāriputra said:
"Why is it clear and pure?
The Buddha said:
"Because the six pāramitās are pure and omniscience (sarvajñatā) is pure; therefore, it is clear and pure."
Śāriputra said: “World-Honored One!
Is nirvāṇa pure?”
The Buddha said,
“It is eternally pure.
[He asked,] “World-Honored One!”
"Why is nirvāṇa pure? The Buddha said:
"Because the five aggregates are boundless, merit likewise neither comes nor goes."
“Because *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is boundless, and merit likewise neither comes nor goes. Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One!”
"Purity is non-attachment.
The Buddha said,
"It is eternally pure."
“World-Honored One!
Who is it that is pure through non-attachment?
The Buddha said:
"Because the nature of the five aggregates is fierce, unattached, and eternally pure, it extends to the nature of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), which is fierce, unattached, and eternally pure."
“World-Honored One!
Is it pure because there is nothing to be attained and nothing to be acquired?
The Buddha said:
“Always pure. “World-Honored One,
for what reason is there purity through neither reaching nor attaining anything?”
The Buddha said:
“The five aggregates are neither attained nor obtained as pure; up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), there is nothing attained and nothing obtained as pure.
[He asked: “World-Honored One!”
"It is pure because it is unarisen.
The Buddha said,
"It is eternally pure."
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is there that which is unarisen, and that which is the purity of the unarisen?
The Buddha said:
"That which is non-arising is the purity of non-arising; up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), that which is non-arising is the purity of non-arising. Śāriputra said:
"World-Honored One!"
“Is it not pure because it does not arise within the three realms?
The Buddha said,
“It is eternally pure.”
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is it that not being born into the three realms is purity?
The Buddha said:
“Because there is no possession of anything within the three realms, non-arising is purity.
“World-Honored One!
Non-cognition is purity.”
The Buddha said,
“Always pure. [He asked,] “World-Honored One!”
"Why is there no purity of that which is known?
The Buddha said:
"Because all dharmas are deaf, there is no purity of that which is known."
“World-Honored One!
I know purity.
The Buddha said:
“Always pure. “World-Honored One,
how is it that the five aggregates are pure through being without cognition?”
The Buddha said:
"Because the characteristics of the five aggregates are empty, there is no knowledge that is pure.
[He asked: "World-Honored One!"
"Are all dharmas pure?
The Buddha said:
"They are eternally pure."
“World-Honored One!
How is it that all dharmas are pure because they are pure?
The Buddha said:
"Because all dharmas are non-apprehendable, all dharmas are pure. Śāriputra said,
"World-Honored One!"
“Prajñāpāramitā neither performs an act of increase nor an act of decrease toward sarvajñatā;
it is pure. The Buddha said, “It is eternally pure.”
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is the *prajñāpāramitā* pure, performing no act of increase or decrease regarding *sarvajñatā*?
The Buddha said:
“Because the Dharma is eternally abiding.
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is pure; all dharmas are without anything to be grasped.”
The Buddha said,
"It is eternally pure.
[He asked,] "World-Honored One!"
"How is it that the perfection of wisdom purifies all phenomena such that there is nothing to be grasped?
The Buddha said:
"Because the nature of phenomena is immovable and unchanging."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Are the five aggregates of the self pure?
The Buddha said:
“Always pure. Subhūti said,
“World-Honored One!”
“For what reason is the self pure and the five aggregates pure?
For what reason is permanence pure?
The Buddha said:
"Because the self does not exist and the five aggregates do not exist, they are eternally pure. Subhūti said:
"World-Honored One!"
"The self is pure; the six pāramitās are pure; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are pure.
The self is pure; the ten powers are pure; the eighteen unique dharmas are pure.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"Always pure. Subhūti asked: "For what reason are 'self' pure, and so on, up to the eighteen dharmas being pure?"
The Buddha said:
“Because there is no ‘self’ whatsoever, and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha do not exist, it is pure.
[He asked: “World-Honored One!”
"The self is pure; the srotāpanna is pure, up to and including the arhat and the pratyekabuddha.
The self is pure, and the Way is also pure.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Always pure. “World-Honored One!
For what reason are the self pure, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas pure, and even the path and the Buddha-path pure?”
The Buddha said:
“The characteristics of all phenomena are empty and pure.
[He asked: “World-Honored One!”
"The purity of the self is the purity of sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
The Buddha said:
"It is eternally pure."
“World-Honored One!
How is it that the purity of the self and the purity of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) are eternally pure?
The Buddha said:
"Because it is without marks and unchanging. Subhūti said,
"World-Honored One!"
"The two purities are non-apprehensible and unattainable.
The Buddha said,
"They are eternally pure."
“World-Honored One!
How is it that the two purities are unattainable and non-apprehensible, being eternally pure?
The Buddha said:
"Because there is neither attachment nor abandonment.
"World-Honored One!
The self is pure and has no place of sinking."
The Buddha said:
"It is pure because nothing is produced. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that the self and the five aggregates are pure, being eternally pure because they are non-arising?
The Buddha said:
“Because space is boundless.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands in this way, this constitutes practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).”
The Buddha said,
"It is eternally pure.
[He replied,] "World-Honored One!"
"How does one come to know that this constitutes the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha said:
"Because it is the matter of knowing the Way."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Suppose a bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* with *upāyakauśalya* were to form this thought: ‘Form does not know form;

feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not know consciousness; past phenomena do not know past phenomena; future phenomena do not know future phenomena; and present phenomena do not know present phenomena.’”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva who has attained the prajñāpāramitā and practices upāyakauśalya does not form this thought:
‘I am practicing the six pāramitās.’”
He says: "I practice giving; I take this giving as being for the sake of this giving.
It is the same even up to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Nor does he say:
"I have performed meritorious deeds; I possess merit. Nor does he say:
"I shall attain the path of a bodhisattva," nor does he say:
"I shall transform sentient beings and purify buddha-fields."
Nor does one say: "I have attained sarvajñatā.
Those who practice the prajñāpāramitā with upāyakauśalya likewise do not harbor such thoughts.
"From internal emptiness and external emptiness up to the emptiness of existence and non-existence," Subhūti, it is because there is no such thought.
"This is the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) without attachment.
Śakra Devānām Indra asked Subhūti:
"For a son of good family or a daughter of good family who practices the bodhisattva path, what constitutes attachment?"
He replied: "Kauśika!

One who practices the bodhisattva path possesses the conceptualization of a self, the conceptualization of giving, the conceptualization of the six pāramitās, the conceptualization of internal emptiness, external emptiness, and the emptiness of both existence and non-existence, the conceptualization of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the conceptualization of the eighteen unique qualities, the conceptualization of the ten powers, the conceptualization of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, and the conceptualization of the merit of making offerings to the Buddhas. Taking all these together and summing them up, one maintains these conceptualizations to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Kauśika! A son of good family who practices the bodhisattva path in this manner is attached; he cannot attain unimpeded wisdom and practice the prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?

The nature of the five aggregates cannot be designated, nor can anything be established therein; even the nature of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) cannot be designated, nor can anything be established therein. O Kauśika!

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva acts for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; he encourages and assists sentient beings, practices the dāna-pāramitā for the sake of sentient beings, and because he keeps sentient beings in mind, he likewise encourages and assists others, causing them to practice the dāna-pāramitā for the sake of sentient beings.

One should not form conceptualizations while practicing the six pāramitās; nor should one form conceptualizations while practicing internal emptiness, external emptiness, or the emptiness of existence and non-existence; nor should one form conceptualizations while practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; nor should one form conceptualizations while practicing the Path.
When sons or daughters of good family practice in this manner, they further exhort and assist others to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Those who provide such exhortation and assistance do not fall into ruin themselves, nor do they cause others to be deprived of the exhortation and assistance of the Buddhas.
"In this way, good sons and good daughters are free from attachment to all extremes.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Excellent, excellent!"
This is to cause all bodhisattvas to understand the attachments to the various limits. Subhūti!
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.
"I shall further explain for you the subtle attachment.
Subhūti joined his palms and said,
"Yes, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said,
"Good sons and good daughters who have set their minds on Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should conceive the thought of the Tathāgata."
Subhūti! As soon as there is conceptualization, one becomes attached to the Tathāgatas.
From the initial resolution until the exhaustion of the Dharma, whatever merit is performed during that interval is all rendered into conceptualization.

If one forms such thoughts while seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then by following those mental conceptions, one becomes attached to the merits performed by the Buddhas, the assembly of disciples, and all sentient beings.
To maintain these conceptions and thereby produce *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is to act according to what is conceived and what is attached.
Why is this? One should not, by means of such conceptions, [grasp] the merits of the Buddhas.
Subhūti said to the Buddha,
“The Prajñāpāramitā is profound.
The Buddha said:
"Because the nature of all dharmas is quiescent. Subhūti said:
"World-Honored One!"
"The Prajñāpāramitā has a great name.
The Buddha said:
"The Prajñāpāramitā has no creator, no one who can accomplish it, no one who can attain it, no one who can reach it, and no one who can awaken to it."
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
Among all dharmas, there is nothing that can be attained.”
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is non-dual.”
The nature of all phenomena is without diversity; it is a single nature.
That which is a single nature is not a nature; that which is not a nature is not an act; and that which is not an act does not create.
“Subhūti! The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is one; it is not something created.
The Buddha said:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva who knows that all dharmas are neither made nor created abandons all attachment to limits.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“The Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to understand and difficult to know.”
The Buddha said:
"There is neither one who knows, nor one who sees, nor one who attains; there is no one who perceives, nor anyone who realizes awakening."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is inconceivable.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“It is not produced from the mind, nor is it produced from the five aggregates, nor is it produced from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, nor is it produced from the ten powers or the eighteen unique qualities.”
44. Chapter on Non-Action, the Great Prajñāpāramitā, Chapter Forty-four. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"The Prajñāpāramitā is that which does nothing.
The Buddha replied,
"Because there is no agent."
"Subhūti! Even all dharmas are non-existent.
"World-Honored One!"
"How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice when practicing the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said, "When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not practice with regard to form; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom."
To not practice with regard to sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is to practice the perfection of wisdom;
even to have no practice with regard to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is to practice the perfection of wisdom.
To not conceive of the five aggregates as being either permanent or impermanent is to practice the perfection of wisdom;
even to not conceive of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) as being either permanent or impermanent is to practice the perfection of wisdom.
To practice the perfection of wisdom is to have neither suffering nor pleasure regarding the five aggregates;
even up to *sarvajñatā*, to practice the perfection of wisdom is to have neither suffering nor pleasure.
To realize that within the five aggregates there is neither self nor non-self is to practice the perfection of wisdom;
even up to the point of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), to realize that there is neither self nor non-self is to practice the perfection of wisdom.

To practice the perfection of wisdom is to have neither purity nor impurity regarding the five aggregates; even up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), to practice the perfection of wisdom is to have neither purity nor impurity.

Why is this? One does not perceive the five aggregates as being either permanent or impermanent; nor does one perceive them as having suffering or happiness, as having a self or being selfless, or as being good or bad.
This applies even up to *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), which is likewise so.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, practicing without fully grasping the five aggregates is practicing the perfection of wisdom;
even practicing without fully grasping up to omniscience (sarvajñatā) is practicing the perfection of wisdom."
Why is this? Because the five aggregates, when not fully realized, are not [truly] the five aggregates; practicing in such a manner is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
This extends even to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*): when omniscience is not fully realized, it is not [truly] omniscience; practicing in such a manner is practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is most extraordinary!”
"One who practices the bodhisattva path is well-spoken regarding the attachments of a bodhisattva.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!"
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has well explained the matters of the bodhisattva’s attachment and non-attachment. Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva is without attachment to the five aggregates, he practices the perfection of wisdom.
To have no attachment to the six sense organs—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—is to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*;
to have no attachment to the six *pāramitās* is to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*;
and even to have no attachment to *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva practices in this manner, they come to know whether there is attachment or non-attachment regarding the five aggregates; likewise, they know whether there is attachment or non-attachment regarding sarvajñatā (all-knowledge); they know whether there is attachment or non-attachment regarding the path of the srotāpanna; they know whether there is attachment or non-attachment regarding the paths of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha; and they know whether there is attachment or non-attachment regarding the path of the samyaksambuddha.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How most marvelous and extraordinary this is!”
"The Dharma is so profoundly deep that whether it is taught, it neither increases nor decreases; whether it is not taught, it neither increases nor decreases.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said, Subhūti."

For example, even if all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas were to praise empty space for the rest of their lives, it would not increase; nor would it decrease if they were to revile and disparage empty space.
For example, just as praising an illusory person does not increase them, nor does disparaging an illusory person decrease them;
they feel no joy upon hearing good things, nor do they feel anger upon hearing evil things.
“Subhūti! The nature of all dharmas is likewise: whether they are spoken or not spoken, they neither increase nor decrease.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is most difficult, most difficult for a bodhisattva to practice the prajñāpāramitā and to keep the prajñāpāramitā in mind.
World-Honored One!”
When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they are neither afraid nor timid; they correspond to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and no longer waver. Why is this?
World-Honored One!
To recollect the *prajñāpāramitā* is to wish to recollect empty space.

In empty space there are no six *pāramitās*, nor are there five aggregates (*skandhas*), nor internal and external emptiness or the emptiness of existence and non-existence; nor are there the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, nor the ten powers, nor the four fearlessnesses, nor the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; nor is there the path of the *srotāpanna*, nor the path of the *sakṛdāgāmin*, nor the path of the *anāgāmin*, nor the path of the *arhat*, nor the path of the *pratyekabuddha*.
"Even space does not possess the path of the Samyaksaṃbuddha,
World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who dons such armor (saṃnāha-saṃnaddha) should be paid homage."
World-Honored One!

One who exerts diligence for the sake of sentient beings, displays power for the sake of sentient beings, strives for the sake of sentient beings, and makes solemn vows for the sake of sentient beings, does so because they wish to exert diligence for the sake of emptiness and wish to make solemn vows for the sake of emptiness.
World-Honored One!
One who makes a solemn vow for the sake of sentient beings desires to deliver emptiness;
this is the great solemn vow of a bodhisattva.
To make a solemn vow for the sake of sentient beings who are like space is to desire to lift up space and place it within the midst of space.
All Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* do so in order to establish the power of great diligence.
World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva who gives rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of sentient beings has already established the great vow.
World-Honored One!
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is one of great courage and valor, who has resolved upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of sentient beings who are equal to space. Why is this?
“World-Honored One! Suppose that all beings within the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were to become Tathāgatas—

just as if an entire forest of sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, rice, hemp, grasses, trees, medicinal herbs, and fruit-bearing trees were all to become Tathāgatas— and each of these Buddhas were to preach the Dharma for a kalpa or even more than a kalpa, with each Tathāgata individually delivering countless and incalculable multitudes of sentient beings, yet one would not perceive any increase or decrease in the nature of those sentient beings.”
Why is this? Because sentient beings are non-existent and quiescent,
World-Honored One!

Setting aside this trichiliocosm, suppose that for every single grain of sand along the banks of the Ganges River in the ten directions, there were one Buddha-land; and in all those Buddha-lands, every being therein were a Tathāgata, teaching and transforming sentient beings in numbers beyond calculation or measure, yet the nature of sentient beings neither increases nor decreases.
Why is this so? Because all sentient beings are empty and quiescent.
Therefore, sentient beings have neither beginning nor end, for they are equal to emptiness.
World-Honored One! For this reason, I say:
"Those who wish to deliver sentient beings merely wish to deliver emptiness."
Then another bhikṣu thought to himself:
"I should pay homage to the Prajñāpāramitā.

Within the Prajñāpāramitā, there is no dharma that can arise, nor any dharma that can cease; yet within it, the nature of precepts, the nature of samādhi, the nature of wisdom, the nature of liberation, and the nature of the vision and knowledge of liberation appear."
There are srotāpannas, sakṛdāgāmins, anāgāmins, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and samyaksaṃbuddhas; thus there are the Three Jewels, and there is the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra said to Subhūti,
"When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), what is it that he practices?
The venerable Subhūti replied to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"One who studies the *prajñāpāramitā* practices emptiness.
Śakra-devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, recites, reads, contemplates, and practices the matters within this *prajñāpāramitā*..."
“World-Honored One!
What kind of protection should I provide?
Subhūti said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
“Kauśika! Have you ever seen any dharma that is worth protecting?
“Indeed, Venerable Sir!”
"In truth, I do not see any dharma that is worthy of being protected.
Subhūti said: "Kauśika!"

Noble sons and noble daughters who abide according to the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā* have already attained protection; as long as they do not depart from the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, neither humans nor non-humans shall ever find an opportunity to harm them.
Those who abide according to the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā should be known as good sons and good daughters who shall never be separated from the Prajñāpāramitā.
If someone says,
"I wish to protect the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas," one should know that this person wishes to protect emptiness.
Kauśika! Could you possibly protect a dream, a mirage in the heat, an illusion, a transformation, a shadow, or an echo?
Could you possibly protect such things as these?
Śakra Devānām Indra said,
"I cannot protect them. "Kauśika!
If a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, it is also like this.
Kauśika! Are you able to protect the Buddha and those transformed by the Buddha?
Śakra Devānām Indra said, "I cannot.
[The Buddha replied,] "When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, there is likewise no one who can provide protection for them."
"Kauśika! Are you able to provide protection for the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), and the inconceivable? "Yes indeed, Subhūti!"
"No. "The Bodhisattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā is likewise; there is no one who can provide protection for them.
Śakra Devānām Indra asked Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, how should they realize that phenomena are like dreams, like illusions, like mirages in the heat, like echoes, and like magical transformations, yet remain free from arrogance?"
Subhūti said: "Kauśika!
When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they do not even think of the five aggregates, nor do they become conceited regarding the five aggregates."
"Even regarding *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), one neither dwells upon it nor is conceited;
even regarding phenomena in dreams up to those that are magically conjured, one neither dwells upon them nor is conceited.

By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the Four Heavenly Kings throughout the trichiliocosm, up to the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, each took celestial powdered sandalwood and scattered it from afar over the Buddha.

Having scattered [the flowers], they approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads touching the ground as a salutation to the Buddha, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the various Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra-devānām-indra, the various Brahmā kings, and the various gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, each thought to themselves:
"Now we should invite a thousand Buddhas from each of the ten directions to turn the chapter on the Prajñāpāramitā."
As soon as the Four Great Kings, Śakra, Brahmā, and the various honored devas had formed this thought, at that very moment, a thousand Buddhas appeared simultaneously from each of the ten directions,
all of whom preached the Prajñāpāramitā chapter; their disciples were also like Subhūti,
and those who posed difficult questions were all like Śakra Devānām Indra, asking questions in exactly the same way.
It is no different from what was taught by Śākyamuni Buddha regarding the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Buddha said:
“Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva shall likewise attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and become an Arhat-Buddha at this very place, and he shall likewise preach the Prajñāpāramitā at this very place.”

The Buddhas who will appear in this Bhadrakalpa shall likewise attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment at this very place, and they too shall preach the Prajñāpāramitā at this very place.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what means, by what characteristics, and with what intention will the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, upon attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, preach the Prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya attains Buddhahood, he will not say that the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are permanent or impermanent; nor will he say that the five aggregates are suffering or happiness, pure or impure, self or non-self, good or bad. He will not say that the five aggregates are bound or liberated, nor will he say that the five aggregates belong to the past, future, or present.

Since the five aggregates are eternally pure, he shall speak of the five aggregates as eternally pure; even unto the fact that omniscience (sarvajñatā) is eternally pure, he shall speak of omniscience as eternally pure."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is pure,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:
“Because the five aggregates are pure, the Prajñāpāramitā is pure.
[Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!”
"How is it that because the five aggregates are pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure?
The Buddha said:
"The five aggregates are neither produced nor extinguished, neither attached to nor severed; for this reason, the five aggregates are pure."
“Subhūti, because space is pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
“World-Honored One,
how is it that because space is pure, the perfection of wisdom is pure?”
The Buddha said:
“Space is neither born nor extinguished; it is non-existent. Therefore, space is pure.
[He asked: “World-Honored One!”
"How is it that because space is non-existent, the *prajñāpāramitā* is pure?
The Buddha said, "Because space cannot be maintained or grasped, the *prajñāpāramitā* is pure like the nature of space; therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* is pure."
“World-Honored One!
In what way is the perfection of wisdom pure because its nature is like space?
The Buddha said:
"Just as space is non-dual and quiescent, by virtue of this fact, the *prajñāpāramitā* is pure.
The Buddha said:
"Just as space is without activity, the *prajñāpāramitā* is pure."
“World-Honored One!
How is it that because space is without activity, the perfection of wisdom is pure?
The Buddha said:
"Because space has no sphere of activity, the perfection of wisdom is pure.
The Buddha said,
"Because space has nothing upon which it relies, the perfection of wisdom is pure."
“World-Honored One!
How is it that because space has nothing upon which to rely, the *prajñāpāramitā* is pure?
The Buddha said:
"Just as space is untainted, so too is the perfection of wisdom pure.
Subhūti! Because all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, neither attached to nor severed, the perfection of wisdom is pure."
“World-Honored One!
How is it that because all dharmas are neither produced nor extinguished, neither attached to nor severed, the Prajñāpāramitā is pure?
The Buddha said:
"Because all dharmas are eternally pure, the Prajñāpāramitā is pure.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If good sons or good daughters uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, reciting, chanting, reading, studying, and practicing its teachings, these good sons and good daughters shall never suffer from eye disease; their ears and noses shall remain free of ailment; and though their bodies grow old, they shall never fall into premature decay.
When their life comes to an end, they die without confusion, with body and mind at peace; they never meet with a death caused by poison, disease, delusion, or falsehood.
They are constantly attended and protected by various devas, from the Four Great Kings up to the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, who always provide them with protection.
When good sons or good daughters who serve as Dharma-preachers recite the Prajñāpāramitā on the fourteenth or fifteenth day of the month, at that time all the devas will assemble there.
When good sons and good daughters speak thus regarding the Prajñāpāramitā, the merit they obtain is incalculable, immeasurable, and inconceivable.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If good sons and good daughters preach the Prajñāpāramitā during the six fast days, the devas will come to the assembly; the merit they thereby obtain is immeasurable."
Why is this? Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is the most supreme and precious treasure.

Within the precious treasure of the *prajñāpāramitā*, one cuts off the three evil destinies and cuts off poverty among humans; it bestows upon people the paths of gods and humans, enabling all beings to be born into great clans such as those of brahmins and householders, and to be born in the heavens from the Four Great Kings up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
it bestows upon people the path of the *srotāpanna*, the *sakṛdāgāmin*, the *anāgāmin*, the *arhat*, and the path of the *pratyekabuddha*;
and it bestows upon people the path of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Why is this? Because within the Prajñāpāramitā, the ten wholesome deeds are explained in detail; having studied therein, one comes to know of the kṣatriyas, brahmins, and great clans of householders; one comes to know of the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
and one comes to know of the path of the srotāpanna, as well as the paths of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha.
One then knows that there are the three vehicles and the three paths of the Buddhas;

one then knows that there are the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Buddha, the eighteen unique qualities, and the four fearlessnesses;
one then knows that there are the six pāramitās, and one knows internal and external emptiness as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence.
One thereby knows that there is *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge);
for this reason, it is called the "Jewel-Crossing" (*ratnapāramitā*) and the "Perfection of Wisdom" (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Within this Jewel-Crossing, there is neither one who arises nor one who ceases; there is neither one who clings nor one who abandons; there is neither one who grasps nor one who discards.
Why is this? Because there is no dharma whatsoever that undergoes arising or ceasing, that is subject to attachment or abandonment, or that involves grasping or relinquishing. Subhūti!

In the Prajñāpāramitā, there are no wholesome dharmas and no unwholesome dharmas; there are no dharmas of the Path and no worldly dharmas; there are no out-flowing and no non-out-flowing dharmas; and there are no conditioned dharmas and no unconditioned dharmas.
For this reason, Subhūti, the jewel-like pāramitā is without dependence.
This jewel-like pāramitā has no dharma that can defile it, and no dharma that can attain it.
"Why is this? Because that which is ungraspable cannot come into proximity with anything; therefore, there is nothing capable of defiling it.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If there is a bodhisattva who practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, and who does not form such knowledge, does not form such thoughts, does not form such attachments, and does not engage in such play, then they are practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, they are mindful of the *prajñāpāramitā*, and they are paying homage to all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; traveling from buddha-field to buddha-field, making offerings to, serving, and revering those Buddhas, while teaching and transforming sentient beings and purifying the buddha-fields."
Subhūti! This prajñāpāramitā has no dharma that can be seen, nor any that cannot be seen;
it neither grasps nor relinquishes, neither arises nor ceases, and neither clings nor...
It is severed, yet neither increases nor decreases; it is neither past, future, nor present;
it does not cause the realm of desire to pass away nor does it cause it to abide; it does not cause the realm of form to pass away nor does it cause it to abide;
it does not cause the formless realm to pass away nor does it cause it to abide; nor does it bestow the six *pāramitās* upon people.

He does not instruct others to discard honey, nor does he give them internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) or the emptiness of existence and non-existence (*bhāvābhāva-śūnyatā*), nor does he discard them;
he does not give them the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*), nor does he discard them;

he does not give them the ten powers (*daśa-bala*) and the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), nor does he discard them; nor does he hold [them as inferior], up to and including the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
In omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), there is nothing given, nor is anything caused to be discarded.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, as for the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), it neither takes up the dharmas of an Arhat to give them away nor does it discard the dharmas of an ordinary person; it neither takes up the dharmas of a Pratyekabuddha to give them away nor does it discard the dharmas of an Arhat; it neither takes up the dharmas of a Buddha to give them away nor does it discard the dharmas of a Pratyekabuddha; nor does it take up the dharmas of a Buddha to give them away while discarding others."
Subhūti! The prajñāpāramitā neither takes up unconditioned phenomena to bestow them, nor does it discard conditioned phenomena. Why is this?
Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, the *dharmatā* abides as it is.
This *dharmatā* is the *dharmakāya*; it abides neither through forgetting nor through diminution.
At that time, the hosts of devas in the void rejoiced and leaped for joy, laughing aloud; they took celestial *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers and scattered them over the Buddha.
They all raised their voices and said:
"We now behold the turning of the Wheel of Dharma once again in Jambudvīpa. Why is this so?"
"Because innumerable sons of gods have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) in mid-air.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"The turning of the wheel of Dharma is neither dual nor non-dual."
“The Prajñāpāramitā does not turn for the sake of dharmas, nor does it fail to turn because there is something to be done; this is because of the emptiness of existence and non-existence.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By virtue of what emptiness of existence and non-existence does the Prajñāpāramitā turn or attain anything?”
The Buddha said:
“The six pāramitās are empty because they are empty by means of the emptiness of the six pāramitās.
Internal and external emptiness is empty because it is empty by means of the emptiness of internal and external emptiness.”
Furthermore, existence and non-existence are empty by means of the emptiness of existence and non-existence.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are empty by means of the emptiness of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
The ten powers are empty by means of the emptiness of the ten powers.
The eighteen dharmas of a Buddha are empty because they are empty of the eighteen dharmas.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are empty because they are empty of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
“Sarvajñā is empty; it is by means of the emptiness of sarvajñā that it is empty.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“That which is called emptiness in the Prajñāpāramitā is the great liberation of the bodhisattva.”

Because the Bodhisattva possesses the Prajñāpāramitā and all things are empty, he attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the supreme perfect enlightenment; yet there is nothing attained or awakened to as he turns the wheel of Dharma. There is no dharma that can be turned, nor does he turn back again, nor does he perceive any dharma.
Why is this? Because even that dharma which could be sought out and turned over cannot be found, for all dharmas are eternally non-existent. Why is this?

That which is empty, signless, and wishless neither revolves nor returns—this is the teaching, this is the designation, this is the differentiation and classification, and this is the proclamation and distribution of the Prajñāpāramitā.
If the Prajñāpāramitā contains such a teaching, it is a teaching of great purity.
In the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, there is no speaker, no recipient, and no one who attains realization.
If there were no teaching, no receiving, and no realization, then in this way there would be no one who enters parinirvāṇa.
If there were no one who enters parinirvāṇa, then within these teachings there would likewise be no venerable field of merit.
