Chapter 46: True Spiritual Friends. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, Chapter Forty-Six: True Spiritual Friends. At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra thought to himself:

“Good sons and good daughters who hear the Prajñāpāramitā pass their ears are all those who performed meritorious deeds during the time of past Buddhas; they have already encountered true spiritual friends.”

How much more so for one who receives, maintains, recites, chants, reads, explains, and practices the matters contained therein; such a person has already made offerings to numerous Buddhas, is able to inquire on behalf of others and to explain for them, and now further receives and maintains the Prajñāpāramitā according to its teachings.
Noble sons and noble daughters who hear the Prajñāpāramitā without fear or terror have already practiced the deeds of the six pāramitās for many hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing this profound Prajñāpāramitā, are neither terrified nor afraid, neither cowed nor fearful, and who, having heard it, are able to receive, uphold, recite, and practice its teachings—these bodhisattvas should be regarded as being like those who are irreversible (avaivartika).”
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is exceedingly profound; those who have not yet practiced the six pāramitās will ultimately be unable to understand it.
Thus it is, World-Honored One!
Furthermore, if there should be a son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to disparage the *prajñāpāramitā*, that person has already treated the *prajñāpāramitā* with contempt.
Why is this? It is because they do not believe or take pleasure in hearing the exposition of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

This is due to their never having heard from the Buddha or his assembly of disciples the practice of the six *pāramitās*; it is due to their not having heard of internal and external emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence; and it is due to their not having heard of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Buddha, and the eighteen unique qualities.
Śakra Devānām Indra asked Śāriputra:
"What kind of wonders does the Prajñāpāramitā possess?
When newly initiated bodhisattvas hear this profound Prajñāpāramitā, how do they understand the six pāramitās?"
"How does one understand internal and external emptiness, as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence?
How does one understand the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, and the eighteen unique qualities?
Śakra-devānām-indra said to Śāriputra:
"The Prajñāpāramitā possesses great renown; those who do not revere the Prajñāpāramitā do not revere the wisdom of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge)."
The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying:
“It is so, Kauśika! To not revere the Prajñāpāramitā is to not revere the wisdom of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).”
Why is this? Because the *sarvajñajñāna* (omniscient wisdom) of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is born from within it, Kauśika!
Good sons and good daughters who wish to dwell in sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) should dwell in the prajñāpāramitā;
those who wish to give rise to the wisdom of the Path should practice and cultivate the prajñāpāramitā.
Good sons and good daughters who wish to be free from all habitual tendencies should practice the perfection of wisdom;
those who wish to turn the wheel of the Dharma of the Buddhas should practice the perfection of wisdom.

Good sons and good daughters who wish to attain the path of the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, or the path of the samyaksaṃbuddha Buddha, should practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā);
those who wish to sustain the community of bhikṣus should practice the perfection of wisdom.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva abide in the six pāramitās?
How does he practice the six pāramitās?"
How does one practice the perfection of wisdom by cultivating internal and external emptiness, as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence?
How does one practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra,
saying: “Excellent, excellent, Kauśika!”
"It is by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power that you are able to ask such questions of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Buddha said:

"A bodhisattva who practices the *prajñāpāramitā* does not dwell in the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). To not dwell in the five aggregates is to practice [the non-attachment to] the five aggregates."

Not dwelling in the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; not dwelling in forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena; not dwelling in the twelve bases (*āyatana*) is the practice of the twelve bases;
not dwelling in the six perfections (*pāramitā*) is the practice of the six perfections;

not dwelling in internal and external emptiness, nor in the emptiness of existence and non-existence, is the practice of internal and external emptiness and the emptiness of existence and non-existence.
Not dwelling in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four fearlessnesses, the ten powers, up to the eighteen unique qualities, is to practice the eighteen unique qualities.

Why is this? Because one does not perceive the five aggregates as having anything in which to dwell or to practice; likewise, one does not perceive even the eighteen unique qualities as having anything in which to dwell or to practice.
"Furthermore, Kauśika!

When a bodhisattva does not unite with the five aggregates, he practices the five aggregates; likewise, up to when he does not unite with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, he practices the eighteen qualities of a Buddha."

Why is this? Because a bodhisattva cannot perceive the five aggregates of the past, cannot perceive the five aggregates of the future, and cannot perceive the five aggregates of the present; even so it is with the eighteen dharmas of a Buddha.
Śāriputra said to the Buddha,
“The Prajñāpāramitā is profound.
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra, the suchness of the five aggregates is also profoundly deep;
even the suchness of the eighteen dharmas is profoundly deep.”
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is profound; it is difficult to uphold and difficult to receive.
The Buddha said:
“Because the five aggregates are difficult to maintain and difficult to accept, the Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to maintain and difficult to accept;
and so on, up to because the eighteen dharmas are difficult to maintain and difficult to accept, the Prajñāpāramitā is difficult to maintain and difficult to accept.”
“World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā has no characteristic of levelness.
The Buddha said:
"Because the five aggregates are of an unlevel nature, the Prajñāpāramitā is of an unlevel nature;
and so on, because even the eighteen dharmas are of an unlevel nature, the Prajñāpāramitā is of an unlevel nature."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, not practicing the depth of the five aggregates constitutes practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*;
likewise, not practicing the depth of the eighteen dharmas, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, constitutes practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*."
"Why is this? Because the five aggregates, being profoundly deep, are in fact not five aggregates; and so on, up to the eighteen dharmas, being profoundly deep, are in fact not eighteen dharmas.
The Buddha said:

"If a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, not practicing [the notion that] the five aggregates are difficult to maintain or difficult to accept, this constitutes practicing the perfection of wisdom. Why is this? "
If the five aggregates are difficult to maintain and difficult to accept, they are not the five aggregates;
if the eighteen dharmas are difficult to maintain and difficult to accept, they are not the eighteen dharmas. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not practice with the five aggregates as having the characteristic of being unlevel; this is practicing the perfection of wisdom. Why is that?
If the five aggregates cannot be characterized as equal, they are not the five aggregates;
likewise, up to the eighteen dharmas of a Buddha, if they cannot be characterized as equal, they are not the eighteen dharmas.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The Prajñāpāramitā is profound, difficult to understand, and its characteristics cannot be leveled. One should not speak of this profound Prajñāpāramitā before bodhisattvas who are newly set out in their training; those who hear it may become afraid or terrified, harbor doubts and obstacles, and neither believe nor rejoice in it.

One should speak of this profound Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive); upon hearing it, they will never be terrified and will never have doubts or obstacles, but will instead believe and understand it as soon as they hear it.”
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked Śāriputra:
"If one were to preach the profound Prajñāpāramitā before a newly initiated bodhisattva, what fault would there be?"
Śāriputra said to Śakra Devānām Indra:

"If one were to speak of this before a newly initiated bodhisattva, that person would become terrified, would engage in slander, would fail to attain liberation, and would incur extremely grave offenses; furthermore, it would take twice as long as usual for them to achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Śakra Devānām Indra asked Śāriputra:
"Is there any bodhisattva who has not yet received a prediction [of enlightenment] who, upon hearing this profound prajñāpāramitā, does not feel fear or dread?"

Śāriputra said: "Those who hear this profound Prajñāpāramitā and do not feel fear or terror will receive their prediction of enlightenment before long; they need not see more than one or two Buddhas before they receive that prediction."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:

“So it is, so it is! If there are those who, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, feel neither fear nor terror, you should know that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have long since resolved their minds for awakening and have long practiced the six *pāramitās*. They have made offerings to various Buddhas, and their practice has progressively surpassed what they previously heard and practiced.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, I have understood what has been spoken by the World-Honored One.”

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon the bodhisattva path practices the six pāramitās even in a dream, or sits upon the seat of a Buddha, you should know that this son or daughter of good family will before long draw near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If one acts in this manner even within a dream, they shall be near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before long;
how much more so for one who practices the six *pāramitās* seeking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—how could such a person not swiftly achieve *samyak-saṃbuddha-hood*?

Good sons and good daughters who, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, are able to practice it in accordance with it, have already accomplished the roots of goodness and merit; they have already made offerings to countless Buddhas of the past, and have associated with true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). By upholding, reciting, and chanting the *prajñāpāramitā*, they will before long receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It should be known that such Bodhisattvas shall no longer waver from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Those who believe now in the present should also be thus, and those who will believe in the future shall likewise be thus.
World-Honored One!

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How most marvelous and extraordinary!

The Buddha said to Subhūti:

What are the four? First, giving; second, loving-kindness; third, benefiting others; and fourth, sharing in their welfare.
One encourages them to practice the ten wholesome paths of action.
They personally practice the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments, and encourage others to practice the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments;
they personally practice the six pāramitās, and encourage others to practice the six pāramitās;

through the prajñāpāramitā, they encourage others to attain the stage of srotāpanna; yet within themselves, they do not encourage others toward the paths of arhat or pratyekabuddha, nor do they within themselves accept the realization of arhat or pratyekabuddha; rather, they assist countless hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas, encouraging them to practice the six pāramitās.
Having themselves transcended the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), they encourage others to abide in the stage of non-retrogression;
having themselves purified their Buddha-fields, they encourage others to purify Buddha-fields;
having themselves perfected the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they encourage others to cultivate the supernormal powers.
Having personally purified the dharani-gates, they encourage others to purify the dharani-gates;
having personally perfected eloquence, they encourage others to practice eloquence;
having personally accomplished the physical marks, they encourage others to accomplish the physical marks.

having themselves attained the ten powers of a Buddha, they exhort others to practice the ten powers;
having themselves established in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they exhort others to establish themselves in omniscience.
"Having personally become free from all habitual tendencies, they encourage others to become free from habitual tendencies;

“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the recollection of the prajñāpāramitā so as to bring it to full completion?
The Buddha said:

"When practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), one does not perceive the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) as having increase or decrease; therefore, the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom attains the fulfillment of mindfulness (smṛti). Even up to omniscience (sarvajñatā), one does not perceive it as having increase or decrease;
this is what constitutes the bodhisattva’s attainment of the fulfillment of mindfulness."

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* does not perceive these dharmas, nor does he perceive non-dharmas; he does not perceive past, future, or present unwholesome or wholesome dharmas; he does not perceive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), nor does he perceive its absence; he does not perceive conditioned dharmas (*saṃskṛtadharma*), nor does he perceive unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛtadharma*); he does not perceive the triple world, nor does he perceive the six *pāramitās*, up to and including *sarvajñatā*, which he likewise perceives as nothing at all.
For this reason, the bodhisattva attains the perfection of mindfulness through the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Why is this? Because the characteristic of all phenomena is that phenomena are empty and indestructible; they possess no solid, deceptive appearance, for phenomena are without birth, without lifespan, and without life-force.
Subhūti said: "That which the World-Honored One has spoken is inconceivable.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Because the five aggregates are inconceivable, that which is taught is inconceivable;
because the six pāramitās up to sarvajñatā are inconceivable, that which is taught is inconceivable."

Subhūti! If there is a bodhisattva who practices the prajñāpāramitā and knows that the five aggregates are inconceivable, then he knows that he is fully endowed with the prajñāpāramitā; up to and including knowing that omniscience (sarvajñatā) is inconceivable, he is fully endowed with the knowledge of the prajñāpāramitā.

“World-Honored One,
who will be able to believe and understand this profound Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said:

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“How does one make offerings to as many Buddhas as there are and come into association with true spiritual friends? The Buddha told Subhūti:

"For this reason, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have long practiced the six pāramitās perform various roots of goodness and encounter true spiritual friends.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
The Prajñāpāramitā is profound. Because the five aggregates are profound, the Prajñāpāramitā is profound.
Because omniscience (sarvajñatā) is profound, the Prajñāpāramitā is profound.
World-Honored One!

The Prajñāpāramitā is an accumulation of rare treasures; it is an accumulation of the treasures of the srotāpanna, arhat, and pratyekabuddha; it is also an accumulation of the treasure of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; and it is an accumulation of the treasures of all dharmas, including the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered wisdoms, the four immeasurables, the four dhyānas of emptiness, the five supernormal powers, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, and sarvajñatā.
"Bhagavān! This Prajñāpāramitā is an accumulation of purity, because the five aggregates are pure, up to and including the purity of sarvajñatā."
“World-Honored One!
This profound *prajñāpāramitā* is truly marvelous; how could there be any obstacles within it?
The Buddha said:
“There are such obstacles.

Sons and daughters of good family who wish to write down this Prajñāpāramitā should write it down with great haste; those who wish to receive and uphold it, or wish to recite it, or wish to maintain its practice, should likewise do so with great haste.”
Why is this? Because there may be obstacles encountered while one has not yet finished copying and practicing it.

If a son or daughter of good family can complete the transcription in one month, or two, three, four, five months, or even a year, they must certainly transcribe, uphold, receive, recite, and study it. If they have completed the transcription and are upholding, studying, and receiving it within one month, they should likewise bring it to completion; if it takes as long as a year, they should likewise bring it to completion.
"Why is this? It is because among many precious jewels, various causes and conditions for obstacles arise. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!

Regarding this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, those who write it down, uphold it, study it, recite it, practice it, and keep its contents in mind—Māra Pāpīyān will constantly intend to cut them off from it.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Even if Pāpīyān should wish to sever [this teaching], he will ultimately be unable to sever it from those who do not abandon their practice and who uphold and study it."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By whose grace is it that Māra Pāpīyān is unable to sever those who study the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“This is the work of the Buddhas, such that Māra Pāpīyān cannot interrupt it.
Furthermore, it is also the grace of the Buddhas of the ten directions who protect this bodhisattva who upholds the Prajñāpāramitā, so that Māra Pāpīyān cannot interrupt it.”
Why is this so? Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva upholds the Prajñāpāramitā and is protected by the Buddhas, Māra, the son of Heaven (Pāpīyān), will ultimately be unable to sever it or create obstacles for them.
Why is this? Śāriputra, all those bodhisattvas who write down,
uphold, receive, study, contemplate, and recite the Prajñāpāramitā should be protected by the dharmas of all Buddhas, so that Māra Pāpīyān cannot create obstacles or hindrances along the way.
Śāriputra! These sons and daughters of good family should form this thought:
"That I now write down, uphold, and study the Prajñāpāramitā is entirely the work of all the Buddhas."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are good men or good women who write down, uphold, receive, and study the Prajñāpāramitā, they shall all be protected and sustained by the grace of the Buddha.”
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is! Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One!

Do the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently residing in the ten directions perhaps know those sons and daughters of good family who write down, uphold, study, recite, and chant this Prajñāpāramitā?”
“Do they possess the Buddha-eye? Do they know? Do they see?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“All those sons and daughters of good family who practice the bodhisattva path, and who write down, uphold, study, recite, and practice the Prajñāpāramitā—those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions have already seen them and already known them as they write down, uphold, study, recite, and practice the Prajñāpāramitā.”
You should know that such a person is now close to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and will attain it before long. Śāriputra!

Furthermore, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family who practices the bodhisattva path writes down, upholds, studies, recites, masters, and practices the *prajñāpāramitā* according to its instructions, and with love and joy makes offerings to the *prajñāpāramitā* with famous flowers, powdered incense, liquid incense, blended incense, silken banners, flower canopies, and flags.
All those who perform such offerings are seen by all Buddhas with their divine eye once they have become these good sons and good daughters.
These good sons and good daughters who write down, uphold, practice, and study the Prajñāpāramitā obtain the greatest merit, attain great virtue, and achieve the supreme practice.

Good sons and good daughters who uphold the merit of their roots of goodness shall never fall into the evil realms and will proceed until they reach the stage of *avaivartika*. They shall never be separated from the Buddhas or the six *pāramitās*, and they shall never be separated from internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) or the emptiness of existence and non-existence (*bhāvābhāva-śūnyatā*).
Until they reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they shall never be separated from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. Śāriputra!

After the Tathāgata has passed away, this Prajñāpāramitā shall remain in the south; the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās of the south shall likewise receive, study, write, and uphold this profound Prajñāpāramitā. By virtue of these merits, they shall never fall into the evil realms, but shall instead receive the blessings of gods and humans.
Having practiced and clarified the six pāramitās, one should further make offerings to and serve the Buddhas; after serving them, one shall attain liberation through the three vehicles.

Śāriputra! In whichever direction the Prajñāpāramitā resides, and wherever it reaches, the four classes of disciples should likewise receive, uphold, write down, and recite this profound Prajñāpāramitā. By upholding these merits, they shall not fall into the evil realms, but will instead receive the blessings of gods and humans.

Furthermore, one should also practice the six pāramitās; having clarified the six pāramitās, one should then make offerings to and serve the Buddhas, and after serving them, attain liberation through the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.

Śāriputra! This Prajñāpāramitā shall turn northward; the fourfold assembly in the north shall likewise receive, write down, uphold, recite, and practice this profound Prajñāpāramitā. By virtue of these merits, they shall not be born in the three evil destinies, but shall instead receive the blessings of the two [noble] paths. They shall also practice the six pāramitās, serve the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and further attain liberation through the three vehicles.
Śāriputra! At that time, the profound Prajñāpāramitā shall perform the work of a Buddha. Why is this so?

Śāriputra! After my parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma is about to perish, I have already foreknown those sons and daughters of good family who will receive, uphold, and maintain this profound Prajñāpāramitā.

I further know that these sons and daughters of good family, having offered their whole hearts to the *prajñāpāramitā* with all manner of famous incenses, silken banners, flowers, and canopies, shall by virtue of this merit not fall into the three evil realms. They shall receive the wholesome blessings of the second stage, practice the six *pāramitās*, make offerings to all Buddhas, and attain liberation through the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
Why is this? Śāriputra, the Tathāgata has already perceived such people; he has already praised these people, and I have already designated the station where these people shall abide.
"The Buddhas of the present in the ten directions likewise praise them; they see these people and have already marked them.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Will this Prajñāpāramitā subsequently be universally present in the northern direction?
The Buddha said, "It is as you have said."

Furthermore, one should know that those sons of good family or daughters of good family who, in future times, receive, study, transcribe, uphold, and practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, have long since set their minds upon the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), and have made offerings to numerous Buddhas and cultivated various roots of goodness.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In the future, how many sons and daughters of good family in the northern direction will practice the bodhisattva path, receiving, upholding, reciting, and explaining the Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"In the future, although there will be many sons and daughters of good family in the northern world who uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, few indeed will be those who achieve the Mahāyāna."

Śāriputra! Those sons and daughters of good family who practice the bodhisattva path, upon hearing the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, do not find it difficult, do not grow weary of it, and do not feel terror.
Why is this? Because these sons and daughters of good family have already seen the Buddhas and have already heard the profound Dharma from those Buddhas. Why is this?

These good sons and good daughters have already fulfilled the six pāramitās; they have already fulfilled internal emptiness, external emptiness, and the emptiness of existence and non-existence; and they have already fulfilled the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
These sons and daughters of good family have performed many meritorious deeds and have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of all sentient beings.
Śāriputra! For the sake of these good men and good women, I teach the wisdom of sarvajñatā;
likewise, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past also taught that which accords with the wisdom of sarvajñatā.

All those who seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi do so for the sake of birth, old age, sickness, and death; for their sake as well, he explains the matters of the various wisdoms of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

These sons and daughters of good family, from their initial resolve until the final goal, seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; even Māra and the gods of Māra can never destroy them, let alone others who engage in evil conduct and wish to slander the profound prajñāpāramitā.
Śāriputra! When these good men and good women hear this profound Prajñāpāramitā, they immediately attain the most sublime joy and establish many people in Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said:
"When I was a bodhisattva, I also made this vow:
'We, too, shall establish countless sentient beings and exhort them to practice the bodhisattva path; we, too, shall receive the prediction of non-retrogression for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.'"
If there are bodhisattvas who resolve their minds [upon enlightenment], I rejoice on their behalf;
and for all those who exhort others to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I likewise rejoice on their behalf.
"Good sons and good daughters who practice the Prajñāpāramitā have already made this vow before the Buddhas of the past; now, once again before me, they vow for the sake of sentient beings:
'I shall benefit and bring peace and security to sentient beings; I shall exhort and assist all sentient beings to establish the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, so that it shall never waver.'"
Why is this? Because the Buddhas of the past likewise rejoiced on behalf of those bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds [on enlightenment] and made such vows. Śāriputra!

I rejoice on behalf of those sons and daughters of good family; furthermore, desiring to bring peace and security to all, I exhort and assist sentient beings so that they may establish themselves in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, remain free from the six defilements (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and attain pure and wondrous conduct.
Having already purified oneself, one further gives pure gifts;
having given pure and wondrous gifts, one then receives the merit and blessings of pure and wondrous virtue;

having received pure and wondrous blessings, one further distinguishes between all internal and external possessions for the sake of sentient beings, enabling them to obtain pure and wondrous blessings.
By virtue of these merits, they will travel throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions to wherever the *prajñāpāramitā* is being taught, there to hear and receive it;
having heard and received it, they will in turn exhort and inspire sentient beings in those places, causing them to establish the mind set upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary, World-Honored One!

Regarding the dharmas of the past, future, and present spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, there is nothing he does not know; he knows the conduct of sentient beings without exception, and there is no matter he does not understand. He further knows all the buddha-works of the future, past, and present Buddhas, as well as the matters concerning the Saṃgha.”

There may be good sons or good daughters who, having attained the six pāramitās, wish to recite and receive them; yet, if their minds fluctuate between progress and retreat, they will be unable to study the six pāramitās.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family seeks the six pāramitās with a mind that neither advances nor retreats, practicing with diligence and without indolence, they will then be able to fully possess the six pāramitās all at once.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family practices in this way, will they obtain the profound sūtras? Is this in accordance with the Prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddha said:
"A profound sūtra such as this corresponds to the Prajñāpāramitā. Why is that?"
This is because they are able to encourage and assist sentient beings, establishing them so that they may resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Śāriputra, these sons and daughters of good family do not abandon birth, old age, sickness, and death within the six *pāramitās*; they practice with diligence and without indolence according to the teaching of the *prajñā-pāramitā*, purifying buddha-fields and transforming sentient beings, causing them to establish the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, never becoming lax or weary.
Chapter 47: Awakening to Māra The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Forty-Seven: Awakening to Māra Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, you have praised these sons and daughters of good family who resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and practice the six *pāramitās*, who take up the Buddha-fields and transform sentient beings; their merit is indeed such as this.”
"How do these good sons and good daughters proceed so as to sever and eliminate obstacles?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If eloquence does not arise immediately, one should know that this is the work of Māra."
Subhūti said: "World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva know that the failure of eloquence to arise immediately is the work of Māra?"
The Buddha said:
"When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, it takes a long time to fulfill the six pāramitās.
For this reason, if a bodhisattva’s eloquence does not arise immediately, you should know that this is the work of Māra."
"Subhūti! If eloquence suddenly arises in a bodhisattva, this too is the work of Māra.
"World-Honored One!"
"Why is this? For eloquence to arise suddenly is also the work of Māra!
The Buddha said, "This is because the Bodhisattva practicing the six pāramitās has suddenly given rise to eloquence."

Why is this? Because their learning lacks both foundation and culmination, and their eloquence arises abruptly and cannot reach its ultimate conclusion; therefore, one should recognize these as the works of Māra.

When Bodhisattvas write this sūtra, they mock one another, their minds become distracted and unsettled, and the assembly’s intentions are discordant—such instances constitute the works of Māra for a Bodhisattva.
While reading this sutra, one may think to oneself:
"I do not find any flavor within this sutra.
To then abandon it and depart—this should also be recognized as the work of Māra.
Subhūti! When this sutra is being preached, if one receives and upholds it while being arrogant, engaging in frivolous speech, or concealing the faults of others, this too is the work of Māra.
While receiving, upholding, reciting, and studying this sutra, they each become arrogant and mock one another.
A bodhisattva should recognize this as the work of Māra.
Subhūti, when this sutra is being received, if each person’s mind becomes distracted and their thoughts are not in harmony, you should know that this is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
How is it that failing to find the flavor within the sutra and then abandoning it should be recognized as the work of Māra?”
The Buddha said:
"These bodhisattvas have never practiced the six pāramitās and have not heard the prajñāpāramitā; they have conceived in their own minds the thought:
'I have received no prediction regarding the six pāramitās.'"
"For this reason, if upon hearing the Prajñāpāramitā one does not feel joy or delight but instead abandons it and departs, you should know that this is the work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
"World-Honored One!"
Why does a bodhisattva say,
"I have not received a prediction," and depart without pleasure?
The Buddha said:
"One who has not yet attained the path of a bodhisattva shall never receive the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore it is said:"
"I have no prediction regarding the six pāramitās," he says,
and then abandons them and departs.
You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
If there is a bodhisattva who thinks to himself:
"In my hometown, the Prajñāpāramitā was not heard, and in the place where I was born,
it likewise was not heard," and then abandons [the teaching] and no longer wishes to study the Prajñāpāramitā.
If the mind turns back for even a single thought-moment, one is immediately set back by one kalpa; according to the number of such mental reversals, one must undergo that many more kalpas.
One will then have to study other sutras once again, neither abiding in *sarvajñatā* nor yet arriving at *sarvajñatā*.
"These bodhisattvas are like those who abandon the root to grasp at the branches and twigs; you should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Subhūti said, "World-Honored One!"
“What sūtras are there that do not emerge from *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), yet you wish to study and recite other sūtras?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the three gates of liberation are what the śrāvakas should practice. If good sons and good daughters abide in these, seeking the path of a srotāpanna, the path of a sakṛdāgāmin, an anāgāmin, or an arhat, but do not take up *sarvajñatā*, they will thereby create an obstacle for themselves.”
Subhūti! This is what it means to abandon the root and cling to the branches. Why is that?
This bodhisattva is likewise born from within the *prajñāpāramitā*; the *prajñāpāramitā* also gives rise to both the supramundane (*lokottara*) dharmas and the mundane (*laukika*) dharmas.
A bodhisattva who studies the *prajñāpāramitā* should study both the supramundane dharmas and the mundane dharmas.
It is like a dog that, having obtained the food of its master, refuses to eat it, and instead eats the food of a servant.
Subhūti, so it will be with those who study the bodhisattva path in the future: having obtained the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will abandon it and instead cling to the branches and twigs.
"Subhūti! You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Suppose there is a person who wishes to see an elephant; having found the elephant, he abandons it and instead seeks the elephant's tracks.
What do you think—would this person be considered clever?
Subhūti said: "They would not be wise.

"In future ages, there will be those who practice the bodhisattva path who, having obtained the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, instead abandon it and further study the sūtras and dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
"What do you think? Is this bodhisattva wise? Subhūti replied, "He is not wise."
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, this bodhisattva should recognize these as the deeds of Māra.”
It is like a person who wishes to see the great ocean; having seen it, they abandon it and instead look at the water in a cow's footprint, saying:
"As for the size of the ocean, how could it possibly surpass this?"
"What do you think, Subhūti? Is such a person wise?
Subhūti replied, "World-Honored One!"
"This is not wise.
The Buddha said:

"In the future, there will be those who study the bodhisattva path; having obtained the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will nevertheless abandon it and instead study the sūtras and dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, receiving instruction and reciting them therein."
Subhūti, these bodhisattvas should recognize such as the work of Māra. Subhūti,
it is like a craftsman who, wishing to measure the patterns of the palaces of the sun and moon, sets up and constructs a palace for Śakra.
"What do you think? Although that craftsman is skillful, would he be able to create it?
Subhūti said, "World-Honored One!"
"This matter is extremely difficult; it is not something that can be accomplished by ordinary people or worldly fools.

The Buddha said, "In a future age, there will be those who practice the bodhisattva path and succeed in studying the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, yet they will abandon it midway and instead seek to fulfill omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and the matters pertaining to omniscience within the sūtras and dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
"What do you think? Would such a person be able to achieve *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge)?
Subhūti replied, "They would not be able to achieve it."
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, this bodhisattva should recognize these as the deeds of Māra.”
It is, for example, like a person who wishes to see a wheel-turning sage king; having seen him, they instead look upon a minor king and examine him closely, saying:
"How does the body of the sage king differ from this?"
"Would this person be considered clever? Subhūti replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"This is not wise," the Buddha said.

"In the future, there will be those of slight virtue who study the Bodhisattva path; having heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will study, uphold, and practice it, yet they will abandon the Middle Way and instead receive the sūtras and teachings of the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas."
Furthermore, he says:
"I shall fully realize sarvajñā within this.
What do you think? Is such a bodhisattva wise?
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One, it would not be wise.”
The Buddha said,
"This is a demonic deed of a bodhisattva.

It is like a hungry person who, having obtained food of a hundred flavors, further thinks of wanting food of sixty flavors, and thus abandons the hundred-flavored food to eat the sixty-flavored food."
"What do you think? Is this wise?
Subhūti replied, "World-Honored One!"
"This is not wise.
The Buddha said:

"In the future, there will be those who study the bodhisattva path; having obtained this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will abandon it and instead seek *sarvajñatā* within the scriptures and teachings of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
“Would this bodhisattva be wise? Subhūti replied,
“He would not be wise.”
The Buddha said:
"This is a demonic deed of a bodhisattva.
It is like a man who, having obtained a priceless maṇi jewel, instead compares it to crystal."
"What do you think? Is this wise?
Subhūti replied, "World-Honored One!"
"They are not wise.

The Buddha said, "In the future, there will be those who study the bodhisattva path; having obtained the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will instead abandon it and take up the sūtras and dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, seeking to attain *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) through the sūtras and dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
"Would one not be clever?
Subhūti replied, "One would not be clever."
The Buddha said:
"This is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Subhūti!..."

If there are good sons or good daughters who, having written out the Prajñāpāramitā, are then prevented from writing it due to external circumstances; or if there are obstacles regarding forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects (dharmas); or if there are obstacles to the dānapāramitā, śīlapāramitā, kṣāntipāramitā, vīryapāramitā, or dhyānapāramitā—even up to obstacles being created against anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi itself.

Why is this? Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is not an obstacle; it is inconceivable and not subject to selection. It is neither born nor extinguished, neither attached nor severed, unimpeded, not a view, not an activity, and not a reliance.
Why is this? Subhūti, the Prajñāpāramitā possesses no such characteristics.
"If there should be any bodhisattva who, while copying this sutra, encounters such obstacles and hindrances, you should know that these are the works of Māra.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Can this Prajñāpāramitā be written down? The Buddha said, "No."

Why is this? Because the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is in its true nature invisible; even up to the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), it is in its true nature invisible, and even up to omniscience (sarvajñatā), it is likewise invisible.
All that exists is invisible.
Why? Because there is nothing that exists.
That which is non-existent cannot be written down. Subhūti!
A son of good family or a daughter of good family practicing the bodhisattva path should form this thought:
"That this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is 'nothingness'—
this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
Those who practice the bodhisattva path, having written out the characters of this profound *prajñāpāramitā* sūtra, enter into these characters and say:
‘I have written the *prajñāpāramitā*.’”
"World-Honored One!
These six pāramitās are dharmas that possess no words. Why is this so?"
The six pāramitās have no letters; the five aggregates likewise have no letters, and even up to sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), there are no letters.
World-Honored One!

Good sons and good daughters who practice the bodhisattva path, from the six pāramitās up to sarvajñatā, if they conceive of entering the prajñāpāramitā by way of non-letters, this too is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.

“Subhūti! When a son of good family or a daughter of good family who practices the bodhisattva path is transcribing the Prajñāpāramitā, if they give rise to thoughts of commanderies, kingdoms, districts, towns, hamlets, or villages; or if, upon hearing the voices of their parents or those they revere, they bring their parents to mind; or if they think of brothers, sisters, or matters of soldiers, bandits, and sensual desire—[they should not do so].”
Having formed this thought, another thought arose.
Māra Pāpīyān further reinforced that thought, creating this obstacle in order to cause an interruption so that [the teaching] would not be written down or upheld.
Subhūti! These are the deeds of Māra for a bodhisattva.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family who practices the bodhisattva path, while copying and upholding the Prajñāpāramitā, should encounter the arising of offerings—such as clothing, wealth and profit, food and drink, bedding, or medicine for the sick—and someone should say:
‘Because I have written out the Prajñāpāramitā, I have received this offering.
Subhūti, one who delights in such thoughts should recognize this as the work of Māra. Subhūti!
While this sūtra was being written, Māra Pāpīyas spoke before the Bodhisattva about various other profound sūtras.
The Bodhisattva, possessing *upāyakauśalya*, did not accept what Māra had said.
Why is this? Because this sutra cannot cause people to reach sarvajñā (all-knowledge). Subhūti!
"If a bodhisattva lacks the mind of *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), upon hearing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they will wish to abandon it and depart.
The Buddha said:

"I have extensively explained the matters of *upāyakauśalya* for the sake of all bodhisattvas; those who wish to attain the matters of *upāyakauśalya* should seek them within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
Subhūti! If good men or good women who seek the bodhisattva vehicle abandon the profound prajñāpāramitā and wish to seek upāyakauśalya from the sūtras and dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Subhūti! You should know that this is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
*The Sutra of the Radiant Prajñāpāramitā*, Scroll Ten.
The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Eleven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mokṣala of Khotan during the Western Jin Dynasty,
by Imperial Decree.
Chapter 48: On Non-harmony, from the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra. Chapter Forty-Eight: On Non-harmony. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
"There may be someone who delights in hearing and receiving the Prajñāpāramitā;
yet the Dharma-preacher’s body may be so utterly exhausted that he is unable to preach it."
"One should recognize this as the work of Māra. The Buddha said:
"If a Dharma teacher is physically at ease and wishes to speak;"
However, those who receive the Dharma may become attached to other causes and conditions and thus disperse;
one should recognize this as the work of Māra, Subhūti!
If the person receiving the sutra wishes to transcribe the Prajñāpāramitā,
while the Dharma master wishes to go elsewhere,
this is the work of Māra.
If the Dharma master desires offerings of bedding, food and drink, and medicine for illness, as well as all manner of clothing and robes,
while the person receiving the sutra has few desires, is content, and dwells in silent non-attachment,
they will not be in harmony; this is the work of Māra.
"Subhūti! The Dharma-preacher is one of few desires and contentment, who observes the precepts without greed, whose will is always diligent, and who delights in meditative concentration;
whereas the recipient of the sūtra does not know contentment, but greedily seeks offerings."
When the two do not harmonize, this constitutes the work of Māra.
Subhūti! A person who is a Dharma-preacher should practice twelve dharmas in the seclusion and tranquility of an araṇya.
Subhūti, those who receive this sutra may be unable to sit in meditative seclusion and may not practice the twelve dharmas; yet, Subhūti,
those who receive this sutra and uphold these twelve dharmas are able to dwell alone in tranquil stillness.
One who acts as a Dharma teacher will never have such an intention;
when these two do not harmonize and cannot engage in writing or study, this is the work of Māra. Subhūti!
The person who receives the sutra is diligent and faithful, upholds the precepts according to the Dharma, and delights in the Prajñāpāramitā;
yet the one who acts as the Dharma master has many desires, violates the Vinaya, and is unable to maintain the precepts.
Subhūti! The Dharma-preacher is diligent, full of faith and joy, and observes the prohibitions and precepts while practicing the Prajñāpāramitā;
yet the person who receives the sūtra has many transgressions, violating the precepts and the Vinaya.
When the two are not in harmony, this constitutes the work of Māra. Subhūti!
One who acts as a Dharma-preacher should have no greedy desires, should delight in giving, and should have vast and universal aspirations.
Those who receive this sutra often seek existence, harbor desires, and are stingy and possessive; their wills are obstructed and their minds are narrow, so that the two do not harmonize. Subhūti!
If the person who receives the sutra has no further desires, delights in giving, is free from greed,
and possesses unimpeded aspirations, yet the Dharma master instead becomes more greedy and insatiable,
with narrow-minded intentions; when these two are not in harmony, this constitutes the work of Māra.
Subhūti! If the person who receives the sutra wishes to provide all the requisites for the Dharma teacher,
yet the Dharma teacher is unwilling to accept them, that person shall not be able to study and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti, it may be that the Dharma-preacher desires offerings of clothing and possessions,
while the person who receives the sutra is more frugal, pure, and observant of precepts, having no longing for gain or sustenance; thus, they do not harmonize with one another.
This is the work of Māra.
Subhūti, those who act as Dharma-preachers are clear regarding the path of the sūtras and possess courageous eloquence and fierce wisdom; yet [they may still fall into such errors].
However, those who receive the sutra may be dark-minded, obstructed, and dull-witted, such that their resolve does not awaken in a timely manner. Subhūti!
Those who receive the sutra possess resolute will, penetrating intent, and subtle wisdom and eloquence, awakening at once.
If those who act as Dharma masters are greedy and ignorant, lacking understanding and failing to harmonize,
this is the work of Māra. Subhūti!
The Dharma Master clearly understands the twelve divisions of the scriptures and explains them in their proper sequence without deficiency;
yet the person receiving the teachings does not know the sequence and has not yet mastered the principles of the direct and the inverse.
Subhūti, if the recipient of the sutra clearly understands its sequence, understands the twelve divisions of the scriptures, and knows matters of reversal and conformity,
yet the Dharma master is unable to comprehend them;
When their aspirations do not harmonize, this constitutes the work of Māra. Subhūti,
those who serve as Dharma-preachers must be fully endowed with the six pāramitās.
The person who receives the sutra may not be complete in their practice;
or, the recipient of the Dharma may be complete in the six pāramitās, while the Dharma master is not.
When these two do not harmonize, this constitutes the work of Māra.
Subhūti! One who serves as a Dharma teacher should be fully endowed with the six perfections and further possess *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means).

Subhūti, if the person who receives the sutra lacks these six things and furthermore lacks *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), these two will not be in harmony; this constitutes the work of Māra. Subhūti!
The Dharma teacher attains dharani, while the recipient of the sūtra and Dharma does not; or,
the recipient of the Dharma attains dharani [while the teacher does not].
Subhūti, when one who acts as a Dharma teacher lacks these two harmonious conditions, this constitutes the work of Māra. Subhūti!
A person who wishes to transcribe the Prajñāpāramitā into a scroll for the purpose of receiving the sutra finds that the Dharma-preacher is unwilling to give it;
yet the Dharma-preacher is just about to give the sutra.
Subhūti, if those who receive the Dharma do not wish to transcribe it,
nor do they harmonize with it, this is the work of Māra. Subhūti!
The Dharma master is entangled and enveloped by the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*),
while the person receiving the sūtra has no such coverings and their resolve is not in harmony.
If the recipient of the sūtra is deluded by the five obscurations;
Subhūti, for one who acts as a Dharma teacher, the hindrances have already been exhausted;
yet, when these two do not harmonize, this constitutes the work of Māra. Subhūti!
While one is writing out this Prajñāpāramitā, suppose someone comes and speaks of the intensity of the suffering in the three evil realms, saying to that person:
"I can cause you to be free from such toil and hardship; why do you practice for the sake of this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
"This is the work of Māra.

Subhūti, when one is copying the Prajñāpāramitā or wishes to preach it, someone may instead come and praise the pleasures of the desire heavens (kāmadhātu), where the five desires are indulged in at will, and food, drink, clothing, and music are provided spontaneously; or they may praise the form heavens (rūpadhātu), where one takes dhyāna as pleasure and sustenance; or the formless heavens (ārūpyadhātu), where one takes tranquility as sustenance and pleasure."

From the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception, although the pleasures of these three realms exist, they are likewise impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; all shall perish and cannot endure for long. It would be better to receive the Dharma of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha than to delight in the three realms and undergo this cycle of birth and death;
this is a demonic deed of a Bodhisattva.
The Dharma master desires to attain a tranquil mind and dwell in solitude;
yet those who receive the teachings of the sutras lead large crowds and delight in clamor and bustle.
If the Dharma master’s inclination is toward leading crowds;
Furthermore, if the recipient of the sutra prefers solitude and quietude and does not harmonize with others, one should recognize this as the work of Māra.
If the Dharma Master desires a large following and keeps many disciples;
The person who receives the sutra differs from his peers in that he desires to remain solitary;
whereas those who receive the Dharma desire a multitude of followers,
while the Dharma Master desires tranquility.
Furthermore, they do not harmonize; this is the work of Māra.
The Dharma-preacher regards himself with self-importance and desires honor, while the recipient of the sutra is arrogant and lacks respect.
If the Dharma teacher has no desire for worldly gain and does not take pleasure in being honored or respected,
yet the recipient of the Dharma delights in practicing such honor and respect,
they will not be in harmony; this is the work of Māra.
If the Dharma-preacher intends to receive and take up the Prajñāpāramitā when it is being written down,
but the person receiving the scripture has no intention to give it,
and their minds do not harmonize, this is the work of Māra.
If one who receives the sutra, while transcribing the Prajñāpāramitā, thinks of turning away from the Prajñāpāramitā and gives rise to the intention to seek wealth and profit therein—
this is the work of Māra.
If the Dharma master wishes to go to a place where life is precarious and grain is expensive,
but the recipient of the sutra does not wish to go and cannot follow him,
and they thus do not act in harmony, this is the work of Māra.
The Dharma Master wishes to go to a place of abundance, joy, and low grain prices;
those who have received the sutra all wish to follow him.
Yet, midway, the Dharma Master creates further obstacles.
"You merely desire to crave offerings and wish to follow me to receive them, yet you do not know whether you will actually obtain them when you arrive there.
Upon seeing these signs of being sent away, those who had received the sutra gradually departed;
this is the work of Māra.
If the Dharma Master says to the recipient of the sutra and Dharma:
"The place I wish to go lies along a road through a desolate marsh; there are bandits, wild men, and hunters there, and it abounds with tigers, wolves, snakes, vipers, and venomous insects."
"Can you follow me and endure this suffering?
When the recipient of the Dharma hears this, their mind is not joyful and they cannot go along with them.
Creating such an obstacle so that they cannot transcribe, study, or receive this sutra—this is the work of Māra.

When the Dharma Master goes to a place where he has previously taught or intends to visit again, and the recipient of the Dharma wishes to accompany him there, the Dharma Master says to the student of the sutra:
"I must now pass through this place for a short while; you should return for now."
The recipient of the sūtra becomes sorrowful and unable to follow along; failing to hear it, they are unable to receive and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā.
This is the work of Māra. "Furthermore, Subhūti!

That Māra Pāpīyān constantly schemes and contemplates in his mind, desiring to don the robes of a śramaṇa; he always seeks to cause disruption and disorder, wishing that there should be no one who writes down, upholds, recites, or studies the Prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
for what reason does Pāpīyān constantly assume the robes of a śramaṇa in a ruined and disheveled manner, desiring not to allow anyone to receive and study the Prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Pāpīyān will don the robes of a śramaṇa and seek to ruin and alienate those who study the Prajñāpāramitā.
He will further say to people:"
"According to the teachings in my sutras and upon examining the matters in your sutras, this is not the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Subhūti! Those who have not yet received their prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) will immediately fall into doubt upon hearing this teaching; having such a doubting mind, they will no longer write down, uphold, or study the *prajñāpāramitā*."
This is a work of Māra for a bodhisattva.
Subhūti, furthermore,
Pāpīyān may take the form of a bhikṣu and say to one who is training in the Prajñāpāramitā:
“Good sons and good daughters who study, recite, and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā will realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and attain the paths of the srotāpanna, arhat, and pratyekabuddha.”
By creating such obstacles, they will no longer study, receive, or uphold the Prajñāpāramitā;
this is the work of Māra, Subhūti!
When this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is being taught, many demonic activities arise with the intent to interrupt it.
Therefore, Subhūti, you should recognize these demonic activities.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
how should a bodhisattva recognize the works of Māra and remain far removed from the works of Māra?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Those matters merely resemble the six pāramitās; if one perceives them as such, that itself constitutes protection and keeps one far removed from the works of Māra."
A bodhisattva should always remain far removed from the sūtras and dharmas practiced by arhats and pratyekabuddhas;
they should distance themselves from them. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

Pāpīyān spoke before the Bodhisattva of internal emptiness, external emptiness, and the emptiness of existence and non-existence; from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to the three gates of liberation—these are the matters of the path attained by Arhats;
these are the works of Māra.
Pāpīyān again transforms himself into the body of the Tathāgata, with its golden light and marks, and approaches the bodhisattva to cause the bodhisattvas to give rise to conceptualizations.
To give rise to such conceptualizations regarding sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) is to cause its depletion;
one should know that this is the work of Māra.
Subhūti! Māra will again manifest in the form of a Buddha, accompanied by a multitude of bhikṣus, and come to where these sons and daughters of good family are.
These sons and daughters of good family will then give rise to the thought, saying:
"If, in a future age, I may attain such a body that my assembly of disciples preaches the Dharma therein just as they do today"—
one who forms such a thought will cause a diminution of sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
Pāpīyān again manifested as countless hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas practicing the six pāramitās before these sons and daughters of good family;
having seen them, they further gave rise to conceptions regarding them.
To give rise to conceptual thoughts is to diminish *sarvajñatā*;
this is the work of Māra. Why is this so?
Subhūti! In the prajñāpāramitā, there are no five aggregates, and even up to the Path, there is nothing at all.
Since there are no five aggregates and no Path, there are likewise no Buddha-dharmas and no assembly of disciples.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are entirely empty and non-existent, Subhūti!
Good sons and good daughters, when writing, reciting, or reading this Prajñāpāramitā, there will be many causes and conditions for its arising.
For example, in the house of a great elder of Jambudvīpa, where there is much gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, and other exquisite, rare treasures, there are many who harbor hatred and envy.
“Noble sons and noble daughters who receive, uphold, recite, and chant the Prajñāpāramitā will encounter many who harbor hatred and jealousy, wishing to destroy them.
Subhūti said, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
There will be many demonic activities and many who harbor hatred and envy. Why is this?
Because foolish and ignorant persons, acting under the influence of Māra, will be intent on obstructing and destroying those who study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"These people who destroy the Dharma will never again set their minds upon this sublime Dharma.
The Buddha said,
"As Subhūti has stated, these foolish individuals are incited by Māra and are solely intent on causing ruin."

These people are foolish destroyers of the Dharma; it is because they are beginners who have only recently heard the Dharma, because they have not performed meritorious deeds and their roots of goodness are few, because they have not associated with true spiritual friends, and because they have not made offerings to the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

Subhūti! If one writes down, maintains, recites, reads, explains, receives, practices, and upholds the Prajñāpāramitā at the proper time, there will be no obstacles and no demonic activities will arise. Being free from such hindrances, one is able to fulfill the six pāramitās, and even upon reaching sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), there will be no further obstacles.
If there are good men or good women who write down, uphold, recite, and chant the Prajñāpāramitā, they will then be fully endowed with the five pāramitās and sarvajñatā;
you should know that this constitutes the work of a Buddha.

Furthermore, if one is fully endowed with internal and external emptiness as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the ten powers, and is fully endowed with sarvajñā (all-knowledge);
one should know that this, too, constitutes the work of a Buddha.
The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently residing in the ten directions likewise perform buddha-works for such good sons and good daughters who practice the Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are currently established in the stage of non-retrogression throughout the ten directions likewise protect these good men and good women who practice the prajñāpāramitā, and they also encourage and assist them.
Chapter 49: The Great Illumination. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā, Chapter Forty-nine: The Great Illumination. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
"Suppose there is a woman who gives birth to children one by one, numbering from one up to a thousand."

If the mother falls ill, each of her sons seeks to provide medical treatment; they administer what is cold or warm, dry or moist, and whatever nourishment is appropriate for her upbringing, so as to ensure the mother’s well-being and comfort.
Why is this? It is because you have enabled us to see the sun and the moon; we were unfilial in our support of you and never repaid your kindness. Thus it is, Subhūti!
The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas always regard with their Buddha-eye those who practice the Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because the profound Prajñāpāramitā is the great illumination of the world.
The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions also constantly behold with their Buddha-eye those who practice the Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?
The profound *prajñāpāramitā* gives birth to all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, enabling them to attain the wisdom of *sarvajñatā*.
For this reason, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas always regard with equal vision those who practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.

The five *pāramitās* of all Tathāgatas are likewise born within this; internal and external emptiness (*śūnyatā*), as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) are all produced therein. The ten powers (*bala*), the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*), and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) are also all produced therein. The paths of the *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, *arhat*, *pratyekabuddha*, and the path of the *samyaksaṃbuddha* are all born from within the *prajñāpāramitā*. All Buddhas of the past, future, and present are born from within the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, having themselves attained the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Subhūti! If there are good men or good women who write down, uphold, receive, and study the Prajñāpāramitā, the Buddhas will constantly behold those who practice the Prajñāpāramitā with their Buddha-eye; the Buddhas will constantly protect them so that they do not waver, until they reach Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi without any diminution.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the World-Honored One has said, the Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of bodhisattvas and is the great illumination of the world."
World-Honored One!
In what way is the perfection of wisdom the mother of bodhisattvas?
In what way is it the great illumination of the world?
"How are the Buddhas born?
How do they manifest as the light of the world?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The Prajñāpāramitā gives birth to the ten powers and eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and it gives birth to sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).

The Tathāgata has manifested that these dharmas are fully complete; therefore, when it is said that all Tathāgatas are born into the world from the Prajñāpāramitā, this refers to what the Tathāgata calls the five aggregates.”
“World-Honored One!
How does the profound *prajñāpāramitā* manifest the five aggregates?
The Buddha said:
"The Prajñāpāramitā is also unarisen; the manifestation of the five aggregates is also unextinguished.

The manifestation of the five aggregates is neither attached to nor severed; it neither increases nor decreases; it neither sustains nor abandons; and it does not belong to the past, the future, or the present."

Why is this? Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are neither manifested as success nor failure; they do not manifest as conditioned, nor do they manifest as unconditioned; they do not manifest as non-arising, nor do they manifest as non-existence, nor do they manifest as the reality of all phenomena.
In this way, Subhūti, it does not manifest success or failure;
this, Subhūti, is how the Prajñāpāramitā manifests the world. Subhūti!

The Prajñāpāramitā also knows the mental activities of all sentient beings; yet the Prajñāpāramitā does not know the location of sentient beings, nor does it know the location of the aggregates (skandhas) or the six sense bases (āyatanas), and even up to omniscience (sarvajñatā), it does not know their location.
Subhūti! This is how the profound *prajñāpāramitā* manifests in the world.
Yet, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not manifest the five aggregates, nor does it manifest anything up to and including *sarvajñatā*.
Why is this? Even deep prajñāpāramitā does not perceive deep prajñāpāramitā; how much less could it perceive the five aggregates, or even up to sarvajñatā, as something to be perceived?
Subhūti! Those who are called "sentient beings" are those in the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
The Tathāgata fully knows the distracted minds and concentrated minds of all beings throughout the world and the ten directions, and he further knows all their innumerable affairs.
Subhūti! How does the Tathāgata fully know the countless other matters of sentient beings?
It is by means of the Dharma.
The Tathāgata fully knows those with distracted minds and those with undistracted minds.
By what dharma does he know whether the minds of sentient beings are distracted or concentrated?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“If even phenomena cannot be perceived, how much less can one expect to find sentient beings who are either distracted or concentrated?
It is for this reason that you should know, Subhūti:”
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, knows that the minds of sentient beings are sometimes distracted and sometimes concentrated. How does he know this?
He knows it through impermanence, he knows it through liberation, he knows it through tranquility, and he knows it through cessation.
Therefore, one knows there is distraction and there is concentration. "Furthermore, Subhūti,
the Tathāgata fully knows those sentient beings who possess lust, anger, and delusion."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does one fully know?”
The Buddha said:
"To know the mind that possesses lust, anger, and delusion as being a mind that is not a mind of lust, anger, and delusion. Why is this?"
Since all things and even mindfulness are invisible, how much more so could lust, anger, and delusion possibly exist?
For this reason, the Tathāgata knows them all.
Subhūti! Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows those sentient beings who possess no thoughts of lust, anger, or delusion; he knows them all. Why is this?
One knows that which is to be known without the intention of lust, anger, or delusion;
yet this intention is not an intentional state. Why is this? Because two intentions do not conjoin. Therefore, the Tathāgata knows all.
Subhūti! By means of the prajñāpāramitā, the Tathāgata fully knows the mentalities of sentient beings; he fully knows those that are vast.
How does he fully know them?

Subhūti! The Tathāgata does not broaden the minds of sentient beings, nor does he narrow the minds of sentient beings; he does not increase the minds of sentient beings, nor does he decrease the minds of sentient beings; he does not bring the minds of sentient beings, nor does he send away the minds of sentient beings.
Why is this? Because the mind cannot be apprehended as advancing or retreating; for this reason, one knows all. Furthermore, Subhūti!
The Tathāgata, by means of the Prajñāpāramitā, fully knows that sentient beings possess great resolve. Why does he know this?
Because the minds of sentient beings neither come nor go, neither arise nor cease, and neither abide nor change; it is for this reason that he knows.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata,
by means of the perfection of wisdom, fully knows that the minds of sentient beings are without limit.
How does he fully know them?
Subhūti! One does not perceive that the minds of sentient beings increase or decrease, nor that they abide anywhere. Why is this?
Because the minds of sentient beings have no abode and are invisible, it is for this reason that one knows. "Furthermore, Subhūti,
it is by means of the *prajñāpāramitā* that the Tathāgata fully knows that the minds of sentient beings are invisible."
How does he know them all?
He knows them all because the minds of sentient beings have no form and possess nothing. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The Tathāgata, by means of the prajñāpāramitā, fully knows that the minds of sentient beings are unobservable. How does he know this? Subhūti!
Because the Tathāgata perceives the mental orientations of all sentient beings with his five eyes,
he knows this. Furthermore, Subhūti,
by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Tathāgata fully knows the contraction and extension, the contraction and expansion, of all sentient beings.
How is this known? Subhūti!
The contraction and extension, the coiling and unfolding of the minds of sentient beings, all arise from being born within the cave of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha).
They do not understand the five aggregates; they know only that there is a self and a world in the out-breath and in-breath. They know only this matter and are ignorant of everything else.
Furthermore, they do not understand the five aggregates nor do they understand the out-breath and in-breath; they know only that there is a self and a world, and are ignorant of everything else.
The body is the life-force, and the life-force is the body;
yet this body is not the life-force, and this life-force is not the body. Therefore, Subhūti!
The Tathāgata, by means of the perfection of wisdom, fully knows the contraction and extension, the contraction and expansion, of all sentient beings. Subhūti!
The Buddha knows the five aggregates.
How is this known?

It is known through knowing the suchness of the five aggregates, knowing the suchness of suchness, knowing the suchness of non-action, knowing the suchness of signlessness, knowing the suchness of non-exertion, knowing the suchness of non-proliferation, knowing the suchness of selflessness, and knowing the suchness of non-reliance.
Therefore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata takes the suchness of sentient beings as the bending, stretching, entering, and exiting of the five aggregates’ suchness.
That which is the suchness of the five aggregates is the suchness of all dharmas.
The suchness of all dharmas is the suchness of the six pāramitās;
the suchness of the six pāramitās is the suchness of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
the suchness of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is the suchness of the eighteen kinds of emptiness.
The suchness of the eighteen emptinesses is the suchness of the eight liberations and the nine successive meditations;
the suchness of the eight liberations and the nine successive meditations is the suchness of the Buddha’s ten powers;

the suchness of the ten powers is the suchness of the four unhindered wisdoms, the four immeasurable minds, the four fearlessnesses, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
The suchness of the eighteen dharmas is the suchness of the wisdom of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge);
the suchness of the wisdom of *sarvajñā* is the suchness of all wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, mundane and supramundane dharmas, and out-flowing and non-out-flowing dharmas;
this suchness of all these dharmas is the suchness of the past, future, and present.
The suchness of the past, future, and present is the suchness of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena;
the suchness of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena is the suchness of the stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, and arhat;
and the suchness of the arhat is the suchness of the pratyekabuddha.
The suchness of the pratyekabuddha is the suchness of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
the suchness of saṃbodhi is the suchness of the Way;
the suchness of the Way is the suchness of the Tathāgata.
The Suchness of the Tathāgata is the Single Suchness; it cannot be destroyed, nor can it be differentiated; it is inexhaustible and non-dual, and it cannot be made otherwise.
Subhūti! This is the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas.
It is by means of the perfection of wisdom that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to the suchness of all dharmas.
Subhūti! This Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Tathāgatas; it is the great illumination of the world. Therefore, Subhūti!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully knows the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena.
It is thus, not otherwise; there is nothing that can make it otherwise.
He fully knows all that is such and all that is thus.
"For this reason, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are called Tathāgatas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
"The suchness of all phenomena, and their being thus and not otherwise, is profound, profoundly profound,
World-Honored One!
Since the path of transformation flows forth from this suchness, who will be able to understand these most profound teachings as spoken by the Buddha?"
"Only an *avaivartika* bodhisattva-mahāsattva and an arhat whose outflows are exhausted (*kṣīṇāsrava*) are able to understand this.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"As for 'the inexhaustible suchness' (*tathatā*), of what is it the inexhaustible suchness?"
This is the suchness of all dharmas, which is inexhaustible.
Subhūti, when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he proclaimed this suchness of all dharmas.

Chapter 50: Inquiry into Characteristics, from the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra. At that time, the devaputras of the desire realm and the devaputras of the form realm throughout the trichiliocosm took various famous flowers and renowned incenses and scattered them over the Buddha. They prostrated, withdrew to stand aside, and each addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What has been spoken of as the *prajñāpāramitā* is exceedingly profound, exceedingly profound.
What is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of this *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha addressed the devaputras, saying:

“Deep Prajñāpāramitā is the mark of emptiness; it is the mark of signlessness, the mark of wishlessness, the mark of non-action, the mark of neither arising nor ceasing, the mark of neither attachment nor cessation, the mark of the emptiness of non-existence, the mark of non-reliance, and the mark of space.”
O sons of the gods!
The Prajñāpāramitā is thus profound.
The Tathāgata, for the sake of worldly convention, does not [act] for the sake of the Path, nor for the sake of cessation.
O sons of the gods!
These marks cannot be produced by gods, nāgas, spirits, or the people of the world; there is no one capable of nourishing them.
Why is this so? Because the devas, nāgas, spirits, and the people of the world are also of this same nature.
Therefore, mark does not nourish mark, and mark does not recognize mark.
Characteristics do not recognize the absence of characteristics, nor does the absence of characteristics recognize characteristics.
Characteristics and the absence of characteristics—both of these are empty; there is nothing that can establish them, nothing that can answer regarding them, and nothing that can recognize them.
O sons of the gods!

This mark is not produced by the five aggregates, nor is it accomplished by the six pāramitās; it is not produced by internal and external emptiness or the emptiness of existence and non-existence, nor is it accomplished by sarvajñatā.
O sons of the gods!
