This mark is neither a person nor a non-person; it is neither with outflows nor without outflows; it is neither the Path nor the mundane; it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the devaputras:
"If someone were to ask:
'What are the characteristics of this space?'"
"What do you think, sons of the gods!
Is the question asked by this person a correct one?
The sons of the gods replied:
“World-Honored One!
This is not an unequal question. Why is this so?
"Space has no marks and no creator.
The Buddha addressed the devas of the desire realm and the devas of the form realm, saying:
"Whether a Buddha appears or not, the marks and the essential nature [of phenomena] abide eternally."
"Because the Tathāgata has realized the characteristics and nature of reality as it truly is, he is called the Tathāgata.
The devaputras addressed the Buddha, saying,
"The characteristics realized by the Tathāgata are profoundly deep."
The Tathāgata, from this unimpeded wisdom of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, abides in signs and gathers them within the *prajñāpāramitā*.
How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
This profound *prajñāpāramitā* is the treasury of all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

Within this treasury, one realizes *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; within this treasury, one practices and attains the characteristics of all dharmas, the characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and the characteristics of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
The Buddha told the devaputras: "Form is the characteristic of shape;

that which is experienced is the characteristic of sensation; that which is perceived is the characteristic of perception; that which is good or evil is the characteristic of volitional formations; and that which is cognized is the characteristic of consciousness."
The Tathāgata has attained perfect enlightenment by virtue of the characteristic of non-appropriation.

That which is without anything to cherish is the characteristic of the dāna-pāramitā; that which is without anything to decay is the characteristic of the śīla-pāramitā; that which does not give rise to thoughts of anger is the characteristic of the kṣānti-pāramitā; that which cannot be overcome is the characteristic of the vīrya-pāramitā; that which gathers together all things is the characteristic of the dhyāna-pāramitā; and that which understands and knows immediately upon hearing is the characteristic of the prajñā-pāramitā.
Thus it is, O sons of the gods!
It is because there is no characteristic of anything apprehended that the Tathāgata has attained perfect enlightenment.

As for the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, these are characteristics of the absence of ill-will; yet the Tathāgata did not attain perfect enlightenment by means of such characteristics.
That which emerges from the three realms is the characteristic of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; yet the Tathāgata did not attain perfect awakening by means of these characteristics.

The characteristic of suffering is the door of wishlessness; the characteristic of tranquility is emptiness; the characteristic of purity is signlessness; yet the Tathāgata did not attain perfect awakening by means of these characteristics.

The characteristic of quiescence is that which is without arising; the absence of common characteristics is the eighteen dharmas, yet the Tathāgata did not attain perfect enlightenment by means of these characteristics.
The characteristic of manifestation is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), yet the Tathāgata did not attain perfect enlightenment by means of this characteristic.
Thus it is, O sons of the gods!
The Tathāgata does not attain the Dharma of perfect awakening by means of the characteristics of phenomena; therefore, the Tathāgata is called "Unobstructed Wisdom."
Thereupon the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying:
“The Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas;
the Prajñāpāramitā is the great illumination of the world for all Buddhas, Tathāgatas.”
The Tathāgatas rely upon this dharma to accomplish their tasks; for this reason, all Tathāgatas revere, honor, and serve this Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?
All Buddhas, Tathāgatas, emerge from within the Prajñāpāramitā; therefore, this is how the Tathāgata repays his debt of gratitude.
Subhūti, there is no one who can repay such gratitude better than the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! How does the Tathāgata acknowledge what has been done for him?
How does he repay what has been done for him?"

One should revere, serve, and pay homage to the Dharma by which the Tathāgata came, the Dharma by which he attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and the qualities of a Buddha, and that Dharma which he maintains and upholds as his vehicle.
Subhūti! This is what the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha knows as gratitude and repays as gratitude. Furthermore, Subhūti!
The Dharma attained by the Tathāgata likewise has no agent, because an agent cannot be perceived.
That the Tathāgata has fully attained this Dharma and realized the state of non-action—this is the Dharma of non-contention.
Subhūti! The Tathāgata knows gratitude and repays kindness; through the *prajñāpāramitā*, he has attained the realization of the dharma within the dharma of non-action. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Tathāgata! One who is without attachment!
Because you practice the prajñāpāramitā, you have attained all wholesome dharmas, yet there is nothing attained.
"Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas and the great enlightened guide of the world.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
All dharmas are without cognition, without vision, and without origination.
How, then, is the perfection of wisdom the mother of the Buddha?
How does she give birth to the Tathāgata?
"How is he the great illuminating guide of the world?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is!"
All dharmas are without cognition and without vision.
Why are they without cognition and without vision?
Because all dharmas are empty; they are non-existent, not solid, and unarisen.
For this reason, all dharmas have no place of arising.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, all dharmas are without cognition and without vision."
What is meant by "no knowledge and no vision"?
It is because all dharmas have nothing into which they enter and nothing to which they cling.
For this reason, the Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of the Tathāgatas and the guide of the world.
Because one does not perceive the five aggregates, it is a guide;
even up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), because there is nothing perceived, it is a guide.
For this reason, the Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas and the guide of the world.
Subhūti asked the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that not seeing the five aggregates constitutes being a guide for the world?”
“Subhūti! Not giving rise to consciousness by means of the five aggregates as its causal conditions is what is meant by not seeing the five aggregates.
Not giving rise to perceptions by means of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) is what is meant by not seeing sarvajñatā.”
For this reason, the Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Tathāgatas and the guide of the world. Furthermore, Subhūti,
in what way is the Prajñāpāramitā the mother of the Tathāgatas and the guide of the world?
Subhūti! The Prajñāpāramitā reveals that the world is empty.
How does it reveal that the world is empty?
He demonstrates that the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements are empty; he manifests the ten unwholesome dharmas of the world;
he shows the root of the self through the twelve links of dependent origination arising from ignorance and craving;
and he demonstrates the emptiness of the world through the sixty-two views.
The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments demonstrate the emptiness of the world;
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the six pāramitās, internal emptiness, external emptiness, and the emptiness of existence and non-existence demonstrate the emptiness of the world;
the nature of the conditioned and the unconditioned, the ten powers, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha demonstrate the emptiness of the world.
Up to the attainment of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), it demonstrates that the world is empty.
For this reason, Subhūti, this prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas and the illuminating guide of the world.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata reveals the world through emptiness, contemplates the world through emptiness, and knows the world as empty.
For this reason, the Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas and the guide of the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom reveals to the Tathāgata that the world is empty.
What kind of emptiness does it reveal?
It manifests the emptiness of the five aggregates, the emptiness of the twelve bases, and the emptiness of the eighteen elements; it manifests the emptiness of sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
For this reason, the Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas and the guide of the world.
"Therefore, Subhūti! The Tathāgata manifests that the world is inconceivable;
he manifests that the five aggregates are inconceivable; and so on, up to manifesting that omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is inconceivable to the world."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* manifests the tranquility of the Tathāgata and the world.
What kind of tranquility does it manifest?
It manifests the stillness of the five aggregates and the stillness of sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
For this reason, the Prajñāpāramitā manifests the stillness of the Tathāgata and the world.
Subhūti, the Prajñāpāramitā reveals that the world is eternally empty.
What kind of emptiness does it reveal?
From the five aggregates up to sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), it reveals that the world is eternally empty.
Furthermore, Subhūti, the Prajñāpāramitā reveals that the Tathāgata and all that exists in the world are empty.
What kind of emptiness does it reveal?
From the five aggregates up to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), it demonstrates that all things in the world are empty. "Furthermore, Subhūti,

the *prajñāpāramitā* manifests the emptiness of both existence and non-existence of the Tathāgata, and the emptiness of both existence and non-existence of everything from the five aggregates up to all-knowledge."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, the Prajñāpāramitā reveals the Tathāgata and the cessation of the world.
What kind of cessation does it reveal?
From the five aggregates up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), this constitutes the cessation of the world.
For this reason, the Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of the Tathāgata and the guide of the world.
The Prajñāpāramitā reveals that in the world there is no conceptualization of a present life or a future life.
Why is this? Because these dharmas possess no characteristics of a present life or a future life.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!

This Prajñāpāramitā arises for a great matter; it arises for an inconceivable matter; it arises for an immeasurable matter; it arises for an unlimited matter; it arises for a matter that has no equal.”
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti! This is a great matter; an inconceivable matter has arisen.”
“What is meant by ‘the great undertaking being undertaken’? He replied: “Subhūti!...”
"Because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas seek to rescue and protect all sentient beings, they do not abandon them.
"In what way does this inconceivable event arise?"
"The Buddha-works, spontaneity, and sarvajñā (all-knowledge) are inconceivable; therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā arises as an inconceivable phenomenon."
“What is meant by ‘the arising of matters that cannot be measured’?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“All sentient beings who have received bodies and possess consciousness are unable to know, measure, or fathom the Buddha’s deeds, as well as his spontaneity (*svayambhū*) and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).”
“What is meant by ‘arising from that which is immeasurable’?
Subhūti, the Buddha-work is immeasurable, and the work of the Tathāgata is likewise without limit.”
There is no one at all who is equal to the Tathāgata, much less anyone who could surpass him.
Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā and the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, arise for the sake of that which is limitless.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Are the deeds of a Buddha, the deeds of a Tathāgata, the deeds of a Self-Existent One, and omniscience (sarvajñatā) inconceivable, immeasurable, and indeed limitless?”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is! Subhūti!"
"This is the work of the Buddha, the spontaneous work, the work of the Tathāgata, and the work of Sarvajñā; it is inconceivable and immeasurable.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"From the five aggregates up to Sarvajñā, they are inconceivable and immeasurable."
“Subhūti, regarding the nature of all dharmas, even if one seeks it through intention and conceptualization, it cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha said:
“The five aggregates are inconceivable and immeasurable; even up to *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), they are inconceivable.”
Subhūti asked, "For what reason?
The World-Honored One replied:
“The five aggregates are inconceivable, and there is nothing equal to them;
even up to omniscience (sarvajñatā), it is inconceivable, and there is nothing equal to it.”
The Buddha said,
“One cannot establish a limit for the five aggregates, nor can one establish a limit even for sarvajñatā. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason can the five aggregates and sarvajñatā not be established as limits?
The Buddha said:
"Because the five aggregates up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) are inconceivable, they cannot be assigned limits.
What do you think, Subhūti? Within that which is inconceivable and limitless, can the five aggregates or the Path be apprehended?"
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
it cannot be apprehended.”
"For this reason, Subhūti, all dharmas are inconceivable and cannot be limited.
The Dharma of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; there is nothing equal to it, and it cannot be limited nor measured. This is what is meant by 'inconceivable.'"
That which is taught is also inconceivable; space is inconceivable, and there is nothing equal to it. Subhūti!
This Dharma of the Tathāgata cannot be conceived by worldly people, nor by gods, nor by asuras.

When he spoke thus of the Tathāgata as inconceivable, immeasurable, and limitless, and when he taught the chapter on having no equal, five hundred bhikṣus and two thousand bhikṣuṇīs attained liberation through the exhaustion of their outflows.
Sixty thousand *upāsakas* and twenty thousand *upāsikās* were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, and the Dharma-eye arose within them.
Two thousand *bodhisattvas* attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*; all shall become Buddhas within this present Bhadrakalpa.
Chapter 51: The Arising of Great Matters. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Fifty-one: The Arising of Great Matters. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is most profound and most deep; it arises for a great purpose, being inconceivable, immeasurable, peerless, and beyond limit.
The Buddha said, “So it is, Subhūti!
The perfection of wisdom arises for a great purpose; it arises for a purpose that has no equal.”
Why is this? Subhūti, the five perfections are all accomplished by means of it and are in accord with the perfection of wisdom.

Internal emptiness, external emptiness, and the emptiness of existence and non-existence all emerge from the *prajñāpāramitā* and are in accord with it; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, and the eighteen unique qualities likewise emerge from it and are in accord with the *prajñāpāramitā*;
even the stage of Buddhahood and the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*) emerge from it and are in accord with the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"For example, when there are matters in the various small kingdoms, each is settled on its own, and the wheel-turning sage king has no cause for concern."
Why is this? Because the various minor kings have already long since accepted the commands and instructions of the Holy King, they no longer have cause for anxiety.

The dharmas of the disciples, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, and the dharmas of the buddhas all equally emerge from the *prajñāpāramitā*; it is the *prajñāpāramitā* that accomplishes their respective tasks.

Therefore, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom arises for a great purpose; it arises for a purpose that has no equal. It does not accept the five aggregates and does not enter the five aggregates, because it should neither accept nor enter them; this applies even up to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*).
From the path of the srotāpanna up to the path of the arhat and the path of the pratyekabuddha, one neither accepts nor enters; even unto anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one neither accepts nor enters.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One,
how is it that the five aggregates are neither grasped nor entered, and so on, up to the fact that unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment is neither grasped nor entered?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"What do you think? Do you perceive that the five aggregates have anything into which they enter or anything by which they are grasped? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
Even up to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I neither accept nor enter into it."
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
I do not perceive that the five aggregates have any receiving or entering, nor do I perceive that the Samyaksaṃbuddhas have any receiving or entering.”
The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”

I do not perceive the five aggregates, nor do I grasp at the five aggregates; even up to the state of *samyaksambodhi*, I neither perceive it nor grasp at it, nor do I perceive that which enters therein.
Subhūti! I do not perceive even the stage of a Buddha, nor do I perceive omniscience (sarvajñatā), nor do I accept or maintain the activities of a Tathāgata.
For this reason, Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should neither grasp nor enter into the five aggregates; likewise, regarding the work of a Buddha, the work of sarvajñā, and the work of a Tathāgata, they should neither maintain nor enter into them.
The devaputras of the desire realm and the devaputras of the form realm together addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep and difficult to comprehend; it is inconceivable, profound, and subtle, known and understood only by the wise."

"O World-Honored One, this profound *prajñāpāramitā* is brought about by the roots of merit and goodness cultivated during the times of past Buddhas, and by having encountered true spiritual friends."
World-Honored One!
Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to have faith in the Triple Gem, and all were to attain the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha.

Whatever wisdom and whatever moral virtue these noble sages and worthies may possess does not equal the merit of a good son or a good daughter who, within a single day, contemplates, observes, praises, and delights in this profound *prajñāpāramitā*; the latter’s merit surpasses the former.
Why is this? O sons of the gods!

From the wisdom of a *srotāpanna* up to that of a *pratyekabuddha*, and from faith up to the realization of the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), none of these compare to a son or daughter of good family who, within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, copies, maintains, recites, and practices it for even a single day to swiftly attain *nirvāṇa*. This surpasses the merit produced by the paths of the *arhats* and *pratyekabuddhas*, or the merit of practicing other sūtras for an entire kalpa; for those who are separated from the *prajñāpāramitā* do not abide in *sarvajñatā*.

Why is this? Within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, the three vehicles are extensively expounded, enabling all *arhats* and *pratyekabuddhas* to each attain their respective faith without losing what is appropriate for them, and likewise enabling all *bodhisattva-mahāsattvas* to realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* therein.
Thereupon, the devas of the form realm and the devas of the desire realm simultaneously exclaimed:
“World-Honored One!

This Mahāprajñāpāramitā is inconceivable. Within it, faith and joy arise, causing all śrāvakas to each attain what they ought to attain—namely, the paths of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha—and further causing all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Yet this profound Prajñāpāramitā neither increases nor decreases.”
The various devas of the Form Realm and the various devas of the Desire Realm each bowed their heads to the ground in prostration before the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
Not far from there, they suddenly vanished and each returned to their respective heavens.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing this profound Prajñāpāramitā, immediately understand it, from where have they come to be born in this world?”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing this profound prajñāpāramitā, immediately understands it, does not grow weary of it, nor harbors doubt, and furthermore is not hindered by it, but constantly contemplates it with a mind desiring to hear it, never departing from it."
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they shall always follow the Dharma Master, their minds never departing from him. Subhūti,
it is just as a newborn calf whose mind never wishes to be separated from its mother.

These sons and daughters of good family, having heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, will recite it from memory until it is mastered; they will delight in upholding its practice and understanding its meaning, and their minds will not wish to be separated from the Dharma teacher for even a moment.
These sons and daughters of good family have originally come from among human beings, and having been born here again, they have once more attained human form.

Why is this? It is because in previous lives these sons and daughters of good family heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, wrote it down, upheld it, recited it, and practiced its contents; they made offerings of flowers, incense, silken canopies, banners, and streamers. By virtue of these merits, they have come from among human beings and now, upon hearing this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they understand it immediately.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Are there any bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, as the Buddha has taught, are fully endowed with the roots of goodness resulting from their meritorious deeds and have made offerings to the Buddhas?”

Furthermore, are there those who have come from that place to be born here, and having again obtained the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, write it down, uphold it, recite it, believe in it with joy, and practice it according to its teachings? Is there anyone such as this?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“There are those who have made offerings to the Buddhas in other directions and have heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
For this reason, they are born here in this world and once again obtain the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.”
Upon hearing it, they immediately understand, believe, delight in,
and practice it. Furthermore, Subhūti,
you should know that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have likewise fulfilled their roots of merit and goodness from the Tuṣita heaven.

Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas have heard this profound sūtra from Maitreya Bodhisattva; for this reason, they have now been born in this world, where they have attained the profound Prajñāpāramitā, and upon hearing it, they immediately understand it, believe in it with joy, and maintain its practice.

Subhūti! If there are bodhisattvas who harbor doubts or feelings of weariness toward the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, these persons, in their previous lives, heard the profound *prajñāpāramitā* but did not inquire into its wisdom. Therefore, although they have now come to be born here and hear of the six *pāramitās*, their minds continue to harbor doubts; they do not believe, do not accept, and do not rejoice in them.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! This person originally heard of internal emptiness, external emptiness, and the emptiness of existence and non-existence, yet did not inquire into the matter of the middle. For this reason, they continue now to lack faith and lack joy."

In their previous lives, these people heard of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, yet they did not believe or take delight in them, nor did they inquire into their inner meaning. For this reason, having now come to hear the Prajñāpāramitā, they are startled, astonished, and filled with doubt; they do not believe and do not take delight in it.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing the Prajñāpāramitā, constantly inquires about its contents from the first day until the fifth day.
For this reason, wherever they are born, they will always hear the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and never be separated from what they have asked.
Why is this, Subhūti?
Such a bodhisattva is merely able to hear and inquire about these matters, but is not yet fully prepared in their practice. Subhūti!

If there is someone who at times wishes to hear the Prajñāpāramitā and at other times does not wish to hear it, whose resolve is not firm, or who might give rise to other causes and conditions therein.
It is like a light garment that is carried here and there by the wind.

You should know that this is because the bodhisattva has only recently begun his training; he has not yet encountered true spiritual friends, has not made offerings to the Buddhas of the past, and has not established the roots of merit and goodness. It is because he has not diligently studied and recited the teachings, has not attained the six pāramitās, has not attained internal and external emptiness as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence, and has not trained in the six supernormal powers, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).

You should know that these are beginners who have little delight in the Dharma; they are unable to write down, uphold, study, or recite the Prajñāpāramitā, nor are they yet able to practice its deeds.

Subhūti! If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who practice the bodhisattva path and obtain the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, yet do not keep it in mind for copying, upholding, reciting, or practicing it—and even do not keep in mind studying, receiving, or drawing near to it, up to and including *sarvajñatā*—you should know that such persons may fall into the two stages.
Why is this? It is because these sons and daughters of good family, having seen the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, do not keep it in mind, nor do they copy, uphold, study, or draw near to it.
Therefore, such a person enters the second stage and shall fall into the level of the Arhat or Pratyekabuddha path. 52.
The Chapter on Similes, the Fifty-second Chapter of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, titled “The Chapter on Similes. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:

“Suppose a ship in the great ocean suddenly breaks apart; if the people on board do not grasp a plank, or if they grasp a corpse and cling to it, you should know that those people will ultimately never be able to cross over, and all shall sink together.”
Why is this so? It is because each of them did not grasp onto their respective supports.

If that person had grasped onto a plank, a piece of wood, or a mast, he would have immediately crossed over; his body would have attained peace and security, for he would have used what he grasped as a support to save himself.

Subhūti! If there are good men or good women practicing the bodhisattva path who have little faith and joy, and although they have obtained the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not recite or receive it, do not rely upon or draw near to it, and do not practice the six *pāramitās*—up to and including not drawing near to *sarvajñatā*—you should know that such persons will encounter obstacles midway and be unable to reach *sarvajñatā*; they shall instead take the realization of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha.

Subhūti! If there are good men or good women who practice the bodhisattva path and possess faith and joy in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and who possess capability, mindfulness, understanding, generosity, and practice; who obtain the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and copy, uphold, study, attend to, recite, and chant it—then you should know that such persons are able to receive and uphold the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. They will achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and reach *sarvajñatā*, never encountering obstacles midway to fall into the paths of the *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*; they will be able to teach and transform sentient beings and purify buddha-fields.
Subhūti! It is as if there were a person carrying an unbaked earthen jar to fetch water; you should know that it will soon decay and break. Why is this?
Because they are immature, Subhūti!

If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who practice the bodhisattva path, and although they possess faith and joy, mindfulness, giving, understanding, intimacy, and practice toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet do not uphold the six *pāramitās* and lack *upāya-kauśalya*; furthermore, if they do not uphold internal emptiness, external emptiness, and the emptiness of existence and non-existence; nor do they uphold the five supernormal powers or the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, up to and including not being intimate with *sarvajñatā*—you should know that such persons will encounter obstacles midway.
Subhūti! What constitutes an obstacle to the Middle Way?
It is falling into the path of the Arhat or the Pratyekabuddha.

For example, suppose there is a person carrying a vessel filled with cooked rice who goes to a river, a well, a pond, or a lake to fetch water; you should know that this person will return safely and without loss, having obtained the water.
Why is that? Because it is accomplished by means of a jar, Subhūti!

If there are good sons or good daughters who practice the bodhisattva path, possessing supreme faith and joy in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, possessing the mindfulness, understanding, practice, and wisdom of giving, receiving the six *pāramitās* and *upāya-kauśalya*, and drawing near to *sarvajñatā*, you should know that such persons will reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without ever encountering any hindrance.

Subhūti! It is as if there were a ship newly constructed upon the great ocean, which has not yet been made sturdy or well-repaired, nor has it yet been properly rigged; if one were to place goods and merchandise within it and set sail for some destination, you should know that this ship will soon be destroyed midway, and the scattered wealth and goods will each end up in different places.
Because these merchants lacked skillful means, they lost their goods and perished from their great treasure. Subhūti!

If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who wish to perform the work of a bodhisattva, and although they possess faith, joy, trust, generosity, mindfulness, and understanding regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet they have little merit; if they do not copy, uphold, recite, or study the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor do they study the six *pāramitās*, nor do they draw near to the matters of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), and lack *upāya-kauśalya* (skillful means).

Subhūti! You should know that such a person will encounter obstacles midway and lose the great treasure—the great treasure being *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge)—and will fall midway into the path of the *śrāvaka* or the *pratyekabuddha*.
It is like a wise person who first repairs and secures a boat, loads it with goods, and sets sail for a destination.
You should know that this person will certainly reach their destination, obtaining precious treasures in safety and without loss.
Why is this? It is because the equipment of that vessel is strong and sturdy.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who practice the bodhisattva path, possessing great faith and joy, and who give, maintain mindfulness, attain understanding, and practice toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and who, having obtained the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, receive, study, write, uphold, recite, and practice it—then they possess merit in all six *pāramitās*. Constantly drawing near to the mind of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), they shall eventually achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, never encountering hindrance, nor falling into the paths of the *arhat* or *pratyekabuddha*.
Subhūti! Suppose there were a person one hundred and twenty years old who suffered from an illness, such as wind-disorder or fever.
What do you think? Would that person be able to rise, sit, or walk about by himself?
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
they cannot.”
Why is this so? This person is already old;

even if they were free from illness, they would still be unable to rise, sit, or walk about, let alone being afflicted by disease until their strength is utterly exhausted—how then could they possibly travel or reach any destination?

“Subhūti! If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who practice the bodhisattva path, and although they have faith and joy in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and possess giving, mindfulness, capability, and practice, yet they possess little of the merit of the six *pāramitās* and do not draw near to the matter of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), lacking *upāya-kauśalya* (skillful means), you should know that such persons will encounter obstacles midway and fall into the paths of the *arhat* or *pratyekabuddha*.
Why is this? Because they have not attained the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Subhūti!
"The illness that the old man suffered from has already been cured. Let two strong men each support one of his armpits and each hold one of his arms, and say to the old man:
'Set your mind at ease and do not fear; we shall carry you wherever you go and will never abandon you.'"
"Would such a person be able to reach anywhere? Subhūti replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"One will be able to reach one's destination. The Buddha said:

"If there are good men or good women who practice the path of the bodhisattva, who possess deep faith and joy in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, who possess capacity, generosity, practice, and wisdom; who possess merit in all six *pāramitās*; who constantly draw near to the mind of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge); and who possess *upāya-kauśalya* (skillful means)."

Knowing this, one understands that such a bodhisattva will ultimately never be hindered; they are capable of attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and will not waver or fall into the paths of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Subhūti, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! For the sake of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, you have now questioned the Tathāgata on this matter."
If there is a bodhisattva who practices the six pāramitās with the conceptualization of a self, saying,
"I am practicing the six pāramitās," he will consequently become arrogant.
If a bodhisattva practices in this manner, they will ultimately fail to cross over the six pāramitās.

These good sons and good daughters will neither know the further shore nor the near shore; they will not be sustained by the six pāramitās, nor will they be sustained by sarvajñatā (all-knowledge). They will fall midway into the stages of the arhat or pratyekabuddha, and will not give birth to sarvajñatā.
Subhūti! What is it for a bodhisattva to lack *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means)?

It is when a son of good family or a daughter of good family practicing the bodhisattva path does not practice the six *pāramitās* with skillful means, but rather maintains the notion of a self (*ātman*) regarding each of the six *pāramitās*.
"I have something for which I act," thinking thus, one practices the six pāramitās while becoming conceited. Why is this?
Within the six pāramitās, from the very beginning there is no such thought or any discrimination.

One who has such thoughts always dwells on this shore; knowing only this shore and not the other, they are not sustained by the six pāramitās, nor are they sustained by sarvajñatā (all-knowledge). They fall midway into the path of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, and do not emerge within sarvajñatā.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva such as this is not sustained by upāyakauśalya (skillful means), they will fall among the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Subhūti!
How does a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, sustained by *upāyakauśalya*, avoid falling into the paths of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha and instead realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, they have no thought of self; they do not become conceited regarding these six pāramitās. Why is this?
Within the six *pāramitās*, there is neither conceptualization nor arrogance.

When a bodhisattva knows this shore and knows the other shore, they are sustained by the six *pāramitās* and sustained by *upāyakauśalya*; thus they give birth to *sarvajñatā* and do not fall into the paths of the *arhat* or the *pratyekabuddha*.

Subhūti! A bodhisattva who practices in this manner does not fall into the path of the arhat or the pratyekabuddha; he is sustained by the six pāramitās, sustained by upāyakauśalya (skillful means), and protected by sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
*The Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 11 and Scroll 12.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mokṣala of Khotan during the Western Jin Dynasty.

Translated by Imperial Decree. Chapter Fifty-three: Following True Spiritual Friends. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Fifty-three: Following True Spiritual Friends. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"How should a newly initiated bodhisattva train in the six pāramitās?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"A newly initiated bodhisattva who wishes to train in the six pāramitās should associate with true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) and constantly serve them; furthermore, they should associate with and draw near to those capable of explaining the prajñāpāramitā."

If there is anyone capable of explaining this Prajñāpāramitā, one should always call upon others and encourage them to assist, causing them to study the six pāramitās; they should maintain and practice them, and by upholding this, they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Do not disparage the five aggregates within anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor disparage the six pāramitās within anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; do not disparage internal and external emptiness or the emptiness of existence and non-existence; do not disparage the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; do not disparage sarvajñatā.

Why is this? It is because one attains *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) without disparaging the five aggregates; one attains *sarvajñatā* without disparaging the six *pāramitās*; and one attains *sarvajñatā* without disparaging internal and external emptiness, the emptiness of existence and non-existence, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
One should say:
"Good son! When practicing the perfection of wisdom, do not give rise to thoughts of conceptual attachment toward the five aggregates."
Why is this so? Good son, these five aggregates are not things to which one should become attached.
Furthermore, do not become attached to the six pāramitās.
Son of good family!
Even the six pāramitās are not objects to which one should be attached.

Furthermore, do not be attached to internal emptiness, external emptiness, or the emptiness of existence and non-existence; do not be attached to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or even up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Do not have any attachment whatsoever.
Why is this? Because *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is itself not characterized by attachment.

One should not give rise to attachment toward the *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, *arhat*, or *pratyekabuddha*; nor should one give rise to attachment toward the *bodhisattvayāna*; nor should one give rise to attachment toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this so? Good son, this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is not something to which one may become attached.
"Why is this? Because the characteristics of all dharmas are entirely empty.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is truly a matter of great hardship for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and seek to attain *abhisambodhi* within the dharmas of emptiness and signlessness.”
The Buddha said, “So it is,
Subhūti! A bodhisattva undergoes great hardship through the dharmas of emptiness and signlessness, gives rise to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and attains *abhisambodhi*.”

Subhūti! For the sake of the world, out of compassion for the world, for the peace and security of the world, and desiring to rescue all sentient beings of the world—for the sake of these beings—they resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
They resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in order to become a refuge for the world, to become a protector for the world, and to become a lamp of light for the world.
For the sake of acting as a general for the world, as a guide for the world, as a shelter for the world, and as a destination for the world, they resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti! How is it that a bodhisattva, for the sake of all sentient beings, resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, delivers them from the five realms of existence,
establishes sentient beings in peace and security, and leads them to the shore of fearlessness— the serene state of *nirvāṇa*?
For this reason, one generates *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of the world.
How does a bodhisattva wish to bring peace and security to the world? Subhūti!
When there are sentient beings who possess suffering, affliction, grief, and lamentation, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva delivers them all to the shore of sorrowlessness—the tranquil state of nirvāṇa.
For this reason, the bodhisattva brings peace and happiness to the world.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva act as a savior for the world?

This bodhisattva-mahāsattva, amidst all the births and deaths within the world, diligently saves sentient beings from the world so that they may be liberated from all suffering; he transforms them through the Dharma and subsequently delivers them by means of the three vehicles.
Therefore, the bodhisattva is a savior of the world.
Subhūti, how is it that the bodhisattva is a protector of the world?
Sentient beings in the world possess the nature of birth and death; [the Bodhisattva] protects them so that these do not arise.
Sentient beings all possess the nature of old age, sickness, and death; [the Bodhisattva] protects them so that they do not grow old, do not fall ill, and do not die.
Those who possess sorrow and grief, he protects so that they may reach nirvana without remainder.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva resolves upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi to act as a protector for the world.
Subhūti! How is it that a bodhisattva serves as a shelter for the world?
When this bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and becomes a fully awakened buddha, he teaches all dharmas to the world without obstruction.
Therefore, the bodhisattva is a shelter for the world.
How is it that the bodhisattva is a lamp and light for the world?
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva, amidst the darkness of the triple world, delivers all sentient beings and establishes them in nirvāṇa.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is a lamp and illumination for the world.
How is it that the Bodhisattva is a leader for the world?

When this Bodhisattva attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he teaches the world that form (*rūpa*) is not "mine" and is thus non-form; feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are also not "mine" and are thus non-consciousness; and so on, up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), which is not "mine" and is thus non-omniscience.
“Subhūti! Just as form is not the self, so it is non-form; just as form is not the self, so it is with all dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the World-Honored One has said, the five aggregates are not mine; all dharmas are likewise.
In this way, would a bodhisattva fail to awaken to all dharmas? Why is this?”
Form is without discrimination, and even up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), there is likewise no discrimination; one does not say it is the five aggregates, nor does one say it is omniscience.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"As you have said, the five aggregates are without differentiation, and up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), there is likewise no differentiation; nor does one say 'these are the five aggregates,' nor does one say 'this is omniscience.'"
"Subhūti! This is also a great hardship.
To constantly practice this Dharma without weariness or indolence—the Bodhisattva says:"
"I, too, shall attain awakening, and I shall uphold this pure Dharma to proclaim it to those who have not yet learned it. Subhūti,
for this reason, the bodhisattva speaks of "non-self" to the world.
Subhūti! How is it that a bodhisattva serves as an island for the world?
It is like a river, stream, or ocean, where the current is cut off and the boundaries are severed, providing a place to rest and halt; this is called an island, which is of benefit to people.
When the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of the future and the past are both severed, the omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) of the future and the past is likewise severed.
When things are severed in this manner, all phenomena (*dharmas*) are also severed; when all phenomena are severed, the future and the past are also severed.
Such cessation is purity; it is bliss; it is reality; it is emptiness. The exhaustion of craving, non-reliance, the absence of remainder, and the absence of defilement—this is Nirvāṇa.

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and becomes a fully awakened one (tathāgata), they immediately disseminate this transformation of the pure Dharma and the transformation of the true Dharma to deliver sentient beings;
for this reason, the bodhisattva is an island for the world.
Subhūti! How does a bodhisattva act as a guide for the world?

When a bodhisattva attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and becomes a truly awakened one (tathāgata), he teaches the dharma of the five aggregates to the sentient beings of the world as being neither arising nor ceasing, neither clinging to nor severing.

When preaching the Dharma in this manner, from the stage of Srotāpanna up to Arhat and Pratyekabuddha, he teaches these classes of beings that the five aggregates are neither produced nor extinguished, and he maintains and disseminates this teaching throughout the world.
Subhūti! When this bodhisattva attains unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, he will preach the Dharma in this manner; he is a guide for the world. Subhūti!
In what way does the bodhisattva serve as a guide for the world?

When the bodhisattva attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and becomes a fully awakened Buddha (*tathāgata*), he teaches that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are like the course of emptiness, and he teaches that omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is like the course of emptiness.
That which is empty of the five aggregates has no destination; it neither goes nor does it not go. Why is this?
Because the five aggregates and emptiness neither come nor go.

One who preaches the Dharma in this way explains to sentient beings that *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is empty; it neither comes nor goes, and though there is a destination, there is no destination. Subhūti!
Therefore, Subhūti, the bodhisattva is a guide for the world. Why is this?
Because all dharmas transcend [the world] like space; they are of a single destination and do not return.
Why is this? Emptiness neither comes nor goes; that which all dharmas reach has neither characteristic nor aspiration. Why is this?
Because their characteristics and vows do not return once passed.

These characteristics and vows neither come nor go; that which all dharmas reach has no destination. There is no activity, no arising, no cessation, no attachment, and no annihilation; they are like a dream, like an illusion, like an echo, like a shadow, like a transformation, and like a flame.
All phenomena are likewise: once gone, they do not return.
Why is this? That which is an emanation neither goes nor comes.

Subhūti! All dharmas reach nowhere, having no limit, nor do they return; all dharmas are neither moving nor non-moving; all dharmas neither come nor go; all dharmas neither unite nor disperse; all dharmas are without self, without life, and without a lifespan.
Subhūti! Since sentient beings themselves do not exist, how much less could there be coming and going? Subhūti!

"The abiding place of all phenomena is permanent; the abiding place of all phenomena is blissful; the abiding place of all phenomena is pure; the abiding place of all phenomena is self. [Yet] all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, impure, and non-self."

Regarding the abiding of all phenomena: there is the view of lust, anger, and delusion, and the view of a self-body; yet this abiding of all phenomena is also like the abiding of suchness, the abiding of the dharma-nature, the abiding of the limit of reality, the universal abiding, the abiding of the inconceivable nature, and the abiding that is immovable and unshakable. This place of abiding neither comes nor goes.
Why is this? All dharmas neither come nor go;
all dharmas abide as the five aggregates do.
Why is this? Since even the five aggregates cannot be perceived, how much less could there be coming or going?
All dharmas abide as the six *pāramitās*, and this abiding, too, has no returning.
Why is this? Even the six pāramitās cannot be perceived; how much less could there be any coming or going?

All dharmas abide as they do in internal and external emptiness and the emptiness of existence and non-existence; they abide as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment do, and they abide as the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha do. Just as these eighteen qualities have neither going nor coming, so it is with all dharmas.
All dharmas abide as they do in the path of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and they abide as they do in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; likewise, there is no coming or going. Why is this?
“Because Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is without coming or going and is non-existent.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Who is able to understand this profound *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha said,

"Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have performed meritorious deeds under past buddhas, who have made offerings to countless hundreds of thousands of buddhas, and who have long been associated with true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*)— only such persons as these can understand this profound *prajñāpāramitā*."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what marks does a bodhisattva mahāsattva possess that enable them to understand this profound prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Subhūti,
if there is a bodhisattva who has severed lust, anger, and delusion, that is his mark."
"One who is able to understand the profound *prajñāpāramitā* has already severed the manifestations of lust, anger, and delusion.
Chapter 54: Understanding the Profound, from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"To what destination does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who understands the profound *prajñāpāramitā* proceed?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva who is able to understand the profound *prajñāpāramitā* shall proceed to *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge)."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“That which accords with the course of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s understanding of the profound prajñāpāramitā.”
"One who is intent upon sarvajñatā acts as a guide for all sentient beings. Subhūti said,
"World-Honored One!"

To contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā is to not contemplate any dharmas; to contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā is to have nothing to contemplate; to contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā is to be without a starting point.
The Buddha asked Subhūti:
"For one who contemplates the *prajñāpāramitā*, what constitutes 'not having anything to contemplate'? Subhūti replied:
“World-Honored One!
One who recollects the *prajñāpāramitā* has no recollection of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
One who recollects the *prajñāpāramitā* has no recollection of a self (*ātman*) or sentient beings (*sattva*).”
One who contemplates the *prajñāpāramitā* has no mental engagement with the six *pāramitās*.

One who contemplates the *prajñāpāramitā* has no mental engagement with internal emptiness, external emptiness, or the emptiness of existence and non-existence, nor with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
"One who contemplates the Prajñāpāramitā does not contemplate anything from the stage of srotāpanna up to sarvajñatā.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
As Subhūti has said, one who recollects the prajñāpāramitā does not recollect the five aggregates, up to and including sarvajñatā, for there is nothing to be recollected.

Subhūti! These six pāramitās are that which should be protected by an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva. There is a bodhisattva who practices the profound prajñāpāramitā, yet does not enter into the six pāramitās, nor does he enter into sarvajñatā.
One who practices the *prajñāpāramitā* does not follow the words of others, nor do they place faith in other paths, nor do they hold them as essential.

An irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not practice the *prajñāpāramitā* mixed with lust, anger, or delusion. They practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

An avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva never departs from the six pāramitās; when hearing the teaching of the profound prajñāpāramitā, they are neither terrified nor weary, and ultimately never turn back.
They constantly reflect upon hearing it; having heard it, they receive, uphold, recite, and practice it in accordance with the teachings of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Subhūti, you should know that such an irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattva has already heard the matters concerning the *prajñāpāramitā* in previous lives, and has likewise recited, received, upheld, and practiced those matters.
"For what reason are they neither afraid nor terrified?
It is because from time immemorial they have constantly practiced this profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing the teaching of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, is neither terrified nor afraid, and does not turn back in agitation, how is it that their practice becomes doubly increased?”
The Buddha said:
"One who practices the prajñāpāramitā accords with sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
How does one practice the prajñāpāramitā so as to accord with sarvajñatā?"
The Buddha said:
“Just as one relies on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), so should one rely on the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.

One who relies on the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is like relying on space; it is like relying on that which is unarisen and like relying on that which is unceasing. It does not rely on attachment but relies on relinquishment; it is like relying on suchness (*tathatā*), relying on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), relying on the inconceivable, and relying on equanimity and non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), just as one relies on a dream.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
To rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā is like relying upon empty space, or like relying upon a dream.”
"A Bodhisattva who practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* does not rely on the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), nor does he practice by relying on *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"A Bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* likewise does not rely on the five aggregates, nor does he rely on *sarvajñatā*."

The five aggregates and sarvajñā (all-knowledge) likewise have no agent, nor are they uncreated; they neither come nor go, they neither abide nor rely upon anything, they neither emerge nor enter, they are without number and without limit.
That which is innumerable and infinite cannot be realized by anyone.

From form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), there is no one who can realize it; nor can it be realized through the six *pāramitās*, nor can it be realized through the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*).
Why is this? The suchness of the five aggregates and the suchness of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) are equal and without distinction.
The suchness of the eighteen dharmas and the suchness of *sarvajñatā* are likewise equal and without distinction; they are one, being without duality.

Chapter 55: Praising the Profundity. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, Chapter Fifty-Five: Praising the Profundity. At that time, the sons of the gods of the desire realm and the sons of the gods of the form realm scattered celestial flowers over the Buddha. Approaching the Buddha’s presence, they prostrated with their heads at his feet and, with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is profound, difficult to comprehend and difficult to understand, and inconceivable.

It is that which is known by the wise and that which is to be trusted by all the world. It is the path of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas; those who attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and become perfectly awakened Buddhas do so entirely through the grace of the Prajñāpāramitā.
This is the single teaching.
As for the single teaching: the five aggregates are *samyaksambodhi*, and *samyaksambodhi* is the five aggregates;
the suchness of *samyaksambodhi* and the suchness of the five aggregates—the suchness of *samyaksambodhi* and the five aggregates are one and the same, without duality.
“The suchness of the Buddha and the suchness of omniscience (sarvajñatā) are likewise non-dual.
The Buddha addressed the devaputras of the desire and form realms: “So it is, so it is!”
As the sons of the gods have said, the five aggregates are *samyaksambodhi*, and *samyaksambodhi* is the five aggregates;
the Buddha is *samyaksambodhi*, and *samyaksambodhi* is the Buddha;
they are one suchness, without duality.
For this reason, O sons of the gods!
The Tathāgata remains serene and unconditioned, and does not preach the Dharma. Why is this?
This Dharma is profoundly deep and pure, difficult to comprehend and difficult to understand, yet it is uniquely worthy of faith.
Regarding the path of all Tathāgatas, there has been no one who has attained awakening in the past, the future, or the present; that which is non-dual with respect to the Dharma is itself the Dharma.
O sons of the gods!
Just as space is profoundly deep and subtle, so too is this Dharma.
Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is profound and subtle, this Dharma is profound and subtle.

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the inconceivable nature, and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) are without bottom or limit; they neither come nor go, are neither attached to nor severed, and are neither born nor extinguished—profound, subtle, and beyond the reach of awakening.
Because there is no one who attains awakening, the Prajñāpāramitā is profound and subtle.
O devaputras! Because all dharmas are profound and subtle, sentient beings, the self, persons, and life-span are likewise profound and subtle.

The five aggregates are profound and subtle; the six pāramitās are profound and subtle; internal emptiness, external emptiness, and the emptiness of existence and non-existence; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, up to sarvajñatā—all these are extremely deep and subtle.
"Because it is so profound and subtle, O sons of gods!
The Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā is profound and subtle.
Then the sons of gods from the realms of desire and form all addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma is uniquely worthy of trust in the world.
To speak in this way is neither to accept the five aggregates nor to not accept them; even regarding the eighteen dharmas, there is neither acceptance nor non-acceptance.”
Speaking in this way, from the stage of srotāpanna up to sarvajñatā, there is neither grasping nor non-grasping.
All those of the world are characterized by grasping.
How does one grasp and maintain [this view]? One thinks: "The five aggregates are mine; I am of the five aggregates.
"The eighteen elements are mine; I am of the eighteen elements."
"From the stage of srotāpanna up to sarvajñatā (omniscience), all these are 'mine,' and I am that which belongs to sarvajñatā.
This is what is called worldly grasping.
The Buddha told the devaputras:
"As the sons of the gods have said, this Dharma does not grasp or maintain the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), nor does it grasp or maintain omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Sons of the gods!

Those who grasp and practice the five aggregates, or who grasp and practice the path to omniscience, are incapable of practicing the six *pāramitās*, and they are also incapable of practicing omniscience."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma does not oppose all dharmas, but rather accords with them.”
What is the dharma that is compliant?

It is this dharma that is compliant with the six pāramitās; it is this dharma that is compliant with internal and external emptiness as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence; it is compliant with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to omniscience (sarvākārajñatā).
This is called the compliant dharma.
This Dharma is unimpeded among all dharmas.
How is it unimpeded? It is not impeded by the five aggregates, up to and including omniscience (sarvajñatā), where it is likewise unimpeded.
This dharma has the characteristic of non-obstruction, just like space. Why is this?
It abides as the nature of reality (dharmatā), as the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), and as the inconceivable nature; it is like emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
This dharma of the prajñāpāramitā is neither born nor extinguished, because the five aggregates are neither born nor existent.
Even up to *sarvajñatā*, there is neither arising nor existence.
These dharmas leave no trace, because the traces of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) cannot be seen;
likewise, even the traces of *sarvajñatā* cannot be seen.
At that time, the sons of the gods of the desire realm and the sons of the gods of the form realm together addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The Venerable Subhūti is a true son of the Buddha among all the disciples."
"Why is this? What has been spoken is merely the teaching of the dharma of emptiness and non-binding.
Then Subhūti spoke to the devaputras of the desire and form realms:
"As you have said, among all disciples I am the true disciple.
In what way am I a true son?
The sons of the gods replied to Subhūti:
“The Buddha arises from Suchness (tathatā), being neither going nor coming;
Subhūti, Suchness likewise neither comes nor goes.
For this reason, Subhūti is born from the Buddha.”
The suchness of the Buddha is the suchness of all dharmas; as is the suchness of all dharmas, so is the suchness of the Buddha. Furthermore, suchness itself is not [even] suchness.
For this reason, Subhūti is born from the Buddha.
Just as the Tathāgata abides in suchness (*tathatā*), Subhūti also abides in suchness.
Just as the suchness of the Buddha is unconditioned (*akṛta*), uncreated (*asaṃskṛta*), and non-existent, so too is the suchness of Subhūti.
Just as the suchness of the Buddha is without obstruction, so too is the suchness of all phenomena without obstruction.
The suchness of the Buddha and the suchness of all phenomena are a single suchness, non-dual and without an agent.
The unconditioned is as it always is; there is nothing that is not so.
Since from the time it exists as such and is not otherwise, it is eternally one and without duality, we know that the Venerable Subhūti is born from the Tathāgata.
Just as the suchness of the Buddha is not subject to destruction, so too the suchness of Subhūti is neither subject to destruction nor is it not subject to destruction.
Just as the suchness of the Buddha is invisible and indestructible, the suchness of Subhūti is likewise.
The suchness of the Buddha is the suchness of all dharmas, and there is no other suchness; the Venerable Subhūti is likewise so.

For this reason, it is known that Subhūti is truly born from the Buddha. Just as the suchness of the Buddha does not belong to the past, the future, or the present, the suchness of all dharmas also has no past, future, or present. Therefore, it is known that Subhūti is born from the Buddha.

The suchness of the past, future, and present is the suchness of the Buddha; the suchness of the Buddha is also the suchness of the past, future, and present. They are equal, one, and without duality.
The suchness of the five aggregates and the suchness of the Tathāgata are one and not two.
The suchness of the self, the life-span, and sentient beings is the same as the suchness of the Buddha; it is also one and not two.

The suchness of the six pāramitās, the suchness of internal and external emptiness, the suchness of the emptiness of existence and non-existence, the suchness of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and even the suchness of *sarvākārajñatā* (all-knowledge), is the same as the suchness of the Buddha; it is a single suchness, without duality.
"What is 'suchness' (tathatā)?
Subhūti, suchness is that which a bodhisattva realizes; it is by attaining suchness that one receives the title of 'Tathāgata'.
When this Chapter on Suchness was being spoken, the earth of this trichiliocosm shook in six ways.

The east rises and the west sinks; the west rises and the east sinks; the south rises and the north sinks; the north rises and the south sinks. When all four sides rise, the center sinks; when the center rises, all four sides sink. These constitute the sixfold quaking.

At that time, the sons of the gods from the desire realm and the form realm throughout the trichiliocosm scattered celestial flowers, famous incenses, and sandalwood over the Buddha and over Subhūti, and simultaneously exclaimed:
"World-Honored One!..."
"How most marvelous, how most extraordinary!
Venerable Subhūti has indeed been born from the Tathāgata as he truly is; he is truly a son of the Buddha.
At that time, Subhūti further addressed the devaputras, saying:
“O sons of the gods!
Subhūti does not arise from the five aggregates, nor does he arise from the suchness of the five aggregates, nor does he arise apart from the suchness of the five aggregates;
he does not arise from the suchness of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), nor does he arise apart from the suchness of sarvajñatā.”
Nor does it arise from the conditioned or the unconditioned suchness, nor does it arise apart from the conditioned or the unconditioned suchness.
Why is this? Because all these phenomena are non-existent, and there is no phenomenon that can be clung to or delighted in.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Suchness, thusness, the abiding of dharmas, and the nature of the Path are exceedingly profound."
"If even the five aggregates cannot be seen, how much less can the suchness of the five aggregates?
Even up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), it cannot be seen; how much less can the suchness of omniscience?
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! Śāriputra, suchness is profoundly deep!"
The five aggregates and even omniscience (sarvajñatā) cannot be seen;
how much less so the suchness (tathatā) of omniscience! Śāriputra!
"The Suchness is profound.

When he spoke of Suchness and Thusness, at that time two hundred bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind; five hundred bhikṣuṇīs gave rise to the dust-free, stainless Dharma-eye; five thousand bodhisattvas, devas, and humans attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); and sixty bodhisattvas attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“These sixty bodhisattvas have already made offerings to five hundred buddhas and have fully practiced the six pāramitās; however, they did not possess upāyakauśalya (skillful means), and though they studied the various five pāramitās, they were devoid of the prajñāpāramitā.”

If one practices giving, precepts, patience, diligence, and meditation without the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of various characteristics, one will not attain the fixed path of a bodhisattva, but instead attains the path of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), an arhat, or a pratyekabuddha.

Śāriputra! Although a bodhisattva may attain the path of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, if they are separated from the *prajñāpāramitā* and do not maintain *upāyakauśalya*, they will immediately realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and attain the vehicle of the disciples (*śrāvakayāna*).
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One,

how is it that one who has attained the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet lacks *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), realizes the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and thereby attains the vehicle of the disciples?”
How is it that by attaining the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and by attaining *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), one then attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"All those who depart from the mind of *samyaksambodhi* (sarvajñatā), who contemplate the dharmas of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), yet do not possess *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), belong to the vehicle of the disciples (*śrāvaka-yāna*)."

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva attains the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and accords with *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) without being separated from *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Śāriputra! Suppose there were a great bird, one hundred yojanas, two hundred yojanas, or three hundred yojanas in length, yet lacking both wings.
It wished to descend from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Jambudvīpa, but having descended halfway, it then wished to return again to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
“Śāriputra! Would this bird be able to travel back and forth at will? Śāriputra replied:
“World-Honored One! It could not.
“Suppose this bird were to descend to the ground; if it wished its body not to suffer pain, could it possibly avoid suffering pain?”
Śāriputra said, “World-Honored One!
It cannot but be painful;”
Some faint and some die. Why is this?
Because their bodies are so large and they have no wings.

“Śāriputra! Suppose this bodhisattva were to practice the five pāramitās for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; though he may attain the Great Way, if he wishes to give rise to the Great Resolve and reach immeasurable awakened wisdom, yet lacks the Prajñāpāramitā and is devoid of upāyakauśalya (skillful means), he will fall into the path of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.”

Why is this? Because if one practices the five *pāramitās* while being devoid of *upāyakauśalya*, devoid of *sarvajñatā*, and devoid of the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*, one will fall into the path of the *arhat* or the *pratyekabuddha*.

Śāriputra! Although a bodhisattva performs meritorious deeds toward the Buddhas of the past, future, and present—whether through the nature of precepts, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, or wisdom—they do so while clinging to signs. This is because they do not understand the Tathāgata’s nature of precepts, samādhi, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; they neither know nor see them, but merely hear from afar of the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
They merely hear the sounds and, desiring to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, form conceptual signs and think:
"This is the dwelling place of a bodhisattva; this is the dwelling place of a Buddha; this is the dwelling place of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
"Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva is separated from the *prajñāpāramitā* and *upāyakauśalya*, yet wishes to take these merits toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this constitutes a sign."

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva gives rise to the thought of *samyaksambodhi*, they do not depart from the six *pāramitās*, nor do they depart from *upāyakauśalya*. They do not depart from the nature of the precepts, samādhi, wisdom, and the knowledge of liberation of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present; yet they do not become attached to these as signs (*nimitta*). Furthermore, regarding emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they likewise do not take them as signs.
Śāriputra, you should know that this bodhisattva does not fall into the path of the arhat or the pratyekabuddha. Why is this?

Since first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, this bodhisattva-mahāsattva has not practiced the six pāramitās with signs, nor has he, with signs, [regarded] the nature of the precepts, samādhi, wisdom, and the vision of liberation of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present;
in all these, he is without attachment to signs.
Śāriputra! To practice the six pāramitās without signs, and to practice sarvajñatā without signs—this is the *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) of a bodhisattva.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I have now heard from the Tathāgata, a bodhisattva who does not depart from the *prajñāpāramitā* and *upāyakauśalya* shall thereby reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”

Why is this? Because since first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, these bodhisattvas have never seen any dharma that has attained awakening, nor do they see any that is about to attain awakening, nor do they see any that has already attained awakening;
it is likewise so for everything from the five aggregates up to omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Śāriputra said: “World-Honored One!

If there are those who practice the bodhisattva path but are separated from the *prajñāpāramitā* and *upāyakauśalya*, you should know that such persons will harbor doubt regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
Why is this? Because they lack the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the *prajñāpāramitā*, their practice of the six *pāramitās* all involves signs (*nimitta*).
Due to these signs, one should know that doubt exists.
Therefore, World-Honored One,
a bodhisattva who wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should not be separated from the *prajñāpāramitā* and *upāyakauśalya*.

Abiding in the perfection of wisdom through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), one practices the five perfections without signs and without attachment; even up to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), there are likewise no signs or attachments.
At that time, the sons of the gods of the desire realm and the sons of the gods of the form realm together addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Those who seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi are difficult to find.”
"Why is this? Because those who are bodhisattvas must fully awaken to all dharmas while remaining without any attainment.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! O sons of the gods,
this is most difficult."
I too shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet there is nothing attained and nothing acquired; nor do I perceive any dharma that is attained or acquired.
Why is this so? O sons of the gods!
Because all dharmas are eternally pure.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As I have now heard from the Buddha, those who seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi are extremely rare to find.”
As it seems to me, how wonderful it would be to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are empty and there is nothing to be realized or awakened to.
Within the dharma of emptiness, all dharmas are unattainable; furthermore, there is no dharma that attains awakening or fails to attain it.

Why is this? Because in accordance with the nature of reality (*tathatā*), there is neither increase nor decrease. One trains in the five *pāramitās* up to *sarvākārajñatā*, yet these dharmas are all empty—neither visible nor attainable.
For this reason, World-Honored One,
how wonderful it is that a bodhisattva attains awakening and achieves *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this so?
"The five aggregates are empty of themselves, and the activity of the wisdom of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is empty of itself. Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"For this reason, *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (unsurpassed perfect enlightenment) is difficult to understand and difficult to attain."
Space also does not have the thought:
"I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The bodhisattva likewise does not think:
"I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are like empty space.
When a bodhisattva understands that all dharmas are like space, they then achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If a bodhisattva knows that all dharmas are like space, how wonderful it is that they achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which is so difficult to accomplish!
"Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* never turn back or retreat.
For this reason, Subhūti!"
"It is most wonderful that it is difficult to achieve, yet one achieves *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti said to Śāriputra: "What do you think?
Do the five aggregates move toward or turn back from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
Śāriputra said: “No. [The Buddha asked:
“...up to and including: would you waver or turn back from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
Śāriputra said, “No. [The Buddha asked:
“What do you think? Is there anyone who, having departed from the five aggregates, returns?”
"Is there anyone who departs from *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) and returns? Śāriputra replied, "No."
Subhūti said: "Śāriputra, what do you think? Does the suchness of the five aggregates return?"
"Would *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) be like returning? Śāriputra replied, "No."
“Is there anyone who, apart from the suchness of the five aggregates, returns apart from the suchness of *samyaksambodhi*? Śāriputra replied, “No.”

“What do you think, Śāriputra? Regarding suchness, the nature of dharmas, the dharma that abides in the path, the limit of reality, and the inconceivable nature—do they ever turn back from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
Śāriputra said: "No. [The Buddha asked:
