"Is there anyone who, having departed from suchness, up to and including the inconceivable nature, returns?"
Śāriputra said: "There is no such principle;
this dharma is also unattainable. [The Buddha asked:
"What dharma could there be that would turn back from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Śāriputra said to Subhūti: “According to the Dharma-patience as taught by the Venerable Subhūti, there is no bodhisattva who would waver or turn back from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"The Tathāgata’s predictions regarding the practices of the three vehicles for bodhisattvas have no basis whatsoever.
As Subhūti has said, there is but the Single Vehicle.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra then spoke to Śāriputra:
“Does Subhūti wish to speak of a single Buddha-vehicle?
We should question Subhūti. Śāriputra then asked Subhūti:
“How is it that you wish to speak of the bodhisattva’s practice of the Single Vehicle?
Subhūti replied, “Do you wish to speak of the Three Vehicles within suchness?”
"The vehicle of the Arhat, the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddha,
and the vehicle of the Bodhisattva-Buddha. Śāriputra said, "No."
Subhūti said: "What do you think, Śāriputra?
Within suchness, are there any three vehicles?"
He replied, "There is none. Subhūti said:
“Is there, within suchness, one thing, two things, or three things? Śāriputra replied, “No.”
“Is it possible to perceive even a single bodhisattva within suchness? He replied, “No.”
"This dharma is called the unconditioned and non-existent dharma; how can one seek the three vehicles—the Arhat, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Samyaksambuddha—within it?"
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears that all dharmas arise from suchness, they are not afraid, not weary, and do not retreat; thus they give birth to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Buddha praised Subhūti: “Excellent, excellent!
All that you have spoken is the work of a Buddha.”

When a bodhisattva hears that all these dharmas arise from suchness, and is neither terrified, nor afraid, nor weary, nor turns back, it should be known that this bodhisattva shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by which path should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva emerge?”
The Buddha said:
"This bodhisattva shall give birth to the path of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva wishes to emerge and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how should they abide?
The Buddha said:
"One should always maintain an impartial mind toward all sentient beings, exercising great compassion and universal mindfulness without partiality.
One should preach for the sake of sentient beings to protect, care for, and bring them peace; one's speech should be harmonious and gentle, never seeking to cause injury."
He regards all sentient beings as equal, like his own father, mother, body, or child.
Out of compassion, he exhorts others not to harm living beings and constantly encourages sentient beings to practice the ten wholesome actions.
When one sees others practicing correctly and remaining free from wrong views, one should rejoice on their behalf.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should abide in this manner.

One practices the Four Noble Truths, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments oneself, encourages others to practice them, and rejoices on behalf of those who do so.
One practices the six *pāramitās* oneself and constantly exhorts and instructs others to practice the six *pāramitās*, rejoicing on behalf of those who do so when one sees them.

One practices internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence (*bhāva-abhāva-śūnyatā*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣāḥ*), the ten powers of a Buddha (*daśa-tathāgatabalāni*), great loving-kindness and great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-mahākaruṇā*), and the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) in both forward and reverse order; one exhorts others to practice these in both orders, and upon seeing those who do so, one rejoices on their behalf.

One practices the wisdom of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas oneself, yet encourages others to practice it without realizing the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); seeing those who practice it, one rejoices on their behalf.

Having ascended to the stage of a bodhisattva oneself, one teaches others to advance; one practices supernatural powers (abhijñā) oneself to purify buddha-fields and transforms sentient beings, encouraging them to study; seeing those who study, one rejoices on their behalf.
Having personally extinguished the traces of habitual tendencies, one encourages others to extinguish them as well.
Having personally achieved longevity and personally abided in the Dharma, one encourages others to abide in the Dharma; seeing those who act in this way, one rejoices on their behalf.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should train in this way and should abide in this way.

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in this way in the *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). Training in this manner and abiding in this way, they will encounter no obstruction regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), nor will they encounter any obstruction even regarding the abiding of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti*).

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), and thus does not grasp the five aggregates, nor does he grasp anything up to and including omniscience (sarvajñatā).
"Why is this? Because that which is not grasped as the five aggregates is not the five aggregates; that which is not grasped as *samyaksambodhi* (perfect enlightenment) is not *samyaksambodhi*.
When this chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Abiding was being taught, two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
56. Chapter on the Avaivartika: The Mahāprajñāpāramitā, Chapter Fifty-Six. Thereupon, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“By what marks and characteristics shall we know him to be an *avaivartika*? The Buddha told Subhūti:

“He understands that the stage of ordinary persons, the stage of disciples, the stage of *pratyekabuddhas*, and even the stage of the Tathāgata are all one suchness (*tathatā*) without distinction; they are a single non-duality of entry.”
One’s own self and suchness are one and the same; entering therein, one does not engage in discrimination.
Having heard this suchness, one passes directly through it without doubt, and there is nothing lost of that suchness.
What is spoken contains neither addition nor subtraction, nor does one look upon the long or the short in others.
"By these characteristics, one should know that this is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva.
"World-Honored One,
by what further marks, signs, or appearances may one know that this is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva?"
The Buddha said:
"All dharmas are likewise formless, without appearance, and without characteristics. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are formless, imageless, and without marks, from what dharma does one turn back to become an avaivartika bodhisattva?”
The Buddha said: "Subhūti,
when one turns back from the five aggregates, know that this is an irreversible bodhisattva."

Subhūti, the bodhisattva turns back from the six pāramitās; he turns back from internal emptiness, external emptiness, and the emptiness of existence and non-existence; he turns back from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; he turns back from the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha, as well as from the stage of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti!
You should know that this is an irreversible bodhisattva.
Why is that? Subhūti!
The five aggregates have no form, and the Way likewise has no form; therefore, the bodhisattva turns away from the five aggregates and proceeds toward the Way. Why is this?
Because the five aggregates and the Way have no location.

"Furthermore, Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not observe or examine the actions, knowledge, or views of non-Buddhists, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas; nor does he observe or examine the wrong views or right views of various non-Buddhist schools, nor does he harbor any doubt."

Nor do they disparage the precepts of non-Buddhist śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; nor do they engage in deceitful play or fall into various false views; nor do they carry incense, flowers, silk canopies, banners, or pennants to offer to celestial deities; nor do they instruct others to follow such false views.
By observing their physical appearance, characteristics, and conduct as being complete, one knows them to be irreversible (*avaivartika*) bodhisattvas. Subhūti!
Irreversible bodhisattvas are not born into low-born families, nor are they born in the eight difficult circumstances, nor do they receive a female body.
By being endowed with these characteristics, one knows this person to be an *avaivartika* bodhisattva.

Subhūti, an *avaivartika* bodhisattva constantly practices the ten wholesome paths of action without transgression; they constantly maintain the practice of the ten wholesome paths even in dreams, teach others to practice them, and feel sympathetic joy on behalf of those who do so.
By being endowed with these characteristics, one knows that this is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva. Subhūti!
For the sake of sentient beings, the *avaivartika* bodhisattva practices the six *pāramitās*, personally studies the twelve divisions of the scriptures, and constantly makes this vow:
"Upholding these twelve divisions of the scriptures, one exhorts and encourages sentient beings to fulfill their aspirations.
Taking these merits and bestowing them all upon sentient beings, one brings them to the realization of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."
"By being endowed with these characteristics, one knows this person to be an *avaivartika* bodhisattva.
Subhūti! An *avaivartika* bodhisattva also harbors no doubt regarding the profound sūtras concerning the mark of equanimity."
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
"How is it that an avaivartika bodhisattva has no doubt regarding the profound teachings of the Dharma?
The Buddha replied:
"This bodhisattva also does not perceive any dharma, nor does he perceive the five aggregates, nor does he perceive any doubt regarding the mark of equality in the Path.
Because he is fully endowed with these characteristics, one knows him to be an Avaivartika."
Subhūti! The conduct of body, speech, and mind of an avaivartika bodhisattva is always compassionate and gentle; his actions of body, speech, and mind are constantly bestowed upon sentient beings.
By being fully endowed with such characteristics, one knows that this is an avaivartika bodhisattva.
Subhūti! An irreversible bodhisattva does not dwell together with the five hindrances, nor does he ever harbor thoughts of longing or attachment toward sensual desires.
By these marks, one knows him to be an irreversible bodhisattva.
Subhūti! An irreversible bodhisattva, whether sitting, rising, walking, lying down, or waking, is composed and never abrupt.
By being endowed with these characteristics, one knows this to be an irreversible bodhisattva.
Subhūti! An avaivartika bodhisattva is pure and delights in cleanliness, free from all dust and defilement; his clothing, bedding, and seating are likewise pure, and he suffers little from illness.
In the bodies of ordinary people, there are eighty thousand kinds of worms that constantly consume them; however, for an Avaivartika [Bodhisattva], these worms no longer exist. Why is this?
Because the merit of such a Bodhisattva surpasses that of all mundane beings, including the devas, ghosts and spirits, and asuras.
Acting as the foundation for all roots of goodness, they gradually increase in merit, with body, speech, and mind purified.
Being fully endowed with these signs, practices, and characteristics, such a person is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“How does a bodhisattva attain purity of body, speech, and mind?
The Buddha said:
"Following all roots of goodness, the body, speech, and mind become pure; defilements are immediately eliminated, merit gradually increases, and impurities are progressively extinguished.
This is what is meant by the purity of body, speech, and mind."
By means of these three purities, he surpasses the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Because he is fully endowed with these marks, practices, and characteristics, he is an irreversible bodhisattva.

Subhūti! An avaivartika bodhisattva does not crave gain or offerings, nor does he crave clothing; he is fully endowed with the twelve dharmas of a śramaṇa. He acts without a mind of envy, nor does he have a mind of delusion or craving for profit. He has no mind of inequality, no mind of indolence, and no mind of immoral conduct.
By being fully endowed with these signs, conducts, and characteristics, one is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva.

Subhūti, the resolve of an *avaivartika* is always peaceful and secure, and their mind is always deeply penetrating. With single-minded focus, they listen to and receive the teachings of the Dharma as they are heard; they practice in accordance with the *prajñāpāramitā* with an equanimous mind, and all worldly affairs are likewise conjoined with the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Those who do not enter into the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) all see themselves as being in union with the Prajñāpāramitā.
Because they are fully endowed with these signs, practices, and characteristics, one knows them to be irreversible (avaivartika) bodhisattvas.

Subhūti! If Māra Pāpīyān were to manifest great and small hells, and within each of those hells there were countless billions of bodhisattvas, all of whom were undergoing various sufferings therein—this is the mark of an avaivartika bodhisattva.
Pāpīyān pointed them out and said to the Bodhisattva:
"These people suffering in misery were all granted predictions by past Buddhas; they are all *avaivartika* bodhisattvas who have now fallen into this state to undergo these various pains."

If you, Minister, were one who had received the prediction of an avaivartika bodhisattva, the Buddha would have bestowed upon you the prediction of niraya, rather than bestowing upon you the prediction of a bodhisattva.
"You would do better to abandon the bodhisattva path so that you may be reborn in heaven and no longer undergo such arduous suffering in the hells. Subhūti,
if the mind of such a bodhisattva is not distracted, they will never fall into the hells.
One should know that such a person is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān again assumes the robes of a śramaṇa and approaches the bodhisattva, saying:

"Regarding the six *pāramitās* you previously accepted and your desire to seek the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, you should now quickly repent of all those practices you have performed; by quickly repenting your transgressions, you may attain liberation."

All the Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples whom you have previously honored, from the first generation of the resolve for awakening until the exhaustion of the Dharma—including the roots of goodness cultivated therein and the merit of exhorting, assisting, and rejoicing with others—seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Quickly abandon this intention and repent at once.
If you abandon it and repent, I shall then speak to you of the essential Dharma of the profound sūtras taught by the Buddha and the instructions of the Tathāgata."
"What you have heard is none of the Buddha's sutras, nor is it the teaching of the Tathāgata; it is merely a compilation by followers of heterodox paths.

If a bodhisattva should experience such mental agitation and doubt, one should know that this bodhisattva has not been granted a prediction of enlightenment by the Tathāgata, and that this bodhisattva has not yet correctly established themselves in the stage of *avaivartika*.

If a bodhisattva is without doubt or confusion, does not shift their resolve, and has nothing to grasp; if they do not rely on other matters nor follow the teachings of others, then by practicing the six pāramitās they will spontaneously become complete and swiftly attain the path of the wisdom of *sarvajñatā*.

Having taken refuge in oneself and not accepting the teachings of others is like an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted, who perceives the Dharma directly before his own face and does not believe in other doctrines; even Māra can ultimately do nothing to him.
“Arhats and pratyekabuddhas can never cause an avaivartika bodhisattva to turn back.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“As you have said, arhats and pratyekabuddhas cannot move or turn back an avaivartika bodhisattva.”
That which cannot be turned back is that which does not regress; such a bodhisattva will certainly reach anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and shall dwell correctly in the stage of avaivartika.
If one does not yet believe in the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, how much less could one believe the words of arhats, pratyekabuddhas, Māra Pāpīyān, or various heterodox teachers?

Why is this? Because from the outset, one does not perceive any dharma that is worthy of being trusted; nor does one perceive the five aggregates as something worthy of being trusted; nor does one perceive the Path as something worthy of being trusted.
Subhūti! One should observe their marks and conduct by means of these characteristics; one should know that such a person is an avaivartika bodhisattva. Subhūti!
Māra further manifested himself in the form and appearance of a bhikṣu and, approaching the Bodhisattva, said to him:
"Good man! All that you practice is merely worldly; it is not the practice of *samyaksambodhi*."
The Māra spoke again, saying:
"I shall sever the root of your diligent suffering.

He then preached to the Bodhisattva the teachings of the Path of Phenomenal Existence (*nimitta-mārga*); that is, those teachings of the Path of Phenomenal Existence pertaining to worldly affairs, which either demonstrated the "corpse-liberation" (*śi-jie*) or explained the four *dhyānas* and the four formless absorptions (*catasraḥ ārūpyasamāpattayaḥ*).
He said:
"Good man! This is the return to the right path; from this one may attain the stage of srotāpanna, and may reach the stages of arhat or pratyekabuddha."
Those who follow my teaching can sever the root of the suffering of birth and death;
why then would they undergo such suffering for the sake of study?
Those who follow my teaching can be born in the heavens of desire and attain birth in the heavens of form.
“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva hears this, he is filled with great joy; he is neither distracted nor wavering, nor does he harbor any doubt. He further reflects in his mind:
‘Now this bhikṣu has brought these semblances of the Dharma to speak for my sake; it will benefit me no small amount.’”

Why is this? That which is taught in the Semblance Dharma does not involve attaining realization as a srotāpanna; nor does it involve attaining realization up to the paths of arhat or pratyekabuddha; nor does it involve attaining realization up to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Now, receiving the kindness of this bhikṣu, he has explained for me that which I ought to awaken to and know.
Having awakened to and known this, I shall come to fully understand the matters of the three vehicles.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān, knowing that the Bodhisattva was joyful, spoke to the Bodhisattva, saying: “Good son!

If you wish to know those who have made offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—Bodhisattvas who have practiced the five *pāramitās* under these past Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and who have heard and questioned them—[you must look no further than here].”
"How should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwell? How should they practice the five pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, great compassion, and great loving-kindness?"
As the Buddhas have taught, one should practice in this way and abide in this way.
As is appropriate for a bodhisattva, from this one shall achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"If one abides according to the teaching, just as those practitioners attain *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).

"The past bodhisattvas performed such practices and accumulated such merit, yet they were still unable to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. You have only just begun your training; how then could you possibly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
If a bodhisattva, upon hearing this, remains unchanging in mind, neither terrified nor afraid, but instead feels redoubled joy and says:
"These bhikṣus have greatly benefited me, enabling me to attain the stage of srotāpanna up to sarvākārajñatā."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas, knowing that the Bodhisattva’s mind was unshakable and would not waver, further manifested himself as a great assembly of bhikṣus and said to the Bodhisattva:
"These bhikṣus have exhausted all outflows (āsrava); though they resolved their minds to seek Buddhahood, they could not attain it, and now they have all taken up the state of Arhat."
"Such people as these cannot achieve it; how much less can you, who desire to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi as a bodhisattva?
One who recognizes this as the work of Māra will not fall into the paths of the Arhat or Pratyekabuddha, but shall instead attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"If there is a bodhisattva who practices the dānapāramitā and proceeds toward sarvajñatā without wavering or turning back, they shall attain anuttarasamyaksambodhi. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If there is a bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā who forms this thought:

"As the Buddha has taught, a bodhisattva fully upholds [the teachings] without departing from the Buddha's instructions, until reaching *samyaksambodhi* (sarvākārajñatā), never allowing them to diminish."
"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they should form this thought:
'One who recognizes and understands the works of Māra will never diminish in their pursuit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
“Subhūti! By being fully endowed with these signs, activities, and characteristics, one should know that this is an irreversible bodhisattva. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
In what respect does a bodhisattva turn so that it is said they do not turn back?
The Buddha said:

"Returning from the marks of the five aggregates, returning from the marks of the twelve bases, returning from the marks of the eighteen elements, returning from the marks of lust, anger, and ignorance, returning from the mark of views, returning from the marks of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, returning from the marks of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and returning from the mark of the Buddha."
Why is this? Because the *avaivartika* bodhisattva, through the empty image, appearance, and dharmic characteristics of form, ascends to the stage of a bodhisattva.

Within the dharma of non-arising there is nothing at all; since there is nothing at all, there is also no action. There is neither doing nor arising; therefore, it is called the "patience regarding the dharma of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
A bodhisattva who has attained this patience is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Subhūti! By being fully endowed with these marks, practices, and characteristics, one knows that he is an *avaivartika* bodhisattva mahāsattva.
The Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 12 and Scroll 13.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mokṣala of Khotan during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Translated by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Fifty-seven: On Firmness. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Fifty-seven: On Firmness. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
“That Māra Pāpīyān will come to where the bodhisattva is and say:”
"Samyaksaṃbodhi is equal to empty space; the matters of existence and non-existence are all empty, and these dharmas as well as their forms are likewise empty.

Within this dharma of emptiness and non-existence, nothing can ever be attained; that which has already passed cannot attain the dharma of emptiness and non-existence, nor can that which is yet to come attain it; the characteristics of existence and non-existence are all empty."
"Just as with space, your diligent toil is in vain; that one should attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is entirely the work of Māra, not what has been taught by the *samyak-saṃbuddha*."
“Virtuous ones, you must recognize the works of Māra. If you harbor such thoughts, you will surely fall into the evil destinies for a long night.
The Buddha said: “If these sons or daughters of good family hear these words, they should immediately recognize them as the work of Māra.”
“Māra wishes to destroy my *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Although these matters of the existence and non-existence of all dharmas are equal to emptiness, there is no sentient being who can see them, nor any who can know them.”

I shall take the emptiness of existence and non-existence as my saṃnāha-saṃnaddha (armor), and having attained sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), I shall preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings so that they may attain liberation.
I shall cause sentient beings to attain the path of srotāpanna, to attain arhatship, to attain the path of pratyekabuddha, and to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Since the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva first resolved his mind [on awakening], he should make that intention firm, remaining unshakable and unwavering, and not placing faith in other matters.
Once his intention is firmly established, he then practices the six pāramitās and ascends to the rank of a bodhisattva."
Subhūti said: "How is it, World-Honored One?
Is a bodhisattva who does not turn back from the path one who is irreversible (avaivartika)?"
"Is one who wavers and turns back an *avaivartika*?
The Buddha replied,
"One who does not move or turn back is an *avaivartika*, and one who moves and turns back is also an *avaivartika*."
Subhūti said: “How is this so, World-Honored One?”
The Buddha said:
"One who wavers from the stages of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha is an Avaivartika.
One who does not waver from the stages of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha is, for that Bodhisattva, one who wavers."
Subhūti! By being fully endowed with these marks, activities, and characteristics, one is an *avaivartika*.
One who possesses such marks cannot be thwarted by Māra Pāpīyān, nor can he be prevented from attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Subhūti! An avaivartika bodhisattva who wishes to attain the four dhyānas is able to attain them; he is likewise able to attain the dhyāna of cessation and liberation; he is able to attain all the dhyānas of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, as well as the dhyānas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and he is able to attain all five supernormal powers.

Although he attains the various dhyānas, he does not take the realization of those dhyānas as his own; nor does he take the realization of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. Rather, he takes for himself that which is appropriate to liberate sentient beings. Subhūti!

By being fully endowed with these signs, practices, and characteristics, one knows this to be an *avaivartika* bodhisattva. "Furthermore, Subhūti, an *avaivartika* constantly contemplates the Path and does not depart from the Path.

He does not crave physical form or color; he does not crave bodily marks; he does not crave a dwelling place; he does not crave the six *pāramitās*; nor does he crave the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*), nor the four meditative concentrations on emptiness (*catasraḥ śūnyatā-samāpattayaḥ*); he does not crave the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); he does not crave the ten powers (*daśa balāni*) or the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharmāḥ*); he does not crave a Buddha-field, nor does he crave the instruction of sentient beings; he does not crave seeing the Buddhas, nor does he crave the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*)."
Why is this so? Because in emptiness there are no phenomena; one does not perceive within the empty, signless, and wishless dharmas anything that can be craved.
For what reason?
Subhūti, because all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—are empty of their own characteristics, the irreversible Bodhisattva is fully endowed with the mindfulness of a Bodhisattva.

He is fully endowed with the four modes of conduct: walking, standing, sitting, and reclining; whether waking or dwelling, he is calm, attentive, and deliberate, never acting impulsively, and maintains his mental focus without forgetfulness.
Subhūti! By being fully endowed with these marks, activities, and characteristics, one is an irreversible bodhisattva. Subhūti!

The avaivartika bodhisattva, for the sake of sentient beings, employs *upāyakauśalya* while remaining amidst the five desires of the household life; he bestows clothing, bedding, food, and drink upon those in poverty and distress, providing them with everything according to their wishes.

One practices the six pāramitās oneself, encourages others to practice the six perfections, constantly praises the merit of the six perfections, and rejoices on behalf of those who see others practicing them.

An avaivartika bodhisattva, while living as a householder, bestows upon sentient beings the treasures filling Jambudvīpa, and even the treasures of the trichiliocosm, never once feeling attachment or stinginess.

Free from thoughts of lust, they always practice the Dharma with equanimity; their speech is humble and they do not treat others with contempt, ensuring that sentient beings do not give rise to anger.
Subhūti! By being fully endowed with these signs, activities, and characteristics, one is an avaivartika. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"
The yakṣa Haripiṅgala constantly follows and protects them.
The yakṣas and others say:
"We shall always protect this bodhisattva until he attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, ensuring his mind remains undisturbed and never strays from it."

Furthermore, there are five Śivā yakṣas who also attend and protect the bodhisattva mahāsattva avaivartika, ensuring that other minor deities and non-human spirits are unable to find any opportunity to harm him.

Subhūti! An avaivartika bodhisattva is fully endowed with the faculty of faith, the faculty of resolve, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of samādhi, and the faculty of wisdom; such a person is courageous among men and never succumbs to cowardice.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What constitutes being courageous?
What constitutes not being timid?"
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"One whose resolve for the path is firm, unshakable, and irreversible is indeed courageous and not timid; you should know that this is the mark of an avaivartika."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! An irreversible bodhisattva is always fully endowed with mindfulness of the path; he does not study incantations or talismanic scripts, does not practice sorcery, does not act as a physician compounding various medicines, and does not study the arts of immortals, external paths, or divination to know the thoughts of other men and women."
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva, regarding emptiness, does not perceive the mark of dharmas; since such marks do not exist, they always aspire to purity.
By being fully endowed with these marks, practices, and characteristics, one knows them to be an *avaivartika*.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"I shall now explain the characteristics, marks, and conduct of an irreversible bodhisattva; listen attentively and receive this well. Subhūti said:
"Yes, World-Honored One!
We shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Subhūti:

"When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not depart from the practice of the path; they accord with the five aggregates, accord with the various natures, and accord with the various constituents."
Why is this? Because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are empty, their nature (*svabhāva*) is also empty; thus, one’s conduct does not oppose the affairs of the state. Why is this so?
Abiding in the dharma of emptiness, one does not perceive any phenomenon as increasing or decreasing.
One does not engage in the act of stealing. Why is this?
Abiding in emptiness, within the dharma of emptiness, one does not perceive any dharma that is brought forth nor any that is taken away.
One does not oppose military affairs. Why is this?
Abiding in emptiness, one does not perceive even within empty phenomena that there is much or little.
One does not engage in conflict or contention. Why is this?
Abiding in the dharma of emptiness, one does not perceive any dharma that is subject to aversion or affection.
One's speech is always in accordance with reality. Why is this?
Because he abides in the emptiness and suchness of all phenomena, and does not perceive even the existence of permanence or impermanence.
Subhūti, an avaivartika bodhisattva does not speak of matters concerning cities or fortresses.
Why is this? Abiding in the emptiness of space, one perceives neither aggregation nor dispersion, nor does one perceive the affairs of villages. Why is this?

Abiding in the ultimate limit, they perceive neither gain nor loss; they speak not of the affairs of the self, nor do they speak of various worldly matters, but speak only of the prajñāpāramitā, which is never separate from the state of omniscience (sarvajñatā).

One practices the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) without being motivated by greed or envy; one practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) without being motivated by immoral conduct; one practices the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) without being motivated by anger; one practices the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*) without being motivated by indolence; one practices the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) without being motivated by distracted mind; and one practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) without being motivated by ignorance.
Practicing the emptiness of all phenomena, one becomes a master of all phenomena, not a master of what is non-dharmic.
One practices within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and praises those who do not destroy the Dharma.

One forms friendships with the Tathāgatas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and Bodhisattvas, as well as with sons and daughters of noble family who have newly resolved upon the Great Vehicle. One constantly wishes to behold the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas; one constantly wishes to see the Buddhas of the ten directions, and wherever one sees a Buddha, one vows to be reborn there. Thus, one attains rebirth there, and day and night, one’s mind never departs from the mindfulness of the Buddhas.

Why is this? Because all *avaivartika* bodhisattvas enter the desire realm in accordance with its nature and practice the ten wholesome deeds, thereby attaining birth before the Buddhas of the ten directions; they give rise to the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, and from the fourth dhyāna proceed to the formless dhyānas, thus attaining birth before the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Subhūti! By being fully endowed with these marks, features, and modes of conduct, one knows this to be an irreversible bodhisattva. Subhūti!

A bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā who dwells in internal emptiness, dwells in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and dwells in the three gates of liberation never says: "I am an avaivartika."
Nor does he say, "I am not an avaivartika. Abiding in his own stage, he never has any doubt.
Why is this? Because from the beginning, one does not perceive any phenomenon that either moves or does not move.
It is, for example, like a stream-enterer who abides in his own path without doubt or perplexity.

The Avaivartika is also like this: abiding securely in his own stage, he transforms sentient beings and purifies the Buddha-lands; as soon as the works of Māra arise, he immediately perceives them, does not follow the teachings of Māra, and destroys the works of Māra.
It is like the mind of a person of the lowest intelligence, who harbors rebellious and evil intentions that do not change until death. Subhūti!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva who is irreversible (avaivartika) and dwells in his own stage is also like this; he cannot be moved or diverted by gods, humans, ghosts, spirits, nāgas, asuras, or the Māra Pāpīyān.
Why is this? Because they have emerged above all those in the world, including the devas, nāgas, and spirits.

Within their own stage, they are fully endowed with the five supernormal powers; they transform sentient beings, purify buddha-fields, travel from one buddha-field to another, plant various roots of goodness in the presence of all buddhas, inquire of the buddhas, and receive their teachings.

If there are demonic activities in the place where one dwells, one immediately recognizes them; through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), one remains amidst those demonic activities and clings to the fundamental limit (*koṭi*).
Thus, regarding that very stage, one neither doubts nor feels weary.

Why is this? Because they have no doubt regarding the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); they know that the limit of reality is neither one nor two, and thus they have transcended the stages of the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas.

Subhūti! Regarding this emptiness and the absence of dharmic characteristics, the bodhisattva neither perceives arising nor perceives cessation; neither perceives annihilation nor perceives attachment; nor does he form the thought:
"I shall attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
Nor does he say, "I shall not attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Why is this?

Because the marks of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* are themselves empty, this bodhisattva abides in a state that is naturally free from deficiency; no longer hoping for anything else, no one is able to destroy this stage.
Why is this? Subhūti! The wisdom possessed by an avaivartika bodhisattva is not shared with others.
That Māra Pāpīyān transformed himself into the likeness of a Buddha and came to where the Bodhisattva was, saying:

"Come, take up the state of an Arhat; there is no one who has bestowed upon you the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. You have not yet attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and thus the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, do not accept your prediction."
"You, too, do not yet possess these things, nor this conduct, nor these marks, nor this appearance that would entitle you to receive the prediction of enlightenment.
Thus spoke Subhūti.
When a bodhisattva hears this, they are neither terrified nor afraid, neither doubtful nor weary; their mind is free from duality.
This bodhisattva should know for themselves:
"I have already received the prediction of enlightenment from all the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas."
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva knows for himself:
"I possess these qualities and am capable of receiving the prediction of enlightenment for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

Then that Māra Pāpīyān again assumes the form and appearance of a Buddha and comes to where the Bodhisattva is, bestowing upon the Bodhisattva the prediction (vyākaraṇa) of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi through demonic deeds.
This bodhisattva immediately realizes: "This may be Māra, or one sent by Māra, who has come in this form; it is not the Buddha.
He merely wishes to cause me to fall into the state of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha."
Subhūti! If Māra Pāpīyān should again manifest in the form of a Buddha and come to where the bodhisattva is, saying to the bodhisattva:
"What you are practicing was not spoken by the Buddha, nor was it spoken by his disciples; it is merely the work of Māra."
"Subhūti! The bodhisattva should then know that this is merely Māra, or one acting under Māra's instigation; this is not a Buddha.
Though they seek to destroy my resolve for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, my mind shall never be turned back."
That this bodhisattva’s intention cannot be turned back is because he has already received the prediction from the Buddhas of the past and thus abides on the stage of *avaivartika*. Why is this?
Because they are fully endowed with these marks, features, and modes of conduct, they are capable of attaining *avaivartika* [irreversibility].
By this, one should know the marks of an *avaivartika*. "Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
A bodhisattva who practices the *prajñāpāramitā* does not spare body or life for the sake of upholding all dharmas.

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, through *upāyakauśalya*, is thus able to uphold the Dharma without sparing body or life, then they have already upheld the dharmas of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bodhisattva, not begrudging body or life, desires to protect the Dharma, what kind of Dharma does he wish to protect and uphold?
The Buddha said:
"I preach the Dharma of emptiness, yet foolish people revile and slander it, saying:
'This is neither the Dharma nor the Vinaya practice, and it is not the teaching of the Honored One.'"
“Subhūti! For the sake of this Dharma, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas protect and uphold the true Dharma.
A bodhisattva should form this thought:”
"Whatever Dharma all future Buddhas shall preach, I am also included among those who receive the prediction [of enlightenment] therein.
This Dharma is also my own Dharma; for the sake of this Dharma, I do not begrudge my body or life."
"Subhūti! For the sake of this Dharma, a bodhisattva does not begrudge even their own body or life.
By means of these characteristics, marks, and practices being fully present, one should know that they are an avaivartika."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when an avaivartika bodhisattva hears the teaching of the profound Dharma, they neither harbor doubt nor feel alarm; they are able to receive and uphold all that the Buddhas have spoken, never forgetting it."
"Why is this? It is because they have attained the dhāraṇīs.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What dharani has the bodhisattva attained that enables him to receive, uphold, and never forget the teachings of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas?”
The Buddha said:
"By attaining dhāraṇīs such as *śrutadhara* (retention upon hearing), a bodhisattva is able to receive and uphold the sūtras and teachings of all Buddhas without forgetting them.
[The interlocutor asked: "World-Honored One!"
What the Tathāgata speaks was not spoken by śrāvakas, nor was it spoken by devas, nāgas, or yakṣas; nor was it spoken by asuras, gandharvas, or mahoragas.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Regarding all names of sounds that exist, when a bodhisattva hears them, they are from the very beginning neither startled nor amazed, and their mind is free from doubt, because they have attained the dhāraṇīs."
"By being fully endowed with such characteristics, marks, and conduct, this is an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva. 58.
Chapter on Profundity: The Fifth and Final Chapter on the Profundity of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“An avaivartika bodhisattva is endowed with great merit; he is endowed with incalculable merit.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!”
The Avaivartika possesses great merit and is endowed with merit that cannot be measured. Why is this?
Because he has attained unimpeded and limitless wisdom, which is beyond the reach of all Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas.
"The Avaivartika dwells within this wisdom and thereby attains the superknowledges (abhijñā), which are such that neither the devas nor the people of the world can surpass them.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Could one, with a lifespan equal to the sands of the Ganges River, extol the merits of an avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva—their perfection of physical marks and characteristics, their profound wisdom of entry and abiding, their practice of the six pāramitās, their fulfillment of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and sarvajñatā—and thereby enable others to know these merits of the avaivartika bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!”
It is well that you are able to inquire about the profound domain of the *avaivartika*.
You speak of the profound emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; you speak of non-existence, and of the absence of arising and ceasing.

To speak of the purity of Nirvana amidst all the defilements of lust; to speak of Suchness, of Quiescence, of the Reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), and of the Dharma-nature—these profound dharmas are all images of Nirvana.
Subhūti said: "World-Honored One!
If it is spoken in this way, does it mean that this is merely the profound nirvāṇa, and not the teaching regarding all dharmas?"
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! Profundity is also the teaching of all dharmas.”
Subhūti! The five aggregates are profound, the six sense-bases are profound, and even the Path is likewise profound. Subhūti!
In what sense are the five aggregates profound?
The suchness of the five aggregates is profound, and because it is identical to the suchness of the Path, the five aggregates are profound and the Path is likewise profound.
What is suchness (*tathatā*)?
Now, as for suchness: it is neither the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), nor is it separate from the five aggregates;
it is neither the Path (*mārga*), nor is it separate from the Path.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are *avaivartika* are so exceedingly marvelous, extraordinary, profound, and subtle is truly such.”
Having eliminated the five aggregates, one dwells in nirvāṇa;
whether they be the dharmas of the ordained or the laity, all that is conditioned or unconditioned, with outflows or without outflows, has been entirely eliminated, and one dwells in nirvāṇa.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva responds to the profound and subtle Dharma of the prajñāpāramitā, whether by recollecting it or upholding it, they should personally reflect that their dwelling must be in accordance with the teaching of the prajñāpāramitā, and their learning must likewise be in accordance with the teaching of the prajñāpāramitā;
this bodhisattva will then fully and completely embody everything as taught in the prajñāpāramitā."

By maintaining this complete mindfulness, one receives immeasurable roots of goodness and merit, and abandons the hardships of birth and death for countless kalpas; how much more so for those who, with a focused mind, maintain their practice and accord with the Prajñāpāramitā and the Way.
Suppose, for example, there is a man who is very prone to negligence and has made an appointment with a beautiful woman.
That woman, due to some business, is unable to go at the appointed time.
Before she has arrived, what do you think—how many thoughts or mental preoccupations would arise in that man?
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
this perception is indeed very much so, it is very much so.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom according to its teachings, and maintains such mindfulness for even a single day without wavering, they will eliminate the defilements of birth and death for as many kalpas.”

The roots of goodness and merit acquired by this bodhisattva while practicing the perfection of wisdom for even a single day surpass those of a bodhisattva who practices only giving for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to give offerings to the Triple Gem for as many eons as there are grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges, what do you think? Would that person plant much merit?"
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
it is very much so, it is very much so!”
"It is incalculable.

The Buddha said, "It is not equal to this bodhisattva mahāsattva who, mindful of the prajñāpāramitā, practices for a single day according to the instructions within the prajñāpāramitā; the merit of that is incalculable."
Why is this? Because by means of this vehicle, bodhisattvas swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti!

If there is a bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā who, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, performs meritorious deeds on behalf of srotāpannas, and likewise performs meritorious deeds on behalf of arhats and pratyekabuddhas, up to performing the roots of goodness for samyaksaṃbuddhas.
"What do you think, Subhūti? Would the merit of that person be great?
Subhūti replied, "World-Honored One, it would be great."
"Very much, very much!
The Buddha said, "It is not equal to the merit of a bodhisattva who practices the prajñāpāramitā according to the instructions herein; that merit is incalculable."

Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they have already transcended the stages of the arhat and the pratyekabuddha, and from the rank of a bodhisattva, they proceed to the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Subhūti! If there were a bodhisattva who, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, practiced the six pāramitās, would that person's merit be great? Subhūti replied:
“Very much, very much!

the Buddha said, “It would not equal the merit of this bodhisattva who, following the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, practices the six *pāramitās* for a single day in accordance with it; that merit is incalculable.”
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; by abiding within this Prajñāpāramitā, they fully perfect all the Buddha-dharmas.

Subhūti! If there were a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom who, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, practiced the gift of the Dharma—what do you think? Would that person’s merit be great?
Subhūti said: "Very much, very much! The Buddha said:
"It would not be equal to this Bodhisattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā according to the instructions herein and giving the Dharma for even one day; its merit would be incalculable. Why is this? "
A bodhisattva who does not depart from the *prajñāpāramitā* does not depart from *sarvajñatā*.
A bodhisattva who wishes to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should not depart from the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Subhūti! If there is a bodhisattva who practices the prajñāpāramitā, practicing for as many lifetimes as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, cultivating the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, as well as emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
"Would the merit of that person be great? Subhūti replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"Very much, very much!
The Buddha said:

"It is not equal to this bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* according to its instructions; if for a single day they practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen dharmas according to the instructions within the *prajñāpāramitā*, their merit would be incalculable."
Why is this? Because from the very beginning, one has never seen a bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* who turns back from *sarvākārajñatā*.
Subhūti, it is because those who are separated from the *prajñāpāramitā* undergo movement and regression.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should not be separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, practiced the six *pāramitās*, giving away all his wealth, food, and drink, as well as gifts of the Dharma and various matters concerning *samādhi*, desiring to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
“Would the merit of that person be great?
Subhūti replied, “It would be great,
World-Honored One!”
"Very much, very much!
The Buddha said:

"It is not as great as the merit of this bodhisattva who practices the prajñāpāramitā according to the teaching herein, performing acts of material giving and the gift of Dharma, and engaging in various samādhis, desiring to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; that merit is incalculable."
Why is this? Because that which is taught as the Prajñāpāramitā is the most supreme among all merits.
To be divorced from mindfulness of the Prajñāpāramitā is to be without mindfulness and without seeking.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! A bodhisattva who wishes to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should seek it through skill in wisdom. Subhūti!"

If there is a bodhisattva who practices the six pāramitās for as many eons as there are grains of sand along the Ganges, they should exhort and assist all Buddhas and their Saṅghas of the past, future, and present in their meritorious deeds, and rejoice in them on their behalf.
"If one were to maintain this joy and dedicate it toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
would its merit not be great? Subhūti replied:
“World-Honored One!
It is very much so, it is very much so!
The Buddha said:
"It would be better for this bodhisattva to accord with the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā for a single day; by upholding this merit, they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
“Subhūti! A bodhisattva who wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should seek it through skill in wisdom.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, for a bodhisattva, non-action is the most supreme.

If there is neither action nor that which is performed, how can one attain right view, the stage of srotāpanna, arhatship, pratyekabuddhahood, up to sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), and achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Subhūti!"
One cannot attain the stage of *srotāpanna* up to *sarvākārajñatā*, nor achieve *anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*, by means of anything conditioned.
When practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, one does not seek even through giving; nor does one harbor the thought that there is such a thing as "giving.
One should constantly reflect: "This giving is empty and non-existent."
Why is this? It is because this bodhisattva has trained well in internal and external emptiness, as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence. Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva dwells in this emptiness and contemplates all activities, performing this contemplation of emptiness, they are already not separate from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Being not separate from the *prajñāpāramitā*, they receive incalculable, limitless, and immeasurable merits and virtues.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the difference between that which has no number, no limit, and no measure?
The Buddha said:
" 'Asaṃkhyeya' means being beyond number.
A numbered body cannot be apprehended, nor can a non-numbered body be apprehended.
That which is immeasurable cannot be delimited, measured, or even conceived of in terms of the future, the past, or the present."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Could it be that the five aggregates are immeasurable, incalculable, and limitless?"
The Buddha said, "There is. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason are the five aggregates immeasurable, incalculable, and limitless?
The Buddha said:
“The five aggregates are empty; they cannot be numbered and cannot be measured.
“How is it, World-Honored One?
Is it only the five aggregates that are empty, while all other dharmas are not empty?”
The Buddha said,
"Did I not originally teach that all phenomena are empty?
[He replied,] "World-Honored One, you have indeed taught that all phenomena are empty."
World-Honored One!
Emptiness is inexhaustible, it is incalculable, and it is immeasurable.
Emptiness cannot be counted, it cannot be measured, and it also lacks any level sign.
“World-Honored One!
This dharma-meaning and its interpretation are likewise unobtainable as manifold.
The Buddha said:
"It is exactly as Subhūti has said, without any difference.
Because all dharmas are unattainable, the Buddha speaks of various things as being unattainable.
These dharmas are empty, signless, wishless, non-existent, and unarisen; this is cessation, this is nirvāṇa, and this is the Tathāgata’s inexhaustibility that extends to nirvāṇa."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is unprecedented, World-Honored One!
It is most marvelous and extraordinary!”

As the Blessed One has spoken of the dharma of non-apprehension, I have heard that all dharmas spoken of by the Blessed One are likewise unapprehendable; because all dharmas are unapprehendable, emptiness is also unapprehendable.
"Is there any increase or decrease in the meaning of 'unattainability'?
The Buddha said,
"There is neither increase nor decrease."

Subhūti said: “The six pāramitās neither increase nor decrease; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment likewise neither increase nor decrease; the eight liberations, the four unhindered wisdoms, the four immeasurables, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, as well as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, also neither increase nor decrease.”
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
If these dharmas, from the six pāramitās up to the four fearlessnesses, were subject to increase or decrease, then one would not achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
“Subhūti! It is so, it is so! That which is a dharma that cannot be apprehended neither increases nor decreases.”
Whether practicing the prajñāpāramitā, recollecting the prajñāpāramitā, or training in the skillful means (upāyakauśalya) of the prajñāpāramitā, one does not even think:
"I am increasing the six pāramitās."
Nor should one think:
"I am diminishing the six pāramitās.
One should instead form this thought:
"Because there are merely names, there are the six pāramitās.
Holding this reflection, holding this resolve, and holding these roots of goodness, one practices for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which is the suchness of all dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, what is the suchness of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and the suchness of all dharmas?”
"What is the suchness of all dharmas that constitutes *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The Buddha said:
"The suchness of the five aggregates and the suchness of *nirvāṇa*—this is therefore *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; it neither increases nor decreases."

Therefore, the bodhisattva does not depart from the *prajñāpāramitā*, but practices the *prajñāpāramitā* with even greater vigor and diligence; yet they do not perceive any phenomena as having increase or decrease. Consequently, that which cannot be apprehended also has neither increase nor decrease.
Subhūti! For this reason, the six pāramitās neither increase nor decrease, and so on up to the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), which also neither increase nor decrease.
A bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā should maintain this intention of neither increasing nor decreasing.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is it attained by means of the initial thought, or is it attained by means of the final thought? Since the former thought and the latter thought do not coexist, how can the roots of goodness be accumulated to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
World-Honored One!
Since this mind is neither conjoined nor distinct, how can it accomplish any meritorious virtue?
Being neither accomplished nor accumulated, it cannot achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"I shall provide you with a simile, for those who possess wisdom attain understanding through similes.
What do you think? For example, when a lamp wick is first ignited, does it burn by means of the initial light?"
Is it by means of the later light that the wick is burned?
When the wick is being consumed, is it by means of the light at the initial moment that it is burned,
or is it by means of the light at the later moment that it is burned?
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
It is not by means of the first flame that the fire is ignited, nor is it apart from the causal conditions of the first flame that it is ignited.”
"Nor is it ignited by the subsequent flame, yet it is not apart from the conditions of the subsequent flame. Subhūti!
Likewise, a bodhisattva does not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the initial thought, yet it is not apart from the conditions of the initial thought."
Nor is it attained by means of a subsequent thought, nor is it attained apart from the causal conditions of a subsequent thought. Subhūti!
A bodhisattva practicing the prajñāpāramitā, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until reaching the tenth stage, accomplishes anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“World-Honored One!
How does one attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the ten stages of abiding?
The Buddha said:

"First, from the stage of wisdom, one contemplates the stages that are fully endowed with *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*: the stage of the eightfold assembly, the stage of attenuation, the stage of freedom from passion, the stage of having accomplished what was to be done, the stage of the *pratyekabuddha*, the stage of the bodhisattva, the stage of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and the stage of the Buddha. Having fully perfected the stage of the Buddha, one then realizes *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
In training in these ten stages, a bodhisattva does not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the initial resolve, nor does he attain it apart from the initial resolve;
nor does he attain it by means of the subsequent resolve, nor does he attain it apart from the subsequent resolve.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
the dependent origination of the twelve links is profound.”
One does not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the initial resolve, nor is it apart from the conditions of the initial resolve;
one does not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the subsequent resolve, nor is the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* apart from the subsequent resolve.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Once the mind has ceased, can it be made to arise again?
“World-Honored One, [it cannot].”
"Once extinguished, it does not arise again.
"Subhūti, is the mind that has already arisen something subject to extinction?"
“World-Honored One!
This is truly a dharma of cessation.
The Buddha said:
“Is that which has already ceased considered ‘ceased’? “No,
World-Honored One.”
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does it abide in that very way?
“World-Honored One, it abides as it abides in suchness.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“If one dwells as suchness, should one dwell in the true limit (bhūtakoṭi) as dwelling in suchness?
“No, [World-Honored One].”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “What do you think, Subhūti? Is ‘suchness’ profound?”
“World-Honored One!
It is profound, most profound. “Subhūti!”
"Is 'suchness' (tathatā) this mind? "No,
World-Honored One."
"Is it not like suchness? "Subhūti! Is the mind separate from suchness?"
"No, World-Honored One. "Subhūti!"
“Do you perceive reality by means of reality as its characteristic? “No,
World-Honored One.”
"Suchness does not see Suchness.
"Subhūti, is one who practices in this manner practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*?"
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
One who practices in this manner is practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.”
Subhūti said: “If one practices in this manner, in what dharma does one practice?
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:
"One who practices in this manner is one who practices nothing.
Why is this? Because..."
"One who practices the perfection of wisdom has no manifold practices.
"World-Honored One!
That which is suchness (tathatā) likewise has no manifoldness, nor does it perform manifold practices."
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, what is it that he practices?
Subhūti replied:
"It is because practice ultimately has no two locations.
The Buddha said:
"Regarding ultimate practice, are there various types of practice?"
"Is it characterized by signs? "No,
World-Honored One."
The Buddha asked,
"Do you regard signlessness as having signs? [He replied,] "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said: “What is mindfulness with signs?”
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not form such thoughts as ‘there is a mark’ or ‘there is no mark.’”
When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, if they do not fulfill the ten powers of a Buddha and the eighteen unique dharmas, they will not achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) consists in neither being mindful of nor being unmindful of any phenomena.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva knows that the characteristics of all phenomena are empty.
Abiding in the dharma of emptiness, for the sake of sentient beings, they practice the three samādhis and maintain these samādhis to transform and teach sentient beings.
World-Honored One!
What are the three samādhis of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
The Buddha said:
"Those who abide in this samādhi are in accord with emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
All sentient beings, however, are attached to emptiness, and attached to signs and wishes."
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva establishes sentient beings in the practice of the perfection of wisdom through the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
By means of these three matters, the Bodhisattva teaches and transforms sentient beings.
Chapter 59: Practicing in a Dream. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Fifty-nine: Practicing in a Dream. At that time, Śāriputra said to Subhūti:

"If a bodhisattva practices the three samādhis—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—within a dream, by practicing these therein, would there be any benefit for the *prajñāpāramitā*?"
Subhūti replied to Śāriputra:
"If there is benefit from the Prajñāpāramitā during the day, there shall likewise be benefit even within a night dream."
Why is this? Because there is no difference between day and night, or between waking and dreaming.

Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), if they possess that perfection of wisdom, they shall then maintain mindfulness of the perfection of wisdom even within a dream.
Śāriputra said to Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva performs some action within a dream, would there be any accomplishment or any experience thereof?
As the Buddha has said, all dharmas are like dreams; therefore, there is nothing accomplished and nothing experienced."
Why is this? Within a dream, one does not initially see any dharma that is established, nor anything that is received, nor is there anything attained.
Once awakened from the dream, would there be anything attained at all?
Subhūti said: "If one were to commit an act of killing within a dream and say, 'It is a pleasure that I have killed this,' [would there be any accumulation of karma?]"
“Having awakened, one reflects on what was done in the dream, thinking:
‘How did this come to be? Śāriputra replied:
“All things have causes and conditions; without causes and conditions, nothing ever arises.”
Subhūti said: “So it is, so it is! Things have causes and conditions.”
Where there is an object of condition, there is mindfulness;
where there is mindfulness, there is an object. An object arises from what is heard or seen, which gives rise to mental application and leads to attachment or cessation;
it does not arise through conditions when nothing has been heard or seen.
"Therefore, Śāriputra, it is by reason of causes and conditions that things arise and thoughts are produced. Śāriputra said:
“Subhūti, how is it that all that is thought and all that is done are said by the Buddha to be quiescent? How is it that there is that which is done,
which has conditions, which arises, and which results in attainment and experience?”

Subhūti said: "When a conceptualization arises, there is a causal condition; when there is a causal condition, there is an objective basis; when there is an objective basis, there is mindfulness. Śāriputra said:
"If a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās while dreaming, and maintains these merits with the intention of attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
does this constitute an act of giving?"
Subhūti said: "Now, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya has been prophesied by the World-Honored One; he may be questioned here.
Since Maitreya is able to explain it, you should question him."
Śāriputra said to Maitreya: "Regarding what I asked, Subhūti said:
'Maitreya will be able to explain it.'"
"Now, O Benevolent One, you should explain this for us.
At that time, Maitreya said to Śāriputra:
"Do you wish for me to dismiss [the self] by means of name, or by form, or by sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness?"
By what means should this be explained? Should it be resolved through the emptiness of form (*rūpa-śūnyatā*), or should it be resolved through the emptiness of sensation,
perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna-śūnyatā*)?
The emptiness of form is also incapable of dispatching anything; the emptiness of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is likewise incapable of dispatching anything.

From the beginning, I have not seen any dharma capable of dispatching another dharma; nor is there anyone who receives a prediction, nor anyone who attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor anyone at whom a prediction is bestowed. These dharmas are entirely without duality.
Śāriputra said: "As you have spoken, O worthy one, it is indeed realized. Maitreya replied:
"Although he has spoken thus, I too have not attained realization.
Śāriputra thought to himself:
"Maitreya Bodhisattva’s eloquence penetrates deeply into the six pāramitās; he employs various expositions yet remains without dependence on anything."
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"Do you see any such dharma by which one attains the realization of arhatship? Śāriputra replied:
“World-Honored One!
I do not see any dharma that can be attained or realized.
The Buddha said:
"When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, he does not think:
'This dharma has already received a prediction; this dharma shall receive a prediction; [this one] will attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
When a bodhisattva practices in this way, they practice the prajñāpāramitā without any doubt;
nor do they doubt whether they will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* or not.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), if he sees sentient beings who are hungry and thirsty, whose clothing does not cover their bodies, or who are orphaned, poor, destitute, and unable to sustain themselves, he should give rise to great compassion and make this vow:
'When I attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), may there be no such miserable and suffering beings within my realm.'"

May all the requisites for clothing and food in my Buddha-field be as they are among the gods of the Four Great Kings and the Sixth Heavenly King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, such that all food, drink, and clothing appear spontaneously.
"Subhūti! A bodhisattva who practices in this manner is one who fulfills the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā). Furthermore, Subhūti!"

When a Bodhisattva practices the Śīlapāramitā, if they see sentient beings who harbor thoughts of non-kindness, slaughter the lives of others, are ensnared by wrong views and doubt, or commit the ten unwholesome actions; or if they see those with short lifespans and many illnesses, those with little majesty, ugliness, and lack of complexion, or those who are physically deformed, weak, and extremely low-born, they give rise to great compassion, thinking:
"By my practicing the Śīlapāramitā, when I attain Buddhahood, may there be no such beings within my realm."
"When a bodhisattva thus fulfills the precepts, they will soon attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment before long. Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), if they see sentient beings harboring thoughts of anger, striking one another with clubs, staves, swords, spears, tiles, or stones, wounding or killing each other, they shall give rise to a great vow, saying:"
"I shall practice patience so that until I attain Buddhahood, there shall be no such persons or evil deeds within my realm.

When I become a Buddha, may all sentient beings in my land share a compassionate mind and harmonious intent, regarding one another as fathers, mothers, elder brothers, or younger brothers, never harboring harm toward each other."
"When a bodhisattva practices in this way, they fulfill patience and will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before long. Furthermore, Subhūti!"

When a bodhisattva practices the *vīrya-pāramitā*, if they see sentient beings who give rise to signs of indolence toward the teachings of the Three Vehicles and lack diligence, they further form this great vow:

"I shall personally exert myself with unremitting diligence; when I attain Buddhahood, may the sentient beings in my land be diligent in the teachings of the Three Vehicles, each attaining liberation."

"In this way, the Bodhisattva fulfills diligence and will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before long. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, if he sees sentient beings engaged in the five hindrances—namely, first, lust; second, malice; third, sloth and torpor; fourth, restlessness and remorse; and fifth, the net of doubt—and observes them to be devoid of the four *dhyānas* and the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), he gives rise to a great resolve: "I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, having attained it, I shall teach the Dharma to these sentient beings so that they may abandon these five hindrances, cultivate the four *dhyānas*, and attain the four formless absorptions. This is called the perfection of diligence of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, if he sees sentient beings who have fallen into the eight wrong paths—namely, being born in hell, as animals, as hungry ghosts, or among the long-lived gods, or being born in the borderlands, or being deaf, mute, or mentally deranged, or being born in a time when there is no Buddha in the world—he gives rise to a great resolve: 'I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, having attained it, I shall teach the Dharma to these sentient beings so that they may abandon these eight wrong paths and be born in the noble realms. "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, if he sees sentient beings who are impoverished, lacking food and clothing, and suffering from hunger and cold, he gives rise to a great resolve: 'I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, having attained it, I shall teach the Dharma to these sentient beings so that they may abandon poverty and always obtain the seven types of wealth. "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, if he sees sentient beings who are subject to various diseases and suffer from many ailments, he gives rise to a great resolve: 'I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, having attained it, I shall teach the Dharma to these sentient beings so that they may abandon all illnesses and attain the supreme, unsurpassed medicine. "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, if he sees sentient beings who are constantly harassed by enemies and suffer from fear and distress, he gives rise to a great resolve: 'I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, having attained it, I shall teach the Dharma to these sentient beings so that they may abandon all enemies and attain the supreme, unsurpassed peace. "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, if he sees sentient beings who are separated from their parents, brothers, sisters, wives, children, and relatives, and suffer grief and sorrow, he gives rise to a great resolve: 'I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, having attained it, I shall teach the Dharma to these sentient beings so that they may abandon all separation and attain the supreme, unsurpassed reunion. "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, if he sees sentient beings who are separated from their friends, companions, and associates, and suffer grief and sorrow, he gives rise to a great resolve: 'I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, having attained it, I shall teach the Dharma to these sentient beings so that they may abandon all separation from friends and attain the supreme, unsurpassed reunion. "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, if he sees sentient beings who are separated from their teachers, preceptors, and spiritual friends, and suffer grief and sorrow, he gives rise to a great resolve: 'I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, having attained it, I shall teach the Dharma to these sentient beings so that they may abandon all separation from teachers and spiritual friends and attain the supreme, unsurpassed reunion. "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, if he sees sentient beings who are separated from their parents and suffer grief and sorrow, he gives rise to a great resolve: 'I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, having attained it, I shall teach the Dharma to these sentient beings so that they may abandon all separation from parents and attain the supreme, unsurpassed reunion. "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, if he sees sentient beings who are separated from their brothers and sisters and suffer grief and sorrow, he gives rise to a great resolve: 'I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, having attained it, I shall teach the Dharma to these sentient beings so that they may abandon all separation from siblings and attain the supreme, unsurpassed reunion. "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, if he sees sentient beings who are separated from their wives and children and suffer grief and sorrow, he gives rise to a great resolve: 'I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, having attained it, I shall teach the Dharma to these sentient beings so that they may abandon all separation from spouses and offspring and attain the supreme, unsurpassed reunion. "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, if he sees sentient beings who are separated from their kinsmen and suffer grief and sorrow, he gives rise to a great resolve: 'I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, having attained it, I shall teach the Dharma to these sentient beings so that they may abandon all separation from kin and attain the supreme, unsurpassed reunion. "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, if he sees sentient beings who are separated from their friends and suffer grief and sorrow, he gives rise to a great resolve: 'I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, having attained it, I shall teach the Dharma to these sentient beings so that they may abandon all separation from friends and attain the supreme, unsurpassed reunion.
