"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, if he sees sentient beings who are separated from their teachers and suffer grief and sorrow, he gives rise to a great resolve: 'I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, having attained it, I shall teach the Dharma to these sentient beings so that they may abandon all separation from teachers and attain the supreme, unsurpassed reunion. "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, if he sees sentient beings who are separated from their preceptors and suffer grief and sorrow, he gives rise to a great resolve: 'I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, having attained it, I shall teach the Dharma to these sentient beings so that they may abandon all separation from preceptors and attain the supreme, unsurpassed reunion. "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, if he sees sentient beings who are separated from their spiritual friends and suffer grief and sorrow, he gives rise to a great resolve: 'I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, having attained it, I shall teach the Dharma to these sentient beings so that they may abandon all separation from spiritual friends and attain the supreme, unsurpassed reunion. "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, if he sees sentient beings who are separated from their parents and suffer grief and sorrow, he gives rise to a great resolve: 'I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, having attained it, I shall teach the Dharma to these sentient beings so that they may abandon all separation from parents and attain the supreme, unsurpassed reunion. "Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā*, if he sees sentient beings who are separated from their brothers and sisters and suffer grief and sorrow, he gives rise to a great
"May I always practice the dhyānapāramitā to transform sentient beings and purify the Buddha-lands.
When I attain Buddhahood, may all sentient beings in my land have no disordered minds."
"In this way, the bodhisattva fulfills dhyāna and will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* before long.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*,

if they see sentient beings who commit evil— whether laypeople or those on the path— who have abandoned right view, who engage in unrighteous deeds, who claim there is no retribution for actions, who claim that [the self] is annihilated, or who claim that there are real sentient beings."
Having formed this vision, he gave rise to a great vow, saying:
"I shall diligently practice the six pāramitās to purify the buddha-fields and transform sentient beings."
"When I become a Buddha, may there be no such matters of false views in my land.
In this way, the bodhisattva fulfills the prajñāpāramitā and swiftly approaches sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, if they see sentient beings situated in three positions—first, the position of right view; second, the position of wrong view; and third, the position that is neither wrong nor right view—they think: 'For this reason, I shall diligently practice the six pāramitās to transform sentient beings and purify the buddha-field.'"
"When I become a Buddha, may the people of my land neither see wrong views nor hear the sound of wrong views.
When a Bodhisattva acts in this way, they are fully endowed with the six *pāramitās* and swiftly draw near to *samyaksambodhi*.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, if they see beings in the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm—including even wriggling insects—they should give rise to great compassion, thinking:
'I shall practice the six pāramitās with diligent effort; when I become a Buddha, let the very names of the three evil paths not be heard within my land.'"
“In this way, the bodhisattva, for the sake of fulfilling the six pāramitās, swiftly approaches sarvajñatā (all-knowledge). Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, if they see the great earth with its mountains, hills, ravines, pits, thorns, grasses, trees, and impure, foul things...”
He made a universal vow, saying:
"I shall diligently practice the six pāramitās; when I attain Buddhahood, may my land be as level as the palm of a hand, and may the people of my land not behold any impurities."
"In this way, the Bodhisattva, by fulfilling the six pāramitās, swiftly draws near to *samyaksambodhi*. Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a Bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, if they see that the great earth contains no gold or jewels but consists entirely of soil."
He made this vow, saying:
"I shall diligently practice the six pāramitās; when I attain Buddhahood, may the ground of my land, from the lower limit upward, be composed entirely of pure gold."
"In this way, the Bodhisattva, by fulfilling the six pāramitās, swiftly approaches *samyaksambodhi*. Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a Bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, if they see sentient beings who have attachments, they make this vow, saying:"
"I shall diligently practice the six pāramitās; when I become a Buddha, I shall ensure that the people of my land have nothing to which they are attached.
When a bodhisattva acts in this way, they fulfill the six pāramitās and swiftly draw near to *samyaksambodhi*.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, if they see the four castes— the kṣatriyas, the brāhmaṇas, the vaiśyas, and the śūdras— or officials, generals, and masters, they should form a vow and resolve:
'I shall diligently practice the six pāramitās to transform sentient beings and purify the buddha-field.'"
"When I become a Buddha, may there be no four castes in my land, but only a single, pure caste.
When a bodhisattva acts in this way, they fulfill the six pāramitās and swiftly draw near to *samyaksambodhi*.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, if they see sentient beings belonging to superior, middling, or inferior families, they further make this vow:
'I shall diligently practice the six pāramitās to transform sentient beings and purify the buddha-fields.'"
"When I become a Buddha, may all sentient beings in my land be without such distinctions of superiority or inferiority, nor of high, middle, or low rank.
When a bodhisattva acts in this way, they fulfill the six pāramitās and swiftly draw near to *samyaksambodhi*.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, if they see sentient beings of various appearances, they give rise to a vow, saying:
'I shall diligently practice the six pāramitās to transform sentient beings and purify the buddha-field.'"
"When I become a Buddha, may the people of my land not have various complexions, but all be upright and handsome, attaining the foremost of colors.
In this way, the Bodhisattva fulfills the six pāramitās and swiftly approaches *samyaksambodhi*.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, if he sees a sovereign ruler, he should form a vow and resolve:
'I shall diligently practice the six pāramitās to transform sentient beings and purify the buddha-field.'"
When I become a Buddha, may my land have no title for a worldly king; rather, let it take the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, as its Dharma King.
"In this way, the Bodhisattva, by fulfilling the six pāramitās, swiftly approaches *samyaksambodhi*. Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a Bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, if they see the conduct of the five destinies, they give rise to a vow and resolve, saying:"
"I shall diligently practice the six pāramitās to transform sentient beings and purify the Buddha-land.

When I become a Buddha, I shall cause all the people of my land to be free from the conduct of the five destinies, and instead cause them to practice equally by means of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment."
“In this way, the bodhisattva fulfills the six pāramitās and swiftly approaches sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās,
seeing the four modes of birth— birth from an egg, birth from moisture, birth from a womb, and birth by transformation— they give rise to a vow and resolve, saying:”
"I shall diligently practice the six pāramitās to transform sentient beings and purify the Buddha-lands.
When I become a Buddha, may there be no three modes of birth in my land; all shall be born through transformation."
"In this way, the bodhisattva fulfills the six pāramitās and swiftly approaches sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, seeing that sentient beings lack the five supernormal powers and lack radiance, he further makes this vow: "
"When I become a Buddha, may all those in my land attain the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), and may they all possess radiance that shines afar.
When a Bodhisattva practices the six *pāramitās*, if he sees sentient beings who have excrement or urine, he makes a vow, saying:
"When I become a Buddha, may the people of my land be like celestial bodies, free from the affliction of excrement and urine."
"When the Bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, he makes this great vow, saying:
'When I become a Buddha, may there not be even one day, one month, one year, or ten years in my buddha-field; may these reckonings altogether not exist.'"
"When a Bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, if they see sentient beings with short lifespans, they make this great vow, saying:
'When I become a Buddha, may the lifespan of the people in my land be exceedingly long and beyond measure.'"
"In this way, the Bodhisattva fulfills the six pāramitās and attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the unexcelled perfect enlightenment.
When the Bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, if he sees sentient beings who lack the marks [of a great man], he makes a great vow, saying:
'I shall diligently practice the six pāramitās; when I become a Buddha, may the people of my land all universally attain the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.'"
"In this way, the Bodhisattva, for the sake of fulfilling the six pāramitās, swiftly approaches *samyaksambodhi*.

When the Bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, if he sees sentient beings who lack the roots of goodness, he thinks: 'When I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, may the people of my land be fully endowed with the roots of goodness, equal to those of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.'"
"One who forms such a thought fulfills the six perfections and swiftly approaches *samyaksambodhi*. Furthermore, Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva practices the six *pāramitās*, he says:"
"I shall exert diligent effort to swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, so that within my land there shall be no three defilements or four diseases.
When a bodhisattva acts thus, they fulfill the six pāramitās and swiftly draw near to sarvajñatā.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, he says:

'I shall exert myself with diligence to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; when I become a Buddha, may there not even be the name of "two paths" in my land, but that all beings everywhere shall equally reach sarvajñatā.'"

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, he thinks: 'Upon attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, may the very name of the stubborn and perverse not be heard within my buddha-field.'"
"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, he should form this thought:

'I shall not yet attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; first I must know my own lifespan, my radiance, and the number of my bhikṣu-saṃgha, and only then shall I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.'"
"There is no one at all who can know the number of kalpas of my lifespan or the number of my bhikṣus.
In this way, the Bodhisattva fulfills the six pāramitās and swiftly approaches sarvajñatā.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, they form this thought: 'When I become a Buddha,
I shall cause my single buddha-field to be as vast as the buddha-fields of the sands of the Ganges.'"
"In this way, the Bodhisattva, for the sake of fulfilling *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, will swiftly approach *sarvajñatā*. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
When a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, they should make this vow:
"The path of birth and death is long, and sentient beings are exceedingly numerous; space is boundless, and the nature of sentient beings is likewise without limit;
within it, there is neither one who is born nor one who enters nirvāṇa."
"One who reflects in this manner will fulfill the six *pāramitās* and swiftly draw near to *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).

Chapter 60: Constantly Exerting Effort (*Nityodyukta*) At that time, there was a woman in the assembly named Nityodyukta. She rose from her seat, adjusted her robes, paid homage to the Buddha, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I, too, shall practice the six *pāramitās* and bring a Buddha-land to fulfillment, just as the World-Honored One has taught regarding the matters of the *prajñāpāramitā*."
Having thus praised the Buddha, the woman scattered upon him golden and silver flowers, as well as flowers from both water and land, necklaces worn upon her body, and golden cotton cloths.
Above his head, it transformed into a four-pillared precious canopy pavilion; its solemnity and purity were thus unprecedented.
This woman said:
"I dedicate these merits to all sentient beings, so that we may all together resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the woman's intention, smiled.

According to the dharmas of all Buddhas, rays of light of various colors issued from his mouth, illuminating the countless Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions; they circled his body three times and then re-entered through the crown of his head.
Then Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha:
"For what reason does the Buddha smile?
I pray that you will tell me the meaning of your smile."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This Elder Tiāodi, Constantly Exerting, shall in a future age become a Buddha, named Suvarṇapuṣpa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Having completed the female body and received a male form, he shall later be born in the Buddha-land of Sukhāvatī, where he will cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
In whichever land this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is born, he shall always possess the name Suvarṇapuṣpa.
Throughout his entire life in that land, he traveled extensively through various realms, passing from one Buddha to another, never being separated from the Buddhas. Ānanda,
it is like a wheel-turning sage king who travels from one palace to another, from birth until the end of his life, his feet never touching the ground.
The Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa was also like this; from his attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* until the very end, he never failed to see a Buddha.
At that time, Ānanda thought to himself:
"When this Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa later becomes a Buddha, the bodhisattvas currently gathered here will constitute the assembly for that Buddha."
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in Ānanda’s mind, addressed him, saying: “It is so, it is so!

You should know that the assembly of bodhisattvas at that time was an assembly of Buddhas; those bhikṣu-saṃghas were so numerous as to be incalculable, beyond thousands, tens of thousands, millions, or billions, and were without limit.”

Ānanda! When this Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa becomes a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, all the various evils and unwholesome matters within his buddha-field shall be entirely non-existent; it will be no different from the pure and wondrous buddha-field of the Prajñāpāramitā as previously described.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
From the time of which Buddha has this younger brother planted the roots of merit?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This younger brother first conceived the noble aspiration in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara; he also scattered golden flowers over the Buddha Dīpaṃkara."
When scattering those flowers before that Buddha, my mind also made this vow:
"By means of these merits, may I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
It was just as when I scattered five flowers upon the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, that Buddha, knowing that my merits were complete, conferred upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
When the Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa saw me receive this prediction, he immediately made a vow, saying:
"I, too, shall receive a prediction, just as this Bodhisattva has received his prediction."
“Ānanda! This Bodhisattva Suvarṇapuṣpa first conceived the aspiration for enlightenment under Dīpaṃkara.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This woman has prepared herself for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"So it is, so it is! This younger brother shall thereby accomplish *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the supreme perfect enlightenment.
