61. Chapter on Questions Concerning Characteristics, Practice, and Vows, the Sixty-first Chapter of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, how does he practice the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of signlessness, and the samādhi of wishlessness?
How should he enter them?
How should one practice?
How should one practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment?
How should one maintain mindfulness?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he contemplates the five aggregates as empty, and likewise contemplates the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm as empty.”
One should contemplate in this manner with an undisturbed mind, seeing nothing among all phenomena.
Since there is nothing seen, one does not realize anything regarding all phenomena. Why is this?
Because they have skillfully studied the dharma of emptiness,
when they reach the point of realization, they neither sever any dharmas nor do they fixate upon any dharmas;
that which is realized is not seen as a realization, nor is it seen as a dharma.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, how is it that,
as the Buddha has taught, a bodhisattva does not realize the realization within empty dharmas?”
"How can one dwell in emptiness and yet further realize it?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"One contemplates emptiness as complete and without deficiency, nor does one think: "
"To say, 'I shall receive realization,' is itself not realization.
The Dharma of a bodhisattva, that which is to be practiced and performed, does not take realization as its goal, but takes practice as its goal."

The bodhisattva likewise does not fixate the mind, nor does he bind the mind to anything; while not diminishing in regard to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, he also does not realize the attainment of the exhaustion of outflows.
Why is this? Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are fully endowed with profound and wondrous dharmas. Why is this?
When a bodhisattva has already established themselves in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, they should have this realization, saying:
"This is the time for practice; it is not the time for realization.
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they should perform this contemplation, saying:
"Now is precisely the time to practice the five pāramitās; it is not the time for realization.
Now is precisely the time to practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; it is not the time for realization."

Now is precisely the time to practice the three samādhis, to practice the ten powers, the four immeasurables, and great kindness and great compassion; this is the time to practice sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), not the time for the realization of the paths of the srotāpanna, arhat, or pratyekabuddha.
"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they practice the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness by means of the three samādhis;
they practice the factors of enlightenment—the faculties, powers, and bases of mindfulness—by means of the thirty-seven auxiliaries, yet they do not realize them as a final attainment."
By means of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, he performs his practices, yet he does not accept the realization of a śrāvaka.

Subhūti, it is as if there were a man who was handsome, brave, and robust, skilled in the art of war; he firmly donned armor and held weapons, was fully equipped, thoroughly understood all matters, and was proficient in all sixty-four arts.

There was no one among the multitude who did not love and revere him; whatever tasks he undertook were invariably accomplished. Seeing the crowd attending upon him with such respect, his joy redoubled.

Even when he had business that required him to travel to a place fraught with calamities, perils, and dangers, where many harbored enmity and resentment—and even if those enemies were themselves fierce and the parents and children of his retinue were all struck with terror—he remained undaunted.
At that time, the courageous one brought peace to his parents and comforted his followers, saying:
"Do not be afraid; I possess skillful means and lack nothing, so I shall surely deliver myself from these various calamities."
Having thus escaped the peril and subdued the enemies without causing them harm, he reached a place of safety; his parents and their entire retinue were all filled with joy.
"Why is this? It is because this man is courageous, valiant, and fierce, fully endowed with all arts and lacking nothing.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“By means of the four immeasurable minds—compassion, pity, joy, and equanimity—a bodhisattva fulfills the six perfections for the sake of sentient beings. Although they have not yet attained the exhaustion of outflows, they open the great path to *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge). Abiding in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they do not take these as a basis for realization; thus they fulfill the state of not falling into the stages of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha.”
For example, when various birds fly through the air, they neither fall to the ground nor do they remain in the sky.

In the same way, the Bodhisattva practices the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness without realizing [nirvāṇa] therein; having transcended the stages of the Arhat and Pratyekabuddha, he shall fully possess the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique dharmas, and the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñatā), never taking realization until the very end.

Subhūti! It is as if there were a man, robust, brave, and of great strength, skilled in the art of archery. He shoots an arrow upward into the air and immediately follows it with subsequent arrows, shooting each one at the preceding one, so that the arrows support one another and none of them falls to the ground.
If he intends to cause him to fall and stops the subsequent arrow, ceasing to shoot any more,
only then will he fall. Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, being sustained by upāyakauśalya (skillful means), he plants all merits and fulfills the root of all wholesome qualities.
If even a single factor is lacking, one will never realize the fruit midway.
Only when one has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and *abhisaṃbuddhi*, with all merits fully perfected, does one then realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
"Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should fully complete these aforementioned dharmas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For a bodhisattva to train in this is a most difficult and arduous task.

To train in this way is to train in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), to train in suchness (*tathatā*), to train in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), to train in original emptiness, to train in self-emptiness, and to train in the three doors of liberation.”
To study in this manner without becoming weary along the way—O World-Honored One!
How great! How truly marvelous and extraordinary!
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Why is this?
Because a bodhisattva possesses a vow and aspiration, and does not abandon any sentient being."
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva possesses the intention not to abandon sentient beings, they shall deliver all sentient beings.
To give rise to the three gates of liberation within the dharma that is without beginning or end—know this to be *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means).
A bodhisattva must ultimately attain the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñājñāna) and shall never realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) midway. Furthermore, Subhūti,

when a bodhisattva wishes to observe and know the spheres of all profound dharmas— namely, internal emptiness, external emptiness, and the emptiness of existence and non-existence, as well as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the three gates of liberation— he should form this thought:
"All sentient beings, throughout the long night, constantly harbor the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a life-span, and the notion of a perceiving subject;
whatever they think or do, it all relies upon these notions."

Therefore, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva perceives that sentient beings possess such conceptualizations, he desires to eliminate these thoughts for their sake; having attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he preaches the Dharma for them, practicing the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Although they perform these practices, they never midway take the realization of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha.
Subhūti! Because this bodhisattva possesses such a vow and because their merit is fully complete, they likewise do not take realization midway.

They do not lose the four dhyānas, nor do they lose the four immeasurables and the four formless attainments; they do not lose the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three gates of liberation, the four fearlessnesses, and the four unhindered wisdoms; they do not lose the ten powers and the eighteen unique qualities. Thus, they become fully endowed with all dharmas and never lose their pursuit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

All bodhisattvas who are sustained by upāyakauśalya are fully endowed with merit; their wholesome dharmas increase further, and their faculties become so sharp and penetrating that they surpass those of arhats and pratyekabuddhas.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva constantly keeps in mind that sentient beings practice the four perversions: the notion of permanence, the notion of purity, the notion of pleasure, and the notion of self."

"For the sake of such beings as these, I shall practice the Way; when I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I shall preach the Dharma for them—preaching impermanence, and preaching impurity, suffering, and non-self."

When a bodhisattva is thus fully endowed with such mental conduct, this constitutes the practice of *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) while practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*. They shall then fully possess the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣyā dharmāḥ*), and the wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*). Only thereafter shall they sit in the Buddha-samādhi at the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and realize the fruit of awakening.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"All sentient beings are constantly possessed of attachments; they are always attached to a self, attached to a life-span, attached to the five aggregates, attached to the six sense-bases, attached to the eighteen elements, attached to the four dhyānas, attached to the four formless attainments, and attached to the four immeasurables."
"When I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I shall cause all sentient beings to be free from this disease of attachment.

Holding this intention, he practices the *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*); until he has fully perfected the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*), the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom (*catasraḥ pratisamvidah*), and the wishless samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*), he will never realize the fruit midway;
only when these vows are fulfilled does he then realize it.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he further reflects in his mind:

'Sentient beings, throughout the long night, are constantly attached to perceptions and mental formations, or to conceptualizations— such as the notions of male and female, or of form and formlessness.'"
"I shall practice diligently so that when I attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, my sentient beings will be free from the disease of conceptual attachment.

With this thought fully established, he practices the *prajñāpāramitā* through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*); yet, as long as the ten powers (*daśabala*) are not yet perfected, and the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*) and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) are not yet complete, he will never take realization.
Only when all merits have been accomplished and the signless samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*) is perfected will he then take realization.

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, the emptiness of the internal, the emptiness of the external, and the emptiness of existence and non-existence, and fully accomplishes the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha—this is their practice; they do not practice in common with the three realms.
Subhūti! When a bodhisattva practices these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, having practiced these thirty-seven factors, one should ask:
"How does a bodhisattva desire to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"

One does not take emptiness as a realization; rather, by awakening to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), one attains the paths of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha. Furthermore, one does not realize the signless (animitta), nor the wishless (apraṇihita), nor cessation (nirodha), nor that which is produced, nor that which arises, nor non-existence, while remaining mindful of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
"Subhūti! If there is a bodhisattva who asks other bodhisattvas:
'If one hears the teaching of emptiness, one should then contemplate emptiness; if one hears the signless and the wishless, one should then contemplate the signless and the wishless;'"
If one hears of non-action, one should contemplate non-action;
if one hears of non-arising and non-existence, one should contemplate non-arising and non-existence.

One should simply practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment through emptiness (*śūnyatā*); one should not practice signlessness (*animitta*), nor wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), nor non-action, nor non-arising.
"Subhūti! You should know that this bodhisattva has not yet received a prediction; he has not yet received a prediction from the Buddhas. Why is this?"

An avaivartika bodhisattva likewise does not form such thoughts, does not engage in such conduct, does not utter such speech, and does not form such perceptions; rather, they perform only the deeds of an avaivartika bodhisattva, contemplate only these matters, and practice, speak, and perceive only these matters.
“Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva has already transcended all stages; he is like one on the stage of an avaivartika, for he has transcended the stage of an avaivartika.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Does this bodhisattva attain the state of *avaivartika*?
The Buddha said:
“If there are bodhisattvas who hear of the six pāramitās or do not hear them, their practice and conduct are like those of an avaivartika bodhisattva.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“There are many people who practice the Buddha-way, but few who act as an avaivartika bodhisattva does.”
Why is this? Because there are few bodhisattvas who receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of the stage of irreversible wisdom (*avaivartika-jñāna-bhūmi*).
Those who receive the prediction of an irreversible bodhisattva have already distanced themselves from all aforementioned attachments to conceptualizations and incomplete matters.
“Such a bodhisattva mahāsattva cannot be surpassed by any among the devas or the people of the world.
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“In a dream, a bodhisattva does not draw near to the stages of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha; nor does he draw near to the three realms, nor does he destroy the three realms. He does not give rise to such thoughts, but views all dharmas as being like a dream, like an echo, like an illusion, like a mirage, and like a transformation. Thus viewing all dharmas as transformations, he does not realize [nirvana] therein.”
Subhūti! These are the marks of an irreversible bodhisattva mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti!
In a dream, the bodhisattva sees the Buddha surrounded by several hundreds of thousands of incalculable members of the fourfold assembly as he preaches the Dharma.

Upon hearing the Dharma from the Buddha, the bodhisattva immediately understands its inner meaning; his actions are never apart from the Dharma, and what he speaks does not deviate from the principles of the Dharma.
Subhūti! You should know that these are the marks of an avaivartika bodhisattva. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

In a dream, the bodhisattva sees a Buddha-Tathāgata leaping up into the void, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, manifesting supernatural transformations and preaching the Dharma to a community of bhikṣus; through these transformations, he causes people to go to other buddha-fields to perform buddha-works.
Subhūti! These are the marks of an avaivartika. Furthermore, Subhūti!

If, in a dream, a bodhisattva sees military uprisings in commanderies and counties with mutual slaughter, or encounters fires, or witnesses tigers, wolves, lions, venomous insects, and other terrifying things that cause anxiety, grief, and suffering; or if they see famine, or the loss of parents, brothers, relatives, friends, and teachers.
Having seen this in a dream, he felt neither fear nor dread.
Upon waking from the dream, he reflected and said:
"All that exists within the three realms is merely like a dream."
"I shall apply myself with diligence; having attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, I shall preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings in the three realms.
Subhūti, this is the mark of an avaivartika [non-retrogressive] bodhisattva.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Subhūti,
how should all people know that this bodhisattva has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
If a bodhisattva sees those undergoing various hardships within the three evil realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals, they should make this vow:
"When I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, may there be no three evil realms in my land."
Why is this? Because all that exists within a dream and all dharmas are such that not a single dharma possesses duality.
You should know that this is the mark of an avaivartika.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! Suppose a bodhisattva sees in a dream the fires of hell burning and boiling sentient beings; having awakened, he reflects:

'The forms and their calamitous transformations that I saw in my dream—if, while dreaming, I have seen for myself the marks of an avaivartika [non-retrogressive] bodhisattva, I shall then make this vow:'"
"As I see it, the fires within the hells shall immediately be extinguished.
If the fire is extinguished and the boiling water becomes cool, you should know that this bodhisattva has received the prediction of enlightenment and shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is the mark of an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) bodhisattva.

If these flames burn one house after another, one village after another, or if they burn some houses but not others, or burn some villages but not others, and if there are those among them who are burned by the fire, one should know that this is caused by the severance of the Dharma by the householders being burned; it is entirely the remaining retribution for their severing of the Dharma.
"From this time forward, the remaining karmic consequences of his violation of the Dharma are completely exhausted; this is the extinction of sin and the arising of merit.
This is the mark of an Avaivartika.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Now I shall explain the marks, signs, and conduct of an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) bodhisattva.
Suppose there is a man or woman possessed by a ghost or spirit, and this bodhisattva then thinks:

'If the past Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas have truly bestowed upon me the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), and if my practiced vows and conduct are pure and stainless—such that I should not fall into the stages of an Arhat or Pratyekabuddha, nor harbor any thoughts of being an Arhat or Pratyekabuddha, but shall attain *anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*—then neither shall I attain it, nor shall I not attain it.'"

If all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently residing in the ten directions—who know all things, see all things, and awaken to all things—should know that I shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then these ghosts and spirits shall depart.
“If these spirits and deities do not depart, you should know that this bodhisattva has not received their prediction from the Buddhas of the past. Subhūti!

If, after this bodhisattva has preached the sūtra for them, the spirits and deities immediately depart, you should know that this bodhisattva has already received their prediction from the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas.”
Subhūti! Being fully endowed with these marks, features, and modes of conduct constitutes the mark of an avaivartika. Furthermore, Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās but lacks upāyakauśalya (skillful means), has not yet practiced the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the three gates of liberation, has not yet attained the rank of a bodhisattva, has not yet reached the state of a bodhisattva samādhi, and has not received a prediction of enlightenment from the Buddhas of the past—[he does not know this].
This bodhisattva goes to where that man or woman is and says again:
"If I have truly received the prediction that I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then this ghost or spirit should depart."
When the spirits and deities did not depart, and this bodhisattva continued to preach the Dharma without ceasing,
Māra Pāpīyas went to that place and thought to himself:
"I shall cause these spirits and deities to leave."
"Why is this? Pāpīyān possesses majestic spiritual power that surpasses that of these spirits.
Thereupon, Pāpīyān commanded the spirits to depart.
This bodhisattva does not know that it was Māra who caused the spirits and deities to depart; instead, he joyfully says, "The spirits and deities have departed because of me.
He then becomes conceited and looks down upon others, saying to them:
"I have already received the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddhas of the past, whereas these others have not yet received it.
Because he treats others with such arrogance and contempt, he departs from *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) and fails to attain the wisdom of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha;
because of this arrogance, he loses *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) and falls into the two stages [of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha].
Regarding the stages of the Arhat and Pratyekabuddha:
because of their sincere vows, demonic activities arise, causing them to distance themselves from true spiritual friends and fall into the net of Māra.
Why is this? Because they do not practice the six pāramitās and do not maintain upāyakauśalya (skillful means).
Subhūti, you should know that such a bodhisattva is creating demonic works for themselves.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva who has not yet practiced the six pāramitās, has not yet attained upāyakauśalya, and has not yet reached the stage of a bodhisattva.”
Due to the machinations of Māra, Pāpīyān again came to where the Bodhisattva was, assuming a different appearance and dress, and said to the Bodhisattva:
"Good son! The Tathāgata has already bestowed upon you the prediction that you shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Your father’s name is so-and-so; your mother’s name is so-and-so; your brothers, sisters, and elder siblings’ names are so-and-so; your friends, acquaintances, and kinsmen’ names are so-and-so; your ancestors for seven generations back have names such as so-and-so; and you were born in such-and-such a village in such-and-such a district of such-and-such a country.
If he sees that the Bodhisattva’s physical conduct is harmonious and gentle, Māra says to him according to his appearance: "In your previous lives, you were likewise soft and pliant.
If he sees that the Bodhisattva’s talent is brilliant, or that he practices the twelve dharmas of a śramaṇa, or that his speech is measured, Māra follows his outward form and says to the Bodhisattva:
"In your previous lives, you possessed all these practices; in your previous lives, you also practiced these twelve dharmas."
When that bodhisattva heard the Māra speak of past events and further observed his own past conduct, he became even more arrogant and looked down upon his fellow students.
The Māra spoke again:
"The Tathāgatas of the past have already bestowed upon you the prediction of enlightenment; as for the merit you have cultivated, it shall never be reversed."
Pāpīyān may appear in the form of a bhikṣu, or as one's father or mother, or in the form of a gṛhapati, and come to say:
"You shall certainly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Why is this? It is because you are fully endowed with all the marks and practices of an *avaivartika* [non-retrogressive] bodhisattva.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Subhūti.

"Regarding the characteristics, marks, and conduct of an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) bodhisattva that I have described, if that bodhisattva does not attain such marks, you should know that this bodhisattva is being incited by Māra; having heard this name, they become arrogant and self-satisfied, treating their fellow students with contempt, mocking others, and no longer regarding them with respect."
Because of using pride and arrogance, this constitutes the work of Māra. "Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva should recognize the work of Māra regarding the conditions for Māra."
Why is this? Because this bodhisattva does not practice the six pāramitās, he does not know the suchness of demonic deeds, nor does he know the suchness of the five aggregates.

Since that bodhisattva has failed to perceive demonic deeds, upon hearing the aforementioned bhikṣu’s prediction of his own enlightenment, and now further hearing the name of that prediction, joy arises in his mind, and he thinks to himself:
"By these signs, I shall certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Thinking thus, he becomes even more arrogant, treats others with contempt, and calls them ignorant.

This bodhisattva lacks the marks of an avaivartika; they have distanced themselves from the *prajñāpāramitā* and *upāyakauśalya*, lost the wisdom of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and having abandoned true spiritual friends, they have instead acquired evil associates. It should be known that such a bodhisattva will ultimately not achieve success and will fall into the stage of the two paths.

If, after a long time has passed and one has undergone further intense sufferings in birth and death over an immense distance, one should then again encounter a true spiritual friend and hear the Prajñāpāramitā; only then will one repent for the attachment to the literal words previously received. Because of this repentance, one shall attain the state of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha.
For example, Subhūti, if a bhikṣu violates the four grave prohibitions, he cannot achieve the four paths in this present life. Yet, Subhūti,
the transgression of that bodhisattva is even heavier than those four prohibitions, because he has accepted a name and become attached to arrogance.
Setting aside this matter of transgression,
Subhūti, whoever commits such arrogance as to accept titles or accept false names, their sin exceeds that of the five heinous crimes. Subhūti!
If there is one who grasps at names, words, or conceptual signs, they must urgently guard against the awakening of Māra’s subtle causes and conditions.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra Pāpīyān may again go to where a bodhisattva resides and praise the practice of seclusion, extolling its merits: "
"What you have practiced is exactly as the Buddha has praised it. Subhūti!

It is not as I have described regarding the dharma of a bodhisattva’s seclusion; if one dwells alone in mountain valleys, under trees, or in solitary, uninhabited places, that is not necessarily the dharma of seclusion.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What is meant by the bodhisattva’s distinct form of seclusion?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Bodhisattvas remain detached, being tranquil regarding thoughts of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and tranquil regarding thoughts of dwelling alone in mountain retreats or beneath trees. Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva acts in this way, it constitutes the dharma of great seclusion.
A bodhisattva should practice in this manner day and night; this is what is meant by a bodhisattva’s tranquil seclusion.
If one is among human beings and follows my teaching of tranquility, even though they dwell near a city, it is no different from being in the mountains or marshes.

If, however, one accepts the teachings of Māra and stops practicing seclusion, they will fall to the level of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha; such a person does not accord with the Prajñāpāramitā and fails to fulfill the requirements for Sarvajña (omniscience).
Those who harbor such thoughts and practices do not possess the pure Dharma.
Intermingling the intentions of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, they instead mock and treat with contempt those among humans who practice purity.
The practitioner among humans does not intermingle with the intentions of arhats or pratyekabuddhas, yet instead treats them with contempt.
Likewise, they treat with contempt those who have attained dhyāna, vimokṣa, and samādhi, as well as those who have attained supernatural powers (abhijñā).

If a bodhisattva lacks *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), even if they dwell for hundreds, thousands, or tens of millions of years in a remote wilderness beyond the reach of beasts, birds, ghosts, spirits, or thieves, and despite remaining there for so long,
because they do not know the dharma of the bodhisattva’s detachment, it will ultimately be of no benefit.

Those who practice seclusion under the instruction of Pāpīyān do not delight in the seclusion taught by me; they are likewise unable to fulfill the dharma of seclusion, nor do they abide within the dharma of seclusion.
Why is this? Because departing is far removed from the dharma of detachment.
As soon as he had departed and become distant from that dharma of detachment, Māra Pāpīyas stood in the sky and exclaimed:
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
This is what has been taught by the Buddha; this is the true Dharma of detachment.”
"You practice this method of seclusion; you shall quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Having received such praise, that bodhisattva who practices false seclusion becomes joyful and arrogant, treating those who truly practice seclusion with contempt. He instead slanders them, saying, "This is merely a state of confusion," claiming it is impure, chaotic, and a state of mental distraction.
Those who are impure they instead call pure; those who are not worthy of respect they instead revere, while those who are worthy of respect they instead treat with contempt. Why is this?
"I am seen, encouraged, and honored by gods, humans, and non-humans; what I practice is truly the practice to be followed.
You, however, dwell on the outskirts of the city—who would come to honor and praise you?"
This person, before good sons and good daughters living near the city who seek the bodhisattva path, speaks with arrogance, saying:
"The devas came and told me the number of days and years when I shall attain the Way."
“Subhūti! You should know that these arrogant bodhisattvas are like caṇḍālas or śvapacas—those who, in the language of Jin, are executioners or jailers.

Such persons constitute a great affliction among bodhisattvas; they are those who rely on the semblance of the Dharma while appearing to be bodhisattvas. They are great thieves among gods and humans, and they are likewise great thieves within the semblance-dharma of the śramaṇas. Furthermore, they are great thieves among good sons and good daughters.”
One should not engage in business with such persons, nor should one sit, rise, speak, eat, or drink in their company. Why is this?
Because such people are arrogant, stubborn, and perverse.

If there are bodhisattvas who do not wish to abandon *sarvajñatā*, who do not wish to abandon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, who desire to adorn themselves with the practice of seeking *abhisambodhi*, and who wish to rescue all sentient beings, they should keep far away from such persons as these.
One should not engage in affairs with them, but should cultivate one's own conduct and refrain from associating with them.

One should always maintain a sense of detachment toward the world and not accept the pleasures of the three realms. One should always extend compassion to all sentient beings and give rise to great pity for those people who hold such inverted views, thinking to oneself:
"May I never have such unrighteous matters in life after life; if such thoughts should arise, may they be swiftly extinguished."
"Subhūti! You should know that these bodhisattvas have themselves given rise to supernormal powers. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
"If there is a bodhisattva who, with utmost sincerity and diligent application, seeks anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should associate with true spiritual friends.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What constitutes a true spiritual friend for a bodhisattva?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are the true spiritual friends of bodhisattvas; the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas themselves are also true spiritual friends of bodhisattvas; and the assembly of disciples is likewise a true spiritual friend.
You should know that these are the true spiritual friends of a bodhisattva.”
A true spiritual friend is one who constantly explains the Prajñāpāramitā to the bodhisattva and analyzes its matters for them.

The six pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, suchness, the limit of reality, and the dharma-nature—these are the true spiritual friends of a bodhisattva.

The six pāramitās are the world-transcending sūtra; the six pāramitās are the path; the six pāramitās are the great illumination; the six pāramitās are the great torch; the six pāramitās are the light of great wisdom; the six pāramitās are protection; the six pāramitās are the refuge; the six pāramitās are the father and the mother; the six pāramitās are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; the six pāramitās are omniscience (sarvajñatā); the six pāramitās eliminate all habitual tendencies of human beings.
Why is this? Subhūti,
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the mothers of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the ten directions.
Why is this? Because all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present are born from within the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva who wishes to achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, purify a buddha-field, and transform sentient beings, should gather in sentient beings by means of four ways of benefiting them:
first, giving; second, kind words; third, beneficial action; and fourth, consistency in purpose.
By means of these four kinds of kindness, one benefits sentient beings.
Subhūti, it is because I contemplate this meaning that I speak of these matters.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the parents of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they are their home, they are their protection, and they are their lamp of light.

Subhūti! A bodhisattva who does not wish to abide according to the teachings of others, who wishes to sever the doubts of all sentient beings, and who wishes to purify buddha-fields and transform sentient beings, should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
"Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā extensively expounds the conduct of bodhisattvas; it is that which all bodhisattvas ought to study.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said, “The perfection of wisdom has the characteristic of space; it is neither a characteristic nor does it produce characteristics.”
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
is there any causal condition by which the characteristics of the prajñāpāramitā can be known?”
"Do you understand all dharmas by means of this mark? The Buddha said, "It is so, Subhūti!"
If one wishes to know the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā*, it is like the characteristic of all dharmas. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are quiescent, and because all dharmas are eternally pure.
"For this reason, Subhūti, the characteristic of the *prajñāpāramitā* is the characteristic of all dharmas, because they are empty and quiescent.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are quiescent and all dharmas are empty, how can one know that there is attachment to or the severance of dharmas?
The emptiness and quiescence of dharmas neither involve severance nor attachment, nor do they constitute the attainment of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
Within emptiness and stillness there is no dharma, nor within emptiness and stillness can one find anyone who attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
World-Honored One,
how should we understand this meaning?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Sentient beings have been attached to the notions of ‘self’ and ‘mine’ for a long night. Subhūti said:
"Yes, World-Honored One! For a long night,
sentient beings have been attached to the notion of self and what belongs to the self."
The Buddha asked:
"Do you understand that the self is empty and quiescent? Subhūti replied:
“Yes, World-Honored One! “Subhūti!
"Do you know that it is because of the notion of 'self' that sentient beings have long remained in birth and death? Subhūti replied, "It is so."
“World-Honored One!
Because sentient beings are attached to a self, they undergo further toil and suffering while remaining in the world; thus one knows that there is attachment. “Subhūti!”
There is no "I" and no self; there is no experiencer. One does not remain long in the world, nor does one undergo suffering for long; one neither clings nor is there cessation.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,

a bodhisattva who practices in this manner does not practice within the five aggregates, nor does he practice within the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, nor does he practice within the four unhindered wisdoms.”
Why is this? Because he does not perceive any dharma that can be practiced, nor does he perceive any dharma that ought to be practiced.
When a bodhisattva practices in this manner, no devas or worldly beings are able to shake him or subdue him, and neither arhats nor pratyekabuddhas are able to equal him.
For what reason?
Because there is nothing that can reach the place where it dwells,
World-Honored One!
The Bodhisattva who practices *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) and abides therein has no equal;
such a Bodhisattva swiftly approaches *sarvajñatā*.
The Buddha said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Suppose all the sentient beings in Jambudvīpa were to attain the human realm and all were to become [practitioners] of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

If there are good sons or good daughters who serve and make offerings to them for the duration of their entire lives, and take the merit of these offerings and dedicate it toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Would the merit of these good sons and good daughters be great? Subhūti replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"Very much, very much.
The Buddha said:

"It is not equal to a son of good family or a daughter of good family who upholds the Prajñāpāramitā and teaches it to others, explaining it in its entirety and elucidating the wisdom within it, with a mind that never departs from the thought of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge)."

Suppose all sentient beings throughout the three thousandfold world system were to become human beings, and some son or daughter of good family were to instruct them all in the practice of the ten wholesome paths of action, establishing them in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments; furthermore, establishing them in the stages of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, and anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and dedicating these merits toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Would the merit of these good sons and good daughters be great? Subhūti replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"Very much, very much.
The Buddha said:

"It is not equal to when a son or daughter of good family upholds the Prajñāpāramitā and proclaims it to others, explaining it fully and elucidating the wisdom within it, with a mind that does not depart from the thought of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge); such a person stands beyond the ranks of the worthy and the noble."
Why is this? Excluding the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, there shall be only these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Why is this?
Because these sons and daughters of good family practice the perfection of wisdom with the practice of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).

As they practice the perfection of wisdom, seeing all sentient beings heading toward the realm of death, they give rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); through this practice, they obtain great protection that is not associated with conceptualization, and they obtain great joy, fully endowed with the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).
Subhūti! This is the illumination of the great wisdom of a bodhisattva.
That which is the illumination of great wisdom is precisely the illumination of the six pāramitās.

Although these good men and good women have not yet attained the Way, they act as saviors for all sentient beings; they do not regress from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Because they practice the Prajñāpāramitā, they will surely repay the merit of the faithful offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and all manner of rare treasures received from sentient beings, and they will swiftly draw near to Sarvajña (omniscience).

Subhūti! If one does not wish to receive the gifts of others through delusion and falsehood; if one wishes to show the path to sentient beings; if one wishes to understand non-existence; if one wishes to deliver those within the prison; if one wishes to grant eyes to all sentient beings—then the conduct of one’s body should accord with the *prajñāpāramitā*, and whatever one speaks should also accord with the intent of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

For one who practices the Prajñāpāramitā, no other external influences shall find an opportunity; they should employ skillful means to contemplate the Prajñāpāramitā day and night without interruption.
Subhūti! It is as if,
for example, a man who had previously obtained a maṇi jewel were to obtain it again and leap for joy with great exultation,
only to lose it once more.

Having lost this jewel, he was filled with great sorrow and anxiety; he constantly thought of that maṇi-jewel, never forgetting it whether sitting or rising, not being parted from it for even a moment, and thought to himself:
"How have I suddenly lost this great treasure?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva who has set aside the thought of omniscience (sarvajñatā) is like that person who has lost a great treasure; whether sitting or rising, they do not forget it for even a moment.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it, World-Honored One,
that all thoughts have no place of rest, being entirely empty and entirely quiescent?"

How is it that a bodhisattva does not depart from the thought of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), yet a bodhisattva cannot be apprehended through departure, nor through the thought, nor through omniscience?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

"If there are bodhisattvas who know that all dharmas are by nature detached, that the dharma-nature is eternally abiding, and that the path-dharmas, suchness, and the limit of reality are eternally abiding;
that these are not made by a Buddha, nor can they be made by arhats or pratyekabuddhas."
Having realized this, the bodhisattva never again departs from the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Why is this? Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is empty and quiescent; it neither increases nor decreases.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the *prajñāpāramitā* is itself empty and quiescent, how can a bodhisattva, being equal to the *prajñāpāramitā*, achieve *anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*?”
The Buddha said:
“A bodhisattva is neither equal to the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor does he increase or decrease; the *bhūtakoṭi* neither increases nor decreases, and the *dharmatā* neither increases nor decreases.”
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is neither one nor two.

If, upon hearing this, a bodhisattva is not terrified, does not find it difficult, and is not afraid, you should know that this bodhisattva already dwells on the stage of *avaivartika* and practices the Prajñāpāramitā.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How is it, World-Honored One?
Is one practicing the perfection of wisdom by contemplating the emptiness of the perfection of wisdom, or by contemplating that the perfection of wisdom is non-existent?”
The Buddha said, “No. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One,
is there anyone who, apart from the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*, practices the *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha said:
"No, World-Honored One," Subhūti said.
"World-Honored One!"
“Does one who practices the perfection of wisdom practice the perfection of wisdom? The Buddha said, “No.”
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
can emptiness practice emptiness?”
The Buddha said, "No. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One,
do the five aggregates practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said:
"No, World-Honored One," Subhūti said.
"World-Honored One!"
"Do the practices of the six pāramitās practice the prajñāpāramitā? The Buddha said, "No."
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
does one practice the perfection of wisdom even to the extent of the four kinds of unimpeded wisdom?”
The Buddha said, “No. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
Are the emptiness of the five aggregates, suchness, the nature of things, the dharma-nature, and the emptiness of the four unhindered wisdoms practicing the prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said, "No. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
Do these dharmas not practice the prajñāpāramitā?
If these dharmas do not practice it, how does a bodhisattva practice the prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said, "What do you think, Subhūti? Do you perceive any dharma that practices the prajñāpāramitā? Subhūti replied:
“I do not see them,
World-Honored One!
Is there any bodhisattva who can be seen as one who practices the prajñāpāramitā?”
Subhūti said: “I do not see them, World-Honored One!”
“What do you think, Subhūti? Is that dharma which you do not perceive obtainable?
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha asked,
"Does a dharma that cannot be apprehended undergo arising and ceasing? [He replied,] "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Just as a bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) is such, so too is the prediction of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).”

If a bodhisattva trains by receiving and practicing these dharmas—the four fearlessnesses and the four unhindered wisdoms of the Tathāgata—they shall never depart from the wisdom of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the wisdom of sarvajñatā, and the wisdom of the Mahāyāna.

Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), it remains without depletion until the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
is the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* bestowed upon bodhisattvas from within the non-arising of all dharmas?"
The Buddha said, “No. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
Are the bodhisattvas granted their predictions of enlightenment from within the dharmas that have arisen?
The Buddha said:
"No," Subhūti replied,
"a bodhisattva does not receive the prediction of enlightenment from dharmas that have no source of arising, nor does one receive the prediction of enlightenment from dharmas that do arise."
"In this way, how does one bestow the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the bodhisattvas?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Do you see any dharma that receives the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!

I do not perceive any dharma that receives a prediction; I do not perceive the attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor do I perceive one who shall attain it, nor do I perceive one who has already attained it.”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Subhūti!"
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva finds nothing to be apprehended among all dharmas.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva does not even think:
"There is an *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Nor does he think: "I shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?

When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not engage in any conceptual differentiation regarding all phenomena, because the perfection of wisdom itself is also without conceptual differentiation.
Chapter Sixty-three: Śakra-devānām-indra. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā, Chapter Sixty-three, “Śakra-devānām-indra. At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep and subtle; it is difficult to comprehend, difficult to understand, difficult to explain, and difficult to know, for it is inconceivable due to its primordial purity.

Those who hear this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, copy it, uphold it, and study it, have already come forth fully endowed with great merit; thoughts of attachment no longer arise, and they remain free from conceptual attachment even until they reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra: "So it is, so it is! Kauśika!"
Those who practice the Prajñāpāramitā do not come from minor merits.
Kauśika, suppose all the sentient beings filling Jambudvīpa were to practice the ten wholesome paths, the four immeasurables, the four dhyānas, and the four formless attainments.

It is not equal to this: when a son of good family or a daughter of good family writes down, upholds, recites, studies, and dwells according to the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, remaining until they reach *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without allowing other thoughts to arise.
"His merit shall be a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred millionfold, and even ten billionfold;
it cannot be compared by means of any analogy. At that time, a certain bhikṣu said to Śakra Devānām Indra: "Kauśika!..."

If these good sons and good daughters maintain and uphold the practice of the Prajñāpāramitā and further teach it to others, their merit will surpass that produced by all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to those bhikṣus:

"Good sons and good daughters, a single thought-moment generated within the Prajñāpāramitā surpasses the ten wholesome deeds, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the five supernormal powers performed throughout Jambudvīpa;
how much more so for those who practice, transcribe, maintain, and recite it according to its teachings—they all transcend the gods, the asuras, and the people of the world."
This bodhisattva not only surpasses all devas and worldly humans, but also surpasses the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha.
Not only does he surpass those mentioned above, but he even surpasses bodhisattvas who practice the five pāramitās without the *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) of the prajñāpāramitā.
A bodhisattva who dwells according to the teachings of the prajñāpāramitā transcends all devas and worldlings; none among the devas or worldlings can equal him.

One who abides according to the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā dwells on the ground that ensures the lineage of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is not severed; they never depart from the name of Tathāgata or the practice of a bodhisattva, and thus they ultimately do not lose the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

The practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is thus: desiring to pull out sentient beings who are submerged in the long-flowing stream, one who trains in this manner trains in what is to be learned by a bodhisattva; they do not train in the learning of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
When a bodhisattva trains in this way, the Four Great Kings shall come to that bodhisattva and say:

"Good son, good daughter, you who train with diligence and swift application shall soon achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. When you sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), we shall present to you, before long, the four alms-bowls formerly held by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, which are now located here."
When one practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, all the Śakras, Indras, will likewise come to encourage and assist these good sons and good daughters;

the Suyāma devas, leading the Suyāma devas, will descend; the Tuṣita devas, leading the Tuṣita devas, will descend; all the Nirmāṇarati devas will descend; all the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas will also descend; and even all the devas of the Akaniṣṭha heaven will descend to the place where this bodhisattva who practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* resides.
The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently residing in the ten directions all constantly keep in mind those sons and daughters of good family who practice the Prajñāpāramitā.
For one who practices this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all the calamities, hardships, and labors that exist in the world will no longer exist at all. Subhūti!
This is the reward for the merit of one who practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in the present life.
Throughout all worlds there are four ailments; when even a single thing is disturbed, none of the faculties within the body fail to experience pain.
Because they experience pain, their minds become afflicted.
However, these various ailments and afflictions no longer attach themselves to the body of this bodhisattva, because he practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*;
this is the retribution for his merit in the present life.
At that time, Ānanda thought to himself:
"Is Śakra Devānām Indra speaking this by his own eloquence,
or is he speaking it as a Buddha-act?"
Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing the thoughts in Ānanda’s mind, said to Ānanda:
"Everything I have spoken is the work of the Buddha.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Whatever Śakra Devānām-Indra may speak is entirely the causal basis for the Buddha's work.
When a bodhisattva trains in and recollects the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Māras within the trichiliocosm all give rise to doubt:
'Will this bodhisattva now realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and take up the path of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha?'"
"Will they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the unexcelled perfect enlightenment? "Ānanda!
If there are bodhisattvas who do not depart from the *prajñāpāramitā*, Māra will again be filled with great sorrow and distress."

At that time, Māra again raised a great wind, wishing to cause this bodhisattva to be terrified and give rise to the thought of indolence due to the arising of difficulties; he wished to cause the bodhisattva to give rise to a single distracted thought within his mindfulness of *samyaksambodhi*.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Does Māra trouble and disturb all bodhisattvas without exception?"
"Are there those who are not disturbed?
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"There are those who practice distraction, and there are those who do not."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Who is it that is afflicted?
Who is it that is not afflicted?"
The Buddha said:
"When a bodhisattva first hears the Prajñāpāramitā, if their mind finds no joy or understanding therein, Pāpīyān will then go to disturb and confuse them."
If, when hearing the profound Prajñāpāramitā being taught, doubt arises in their minds such that they say:
"Is this truly existent? Or is it non-existent?"
For this reason, Pāpīyān goes to harass them.

Furthermore, Ānanda, if there is a bodhisattva who distances himself from true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), he will neither hear nor know the Prajñāpāramitā; failing to understand its meaning and purpose, he will find no joy in it, and for this reason, Pāpīyān again goes to harass and disturb him.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
If there is a bodhisattva who distances himself from the prajñāpāramitā and instead upholds what is not the Dharma, for this reason Māra gains an opportunity."
"Furthermore, Ānanda! If a bodhisattva loses the prajñāpāramitā and instead praises what is not the Dharma,
Māra will immediately rejoice and think to himself:"

"He speaks of unrighteous matters; he shall have a certain number of followers who will fulfill my wishes, and furthermore, cause others to fall into the two stages—namely, those of the Arhat and the Pratyekabuddha."
"Furthermore, Ānanda! If there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, thinks to himself:
'Is this profound [teaching] not truly profound?'"
When one forms such a thought, Māra immediately thinks to himself:
"I have now found an opening through my son. Furthermore, Ānanda!
If there is a bodhisattva who speaks with arrogance toward others, saying:
"I am able to practice the six pāramitās, whereas you cannot," this bodhisattva provides an opportunity for Māra to gain an advantage.
"Ānanda! At that time, Māra Pāpīyān was filled with great joy and leaped for delight. Furthermore, Ānanda!"

If there is a bodhisattva who relies on his own wisdom, relies on his own lineage, relies on his own goodness, and relies on his own spiritual friends, he then gives rise to arrogance and looks down upon others. He lacks the marks, conduct, and appearance of an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) bodhisattva; being solely arrogant and disparaging others, he says to them:
"You do not even appear to be within the lineage of bodhisattvas, nor do you abide in the Mahāyāna."
At that time, Pāpīyān thought with joy:
"Now my realm and palaces are no longer empty; the three evil destinies have increased, and my lineage has not been diminished."

Māra constantly watches for such bodhisattvas, wishing to cause them to speak what is not the Dharma, wishing that all people hear what is not the Dharma, and further desiring to increase their wrong views, defilements, and weariness, leading them to create perverted practices and become inverted regarding the Dharma, with errors in body, speech, and mind, greedily attached to false blessings.
Due to these causes and conditions, the three evil realms increase, and the palaces of Māra’s retinue become more numerous.
At that time, Pāpīyān is doubly joyful and exultant, indulging himself in pleasure.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
If one who practices the bodhisattva path disputes with those of the śrāvaka vehicle, Māra then thinks to himself: "
"This good man is far removed from *samyaksambodhi* (perfect enlightenment) and does not draw near to great wisdom. Why is this so?
Strife, contention, and resentment are not the path to *samyaksambodhi*; they are the karma of these three evils.
"Furthermore, Ānanda! When bodhisattvas and bodhisattvas quarrel with one another, Pāpīyān thinks to himself:
'Both have distanced themselves from the Buddha and lost their way toward sarvajñatā; these two bodhisattvas shall both fail to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
"Why is this so? Because these three evil karmas were committed by this son of good family; they do not pertain to omniscience (sarvajñatā). Furthermore, Ānanda!"

Those who have not yet received a prediction will contend with bodhisattvas who have attained the prediction; by giving rise to malicious intent, for as many moments as that intention arises, they shall be set back by that same number of kalpas.

Even if they give rise to thoughts of contention, as long as they do not abandon *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) as before, they shall eliminate a certain number of kalpas and various pathways, and only thereafter will they achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When those kalpas have passed, will there be any cessation [of suffering] during that interval?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“I teach the Dharma for the sake of the three vehicles; according to the extent of their respective inclinations, each fulfills their task to the end, without any intermediate reduction or omission.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If bodhisattvas quarrel with one another, or if they harbor anger, revile each other, or maintain resentment without repentance, I do not say that there is purification for them; they must practice *saṃnāha* (armor-like diligence) for further kalpas before they finally achieve it."
If there is a bodhisattva who, having engaged in conflict and become angry, then repents and says:

"This benefit is difficult to obtain; I shall now humble myself for the sake of all beings, and in this life and in future lives, I shall cause all sentient beings to live in harmony and reconciliation."
"How can I now add evil words to others and dwell on their faults?
I shall never again dare to do such a thing; I shall be like a deaf sheep, removing my own transgressions, and attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi to deliver all sentient beings."
"How can one give rise to anger and thereby sink into ruin?
One should not harbor resentment, nor should one allow oneself to sink into ruin.
At that moment, as soon as the Bodhisattva had formed this thought, Māra Pāpīyān was unable to find an opportunity.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
A practitioner of the bodhisattva path should not dwell together with those of the śrāvaka family; if they do dwell together, they should not engage in disputes with them. Why is this? "
One should reflect to oneself:
"I ought not to give rise to anger or engage in contention with such people; I shall instead accomplish anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and deliver all beings from suffering and distress."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When bodhisattvas dwell together with one another as bodhisattvas, what is their method?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Regarding the rule for Bodhisattvas dwelling together with other Bodhisattvas, they should regard one another as they would the World-Honored One when dwelling together. Why is this? Because—”
One should form this thought:
"This is my true companion; we ride upon the same boat.
He trains as I train; he is my fellow student, and together we practice the *dānapāramitā* until reaching *sarvākārajñatā*."
If his mind is distracted and does not accord with *samyaksambodhi*, it is not appropriate for me [to remain].
If his mind is concentrated and does not depart from *samyaksambodhi*, I likewise should be so.
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this manner, they train in equality.
Chapter Sixty-Four: Inquiry into Training in Equality, from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“What is that which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should equally study?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Internal emptiness and external emptiness are what Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should equally study.”
The five aggregates are empty by nature, and so on up to the Path— the Path itself is also empty by nature. Subhūti,
this emptiness is the very equality of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
"In this way, by equalizing emptiness, one achieves *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti said,
"World-Honored One!"
Does a bodhisattva train in the realization of *sarvajñatā* by training in the elimination of the five aggregates?
Does he train in the realization of *sarvajñatā* by training in the non-defilement of the five aggregates?
Does he train in the realization of *sarvajñatā* by training in the cessation of the five aggregates?
“Is the non-arising of the five aggregates training for *samyaksambodhi*?
Is even training in the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) training for *samyaksambodhi*?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“As it has been said: ‘To train in the dissolution of the five aggregates is to train in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); even to train in non-arising is to train in omniscience.
The Buddha said:
‘What do you think, Subhūti? Is the suchness (*tathatā*) of the five aggregates, the suchness of all things, the suchness of the Path, and the suchness of the World-Honored One [identical]?’”
"Regarding these suchnesses, is there any time when they decrease,
exhaust, or cease? Subhūti replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“When a bodhisattva trains in this way, they are training in suchness; they are training in omniscience.”
Suchness is neither exhausted, nor diminished, nor extinguished.
To train in this way is to train in Suchness; it is to train in omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

When a bodhisattva trains in this manner, they are training in the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), training in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), training in the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), and training in omniscience.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“When a bodhisattva trains in this way, he trains for the sake of transcending all other trainings; it is the foremost training.
One who trains in this manner cannot be defeated or corrupted by the devas or Māra.”
Training in this way, one swiftly approaches *avaivartika* (non-retrogression).
One who trains in this way practices the noble task; one who trains in this way practices as a Tathāgata;
one who trains in this way guides and governs sentient beings.

One who trains in this manner does so for the sake of purifying the Buddha-field, for the sake of training in great loving-kindness and great compassion, and for the sake of training in the transformation and guidance of sentient beings. Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva trains in this way, they train in turning the twelvefold wheel of Dharma in its three aspects to deliver and liberate sentient beings.
One who trains in this way trains to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed.
One who trains in this way trains to open the Dharma-gate of the Deathless (amṛta).
Training in this way, one trains to demonstrate the unconditioned dharma (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
Subhūti! Inferior persons are unable to study this.
Those who study in this way do so because they desire to uproot the root of birth and death for all sentient beings.
One who trains in this way will not enter the three evil destinies, will not be born in a borderland, and will not be born into the family of a caṇḍāla.
One who trains in this way will no longer suffer from deafness, blindness, muteness, or lameness.

One who trains in this manner will have all faculties complete and never deficient; they will be free from harsh sounds, refrain from committing the ten unwholesome deeds, and never train in heterodoxy for the sake of making a living. They will not be devoid of gratitude, nor will they associate with evil persons.
Subhūti! One who trains in this manner does not take birth in the long-lived heavens because of their *upāyakauśalya*.
What is meant by *upāyakauśalya*?

The skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, as well as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, do not involve calculating after those meditative states.
One who trains in this manner purifies the power of all dharmas, and purifies the powers of the arhats and pratyekabuddhas.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since the nature of all dharmas is inherently pure, how can a bodhisattva wish to purify all dharmas?”
The Buddha told Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!
The bodhisattva has already purified the very basis of their nature.”
To study the Prajñāpāramitā without weariness or indolence is what constitutes studying the Prajñāpāramitā.

This Dharma is not something that can be studied, known, or perceived by ordinary, foolish people; rather, for the sake of sentient beings, the Bodhisattva practices the Dānapāramitā up to the attainment of Sarvākārajñatā (all-knowledge).
When a bodhisattva studies suchness, this constitutes studying the ten powers and studying the power of the fearlessnesses.
One who studies in this manner transcends all that is done by sentient beings.
Subhūti! It is as if the earth produces gold, silver, and various rare treasures, yet these emerge only from a few places.
In the same way, Subhūti!
Few people study the Prajñāpāramitā; many give rise to the aspiration for the state of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha.
Few people are able to practice the merit of a Cakravartin king; many more practice the deeds of minor kings who rule over small territories.
"Subhūti, only a few sentient beings are able to enter into *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge); many more enter the path of the arhat or the pratyekabuddha.
Subhūti, although many people aspire to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, those who achieve it are but few; most remain at the stage of the arhat or the pratyekabuddha."
Subhūti! Although many people practice the bodhisattva path and study the prajñāpāramitā, those who reach the stage of *avaivartika* are but very few indeed.
For this reason, Subhūti,
those who wish to dwell firmly in the stage of *avaivartika* should study the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Furthermore, Subhūti:
When a bodhisattva studies the *prajñāpāramitā*, the mind of envy does not arise, nor does the mind of transgression against the precepts arise.
The mind of anger does not arise, nor does the mind of distraction arise.

The mind of indolence does not arise, the mind of ignorance does not arise, the minds of the three poisons do not arise, the mind of doubt does not arise, and the mind of the five aggregates does not arise, even up to the mind of the [arhat] path not arising.
Why is this? Subhūti!
When this bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not perceive any dharma that arises; regarding dharmas that are non-arising, they neither obtain nor give rise to anything.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva studies and maintains the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they are maintaining all the *pāramitās* in their entirety. Why is this?
Because when a bodhisattva studies the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all the other *pāramitās* follow along with it.
For example, just as those who cling to a self grasp all sixty-two views,
so too, when a bodhisattva studies the prajñāpāramitā, all the other pāramitās follow along with it.
Subhūti, it is like when a person is about to die: the vital winds depart first, and all the sense faculties are extinguished.
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, all the *pāramitās* enter therein.
A bodhisattva who wishes to transcend all other pāramitās should study the profound Prajñāpāramitā.
One who studies the profound Prajñāpāramitā is the most honored and supreme among those who study.
“Subhūti! Are the sentient beings within this trichiliocosm many? Subhūti replied:
“World-Honored One!
The sentient beings of a single Jambudvīpa are already numerous; how much more so are all the sentient beings within the trichiliocosm?
The Buddha said:
"May all these sentient beings fully enter the Path and all attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
If there are Bodhisattvas who, one by one, provide them with clothing, food, drink, and all that they require for their livelihood, throughout the entirety of their lifespans."
"Would that merit not be great? Subhūti replied,
"It would be very great, indeed very great."
The Buddha said:
"It is not equal to the way these sons and daughters of good family bring the *prajñāpāramitā* to mind with right mindfulness. Why is this? Because..."
This profound prajñāpāramitā is the great benefit for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it enables bodhisattvas to achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Subhūti! If a bodhisattva wishes to stand above all sentient beings; if all sentient beings have no refuge and no one to rely upon, and he wishes to receive them as his refuge and act as their reliance; if he wishes to be a guiding light for the blind; if he wishes to seek to become a Buddha; if he wishes to attain the realm of a Buddha; if he wishes to perform the strides of a Buddha; if he wishes to produce the lion’s roar of a Buddha; if he wishes to strike the bells and drums of a Buddha; if he wishes to sound the great conch shell; if he wishes to expound the meaning of the Buddha-dharma at the assembly of a Buddha and resolve the various doubts of the multitude—if he desires to attain all these things, he should study the profound *prajñāpāramitā*.
“World-Honored One, for a bodhisattva who practices the perfection of wisdom, there is no merit of any wholesome deed within the triple world that cannot be attained. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!”
“Would a bodhisattva further obtain the merit of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha?
The Buddha said,
“He would indeed obtain the merit of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha, yet he does not realize it therein.”
By observing with wisdom, one immediately transcends the wisdom of the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas; not dwelling therein, one ascends to the stage of a Bodhisattva.
A Bodhisattva who trains in this manner is not far from *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) and will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva who trains in this way becomes a source of blessing and protection for the devas and asuras.
One who practices in this manner surpasses all arhats and pratyekabuddhas and swiftly approaches sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
Subhūti! One who trains in this manner will not long practice the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor will they ever depart from the *prajñāpāramitā*.

When a bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, you should know that this is a dharma that does not diminish; it is not distant from *samyaksaṃbodhi*, and one swiftly approaches the wisdom of the three vehicles.
If a bodhisattva, on the contrary, should further think:
"This prajñāpāramitā does not lead to sarvajñatā," one who forms such a thought is not practicing the prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, if one does not know this or that profound *prajñāpāramitā*, nor perceives the *prajñāpāramitā*, nor knows for whom the *prajñāpāramitā* is, nor knows who shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within the *prajñāpāramitā*.
If one further forms this thought:

"The Prajñāpāramitā is neither that nor this, nor does anything emerge from within it; the dharma-nature is eternally abiding—the Suchness and the Reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) remain eternally abiding whether a Buddha exists or not."
"When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva trains in this manner, he is training in the Prajñāpāramitā.
*The Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 14;
*The Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll 15.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mokṣala of Khotan during the Western Jin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Sixty-Five: Approaching. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Sixty-Five: Approaching. At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra thought to himself:

“If even a bodhisattva practicing the six pāramitās up to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha already surpasses all sentient beings, how much more so one who has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”

If there are those who give rise to the thought of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), they have attained the most supreme among lifespans and the greatest benefit among humans; how much more so for those who give rise to the thought of seeking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
"Those who have resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, those who have not yet so resolved, should draw near to them.
Śakra Devānām-Indra then scattered heavenly *mandārava* flowers over the Buddha. Having scattered them, he made this vow:

"We have already crossed over; we shall further cross over those who have not yet crossed.

"I have already entered nirvāṇa; I shall further deliver others so that they may attain nirvāṇa.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Noble sons and noble daughters who rejoice on behalf of bodhisattvas who have first resolved to attain awakening—how much merit do they obtain?

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva who is in his final birth before buddhahood rejoices on their behalf, how much merit will they obtain?
The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying:
“Kauśika! This four-continent world system may still be weighed to know its weight in *jin* and *liang*;”
The merit of one who rejoices on their behalf is beyond measure.

Kauśika! As for the waters of the oceans within the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system, if one were to take a single hair, split it into a hundred parts, and use each part to draw out drops of seawater, one might still be able to count how many drops there are;

however, the merit from this successive joy—wherein thirty-five characters have been repeated here—is such that its blessings cannot be measured, according to the transcription based on the Danben (Dan-zang) edition.
Kauśika! Even if one were to measure the space within the realms of incalculable buddha-fields using measures such as bushels, pecks, pints, and gills, one might still be able to know its extent;
yet the merit from rejoicing in [the Buddha's] successive generations is beyond all calculation.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Those who do not rejoice in bodhisattvas who have first resolved to attain enlightenment are those sent by Māra."
Those who do not rejoice in [the bodhicitta] on behalf of others are the followers of Māra, coming from among the ranks of Māra.
Why is this? Because those who do rejoice upon generating the resolve for awakening do so for the purpose of destroying Māra.

Without abandoning the various desires, yet revering the Triple Gem, and being neither of a single characteristic nor of two, one should maintain this mind of sympathetic joy and seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said, “It is so,

Why is this? By upholding these merits, one will swiftly draw near to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having attained abhisambodhi, immeasurable, ineffable, and asaṃkhyeya sentient beings shall all be delivered.
For this reason, Kauśika!

Those sons and daughters of good family who have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment should, by means of upholding the merit of sympathetic joy, seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; they should seek it neither with the mind nor apart from the mind.

On behalf of those who have attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) and those who are in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), he rejoices in seeking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; yet he does not seek it with a conceptual mind, nor is he separated from that mind.
Subhūti said: "This mind is like an illusion; how can it attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said:
“What do you think, Subhūti? Do you perceive this mind as being like an illusion? Subhūti replied, “I do not.”
“World-Honored One!
I do not perceive that which is like an illusion, nor do I perceive that the mind is not an illusion.
The Buddha said:
"Furthermore, do you see this mind as being non-dharmic?
