Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they neither approach anything nor are attached to anything."
“World-Honored One!
When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, is it thus that they dwell nowhere?
The Buddha said:
"In this way, a bodhisattva who practices the perfection of wisdom in such a manner does not dwell in the five aggregates, nor does he dwell in sarvajñatā (all-knowledge)."
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does it not abide?
The Buddha said:
"Because there is nothing to enter, one does not abide. Why is this?
Because one does not perceive any dharma that abides or enters."
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, there is nothing to enter and thus they should have no abiding place.
When a bodhisattva abides in this way and practices in this way, they are practicing the perfection of wisdom; they are abiding in the perfection of wisdom.
If anyone should say,
"I practice the prajñāpāramitā; I contemplate the prajñāpāramitā," they are then far removed from the prajñāpāramitā.
One who has already distanced themselves from the Prajñāpāramitā has, in fact, distanced themselves from the five pāramitās, and has distanced themselves from sarvajñatā (all-knowledge). Why is this?
The Prajñāpāramitā has no place of entry, nor is there anyone who can enter the Prajñāpāramitā.
Why is this? Because there is no form that can serve as a point of entry.
If a bodhisattva has a cognition regarding the perfection of wisdom, they have already fallen.
One who has fallen regarding the perfection of wisdom has already fallen regarding all dharmas.
If one further thinks:
"The *prajñāpāramitā* upholds the five *pāramitās* and also causes the *sarvajñatā* to be upheld," then one has once again fallen away;
one is not practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* and cannot achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If, moreover, they should give rise to the thought:
"In this Prajñāpāramitā, I shall receive the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," then they have already fallen away.
Those who fall away from the *prajñāpāramitā* do not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, if one should think:
"I shall, by means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, practice the five *pāramitās* and practice great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*)."
"Then one again falls into error; those who fall cannot fulfill the five pāramitās, nor can they achieve great compassion.
If, however, one further reflects:
'Just as all Tathāgatas, regarding all dharmas, have no grasping and no activity, yet naturally attain awakening and thereby teach and transform sentient beings.'"
"Then one would again fall into error. Why is this?
The Tathāgata has nothing among all dharmas that he has attained or awakened to; therefore, he does not abide in dharmas, let alone any dharma that could be attained or awakened to."
"That is not so. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How should a bodhisattva practice the prajñāpāramitā so that there are no such flaws or gaps?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should reflect:
‘These dharmas are non-existent.’”
"In the state where nothing exists, dharmas are neither grasped nor realized.
One who practices in this manner is practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
If one wishes to enter the dharma of non-existence, one is then separated from the Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?
Because the Prajñāpāramitā has nothing into which to enter, nor is there anyone who enters.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
If the prajñāpāramitā is not separate from the prajñāpāramitā, and the dānapāramitā is not separate from the dānapāramitā, and so on up to the case where sarvajñatā is not separate from sarvajñatā;”
"If they are not separated, how can one enter the *prajñāpāramitā*,
and even up to the *sarvajñatā*, how can there be an entry?
The Buddha said:
"When a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they neither enter into the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), nor do they disparage the five aggregates, nor do they reject the five aggregates;
this applies even unto *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), which is likewise."
Nor does one say:
"The five aggregates are permanent or impermanent, suffering or happiness, self or non-self, empty or quiescent.
This applies even unto *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), which is likewise so.
Whether it be permanence or impermanence, suffering or pleasure, self or emptiness and stillness—these dharmas neither enter into that which has form nor enter into that which is formless. Subhūti!

When a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās and practices sarvajñatā, it is like when a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin) sets out and his fourfold army all follows him; likewise, the five pāramitās all follow the prajñāpāramitā until they reach and abide in sarvajñatā.

"Just as a skilled charioteer driving a team of four horses does not lose the track, so too does the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) drive the five perfections (pañca-pāramitā) straight toward omniscience (sarvajñatā).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is this bodhisattva path?"
"What, then, is not the Way?
The Buddha replied, "The paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not the path of the bodhisattva; omniscience (sarvajñatā) is the path of the bodhisattva."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Prajñāpāramitā is that which gives rise to the great enterprise for all bodhisattvas; it is capable of discerning what is the Path and what is not the Path.”
The Buddha said:

“As Subhūti has spoken, the Prajñāpāramitā arises for the sake of incalculable, asaṃkhyeya sentient beings; although it praises the performance of deeds, it neither accepts the five aggregates nor accepts the two stages.”
The Prajñāpāramitā is the charioteer of sentient beings; it guides sentient beings to reach sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), yet it does not act as a charioteer for the two [lower] stages.
Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā gives rise to nothing and extinguishes nothing among all dharmas, because the nature of dharmas is equal.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the Prajñāpāramitā neither gives rise to any dharmas nor extinguishes any dharmas, how does a bodhisattva practice the six pāramitās?”
The Buddha said:

"One should contemplate the six pāramitās by means of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), and, taking these merits, share them with all sentient beings for the sake of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment)."

When a bodhisattva maintains these merits while seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they then fulfill the mindfulness of the six pāramitās; the loving-kindness practiced by such a bodhisattva is itself sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).
If a bodhisattva were to abandon the six pāramitās, they would be abandoning omniscience (sarvajñatā).
For this reason, a bodhisattva who wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should study the six pāramitās; by fulfilling all virtuous merits, they will then reach omniscience.
"Therefore, a bodhisattva should practice the six pāramitās.
"World-Honored One,
how does a bodhisattva train in the six pāramitās?"
The Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva should contemplate in this way: the five aggregates are neither practiced nor not practiced; and so it is even for up to sarvajñā (all-knowledge)."
A bodhisattva should practice in this way regarding the six pāramitās. Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva does not practice abiding in the five aggregates, nor does he practice abiding even in sarvajñatā.
Why is this? Because the five aggregates and sarvajñatā have no place of abiding.
A bodhisattva who wishes to realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should practice non-abiding.

Subhūti! It is like a man who, desiring sweet fruit, plants a fruit tree; he buries the roots deep and irrigates them at the proper times, causing them to become moist and the sprouts to emerge. Then, with branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit, he is able to eat from it.

A bodhisattva who wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should study the six pāramitās, and by means of these six pāramitās, they should gather in sentient beings and deliver them across [to liberation].

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva who wishes to walk alone through the triple world, who wishes to purify a buddha-field, who wishes to sit at the site of enlightenment, and who wishes to turn the wheel of Dharma, should train in the six perfections.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
should one study the Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha said:
"It is so; you should train thus.
The Buddha said:
"If you wish to attain mastery over all phenomena, you should study the Prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?
Because the Prajñāpāramitā walks alone among all phenomena."
The Prajñāpāramitā is the face of all dharmas.
It is, for example, like the great ocean being the face of the ten thousand rivers and four currents.
Those who wish to study sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should study the six pāramitās and should study sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
It is like a skilled archer who, grasping his bow and arrows, has no fear of enemies.
When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they do not fear Māra or the devas of Māra.
Therefore, a bodhisattva who wishes to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should study the prajñāpāramitā.
“Those who practice the perfection of wisdom are all held in the mindfulness of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“How is it that a bodhisattva practicing the six pāramitās is remembered by all the Buddhas?
The Buddha said:
“They do not remember them because of the existence of the six pāramitās, nor do they remember them because of the existence of sarvajñatā.”
One who dwells in this manner is remembered by all Buddhas.
Furthermore, Subhūti, they do not remember [him] on account of the five aggregates, nor do they remember [him] on account of anything up to and including *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
That which a bodhisattva studies is exceedingly vast, yet it is as if there is nothing to study.”
The Buddha said: "It is so;
there is much that is studied, yet there is nothing that is studied.
Why is this? Because..."
"There is no dharma to be found that a bodhisattva should study. Subhūti said:
"World-Honored One!"
Whatever amount of Dharma is taught, the bodhisattva should receive and practice it all.

A bodhisattva who wishes to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should receive and practice the matters of the six *pāramitās*, whether they be many or few; they should uphold them firmly and constantly contemplate them so that the mind does not waver.
“A Bodhisattva should fully study all six perfections; they should also fully study and understand all dharmas, whether they be many or few.
Subhūti said, “World-Honored One!”
"How should one know the extent and limit of all dharmas?
The Buddha said:

"The suchness of the five aggregates and the suchness of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge)—by knowing the suchness of the five aggregates and sarvajñatā, one thereby knows the extent and limit of all dharmas."
“World-Honored One!
How can one know that the suchness of the five aggregates is the suchness of *sarvajñatā*?
It is neither known to arise, nor known to cease, nor known to diminish; it is eternally abiding and unchanging.”
The Buddha said:
"By contemplating the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), one comes to know the measure of all phenomena.
[He asked: "World-Honored One!"
"What is meant by contemplating the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)?
The Buddha said:
"The limit of reality is not a limit."
When a bodhisattva trains in the non-limit (akoṭi), they come to know the measure of all phenomena.
By knowing the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they come to know the measure of all phenomena.
Knowing that the nature of form and the nature of phenomena are without interruption, they come to know the measure of all phenomena.
Subhūti said: "World-Honored One,
how does one know the measure of all dharmas?"
The Buddha said:
"All phenomena are neither coupled nor uncoupled.
[He asked: "World-Honored One!"
"What dharmas are neither conjoined nor non-conjoined?
The Buddha said:
"The five aggregates are neither conjoined nor non-conjoined; even so, the nature of the conditioned and the nature of the unconditioned are neither conjoined nor non-conjoined."
Why is this so? Because these dharmas have no form that can be said to be joined, nor any that is not joined. Why is this?
"All things are without possession; they neither conjoin nor disperse.
One should understand all phenomena in this way. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the tenth stage, Bodhisattvas should all train in this manner; by means of calculation and deliberation, they shall subsequently know the quantity of all dharmas.”
This is the entrance of Bodhisattvas with sharp faculties, not the entrance of those with dull faculties, nor of those of intermediate faculties, nor of those who are few or many.

Those who wish to train in and enter this [path] are not those who are indolent, nor those who harbor expectations; it is the entrance of those who are diligent, those of powerful discernment, and those who are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) and have attained *sarvajñatā*. Upon receiving the instructions of the six *pāramitās*, they immediately enter *sarvajñatā*.
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, if demonic activities arise, they are able to recognize them and extinguish them.
Those who wish to attain *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) should study the perfection of wisdom.
When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, whether recollecting it or entering into it, all the Buddhas of the ten directions in the present keep this bodhisattva in mind.
All Buddhas of the past, future, and present are born from within the prajñāpāramitā.
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should form this thought:
"The Dharma attained by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, I too shall attain.
A bodhisattva who practices the perfection of wisdom should train in this manner.
One who practices in this manner will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should not be separated from the mindfulness of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).
Suppose all sentient beings within the great trichiliocosm were taught to practice the six *pāramitās*, and were all led to attain the stage of *srotāpanna*, up to *arhat*, and even *pratyekabuddha*.
It is not equal to this Bodhisattva practicing the Prajñāpāramitā for even as long as a finger-snap. Why is this?
Because the five pāramitās, the stage of Srotāpanna, the Arhat, and the path of the Pratyekabuddha are all born from within it.
All the Buddhas of the past, future, and present are likewise born therein.
Suppose there were as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in one *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*; one were to instruct them all to practice giving, up to the stage of *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*.

It is not equal to a bodhisattva’s mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā* in accordance with *sarvajñatā*; that mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā* in accordance with *sarvajñatā*, maintained for one day up to a hundred days, or even for a hundred kalpas.
Why is this? Because all Tathāgatas emerge from within it, establishing the teaching of *dāna* as well as the teachings of the *arhats* and *pratyekabuddhas*.

If there is a bodhisattva who abides according to the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā*, one should know that this is a bodhisattva of the *avaivartika* stage whom the Tathāgata keeps in mind; one should know that this bodhisattva has already practiced the six *pāramitās*, has already attained *upāyakauśalya*, has already served various Buddhas, has already obtained true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), has already attained the fulfillment of the eighteen kinds of emptiness, has already perfected the four unhindered wisdoms (*pratisaṃvid*), and has already attained the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Having already dwelled in the pure conduct of a youth and fulfilled all vows, it should be known that this bodhisattva is never apart from the Buddhas, never apart from various wholesome merits, and never apart from the Buddha-fields; having attained dhāraṇī, they do not lose their eloquence, possess all faculties complete, and have achieved the prediction of enlightenment.
One should know that for such a bodhisattva, the three realms and the eight difficult conditions are forever severed.

One should know that this bodhisattva skillfully enters into all matters and skillfully enters into the meaning of the signless; they are skilled both in speech and in silence, skilled in much speaking and skilled in a single word; they are skilled in instructing men and skilled in instructing women; they are skilled in the five aggregates and skilled in nirvāṇa, and skilled in the characteristics of dharmas.

He is skilled in the nature of the conditioned and the unconditioned; skilled in existence and non-existence; skilled in this and that; skilled in conjunction and dispersion, and skilled in neither conjunction nor dispersion; he is likewise skilled in suchness, skilled in pure dharmas, and skilled in that which has conditions and that which is without conditions.

He is skilled in the five aggregates, skilled in the six sense-bases, and skilled in the eighteen elements; he is skilled in the four noble truths and skilled in the twelve links of dependent origination. He is also skilled in dhyāna, skilled in the four dhyānas, and skilled in the four formless attainments; he is skilled in the six pāramitās, skilled in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and skilled in sarvajñatā (all-knowledge).

He is skilled in the conditioned and the unconditioned; he is skilled in having a body and skilled in being bodiless; he is skilled in mindfulness of the five aggregates up to and including omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and skilled in that mindfulness; he is skilled in the self-emptiness of the five aggregates up to and including the Path, and skilled in the emptiness of the Path; he is skilled in the emptiness of believing in the Path and skilled in the emptiness of not believing in the Path; he is skilled in arising and ceasing; he is skilled in abiding in a single concentration without further change; he is skilled in lust, anger, and delusion, and skilled in the absence of lust, anger, and delusion; and he is skilled in right view.
He is skilled in wrong view, skilled in false view, skilled in non-false view, and skilled in all views; he is skilled in name-and-form, skilled in what is done, and skilled in reverent service.
He is also skilled in signs; he is skilled in suffering, skilled in its origin, skilled in its cessation, and skilled in the path;
he is skilled in the hells, skilled in the realm of hungry ghosts, and skilled in the animal realm—skilled in the three evil destinies;
he is also skilled in humans and skilled in the human destiny, and skilled in...

It is skillful regarding the heavenly realms; it is also skillful regarding the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, skillful regarding the path of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, skillful regarding omniscience (sarvajñatā), and skillful regarding the path of omniscience (sarvajñatāmārga);
it is skillful regarding the powers (bala) and skillful regarding the possession of powers; it is skillful regarding sudden knowledge and skillful regarding subtle knowledge.
He is skilled in the knowledge of revulsion, skilled in great wisdom, and skilled in boundless and bottomless wisdom;
he is skilled in the insight of the three periods of time—past, future, and present—and likewise skilled in expedient means.
He is skilled in observing sentient beings, skilled in meaning, and skilled in interpretation; he is skilled in severing the three evil destinies.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This is the bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom, recollecting the perfection of wisdom, and entering into the virtues of the perfection of wisdom."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does one practice the perfection of wisdom?”
"What is mindfulness?
How does one enter?
The Buddha said:

"You should know that the five aggregates are both permanent and impermanent, both solid and not solid, both real and not real; you should understand them in this way—this is practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*."
"Entering the Prajñāpāramitā should be like entering the contemplation of emptiness;
one should form this thought: 'All that exists is non-existent. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
For how long must a bodhisattva study the *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha said:

“From the first production of the thought of enlightenment until sitting at the site of awakening, a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should act in this way, contemplate in this way, and enter into this way.”
Subhūti said: "World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva contemplates the prajñāpāramitā, should they do so with a single thought?"
The Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva should always maintain single-minded, focused mindfulness of the prajñāpāramitā, not allowing other thoughts to find an opportunity within their mind."
When practicing the perfection of wisdom, one should enter it in this way and contemplate it in this way, never departing from the mindfulness of *samyaksambodhi*.
One should contemplate the perfection of wisdom according to the Dharma as it is, remaining in accordance with that intention without ever departing from it.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
does one attain *sarvajñatā* by upholding, practicing, recollecting, and entering into the *prajñāpāramitā*?”
The Buddha said, “No. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by maintaining this non-recollection, does one attain *sarvajñatā*?
The Buddha said:
"No, indeed. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Having maintained mindfulness and then not being mindful, can one attain *samyaksambodhi*? The Buddha said, “No.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is it by neither thinking nor not thinking that one attains *samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
The Buddha said, “No. Subhūti said:
"How should one attain *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge)?
The Buddha said, "As it truly is (*tathatā*)."
“What is suchness? The Buddha said, “It is like the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).”
“What is it like the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)?
The Buddha said:
“It is like the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), like the nature of sentient beings (sattvatā), like the nature of life-span (āyustā), and like the nature of vitality (jīvitatā).”
“World-Honored One!
How is it that they are like the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), like the nature of sentient beings, and like the nature of life-span?
The Buddha said:
“What do you think, Subhūti? Can a self, a life-span, or a sentient being be apprehended?
Subhūti replied, “World-Honored One, [they cannot].”
"It cannot be apprehended.
The Buddha said:
"The self, the life-span, and sentient beings cannot be apprehended; how then can there be that which is called 'sentient beings'?"
A bodhisattva should understand this: one does not enter the *prajñāpāramitā* by means of names, nor does one attain *samyaksambodhi* by entering into all dharmas by means of names.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
Should these six pāramitās not be regarded by way of their names?”
The Buddha said:
“The six pāramitās and all dharmas are none of them [defined by] conditioned or unconditioned dharmas, nor by the dharmas of the three vehicles. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
If all dharmas cannot be named and have no names, how can they be said to have names?
How can there be the five destinies of birth and death, as well as the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, and samyaksaṃbuddha?”
The Buddha said, “What do you think, Subhūti? Can the designation ‘sentient beings’ be perceived as having a location?
[Subhūti replied,] “World-Honored One!”
"It cannot be seen.
The Buddha said,
"If even the dwelling place of sentient beings cannot be found, how much less can there be the dharmas of the five destinies or the three vehicles?"
“A bodhisattva who practices the perfection of wisdom should train in non-abiding; this is called the non-abiding of all dharmas.
Subhūti said, “World-Honored One!”
"As the World-Honored One has taught, should one not train in the five aggregates?
Should one not even train in the *sarvajñatā*?
The Buddha said:
"One should study the five aggregates, and one should also study omniscience (*sarvajñatā*);
yet, though one studies, there is no place of abiding.
"How is it that one studies while having no place of abiding?"
The Buddha said:
"To study the five aggregates and *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) is likewise neither to give rise to anything nor to extinguish anything.
He asked again:
“How should one train in that which is neither produced nor extinguished?
The Buddha said:
“One should train in the non-existence of all conditioned activities.”
“How should one train in the non-existence of what is done?
The Buddha said:
“To contemplate phenomena as being like the mark of non-existence when one contemplates oneself—this is training in the non-existence of what is done.”
“How does one contemplate for oneself the mark of non-existence?

The Buddha said: “It is like contemplating the emptiness of the five aggregates; like contemplating the emptiness of the six sense bases; like contemplating the emptiness of the internal and external; like contemplating the emptiness of existence and non-existence; like contemplating the emptiness of dhyāna; like contemplating the emptiness of the dhyānas of cessation and liberation; like contemplating the emptiness of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; and like contemplating the emptiness of the Path.”
"Subhūti! When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they should contemplate in this way: they should contemplate that the dharmas of their own marks are empty.
Subhūti said, "World-Honored One!"
"If the five aggregates are empty, and even the Path is empty, how should a bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said:
"When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, it is a practice of non-attainment."
"What is the practice that is not established?
The Buddha said:

"Because the *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be perceived, the bodhisattva cannot be perceived, the practice cannot be perceived, there is no one who practices, there is no one who will practice, and there is no one who has already practiced."
All these are unattainable; this is the practice of non-attainment of the bodhisattva’s prajñāpāramitā. Why is this?
Because all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) cannot be perceived.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One, if a bodhisattva practices in this manner, they do not accomplish the practice; how then should one who has newly resolved their mind practice the *prajñāpāramitā*?”
The Buddha said:
“From the moment a bodhisattva first resolves upon enlightenment, they should not rely on any dharma.
In practicing the six pāramitās, they should in all cases remain without reliance, and even up to the attainment of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), they should maintain mindfulness of non-reliance.”
“What is reliance? What is non-reliance?
The Buddha said:
"The second is dependence; the first is non-dependence. "What is the second? What is the first?"
The Buddha said:
"The eye and forms constitute a duality; the six sense bases and the recollection of dharmas constitute a duality; the path and the Buddha constitute a duality—these are dualities."
“World-Honored One, how is it that from that which has dependence there is no dependence,
and from that which has no dependence there is dependence?
The Buddha said:
“Nor does leaning arise from that which has leaning, nor does leaning arise from that which is without leaning.
That which enters into the single equality of leaning and non-leaning is called ‘non-leaning.’”
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva regards both attachment and non-attachment as equal, this is called "non-attachment"; thus should they train.
When a bodhisattva trains in the *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, this constitutes being without attachment.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
when a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, they neither practice by relying [on anything] nor practice by not relying.”
"How does one practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) so as to fulfill all the stages (bhūmi) and attain omniscience (sarvākārajñatā)?
The Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva fulfills all the stages by not dwelling in dependence."
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā does not rely on anything, the Path likewise has nothing upon which to rely, and even the one who practices the Prajñāpāramitā cannot be apprehended.
“A bodhisattva should practice in this manner.
“World-Honored One!
The *prajñāpāramitā* cannot be perceived; the Path cannot be perceived, nor can the one who practices the Path be perceived.”
“How does a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom discern that these dharmas are the five aggregates and these are the Path?
The Buddha said:
“When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, they do not rely on the five aggregates, nor do they rely on the Path.”
He asked again:
"If a bodhisattva does not rely on the five aggregates nor rely on the Way, how does he fulfill the six pāramitās and transcend the stage of a bodhisattva?"
How does one purify Buddha-fields and transform sentient beings?
How does one attain *samyaksambodhi*?
How does one turn the wheel of Dharma?
"How should one perform the work of a Buddha?
How should one liberate sentient beings from birth and death?
The Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva does not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the five aggregates, nor do they practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of the Path.
He asked again:
"For whose sake, then, does one practice the perfection of wisdom?"
The Buddha said:
"One practices the Prajñāpāramitā precisely because there is nothing to be done. Why is this?"
All dharmas have no agent, and the prajñāpāramitā likewise has no agent and no one who accomplishes it.
The Path also has no agent and no one who accomplishes it; the bodhisattva likewise has no agent and no one who accomplishes it.
“A bodhisattva should practice the perfection of wisdom in this way: they should have nothing to do and nothing to accomplish.
Subhūti said, “World-Honored One!”
"If all dharmas are without action and without accomplishment, then there will also be no place for the three vehicles.
The Buddha said:
"The locus of dharmas that are without action and without accomplishment cannot be found."

Why is this? Because foolish and ignorant people enter into the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and, relying on these five aggregates, become conceited; relying on the Way, they likewise become conceited, thinking to themselves:
"I shall attain the Way and deliver sentient beings."
Why is this? Subhūti!

Even with the five eyes, a Buddha cannot find the five aggregates or the Path; how much less can an ordinary person, who is foolish and sightless, enter the five aggregates and seek to deliver sentient beings?

Subhūti said: “World-Honored One, since you do not apprehend sentient beings by means of the five eyes and do not see anyone who can be delivered, how do you achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and how do you establish sentient beings within the three periods of time?”
The Buddha said:

"I do not perceive the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor do I perceive sentient beings; I do not perceive the three periods of time, neither attaining nor perceiving them, because sentient beings have no self-body."
Furthermore, regarding the notion of a self-body, one merely restrains oneself through these precepts.
The teachings that have been spoken exist only because of worldly convention; they are not the ultimate, ineffable teaching of the primary truth.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
does one not abide in the most supreme essential meaning to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
The Buddha said, "No. Subhūti said:
“Is one awakened to unexcelled perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) by means of the four perversions? The Buddha said, “No.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If it is not attained through the primary essential meaning, nor through the four inversions, will it not be the case that the World-Honored One has failed to realize perfect enlightenment?"
The Buddha said: "No. The Buddha said:
“The Tathāgata, having attained perfect enlightenment, likewise does not abide in the nature of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), nor does he abide in the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

For example, it is as if the Tathāgata were to manifest a transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) Tathāgata; this [manifestation] likewise has no fixed abode, yet it comes and goes, stands and sits, and furthermore practices the six *pāramitās*, is able to practice dhyāna, practices the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions, is able to practice the five supernormal powers and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, is able to practice the three gates of liberation, practices internal and external emptiness as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence, and also practices the eight liberations, the nine successive absorptions, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and is even able to turn the wheel of Dharma.”
These emanated Buddhas further emanated countless people, and the emanated Buddhas said to those people:
"There is a deliverance, there are sentient beings, and there are the three periods of time. The Buddha asked Subhūti:
“Are there any three periods of time or sentient beings within that which is emanated by this emanation-Buddha? Subhūti replied, “No.”
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"For this reason, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, knows that all dharmas are like transformations; there is nothing to be delivered or liberated."
“A bodhisattva should practice the perfection of wisdom in this way and should understand it in this way.
Subhūti said, “As the World-Honored One has said, all dharmas are like magical illusions.”
“What difference is there between the body manifested by the Tathāgata and the body of the Tathāgata himself?
What distinction is there?
The Buddha said:
“There is neither difference nor distinction. Why is this?
The Tathāgata has his own activities, and the emanation likewise has its own activities.”
He asked again:
"If there is no Tathāgata, can a transformation-body alone perform any actions?
The Buddha said:
"It is capable of performing an action. "In what way,
World-Honored One?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“In the past there was a buddha named Suśānta—Suśānta means ‘Utterly Pure’ in the language of Jin (Chinese)—the Tathāgata. During the time of that buddha, there were no people who practiced the bodhisattva path.”
Then the Buddha manifests *parinirvāṇa*, creating a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇabuddha*) who remains for one eon.
Having performed the work of a Buddha for that eon, the transformation Buddha subsequently bestows predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) upon those bodhisattva practitioners and then passes into *parinirvāṇa*.
Everyone calls this "entering parinirvāṇa," yet they do not know that it is a transformation.
The Buddha said,
"A transformation has neither arising nor nirvāṇa."
“Subhūti! A bodhisattva who practices the perfection of wisdom should understand that all phenomena are like magical illusions. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
If there is no difference between what is done by a transformation-body and what is done by a Tathāgata, how can the merit performed bring the debt of gratitude to completion?”
"If one makes offerings to an emanation Buddha or makes offerings to a Tathāgata, will the merit of that donor be exhausted and extinguished by the time of parinirvāṇa?
The Buddha said:
"The Tathāgata is a field of merit for all devas and humans; an emanation Tathāgata is likewise a field of merit for all, being equal and without distinction."
The Buddha said:
"Setting aside the merit produced by making offerings to the Tathāgata or to a manifested Tathāgata,
if there is someone who constantly recollects the Buddha with a mind of loving-kindness, their merit will continue until the end of suffering."
The Buddha said,
"Setting aside the merit of this benevolent intention,
if a person were merely to scatter a single handful of flowers into the air while for a moment recollecting the Buddha, that merit would likewise lead to the end of suffering."
The Buddha said:
"Set aside the merit of scattering these flowers.
If there is anyone who can simply utter 'Namo Buddha,' their meritorious virtue shall likewise lead to the end of suffering."
Subhūti! The merit of giving to the Tathāgata is exceedingly great, vast, and universal. Subhūti!
One should understand it thus: all dharmas are equal, and there is no distinction between a transformation Buddha and a [true] Buddha.

A bodhisattva should practice the *prajñāpāramitā* in this way; they should understand the nature of all dharmas as neither to be extinguished nor to be abandoned. This dharma of the *prajñāpāramitā* is also not to be differentiated, and so it should be for all dharmas up to that point.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
If all dharmas should not be distinguished, why does the Tathāgata say:”
"Is this form? Is this sensation? Is this perception? Are these volitional formations?
Is this consciousness? How can it be said:

"This is an internal phenomenon, this is an external phenomenon; this is wholesome, this is unwholesome; this is with outflows, this is without outflows; this is mundane, this is supramundane; this is birth, this is death; this is a conditioned phenomenon, this is an unconditioned phenomenon?"
“World-Honored One!
Would these dharmas not be without discrimination?
The Buddha said:
"No, World-Honored One.
It is merely by means of names and numbers that you indicate this to sentient beings, desiring only to cause them to understand; yet there is no discrimination therein.
"World-Honored One! [The interlocutor continued.]
"This Dharma is without name or designation; how can one teach sentient beings by means of names and characteristics, desiring to bring them to understanding?
The Buddha said:
"Practice is without name, without characteristic, and without entry; practice is also without suffering, without characteristic, and without entry."
The Buddhas and their disciples likewise do not enter into marks.

If names were to enter names, then marks would also have to enter marks; emptiness would have to enter emptiness, signlessness would have to enter signlessness, wishlessness would have to enter wishlessness, the reality-limit would have to enter the reality-limit, the dharma-nature would have to enter the dharma-nature, and unconditioned dharmas would also have to enter unconditioned dharmas.
These dharmas are merely names; yet even a name does not enter into a name.
When a bodhisattva dwells in the practice of the perfection of wisdom by means of names and signs, they likewise should not enter into those names and signs.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
If all conditioned phenomena exist merely by way of names and signs, for whose sake does a bodhisattva resolve upon the mind of enlightenment?”
For whose sake do they undergo various arduous practices and cultivate the six pāramitās?

For whose sake do they practice dhyāna and formless dhyāna, as well as the four immeasurables and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, encompassing the three gates of liberation and perfecting great compassion—all these practices are performed for whose sake?
The Buddha said:

"By means of names, characteristics, and numerical signs, all conditioned phenomena are not empty of names and characteristics; for this reason, the bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva path and attains sarvajñatā."

Furthermore, when turning the wheel of Dharma and delivering sentient beings by means of the three vehicles of the Dharma, these names and characteristics are likewise neither born nor extinguished; they remain as they are, without any difference.
Subhūti asked: "Does the World-Honored One speak of sarvajñatā (all-knowledge)?
The Buddha said:
“Yes, it is so.
What I have taught as ‘sarvajña’ (all-knowledge) and the ‘matter of sarvajña’ is the teaching on the matter of the wisdom of the path.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is the distinction between these?
The Buddha said,
"Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is the domain of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
"The matter of the wisdom of the Path is the matter of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
The matter of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is the matter of all buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
He asked again:
“What is meant by saying that *sarvajña* (the All-Knowing One) performs the work of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*?
The Buddha said:
“The Arhats and *pratyekabuddhas* fully know all internal and external phenomena.”
"Although he knows them, he does not abide in the affairs of the various paths.
[The interlocutor asked: "What is the bodhisattva’s matter of the wisdom of the path?
The Buddha said:

"A Bodhisattva should explain and know all paths, and should also fully understand the paths of the three vehicles; they should perform the deeds of the three paths, yet they do not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)."
He asked again:
"How is it that a bodhisattva fulfills the Buddha-work yet does not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi)?
The Buddha said:
"One should not realize the awakening to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) as long as the Buddha-field is not perfected and sentient beings have not been transformed.
He asked again:
"Should a bodhisattva dwell within the path to realize the witness of the limit of reality?"
The Buddha said, "No.
[The interlocutor asked,] "How then could it be from non-Path?"
The Buddha said,
“No. [He asked,] “World-Honored One!”
"Can one proceed by means of both the path and what is not the path? The Buddha said, "No."
“Is it neither the path nor not the path? The Buddha said, “No.”
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One, how should it be?”
The Buddha said:
"What do you think, Subhūti? Did you originally abide in the path such that you extinguished all outflows? Subhūti replied:
"No," [he replied]. The Buddha said,
"Did you extinguish all outflows by means of a non-path?"
“World-Honored One! No. The Buddha said:
"Do you extinguish all outflows by means of the path or by means of what is not the path? "World-Honored One, no."
The Buddha asked,
"Do you extinguish all outflows by means of the Path, or by what is not the Path, or by what is neither the Path nor not the Path?
[He replied,] "World-Honored One!"
"No, it is not so. I have extinguished all outflows (āsrava) while dwelling nowhere; though I have extinguished all outflows, I dwell nowhere.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
“The Bodhisattva is also like this.
Although he realizes the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), he does not dwell anywhere.
Although one speaks of ‘sarvajñā’ (omniscience) and the matters of sarvajñā, they are in fact but a single matter.”
“World-Honored One!
What is this one thing?
The Buddha said:
"It is the one who is tranquil.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All that is spoken, all forms and images, and all matters of arising and ceasing—the Buddha has fully awakened to them; for this reason, he is called Sarvajña (the All-Knowing One)."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Are there any distinctions among these three categories: sarvajñatā (all-knowledge), the matter of sarvajñatā, and the matter of the wisdom of the path?"
“Is there a distinction between those whose residual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are exhausted and those whose residual tendencies remain? The Buddha said:

“There is no difference in the exhaustion of residual tendencies; however, for a Buddha, all residual tendencies are completely exhausted, whereas for a śrāvaka, residual tendencies are not entirely exhausted.”
“World-Honored One!
Is it that by exhausting the causal threads one attains nirvāṇa?
The Buddha said:
"No, World-Honored One! Is there any distinction within Nirvana?"
The Buddha said: “No.
[The interlocutor asked:
“If there is no distinction, World-Honored One, why do you say that the various latencies (anuśaya) are not yet exhausted?”
The Buddha said:
"Those who practice do not possess the continuity of practice.
Although lust, anger, and delusion cause exhaustion to the body of an ordinary person, they do not constitute such a continuity."
“The Tathāgata has no lineage. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!”

The Path also has no existence, and Nirvana likewise has no existence; how then can one speak of "this is a srotāpanna," "this is an arhat," "this is a pratyekabuddha," or "this is a samyaksaṃbuddha"?
The Buddha said:
"All these are names that exist because of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta); they are merely the name 'stream-enterer,' 'arhat,' 'pratyekabuddha,' or 'samyaksaṃbuddha.'"
“World-Honored One!
Does a name arise from the unconditioned?
The Buddha said:
"No, it is not so. It is merely through conventional speech that such words exist; they do not accord with the most essential and primary meaning. Why is this? Because..."
"First, one must have no manifold practices within; nor should one bestow anything manifold. One gives for the sake of those who have severed craving, and thus gives toward the future limit.
"World-Honored One! [he said.]
"The characteristics of all dharmas are each empty, and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) cannot be known; how then can one know of a subsequent limit?
The Buddha said: "It is so!"
The characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmas*) are empty, and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) cannot be known; how much less can there be a subsequent limit?

For those who do not know that the characteristics of all phenomena are empty, I speak of a prior and a subsequent limit for them; yet the characteristics of all phenomena themselves have neither prior nor subsequent.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva who practices the *prajñāpāramitā* should know that the characteristics of all dharmas are empty.

Thus practicing the emptiness of all dharmas, they do not enter into any dharmas; they do not enter internal dharmas, nor do they enter external dharmas, nor do they enter conditioned or unconditioned dharmas, nor do they enter the dharmas of the Three Vehicles.
He asked again:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called ‘prajñāpāramitā,’ for what reason is it called ‘prajñāpāramitā’?”
The Buddha said:

“It is the foremost attainment among all dharmas that cross over; it is the most supreme vehicle for crossing over the path of the Three Vehicles. All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas ride upon the Prajñāpāramitā to reach the other shore; therefore, it is called Prajñāpāramitā.”
Furthermore, because one transcends the dust of all phenomena and does not grasp at their solid core, it is therefore called the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Since the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and suchness (*tathatā*) all enter into the *prajñāpāramitā*, it is therefore called the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Subhūti! In these dharmas, the prajñāpāramitā is neither conjoined nor dispersed; whether there is seeing or non-seeing, obstruction or non-obstruction, it is neither conjoined nor dispersed with respect to these dharmas.
Because the prajñāpāramitā is formless, invisible, and without counterpart; it is a single mark, which is to say, no mark.
Why is this? Because it gives rise to all dharmas and all eloquences.

Neither the devas and the world, nor Māra and his adversaries, nor followers of other paths, nor the families of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—none of these are able to sever or obstruct a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom.
Why is this? Because all Māras, adversaries, and those of the two stages are unattainable. Subhūti!
Regarding the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*, a bodhisattva should understand it in this way and practice it in this way.

Furthermore, Subhūti, regarding the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*, a bodhisattva practices the meaning of impermanence, the meaning of suffering and non-self; they know the meaning of the origin of suffering, the meaning of cessation and the path; they know the meaning of extinction, the meaning of non-arising, the meaning of phenomena (*dharma*), the meaning of seeing once and knowing all, the meaning of self-knowledge, and the meaning of knowing the welfare of others; they act according to what they have spoken.
“Subhūti! Regarding the perfection of wisdom, a bodhisattva should understand this meaning and should practice in this way.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Within this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, neither meaning nor non-meaning can be apprehended; how then should a bodhisattva practice various meanings within the *prajñāpāramitā*?”
The Buddha said:
"The profound meaning of a bodhisattva is the *prajñāpāramitā*; one should practice in this manner.

Because a bodhisattva has diminished lust, anger, and ignorance, they should not practice the meaning of false views, nor should they practice the sixty-two views; knowing them to be without meaning, they should not practice them either."
Why is this so? Because the suchness of lust, anger, and delusion neither benefits nor diminishes any dharma.
Likewise, the meaning of the suchness of all views neither benefits nor diminishes anything.
To say that the five aggregates are beneficial or not beneficial is also something one should not practice;
even down to saying that the Path is beneficial or not beneficial, this too is something one should not practice.
Why is this? When the Tathāgata attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he likewise perceived neither that which was beneficial nor that which was not beneficial.
Whether a Buddha exists or does not exist, all dharmas remain tranquil; they neither increase nor diminish.
"Subhūti! A bodhisattva should eliminate what is beneficial and what is not beneficial; in this manner, they should practice the perfection of wisdom.
[Subhūti said: "World-Honored One!"
“How is it that the perfection of wisdom neither benefits nor harms?
The Buddha said, “All conditioned phenomena are eternally quiescent and perform no action; therefore, the perfection of wisdom neither benefits nor harms.”
“World-Honored One!
Are all conditioned phenomena not the domain of the Buddhas and their disciples?
The Buddha said:
"All conditioned phenomena are the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas; they neither increase nor diminish.
They are like the suchness of space, which does not arise through action, nor does it arise through non-action."
“Prajñāpāramitā is also like this: it does not arise for the sake of providing any benefit, nor does it arise for the sake of causing any loss.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One!”
“Does a bodhisattva not attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment by training in the prajñāpāramitā of non-existence and the unconditioned?
The Buddha said, “It is so!”
“A Bodhisattva does not train in the profound *prajñāpāramitā* by means of conditioned phenomena to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they do not respond by means of duality.
“World-Honored One!”
"What is this one dharma?
Is it for the sake of attaining this one dharma?
The Buddha said:
"No, World-Honored One. Does that which is not one arise from two dharmas?"
The Buddha said,
“No. [He asked,] “World-Honored One!”
"How is it that one neither follows from one nor follows from two, yet there is attainment?
The Buddha said:
"Attainment is non-attainment; it is neither by means of attaining nor by means of not attaining that one attains."
Chapter 71: Planting Trees. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Seventy-one: Planting Trees. At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
The Prajñāpāramitā is profoundly deep and devoid of sentient beings, yet the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, for the sake of sentient beings, undergoes humble hardships in seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"It is as if a man wished to plant a tree in the air; so too does a bodhisattva, for the sake of sentient beings, wish to attain *sarvajñatā*.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!"
Subhūti! Those who wish to enable sentient beings to attain *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) do so by conceiving of them as "sentient beings" and thereby delivering and liberating them. Subhūti!
It is like a person who wishes to plant a tree but does not know its roots, nor its trunk, joints, branches, leaves, flowers, or fruit.

They take a cutting and plant it, irrigating and nurturing it according to the seasons. Gradually, the trunk, joints, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit each become fully developed; they then take the branches, leaves, and trunk for whatever purposes they serve, and finally take the fruit to eat.

Subhūti! A bodhisattva, for the sake of all sentient beings, generates the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; subsequently, by practicing the six *pāramitās*, they attain *sarvajñatā*. Their branches, joints, stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits benefit all sentient beings.
By means of its leaves, it delivers beings from the three evil realms;
because it possesses flowers, there arise the four classes of noble ones and the various gods of the Four Heavenly Kings, up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception.

As for its fruit, it is like a Bodhisattva who achieves *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and attains *sarvajñatā*, whereby there then come to be the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*, as well as the path of the *pratyekabuddha*.
There is a bodhisattva who attains the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the benefit of sentient beings.
Because sentient beings abide in this fruit, even though they may attain *abhiṣambuddha* (perfect enlightenment) through the three vehicles, one does not perceive the abiding of sentient beings.

One delivers sentient beings by means of conceptualization, yet one does not perceive the acquisition of sentient beings, nor is there any place where one can attain unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Subhūti!
"A Bodhisattva should train in this way; practicing the Prajñāpāramitā, they should maintain this reflection.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One!"
You should know that such a bodhisattva is also like a Tathāgata. Why is this?
Because through the coming and going of bodhisattvas, the three evil destinies are cut off.
"The eight states of difficulty are all severed; all states of poverty and low birth are severed; all states within the three realms are severed.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!"
Subhūti! You should know that such a bodhisattva is no different from a Tathāgata.

If a bodhisattva were to become weary or indolent, they would ultimately fail to attain the path of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present; there would likewise be no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas in the world, and the three evil destinies and the three realms would never cease to exist.
The Buddha said:
"You should know that this bodhisattva is like the Tathāgata, just as you have said. Why is this?
By means of suchness (tathatā), one knows that there is a Tathāgata, one knows that there are pratyekabuddhas, and one knows that there are the various noble ones;
by means of suchness, one knows that there are the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), and one knows that there are the conditioned (saṃskṛta) and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) natures.
These various *tathatās* (thusnesses) are themselves *tathatā*; therefore, it is called *tathatā*.
The Bodhisattva studies this *tathatā* and attains *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).
Because he comes from within this, he is therefore called a *Tathāgata*.
Because they are equal to suchness, you should know that this bodhisattva is indeed a Buddha. Subhūti,
a bodhisattva should train in the suchness of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Having studied the suchness of the *prajñāpāramitā*, one should study the suchness of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
Having studied the suchness of all phenomena, one should study the perfection of the suchness of all phenomena.
Having fulfilled suchness, one attains mastery over all suchnesses.
Having attained mastery over suchness, one becomes skilled in the faculties of all phenomena.
Being skilled in the faculties, one then perceives the destinies into which sentient beings follow according to their conduct.
Having known the various realms of existence, one then fulfills the aspiration for wisdom.
Having fulfilled the aspiration for wisdom, one then purifies the wisdom of the three periods of time.
Having purified the wisdom of the three periods of time, one then practices the bodhisattva path.
Having practiced the bodhisattva path, one brings benefit to sentient beings.
Having brought benefit to sentient beings, one purifies the buddha-fields.
Having purified the buddha-fields, one attains sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
Having attained *sarvajñatā*, he then turns the wheel of Dharma.
Having turned the wheel of Dharma, he establishes sentient beings in the three vehicles of the Dharma.
Having established sentient beings therein, he enters *parinirvāṇa* in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Subhūti! A bodhisattva mahāsattva, observing for themselves the virtues of all wholesome qualities as well as the virtues of others, should resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
The devas, asuras, and the people of the world should all pay homage to the bodhisattva who practices the prajñāpāramitā.”
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!
All devas and people of the world should pay homage to him."
“World-Honored One!
For the sake of sentient beings, how much merit does a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* obtain?”
The Buddha said:
"If there were good sons or good daughters who taught all sentient beings within a trichiliocosm, establishing them all in the path of Arhatship or Pratyekabuddhahood."
"What do you think? Would the merit obtained not be great?
Subhūti said, "World-Honored One!"
"Very much, very much.

The Buddha said, "It is not equal to the merit of this bodhisattva who, for the sake of sentient beings, gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; that merit is many times greater—twofold, hundredfold, thousandfold, and even hundreds of billions of times greater."
The Buddha said:

"Setting aside this trichiliocosm for a moment, suppose there were someone who taught the sentient beings within a trichiliocosm to establish themselves on the stage of intelligence, the stage of faith, the eighth stage, the stage of vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of purity, the stage of completion, and the stage of the pratyekabuddha. The merit of that person would not equal that of a bodhisattva who has resolved their mind toward awakening and gives rise to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of all sentient beings; the latter’s merit is far greater—hundredfold, thousandfold, and hundreds of billions of times more."

Subhūti! Even if all sentient beings within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were to have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment, their merit would not equal that of a bodhisattva established in right concentration; the latter’s merit exceeds the former by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of times.

"Furthermore, even if the three-thousandfold world system were filled with bodhisattvas who have attained perfection, their merit would not equal that of a Tathāgata, falling short by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of times.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What should a bodhisattva who has newly resolved upon awakening keep in mind?"
The Buddha said:
"One should keep sarvajñatā (all-knowledge) in mind.
[He asked: "World-Honored One!"
"What is the task of *sarvajñatā*?
What is its venerable characteristic?
The Buddha said:
“Sarvajñā is non-existent; it is neither with perception nor without perception, neither arising nor manifesting.
Subhūti said, “World-Honored One!”
Is it only *sarvajñatā* that is non-existent?

Are the five aggregates, internal and external emptiness as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the three samādhis, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great loving-kindness and great compassion, the four unhindered wisdoms, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the six supernormal powers—all these, as well as the natures of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, likewise non-existent?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is itself non-existent.
That which is itself non-existent is empty."
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is there nothing?
The Buddha said:
"That which has no agent is non-existent.
For this reason, the existence and non-existence of all phenomena are empty.
Furthermore, Subhūti!"

All dharmas are empty, signless, and wishless; all dharmas are suchness, all dharmas are like the limit of reality, and all dharmas are like the nature of phenomena. Therefore, whatever exists among all dharmas is non-existent, and all are empty.
“World-Honored One!

If all that exists in all dharmas is non-existent, what is the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva who has first resolved on awakening, such that they practice the six *pāramitās*, practice the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions; practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; practice internal and external emptiness as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence; practice the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and practice the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*), purifying buddha-fields and transforming sentient beings?”
The Buddha said:
"To perform any action within all dharmas that are empty is precisely what constitutes *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means);
it is by this that one can purify buddha-fields and transform sentient beings, knowing that both the buddha-fields and all sentient beings are ultimately non-existent."
The bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās as conditions for the Buddha-way; even up to sarvajñā (all-knowledge), these also serve as conditions for the Buddha-way.
He knows that all things pertaining to the path are in fact non-existent.

When a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās, they create the causal conditions for the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), leading to the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four kinds of unimpeded wisdom, four immeasurables, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha. For the sake of fulfilling the path through the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñājñāna), with a single moment and a single intention, they unify everything simultaneously through wisdom; thus, they shall immediately attain omniscience.

At that time, having completely extinguished all traces of past habitual tendencies because there is nothing from which they arise, one observes the three thousandfold world-system with the Buddha-eye; therein, one does not even perceive non-existence, let alone existence.

Subhūti! When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, they perceive neither existence nor non-existence in all phenomena; this is the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
One does not even perceive non-existence, much less existence.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), they do not know that the gift is non-existent, nor do they know that the recipient is non-existent, nor do they know that the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) is non-existent; this extends even to not knowing that omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is non-existent. They do not know that the one who has attained awakening, the one who will attain awakening, or the one who has already attained awakening are non-existent.
Why is this? All dharmas are non-existent; they are not made by the Buddha, nor are they made by disciples or pratyekabuddhas.
All dharmas are uncreated, for they are free from all creation.
Subhūti said: "World-Honored One, is it that there is no dharma apart from dharma?"
The Buddha said:
"Though it is called 'Dharma,' it is for the purpose of transcending Dharma. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
If dharmas are separated from the characteristics of dharmas, how can one know that a dharma is separated from a dharma?

Among all dharmas, there is ‘non-existence’; a dharma of non-existence does not know a dharma of non-existence, nor does an existent dharma know an existent dharma, nor does an existent dharma know a dharma of non-existence, nor does a dharma of non-existence know an existent dharma.”
"How should a bodhisattva understand all phenomena, whether they exist or do not exist, within the dharma that is itself unknowable?
The Buddha said, "Because of the habitual tendencies of worldly affairs, a bodhisattva manifests both existence and non-existence; these are not the foremost or most essential meaning."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is there a difference between worldly matters and the most essential meaning?”
The Buddha said:
"There is no difference.

The suchness of worldly phenomena and the suchness of the most essential meaning are identical. Because sentient beings do not know this suchness, they perceive worldly phenomena as either existing or non-existing."
Furthermore, Subhūti!

Sentient beings perceive the five aggregates as having marks and do not know them to be non-existent; for this reason, I thus differentiate and teach the Dharma, desiring to cause sentient beings to know that they are non-existent.
"A Bodhisattva who wishes to practice the Prajñāpāramitā should train in this manner. 72.
Chapter on the Practice of the Bodhisattva, the seventy-second chapter of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra. Thereupon, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Yes, World-Honored One!"
“What is the practice of a bodhisattva, and for what purpose does one practice as a bodhisattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“The practice of a bodhisattva is the practice of the Way; therefore, it is called the practice of a bodhisattva.”
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
where does a bodhisattva practitioner practice?”

The Buddha said: “To practice within the five aggregates while being empty of internal and external phenomena; to practice the six *pāramitās*; to practice the four *dhyānas* through the emptiness of the internal and external, as well as the emptiness of existence and non-existence; to practice the four formless meditations (*ārūpya-dhyāna*); to practice the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*); to practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*); to practice the three samādhis; to practice the ten powers of a Buddha; to practice the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*); to practice the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); to practice the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*); to practice the purification of the Buddha-lands; to practice the transformation of sentient beings; to practice entering into words and letters, yet practicing not entering into words and letters; to practice the *dhāraṇīs*;

to practice the nature of the conditioned and the unconditioned—performing these practices without allowing duality to arise in the Path, this is the practice of the Path, and this is the practice of emptiness of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.”
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what constitutes a Buddha?"
The Buddha said: "One is called a Buddha because of awakening through the Way.
Furthermore, Subhūti!..."
Having attained the dharma of thorough examination, he is called a Buddha because of his awakening to that dharma.
Because he has transcended the dharma of thorough examination, he is named Buddha.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
“Because he has truly awakened to all dharmas, he is called a Buddha. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!”
"What is meant by 'the Awakened One'?
The Buddha said:
"One awakens through the dharma of emptiness, one awakens through suchness, one awakens through the dharma; it is merely a name consisting of syllables."
Subhūti! The meaning of awakening is the meaning of that which cannot be severed; it is suchness and thusness, abiding without change. For this reason, it is called awakening.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
It is merely by means of names and signs that one is called a Buddha.
Because it is the path of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, it is therefore called "Awakening" (bodhi).
"Because all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have awakened together [to this], it is called 'Awakening'. Subhūti said:
"World-Honored One!"
When a bodhisattva practices the path, does he practice the six pāramitās?
Does he practice sarvajña (omniscience)?
What kind of goodness does he accomplish?
"What merit does this increase?
Is there arising and ceasing, or attachment and severance?
The Buddha said:

"When a bodhisattva practices the path and practices the six pāramitās until reaching sarvajñatā, they neither achieve nor destroy any dharmas; there is neither increase nor decrease, neither attachment nor abandonment."
The Buddha said:

“A bodhisattva who practices the path of the *prajñāpāramitā* does not fall into any phenomena; nor does he bring about the formation or destruction of any phenomena, nor their increase or decrease, nor their arising or ceasing, nor does he cling to them or sever them.”
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva does not fall into any dharmas and does not observe any [characteristics], how can they uphold the six pāramitās while personally practicing emptiness regarding marks?”
How does one practice the four dhyānas?
How does one practice the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions?
How does one practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the three gates of liberation?
How does one practice the ten powers and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha?
How does one practice great loving-kindness and great compassion?
How does one practice the ten stages of a bodhisattva?
"How does one transcend the two stages?
How does one transcend the rank of a bodhisattva?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva does not practice the six pāramitās by means of duality, nor do they practice sarvajñatā by means of duality. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!...”

If a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās and practices sarvajñā without relying on these two things, how does one proceed from the initial generation of the thought of enlightenment to the subsequent generation of that thought?
"How can one increase one's merit?
The Buddha said,
"Those who practice by means of duality— such people achieve no increase."
Why is this? Those who practice by means of these two things may find some benefit among ordinary, foolish people.
However, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the final production of the thought, a bodhisattva does not increase their merit by means of these two things.
For this reason, neither gods nor humans can cause a bodhisattva to fall into the two stages; nor can any other evils restrain a bodhisattva from practicing the six pāramitās and sarvajñatā.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
does a bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of merit?”
The Buddha said:
"One does not practice the Prajñāpāramitā because of merit, nor does one practice it because of a lack of merit.

A bodhisattva must, however, make offerings to all Buddhas, must fully perfect all virtuous merits, and must associate with true spiritual friends; only then can they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva make offerings to the Buddhas, fulfill their merits, obtain true spiritual friends, and thereby attain *sarvajñatā*?”
The Buddha said:

“From the first moment a bodhisattva resolves upon the bodhicitta, they constantly make offerings to all Buddhas. They should always receive and uphold the twelve divisions of the sūtras spoken by those Buddhas, maintaining them firmly and keeping them in mind; thus, they attain dharanī and give rise to the various forms of non-obstruction.”

Having attained unimpededness, in whatever place they are born, until they reach *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), they shall never forget what they have known or retained, nor the merits of making offerings to the Buddhas; they shall never be reborn in the evil destinies or the eight states of non-leisure, and shall instead receive a pure mind.
Having attained a pure mind, they purify Buddha-fields and transform sentient beings.
By virtue of these merits, they shall never be separated from true spiritual friends, nor ever be separated from the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, the True Persons, and those who praise the Buddhas.
Thus it is, Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the prajñāpāramitā should make offerings to all buddhas, should fulfill all dharmas and receive all merits, and should associate with true spiritual friends.
Chapter 73: On Attaining True Spiritual Friends. In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Seventy-Three: On Attaining True Spiritual Friends, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who does not make offerings to the Buddhas, does not fulfill all merits, and does not encounter true spiritual friends, will they not be unable to attain sarvajñatā?
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“There is no bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not made offerings to all Tathāgatas; there is none who has not fulfilled all meritorious qualities; and there is none who has not obtained true spiritual friends.”
Why is this? Although one may make offerings to the Buddhas, perform meritorious deeds, and encounter true spiritual friends, one has not yet attained *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge);
how much less so can one who does not make offerings to the Buddhas, does not perform meritorious deeds, and does not encounter true spiritual friends hope to attain *sarvajñatā*?
This is not so. Therefore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to study the prajñāpāramitā should make offerings to the Buddhas, should cultivate merit, and should obtain true spiritual friends.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
for what reason should a bodhisattva make offerings to the Buddhas, cultivate all manner of meritorious deeds, and obtain true spiritual friends before attaining sarvajñatā?”
The Buddha said:

"It is because they lack *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), have not heard the matters concerning *upāyakauśalya* from the various Buddhas, have not yet fulfilled their merit, and have not yet attained true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*)."
“World-Honored One!
With what kind of *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) should a bodhisattva be fully endowed in order to attain *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge)?
The Buddha said:

"From the time a bodhisattva first resolves upon enlightenment, they practice the perfection of giving with the mind of sarvajñā (all-knowledge), bestowing gifts upon those of the three vehicles, as well as upon humans and non-humans; yet they remain fully endowed with the mindfulness of sarvajñā, maintaining no perception of a giver, no perception of a recipient, and no perception of practicing the perfection of giving."
Why is this? All phenomena that are conceived as "dharmas" are non-existent, neither arising nor ceasing.

When one contemplates and perceives all dharmas, there is no coming or going; one transcends all characteristics of dharmas and sees no activity within them. By being fully endowed with *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), one thereby increases all merits.

Having already increased their merit, they practice the *dānapāramitā*, transforming sentient beings and purifying Buddha-lands; yet they do not personally receive the retribution for these deeds, desiring only to benefit sentient beings.
They do not accept the rewards for what they have done, practicing the *dānapāramitā* solely with the wish to deliver all sentient beings.
The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Sixteen;
The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Seventeen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mokṣala of Khotan during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Translated by Imperial Decree. Chapter 74:
Teaching and Transforming Sentient Beings. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, Chapter Seventy-Four: Teaching and Transforming Sentient Beings. "Furthermore, Subhūti,..."

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, through the mindfulness of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), from the first production of the thought of enlightenment does not depart from the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) while maintaining the mindfulness of *sarvajñatā*. From the very beginning, their mind does not fall into lust, anger, or delusion; nor do they give rise to thoughts of lust, anger, or delusion, nor are they entangled by them.

All matters that do not enter the discipline of the Path—envy, evil precepts, and malice; indolence and distraction; folly and stubbornness; self-will and attachment to a self, as well as the mentalities of the two stages—are all entirely absent.

Why is this? Because they know that the characteristics of all dharmas are empty; they know that all dharmas are non-existent and unformed; they perceive that all dharmas neither proceed nor return; they fully understand the characteristics of all dharmas and transcend all worldly affairs; they abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), perfecting *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) and increasing their merit; and while practicing the *dāna-pāramitā* (perfection of giving) to teach and transform sentient beings and purify Buddha-fields, they do not receive the retribution for the *dāna-pāramitā* within the world.
Upon reaching the Prajñāpāramitā, one desires only to benefit all and to teach and transform sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva practices the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions."
Although he practices the various dhyānas, he does not receive the blessings of dhyāna.
Why is this? Because through *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), he knows that the characteristics of all dhyānas are empty, and he also knows those who move toward and return from them.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom, from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, they practice with upāyakauśalya (skillful means) and practice the purity of contemplation; yet they do not proceed toward the stage of srotāpanna, nor do they take up the fruit of srotāpanna, continuing in this way until they reach arhatship, yet they do not take up its fruit either."

Why is this? Because they know that the characteristics of all dharmas are empty, and they know the dharma that does not turn back; furthermore, they practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and transcend the two stages. Subhūti!
This is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s endurance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
