Why, then, do you further say that by doing this one attains this, and that those who practice evil enter the three evil realms while those who practice good attain birth in the human realm or are born in the heavens?

How does one practice the path to attain the stage of *srotāpanna* up to the attainment of *arhat*, *pratyekabuddha*, or by practicing in this way attain the Dharma of a bodhisattva, and by practicing in this way attain *samyaksaṃbodhi*?
World-Honored One!

That which is the dharma of non-existence has no activity, no practice, no practice of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, no practice of bodhisattvas, no practice of the three types of buddhas, and no one who attains sarvajñatā to liberate sentient beings.
"What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha replied to Subhūti: "So it is, so it is!"
That which is non-existent is without action, without practice, and without attainment.

Ordinary people, shrouded in ignorance, are unable to know the Dharma of the noble ones; furthermore, they do not understand the nature of existence and non-existence. Deceived by the four inverted views, they perform various actions and receive various retributions, thereby falling into the cycle of birth and death within the five destinies.
Since there are no dharmas that exist, there is neither practice nor reception.
Subhūti, what do you think?
From the stage of a srotāpanna up to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, does anything exist?
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
From the stage of srotāpanna up to the path, all are non-existent.”
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Can that which is non-existent attain the dharma of non-existence? He replied:
"No, World-Honored One!

"Therefore, Subhūti, that which is non-existent and the Path—all dharmas—are neither conjoined nor dispersed; they have no form, are invisible, and are without opposition. They possess a single mark, and this single mark is the absence of marks."

Therefore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they perceive sentient beings as entering into [false] views, entering into perversions, and regarding the five aggregates—which are impermanent—as having the notion of permanence; regarding what is suffering as having the notion of pleasure; regarding what is non-self as having the notion of self; and regarding what is impure as having the notion of purity. Thus they enter into the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Yet, by means of skillful means, the bodhisattva causes sentient beings to depart from existence (*bhava*).
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The realms into which sentient beings enter do not depart from the five destinies; by what causes and conditions are they obstructed?”
"Is there perhaps any real essence?
The Buddha replied to Subhūti:
"There is not, there is not even as much as a hair's breadth of any other practice; it is only because sentient beings are attached to the four perversions that there are the five destinies."
Subhūti! Listen attentively, listen attentively!
For this reason, I shall now speak so that you may attain understanding.
"What do you think?
Is there an agent who creates the five pleasures enjoyed for one's own amusement within a dream? He replied:
“World-Honored One!
Even a dream does not exist; how much less so the five pleasures!
The Buddha said:
"What do you think? Among all phenomena—whether conditioned or unconditioned, with outflows or without outflows—is there any phenomenon that is not like a dream? He replied:
“World-Honored One!
All dharmas are merely like dreams; there is no dharma that is not like a dream.
The Buddha said:
“What do you think?
Is there any real existence of the five destinies for a person seen in a dream? “No, World-Honored One.”
“Subhūti! Does a person in a dream have any thought of the Path, or any matter of attachment or severance? He replied:
"There is not. Why is this? World-Honored One!"
“The formless Dharma has no place of creation, and the dharmas of attachment and severance likewise have no place.
“How so, Subhūti? When a mirror reflects an image, does it constitute any activity, or does it entail the retribution of birth and death within the five destinies?”
He replied, “No, World-Honored One! Why is this? Because...”
An image in a mirror is non-existent; yet ordinary beings, deluded, call it existent.
An image in a mirror likewise lacks the five destinies, and is without action or activity.
“Subhūti! Does a reflection in a mirror possess the thought of a path, or does it have attachment or cessation? He replied:
"There is none. Why is this?
Because a formless dharma is without fabrication, without attachment or cessation, and has no location."
The Buddha said, “What do you think, Subhūti?
Does an echo that issues from a mountain valley ever perform any action such as being born into the five destinies?”
He replied: "No. Why is this?
The formless Dharma has no activity, no action, and does not give rise to rebirth in the five destinies."
“What do you think, Subhūti? Does an echo have any thought of the Path, or does it have any attachment or cessation? He replied:
"There is none. Why is this?
Because dharmas that possess nothing are without fabrication; they are neither attached to nor severed, nor do they have a location."
“What do you think, Subhūti? It is like a mirage in the heat:
where there is no river, there is the perception of a river; where there is no city, there is the perception of a city; where there is no park, there is the perception of a park.”
"What do you think?
Does that flame perform any action such that there are five destinies? He replied:
"A flame has no substantial existence; it merely deludes the eyes of the foolish and is nothing but a reflection.
"Subhūti, does this flame have any thought of the path, or any attachment or cessation?"
He replied: "There is none.
A formless dharma is without fabrication; it is without attachment or cessation, and it has no location."

“Subhūti! For example, suppose a magician conjures up elephants and horses, or manifests various kinds of human beings. Does that conjured person truly have any activity or belong to any of the five destinies?”
He replied: "There is none. Why is this?"
“Because an illusion has no form.
“Subhūti! Does that which is conjured by an illusionary person have any thought of the Path, or any attachment or cessation?”
He replied: “There is none.
The formless Dharma is not something that can be constructed or established; it is neither subject to attachment nor to cessation, and it has no location.”
“Subhūti! Does that which is emanated by the Tathāgata have any activity or existence within the five destinies? He replied:
"There is none. Why is this?
Because that which is created has no intrinsic existence."
“Subhūti! Does a transformation being have the thought of a path, or does it have attachment or cessation? He replied:
"No, it is not so. A formless dharma has no thought of the Path, nor does it have attachment or cessation, nor does it have a location. "What do you think, Subhūti?"
"Are there any attachments or cessations regarding these dharmas?
He replied, "No,
there are neither attachments nor cessations."
The Buddha said:
"If there were no attachment or cessation, that would be non-attachment and non-cessation. Why is this?"
Sentient beings merely abide in the notion of "self" and thus fall into attachment or nihilism.
Those who clearly perceive the Truth neither cling nor sever; because the perceptions of sentient beings are not clear and true, they consequently fall into attachment and severance.
The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Nineteen;
The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll Twenty.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mokṣala of Khotan during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Translated by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Eighty-Six: The Equality of All Dharmas. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, Chapter Eighty-Six: The Equality of All Dharmas. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

That which is thoroughly examined is neither attached to nor severed; that which is not thoroughly examined is likewise neither attached to nor severed. Regarding all things and non-existence, there is neither attachment nor severance; both that which is thoroughly examined and that which is not thoroughly examined are equally neither attached to nor severed.
"What do you think of this matter?
The Buddha replied to Subhūti,
"Because all dharmas are equal, I say they are severed."
“World-Honored One! What does this mean?
The Buddha replied:

Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, suchness and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) remain as they are; the dharmic reality never changes from its original state and eternally abides as suchness. This is called "cessation.
It is only by means of conventional usage that names are given and words and teachings exist.
“Worldly sounds and voices, though they possess verbal teachings, are all non-existent. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!”

If all dharmas are like a dream, like an echo, like a reflection in a mirror, like a mirage, like a magical illusion, and like a transformation, how can a bodhisattva resolve their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* regarding dharmas that are empty and non-existent, saying:

"I shall fulfill the six pāramitās; I shall fulfill the superknowledges (*abhijñā*); I shall fulfill the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) and the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*); and I shall fulfill the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) and the nine successive meditative absorptions (*anupūrvasamāpatti*)?"
He said: "One should be fully endowed with the ten powers and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. He said:
"One should be fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
He said: "One should be fully endowed with the gates of dhāraṇī."
How can one say: "I shall produce light to universally illuminate the dark and obscure places"?
And how does one know the inclinations of the minds of sentient beings in order to preach the Dharma for them?
The Buddha said, “Subhūti, what do you think?”
"Is it as you have asked, that all things are like an illusion or a transformation? Subhūti replied,
"If all dharmas are like a dream or an illusion, how does a bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?"
World-Honored One!
Since dreams and magical illusions are not real, unreal dharmas cannot practice the six pāramitās, nor can they practice even the eighteen dharmas.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! Just as you have said, one who is like a dream-transformation cannot practice the six pāramitās, and thus cannot achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
These dharmas are all conditioned phenomena; yet within these conditioned phenomena, one cannot find *sarvajñatā*.
These dharmas are also the Path and they are also *nirvāṇa*, because these dharmas are unarisen and without marks.

For this reason, from the time a bodhisattva first resolves upon awakening, they practice all wholesome dharmas, from the six pāramitās up to the eighteen dharmas. Knowing that these dharmas are like dreams and like illusions, one who does not fulfill the six pāramitās and the eighteen dharmas is likewise unable to transform and teach sentient beings.
The bodhisattva practices all wholesome dharmas and contemplates all dharmas as being like dreams and like illusions.

The bodhisattva contemplates the *prajñāpāramitā*, contemplates *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), and contemplates sentient beings, likewise as being like dreams and like illusions. When the bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, they do not take form therein; nor do they take form within illusory and transformative dharmas, yet they say that they shall attain *sarvajñatā*.
When a bodhisattva practices the prajñāpāramitā, there is nothing to be grasped; even regarding the eighteen dharmas, there is nothing to be grasped.
Because the bodhisattva knows that all dharmas are without anything to be grasped, they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Why is this? Because all phenomena are formless; they cannot be grasped and cannot be maintained. Although there is nothing to grasp among phenomena, there is that which is attained, yet one does not perceive such a phenomenon.

Therefore, for the sake of sentient beings, the bodhisattva resolves upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; from the moment he first conceived this intention, he practices the six pāramitās solely for the sake of all beings and not for his own self.

When a bodhisattva gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is solely for the sake of sentient beings; yet because sentient beings do not exist, they nonetheless harbor the notion of "sentient beings," they do not see what exists but harbor the notion of seeing, and they do not know what exists but harbor the notion of knowing.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva pulls sentient beings out from amidst the inversions and, upon the ground of ambrosia, severs all habitual conceptualizations.

Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they do not enter into any phenomena, yet they establish sentient beings in non-entry; this is done merely by way of conventional designation, not in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
is the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata according to worldly conventions?”
"Is it by means of the ultimate truth?
The Buddha replied, "The Tathāgata attains awakening through conventional designations; furthermore, there is no dharma whatsoever that can be apprehended."
Why is this? If one were to say, "I have attained the Way," that would be a great disgrace;
if there were duality, there would be neither attainment nor awakening.
He asked again:
“World-Honored One!
Suppose there are two who have not yet attained awakening; would one of them attain awakening as a result?”
The Buddha replied:
"It is neither from two, nor is it from one.
That which has attained awakening is neither one nor two; this state of being neither one nor two is itself awakening."
"Why is this? For one who has attained awakening, playfulness constitutes arrogance; for one who has realized equal awakening, there is neither playfulness nor arrogance. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
Since all dharmas possess nothingness, how can there be such a thing as perfect enlightenment?
The Buddha replied:
"Neither is there existence, nor is there non-existence; there is also no verbal expression—this is perfect awakening (*samyaksambodhi*).
Regarding the dharma of perfect awakening, there is neither verbal expression nor any dharma that can be called 'perfect awakening'."
"The Fully Awakened One has transcended all phenomena, whereas ordinary, foolish people are far removed from the Fully Awakened One.
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!"
“Is the Tathāgata far removed from the dharma of awakening?
The Buddha replied,
“The Samyaksaṃbuddha does not abide in the realm of the various sages, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or buddhas.”
He asked again:
“World-Honored One!
Does the Tathāgata attain mastery over all dharmas?”
The Buddha replied:
"Ordinary worldlings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and tathāgatas are all equally one awakening.
This single awakening is neither dual nor manifold; there are no ordinary worldlings, no pratyekabuddhas, and even for the tathāgata, there is no plurality."
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
If there were no distinctions within perfect enlightenment, then there would be no difference between ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.”
The Buddha said: “So it is, so it is!
There is no distinction between ordinary beings and even the Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
“If there were no distinction between ordinary beings and even the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, for what reason would there be the Three Honored Ones?
The Buddha said, “What do you think, Subhūti?”
"Are the Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Bhikṣu Saṅgha Jewel different from Equal Enlightenment? He replied:

"As I have heard from the World-Honored One, the Three Jewels and Equal Enlightenment are not different. The Three Jewels and Equal Enlightenment neither conjoin nor disperse; they have no form and are invisible. They are of one mark, which is the markless, being the dharma of non-characteristic. To treat them as numbers or locations is to attribute proximity and spatiality to them."
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“When the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he established a locus for all dharmas; therein he knew of the three evil destinies, he knew of the human realm, and he knew of the Heaven of the Thirty-three Gods.

He further knew of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, up to internal and external emptiness and the emptiness of both existence and non-existence, and he knew of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.”
Therefore, Subhūti, this is the distinctive excellence of the Tathāgata, the Great Being: without wavering from the dharma of equal enlightenment, he establishes a locus for all dharmas.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One, is the World-Honored One likewise unmoving in his perfect enlightenment?”
Ordinary persons, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas likewise do not move from equal and perfect enlightenment.
Are the dharmas of a Buddha, the dharmas of ordinary persons, the dharmas of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and the dharmas of a Tathāgata one and the same dharma?
Are formless phenomena, material phenomena, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousness distinct from one another?
Are the eye-faculty, ear-faculty, nose-faculty, tongue-faculty, body-faculty, and mind-faculty distinct from one another?
Are the dharmas of earth, water, fire, wind, consciousness, and space different?
Are the dharmas of lust, anger, and delusion different?
Are the sixty-two views different?
Are there differences among the dharmas of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments?

Regarding the dharmas of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three gates of liberation, internal and external emptiness, and the emptiness of both existence and non-existence; the eight liberations, the nine successive meditations, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered wisdoms, the ten powers, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and all conditioned and unconditioned dharmas—all these dharmas have names. Why is it that they cannot be apprehended in any location?
If a bodhisattva does not abide in these states and does not discriminate among dharmas, they will ultimately be unable to practice the *prajñāpāramitā*.
When a bodhisattva practicing the *prajñāpāramitā* traverses the ten stages (*daśasthāna*), they then ascend to the rank of a bodhisattva and transcend the two stages.

Having transcended the two stages and perfected the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they become fully endowed with the five *pāramitās* within those supernormal powers. They travel through various buddha-fields to serve and honor the Buddhas, planting the roots of all manner of goodness; by means of these merits, they transform sentient beings and purify the buddha-lands.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Regarding your question concerning the dharmas of the Tathāgata, the dharmas of ordinary persons, and the dharmas of the two stages—why do you ask this? What do you think?”
"Are the dharmas of the five aggregates empty and the dharmas of the Tathāgata different?
Subhūti replied, "They are equal in emptiness."
The Buddha said:
"In emptiness, can the signless dharma be seen?
Can the marks of the five aggregates and the marks of a Buddha be seen?"
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,
it cannot be seen.”
"Therefore, Subhūti! The dharma of all dharmas is also non-existent.
An ordinary person does not depart from being an ordinary person, yet it is not the dharma of a Tathāgata, nor does it depart from the dharma of a Tathāgata."
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!
Is this dharma a conditioned dharma?"
"Are these conditioned phenomena or unconditioned phenomena? The Buddha said:
"One does not find conditioned phenomena apart from the unconditioned, nor does one find the unconditioned apart from conditioned phenomena."
Subhūti! Conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena are a single dharma without duality; they neither conjoin nor disperse; they have no form, are invisible, and are of one mark.
The single characteristic is the absence of characteristics; it is only through conventional designations that there is activity, but this is not the ultimate truth.
The ultimate truth is not something produced by body, speech, or mind, yet it is not separate from body, speech, and mind; one attains the ultimate truth through the equality of all phenomena.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), they do not even apprehend that ultimate sense while performing the deeds of a bodhisattva.
Chapter Eighty-Seven: The Sublime Transformation of All Dharmas The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Eighty-Seven: The Sublime Transformation of All Dharmas Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are equally empty and there is no activity regarding any dharma, how can a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom fail to attain the ultimate truth, yet still perform the deeds of a bodhisattva and provide the four kinds of benefit for sentient beings?
The Buddha told Subhūti: “As you have said, that which is empty neither acts nor does not act. If sentient beings knew emptiness, there would be no Tathāgata nor the realm of the Buddhas.

Without wavering from emptiness, they would transcend all notions of a self and the characteristics of the four great elements; they would transcend the characteristics of the five aggregates and the notions of knowledge and vision; they would transcend the characteristics of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), thereby establishing the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*).”
“This unconditioned nature is empty; in what way is it empty? The Buddha replied: “It is empty of all marks;

it is empty like a person created by a magician. Since that which is not a magical creation and emptiness itself are neither conjoined nor dispersed, they are empty through emptiness. There is no one who can distinguish between this emptiness of emptiness and the magically created person.”
Why is this? Because both are empty, Subhūti!
"Among the five aggregates, there is nothing that is not empty; it is because they are empty that one speaks thus, saying 'the five aggregates are empty.
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!"
If worldly phenomena are like an illusion, are the dharmas of the Path likewise like an illusion?

If the dharmas of the Path are indeed illusions, then from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and the three vehicles, they too are like illusions; even those who practice the three vehicles are likewise like illusions.
The Buddha replied:
"By whom were these transformed dharmas produced? Were they produced by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas?
Or were they produced by bodhisattvas or buddhas?"
"These are transformations produced by the traces of habitual tendencies;
these are transformations produced by conditioned activities. He replied, "There is no one who transforms."
The Buddha said:
"For this reason, all dharmas are like transformations.
He asked again:
“World-Honored One!
Are the cessations achieved by those from the *srotāpanna* up to the *arhat*, as well as the cessation of all residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the Buddha, likewise like an illusion?”
The Buddha replied,
"All that arises and all that ceases are entirely like transformations.
He asked again:
“World-Honored One!
What dharmas are not like a transformation?
The Buddha replied:
"That which neither arises nor ceases is not a transformation.
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is it that neither arises nor ceases, and yet is not a transformation?
The Buddha replied,
"Nirvāṇa is not a transformation."
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
You have always taught that emptiness is immovable and unchanging, that there are no dualistic dharmas, and that nothing is not empty; therefore, even nirvāṇa is like an illusion.”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is!
All things are empty; this emptiness is not something created by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor is it something created by bodhisattvas or buddhas. To realize emptiness is nirvāṇa."
He asked again:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the practice of those who have passed away in emptiness, how should one enter it, how should one train in it, and how should one explain it?”
The Buddha replied: "What do you think, Subhūti?
Is there only a past world, and no future world?"
Chapter 88: Sadāprarudita The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Eighty-Eight: Sadāprarudita. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to seek the prajñāpāramitā should follow the example of the bodhisattva Sadāprarudita;
he currently resides in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ghoṣadatta, constantly practicing the pure conduct of brahmacarya."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how did the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita seek the Prajñāpāramitā?”
The Buddha replied:

"When the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita sought the Prajñāpāramitā, he did not spare his own body or life, nor did he hope for offerings or seek renown. He constantly dwelt in solitude and heard a voice from the sky saying:

'Dwell, O son of good family! Do not give rise to thoughts of weariness, fatigue, or sleep; do not think of food or drink; do not think of day or night; do not think of cold or heat; do not allow your mind to be attached to the internal or external; do not look around to the left or right.'"
While practicing, one should maintain this intention: one should act as if not acting, and regarding the five aggregates of the body, no signs of arising should be produced. Why is this?

One who produces signs of arising will encounter obstruction and hindrance regarding the Buddha-dharma; one who encounters such obstruction and hindrance remains within the suffering of birth and death; and one who remains within the suffering of birth and death cannot attain the *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, Sadāprarudita replied to the voice in the sky, saying:
"I shall follow your instructions. Why is this?"
"I wish to act as a great light for sentient beings and widely proclaim the Buddha-dharma; I wish to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having spoken these words, he heard a voice from the air saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

"Good son! If you wish to hear the dharmas of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), you should seek the *prajñāpāramitā*; you should abandon thoughts of signs; you should abandon the view of a life-force (*jīvadr̥ṣṭi*); you should abandon the view of a person (*pudgaladr̥ṣṭi*); you should distance yourself from evil associates (*akalyāṇamitra*); you should attend upon virtuous associates (*kalyāṇamitra*); you should make offerings to true friends; they shall explain to you the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they shall explain the dharma of non-arising and non-extinction; and they shall encourage and assist you in seeking *sarvajñatā*."
One who practices in this manner will, before long, hear the Prajñāpāramitā—either hearing it from within the sūtras or hearing it from the mouth of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Noble son, you should regard the person from whom you hear the Prajñāpāramitā as if they were Śāstṛ (the Teacher).

You should cultivate a spirit of reciprocity toward this Dharma-preacher and must not turn your back on their kindness. The one from whom you hear the Prajñāpāramitā is your true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Having heard this sūtra, you shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and never again regress.

You should think to yourself: 'I am not far from all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; in whatever place I am born, I shall always encounter the Buddhas; I shall always remain far removed from the eight unfavorable conditions (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*), and I shall attain the eight favorable conditions.'"
"Maintaining these virtuous qualities, you should revere the Dharma Master as you would the World-Honored One, and not with worldly expectations;
toward the Dharma Master, you should give rise to the perception of the Dharma and the perception of reverence. Know that those who harbor expectations are engaged in the work of Māra."

If Māra Pāpīyān should bring the five kinds of music, or present the dharma master with fine and smooth forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and textures as offerings, the dharma master, through *upāya-kauśalya* (skillful means), may accept them in order to deliver sentient beings.
If you see them, do not give rise to defiled thoughts; you should simply reflect:
"I have not yet attained this *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means).
As for the practice of the Dharma Master, a bodhisattva who has already attained *upāyakauśalya* is without any hindrance.
For example, just as a diamond penetrates everything without being defiled by dust or grime, one should regard the Dharma teacher through the practice of a single method of discipline.
What is this single method of discipline?
This means that all phenomena are without attachment and without cessation. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are empty, devoid of self, person, life, or soul; they should be viewed as being like illusions or a mirage in the heat of the sun.
Dharma Master, for a guide who practices this contemplation, it will not be long before they attain the Prajñāpāramitā.
Son of good family,
you must guard against the works of Māra.

“Good son! If you come upon the place where the Dharma Master resides but do not see him, do not give rise to thoughts of obstruction; rather, for the sake of the Dharma, you should show reverence to the Dharma Master.
At that time, having heard the voice from the sky, Sadāprarudita proceeded eastward.
After traveling east for no long time, he thought to himself:
"I did not ask earlier where I should go or how far it was from here."
"From whom shall I hear it?
Thereupon he wept bitterly; having finished weeping, he thought to himself:
"From this moment forth, I shall no longer eat or drink, nor shall I move or turn about; from the first day until the seventh day, I will not rise until I have heard the Prajñāpāramitā."
The Buddha told Subhūti: “Suppose an elder has an only son who dies;
the parents grieve, having no other thought but only thinking of their son.”
"Subhūti! At that time, Sadāprarudita had no other thought whatsoever; his mindfulness was directed toward the Prajñāpāramitā alone, just so.
While he was weeping in this manner, there appeared before him the likeness of a Tathāgata, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics."
That Buddha praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O son of good family!"
When the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past were practicing as bodhisattvas, they sought the Prajñāpāramitā in this very same way.
Maintaining this spirit of courageous exertion, travel eastward from here for twenty thousand li; there is a land named Gandhavatī.

Its city walls were encircled by seven layers of the seven treasures; moats with flowing water surrounded it in ten tiers, lined with rows of trees made of the seven treasures and filled with ditches of the seven treasures.
The city was four hundred and eighty li in length and breadth; the kingdom was prosperous and joyful, with a vast population, and all their clothing and ornaments were of rare and exquisite jewels.

Within the city were five hundred railings, and the streets, lanes, and marketplaces were arranged in orderly rows. Various precious substances, gold, and silver were inlaid upon them, and silken banners and streamers were suspended from them. Like celestial brocade, the towers, pavilions, gabled buildings, and battlements atop the city walls were all fashioned from the seven treasures. Rows of jewel-trees stood marvelously along the walls, and canopies of Jāmbūnada gold formed decorative lattices above.

Bells made of the seven precious gems were suspended from its pavilions; when the wind arose, it blew upon the bells, and their sound was harmonious and elegant like celestial music. Any sentient beings who heard the sound of the bells found delight therein.

The water surrounding the city moats is temperate—neither cold nor hot—and is always full without diminishing. Within these waters are boats made of the seven treasures; the people ride these boats to sport and play within the moats. It is because those people possessed merit and virtue from their past lives that they have attained this.

Within the waters of that pond were *pundarīka* flowers, *puṇḍarīka* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, and *utpala* flowers; furthermore, there were other flowers of various kinds and diverse colors numbering in the thousands and hundreds, such that no exquisite flower existing throughout the trichiliocosm was not present there.
Circling the city in due order, there were five hundred pavilions, each likewise fashioned from the seven treasures and exquisitely adorned.

Within each pavilion were five hundred ponds, each twenty *li* in length and breadth. These ponds were filled with wonderful flowers of various colors made of the seven treasures; the flowers were as large as carriage canopies, and their five colors—blue, yellow, red, white, and crimson—were each distinct and vivid.
Within that pond were ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, peacocks, and cormorants—several thousand species of rare and extraordinary birds.

All the precious objects within the city’s houses and pavilions likewise had no owners and no guardians; this was due to the accumulated merit of the people of that land and their constant practice of the Prajñāpāramitā, whereby they have long enjoyed such blessings.
“Good son! There is a bodhisattva there named Dharmodgata.

In the center of that land is a palace, forty *li* in length and breadth. Its walls are made entirely of the seven treasures and are sevenfold; its railings, jeweled trees, gardens, pavilions, and bathing pools are likewise sevenfold. Its towers, balconies, palaces, and gatehouses are all made of the seven treasures, adorned with sevenfold carvings and engravings.”
Within the palace of Dharmodgata, there are four pavilions:
the first is named Constant Joy, the second is named Removal of Sorrow, the third is named Variegated Flowers, and the fourth is named Variegated Fragrances.
Within each pavilion, there are eight pools of water.
The first is named Bhadra; the second, Bhadrottama; the third, Rati; the fourth, Ratottama; the fifth, Śrī; the sixth, Śreṣṭhaśrī; the seventh, Haṃsa; and the eighth, Anivartin.
On each of the four sides of that pond was one kind of treasure:
gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Its bottom was made entirely of purple-polished gold, and it was covered with a canopy of golden mesh.
In each of these ponds, the steps are made of gold, composed of various colors of *śaṅkha*, *aśmagarbha*, and diverse precious gems.
On both sides of these steps, there are plantain trees made of purple gold, their flowers soft and supple, drooping gracefully as they sway in the wind.
Within the waters of that pond there are also various flowers, just as those previously mentioned.
Along the banks of the pond there are further flowering trees; when the wind blows the flowers down into the water, they immediately appear as if they have grown from roots.
The water of that pond was as fragrant as celestial sandalwood.
Within the palace of Dharmodgata, sixty-eight thousand ladies and court maids surrounded him in joyful diversion.
Men and women from the city of Gandhavatī all came together to the pond of Constant Joy (Nityasukha) to observe and enjoy themselves.
The emanated Buddha said:
"Good son! This Bodhisattva Dharmodgata is enjoying himself together with his retinue."
As the Dharma was being preached during the three periods of the day, the people within the city of Gandhavatī prepared a Dharma-seat for the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.

In the center of the city, they fashioned a seat of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli; it was covered with a cushion of fine, soft karpāsa cloth, which was perfumed with various celestial incenses.
The seat was ten *li* high; upon it were men and women holding dangling pearls, scattering famous flowers, and burning renowned incenses.
For what reason?
"Out of reverence for the Dharma,
the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata sat upon his seat and preached the Dharma to sentient beings by means of the Prajñāpāramitā.
The emanated Buddha spoke again:
“Good son! Such was the manner in which the people of the land of Gandhavatī reverently served and attended upon the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.

Hundreds of thousands of devas came to the assembly to hear and receive the Prajñāpāramitā; among them were some who wrote it down, some who recited it, some who received it orally, some who contemplated it, and some who practiced it through silent contemplation.”
"All sentient beings within this land are all *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, never again to turn back.
"O son of good family!
"Go from here to the east to where the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata resides; there you shall be able to hear the Prajñāpāramitā.
This Dharmodgata was your true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) in previous lives, who constantly exhorted and assisted you toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
When the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata formerly sought the Prajñāpāramitā, he was just like you.
Go now, son of good family!
Do not let your mindfulness cease by day or night, and before long you shall hear the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, having heard these words, Sadāprarudita leaped for joy and said:
"When shall I behold this Dharma Master and receive from him the teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā?"
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Suppose there were a person who, having been struck by a heavy poisoned arrow, had no other thought in mind except to think:
'When shall I find a skilled physician who will extract this poisoned arrow from me and heal the wound!'"
Sadāprarudita had no other thought; he desired only to see the Dharma Master and hear the Prajñāpāramitā from him, and having heard the Prajñāpāramitā, to extinguish all attachments.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita immediately perceived the unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena and attained immeasurable gates of samādhi.

The names of these samādhis were: the samādhi of seeing the nature of all phenomena; the samādhi of non-apprehension of all phenomena; the samādhi of subduing all ignorance; the samādhi of attaining the non-differentiation of all phenomena; the samādhi of attaining the immutability of all phenomena; the samādhi of the non-existence and non-accumulation of all phenomena; the samādhi of extinguishing all darkness; the samādhi of the sequential non-distinction of all phenomena; the samādhi of non-seeing of all phenomena; and the samādhi of scattering flowers.
They attain such immeasurable and various gateways of samādhi.
Abiding in these samādhis, they see the innumerable Buddhas of the ten directions preaching the Dharma for the sake of all bodhisattvas by means of the Prajñāpāramitā.
"At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions all praised him, saying:
'Excellent, excellent! O son of good family!'"

"When we were originally bodhisattvas, our seeking of the prajñāpāramitā was likewise accomplished by abiding in this samādhi; having attained this samādhi, our entry into the prajñāpāramitā was also thus, whereby we achieved upāyakauśalya and established ourselves in the dharma of avaivartika."

When we attain this samādhi, we do not perceive any dharma that practices the samādhi, nor any that departs from the samādhi; we do not perceive any who practice the Path, nor any who attain unexcelled perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
The Prajñāpāramitā is free from arrogance.
Sons of good family!

Because we abide in non-arrogance, we have attained the golden-hued body with the thirty-two marks and boundless radiance; we have attained inconceivable wisdom, the unsurpassed enlightenment, samādhi, and the Buddha-knowledge.
He is fully endowed with all merits, which even the Buddhas cannot measure or exhaustively describe, let alone the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas!
Therefore, son of good family!
Within this Dharma, you should redouble your reverence.
Son of good family!
For one who possesses resolve and diligence, it is not difficult to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good son! One should give rise to a mind of reverence and affection toward a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), regarding them as one would the World-Honored One.
A bodhisattva who encounters a true spiritual friend will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita addressed the Buddhas, saying:
"Who is this true spiritual friend whom I have always revered?"
The Buddhas replied:
"The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has, in every lifetime, constantly instructed you in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata is always fully endowed with the *prajñāpāramitā* and *upāyakauśalya*; he is your venerable teacher and your true spiritual friend."
"O noble son! Accept this with the crown of your head, for the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.

Even if one were to spend from kalpa to kalpa, or even up to a hundred kalpas, making offerings with everything contained within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system, one would still not be able to repay even a moment’s debt of gratitude."
"Because hearing this honored Dharma brings forth merit that is difficult to repay, it shall enable you to attain the benefits of the Prajñāpāramitā and upāyakauśalya.
Having spoken these words, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas suddenly vanished from sight.
"At that time, Sadāprarudita arose from his samādhi, looked around in the four directions, and thought to himself:
'From where have these Tathāgatas come?'"
"Where has he gone?

"Where shall I go? Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, out of reverence, affection, and deep humility for the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, reflected:

One who wishes to honor the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata by means of the *prajñāpāramitā* should not go to Dharmodgata’s presence empty-handed;
for one who possesses reverence yet has nothing to offer is not as good as one who sells their own body to make an offering to the *prajñāpāramitā* and the Teacher.
From the past until now, we have destroyed our bodies many times, yet they have not ceased;

in all those previous destructions of the body, we sat amidst lust, anger, and delusion, undergoing various sufferings and pains—not for the sake of the Dharma, nor for the sake of the Teacher, but solely for the sake of craving, the five aggregates, and the six sense-fields.
"At that time, the Bodhisattva passed through a city and cried out loudly, saying:
'I wish to sell myself; who wishes to buy me?
Then, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:"

"Now this bodhisattva, for the sake of the prajñāpāramitā, has sold his own body, desiring to make an offering to the bodhisattva Dharmodgata, and wishing to hear the prajñāpāramitā and upāyakauśalya."
"How does a bodhisattva practice the prajñāpāramitā so as to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? Having heard this, you must certainly receive it with reverence and prostration."
"I shall not allow those who do not destroy [the truth]—namely, the countless hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas and all sentient beings—to pass beyond my realm.
Now I must go and destroy them."
Pāpīyān immediately caused all the men and women of the kingdom to neither see his form nor hear his voice.
At that time, Sadāprarudita could not sell himself; filled with grief and weeping, he said:
"My distress is extreme; I wish to sell my own body to make an offering to my teacher, yet I am unable to find a buyer!"
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra thought to himself:

"Now this bodhisattva wishes to make an offering to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata for the sake of the Prajñāpāramitā. I shall now go and observe this person to see whether, for the sake of the Dharma, he possesses any flattery or deceit."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra transformed himself into a young brahmin, went to where the Bodhisattva was, and asked Sadāprarudita:
"O son of good family!..."
"Why do you not rejoice, but instead grieve and weep? He replied, "Young man!"
"Because of my devotion to the Dharma, I wished to sell myself to provide for my venerable teacher, yet I could never find a buyer; it is for this reason that I weep.
I reflect upon my own meager merit, having no wealth or treasures with which to serve my teacher."
At that time, the youth said to the Bodhisattva:
"I do not need a man; for my current sacrifice, I desire human blood, I desire human marrow, and I desire a human heart."
“Whoever can give this to me, I shall give you even more treasure.
At that time, the Bodhisattva joyfully replied,
“I have gained a great benefit!”
"Young man!
Buy my heart, marrow, and blood with your wealth and treasures so that I may make offerings to my teacher, enable me to hear the Prajñāpāramitā and Upāyakauśalya, and truly fulfill my aspiration."
The youth asked again: "How much do you seek for the marrow, the blood, and the heart?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Give me as much as you can, according to your young heart's desire.
Sadāprarudita then pierced his own left arm with his right hand and gave him the blood that flowed forth.
When he further intended to break his bone to extract the marrow, there was a daughter of an elder in the city who had transcended the ways of Māra, such that Māra could not subdue her.
At that time, the daughter of the elder saw from atop the multi-storied pavilion that the Bodhisattva had thus taken his own life.
She thought, "I shall now go down and ask him the reason for his intent.
Then, the daughter of the elder immediately descended to where the Bodhisattva was and asked:
"O man! Why have you come to this?
Why do you so cruelly and painfully cut yourself—what use is this blood?
And now you wish to break your own bones!"
Sadāprarudita replied to the daughter of the elder, saying:
"I wish to give myself to this youth; having sold myself to obtain wealth and treasures, I intend to make offerings to my teacher so that I may hear the noble scripture, the Prajñāpāramitā."
Then the daughter of the elder said to the Bodhisattva,
“By making offerings to the Teacher, what kind of extraordinary merit will one obtain?
The Bodhisattva replied:

“Master, you should teach me the *prajñāpāramitā* and *upāyakauśalya*, and instruct me in the dharmas practiced by bodhisattvas; then I shall study them so as to act as a broad bridge for all sentient beings and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

I shall personally attain the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics—the unsurpassed radiance—and obtain the four immeasurable minds, the four fearlessnesses, the ten powers of a Buddha, and the eighteen unique dharmas, as well as the six supernormal knowledges and inconceivable pure precepts.
Having become a Buddha, I shall attain unimpeded wisdom and obtain the supreme treasure that eliminates all poverty.”
"I shall surely attain such a Dharma as this.
When the daughter of the elder heard these words, she leaped for joy and spoke to the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O Worthy One!
How extraordinary, how marvelous!
You have indeed spoken such a subtle and profound Dharma."
To speak with emphasis: by means of this single dharma, the wise person should seek dharmas as numerous as the sands of countless Ganges Rivers. Why is this?
Because this dharma is exceedingly profound and subtle in its application.
"O noble son! Regarding that which you desire to obtain, do not harbor self-doubt or hesitation.

Whether you wish for lapis lazuli, mani-jewels, various gems, pearls, gold, silver, amber, sandalwood, famous incense, silken banners, or flowered parasols—obtain whatever you desire at will. I shall now give them to you; you may take them to offer as worship to the Honored Teacher of the Dharma. Do not thus mutilate and destroy your own body."
Now I also wish to go to that place and follow you, so that we may together plant the roots of goodness.
Whatever you have spoken of, I desire to attain it all.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra immediately extinguished the form of the young brahmin and restored his own body as Śakra; standing before the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, he praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!

"Noble son! Just as you have resolved your mind, so too did all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, while practicing the bodhisattva path, seek the Prajñāpāramitā and upāyakauśalya to achieve anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi, just as you do now, O worthy one."
"Today I do not require your heart, marrow, or blood; I have come here only to test you.
What wish do you desire? Sadāprarudita replied:
"I require nothing else; grant me the vow for Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śakra-devānām-indra replied, "O son of good family!
"This is the realm of the Buddha; it is not something I can accomplish. Please seek other vows for me, and grant me some small measure of merit.
The Bodhisattva replied, "Even if these great vows are beyond your capacity, may my body be restored so that it is free from wounds and sores; let this be your merit."
As soon as these words were spoken, Sadāprarudita’s body was restored to its former state.
Thereupon, Śakra suddenly vanished.
At that time, the daughter of the elder said to the Bodhisattva:
"Follow me back home to see my parents, and on my behalf, report this to them; whatever articles of offering you desire shall be provided to you.
I, too, shall go along, attending to you at your side until we reach the place of the Dharma."

At that time, Sadāprarudita followed the daughter of the elder to her home and stood outside the gate. The daughter of the elder went inside and said to her parents: "Now you must give me gold, silver, precious gems, lapis lazuli, and mani-jewels;

fragrant incense, sandalwood, flower canopies, banners and streamers, various colorful garments, articles for making offerings, and all manner of rare curiosities, as well as five hundred female attendants. For the sake of the Dharma, I wish to follow the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita to the land of King Gandhavatī, to the abode of the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, so that I may hear the honored sutras and all the teachings of the Buddha. Having attained them, I shall bring liberation to sentient beings."
The parents asked the daughter,
"Who is this Sadāprarudita now?
The daughter spoke again, saying:
"This person is now standing outside the gate, having made a firm vow to seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, desiring for the sake of all sentient beings to rescue them from boundless suffering."
There is a great and wondrous Dharma called Prajñāpāramitā, which all bodhisattvas ought to study.
For the sake of this Dharma alone, these sons of good family sell their own bodies, not begrudging their lives, and cut themselves apart, desiring to make offerings to the Great Master Dharmodgata.
This person’s utmost sincerity moved Śakra Devendra; seeing this transformation, I went to him and asked:
"What is so extraordinary that you would so cruelly cut and pierce yourself?
He then replied to me:
"I shall sell myself to this youth in order to obtain wealth to make offerings to my teacher.
I shall attain the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics of a Buddha, and I shall turn the wheel of Dharma to deliver and liberate sentient beings."

Having heard this, I am filled with great joy. Who, upon hearing such a Dharma, would not find delight? I promise that I shall grant them precious jewels, articles for worship, and attendants to serve at their side; therefore, parents, you should provide me with all my precious treasures and female attendants.
The parents said to their daughter:
"As you have said, this man is truly extraordinary in his diligence; he does not begrudge even his own body or life in his desire to seek the inconceivable Dharma."

As you have said, this son of good family will surely be able to accomplish the unsurpassed Dharma, bring peace and security to sentient beings, and establish the great armor of the *saṃnāha-saṃnaddha*; how could I possibly go against such a vow of yours?
If you wish to go and see and make offerings to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, I rejoice for you according to your aspiration; however, I myself am too old and cannot go.
"Grant me whatever precious and rare treasures you desire; I shall never frustrate any of your wishes.

At that time, the woman took five hundred chariots adorned with the seven treasures, along with five hundred handmaidens beautifully arrayed as her attendants, and loaded them with various flowers and multicolored jeweled garments such as those mentioned above, using them for her own transport.
Sadāprarudita took another carriage and was followed by five hundred women surrounding him.

Thereupon he traveled eastward, gradually making his way until he saw from afar the city of Gandhavatī, adorned with the seven treasures in various colors and wondrous jewels, such as had never been seen before, as described above.

Furthermore, from afar he saw that in the center of the city, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata was preaching the Dharma, surrounded by a great assembly numbering hundreds of thousands of myriads; having seen this from afar, he felt immense joy, and his body became as tranquil and secure as a bhikṣu who has attained the fourth dhyāna.
He further thought to himself:
"I must not ride upon a carriage now; I shall proceed on foot.
He then entered through the city gate, surrounded by the daughter of the elder and five hundred women.
He saw a pavilion made of the seven treasures, adorned with red sandalwood and draped with pearls.

At the four corners of the pavilion were four precious vases filled with *maṇi* jewels that shone constantly day and night; there were also precious incense burners where famous incense was perpetually burned, making it fragrant constantly day and night.

In the center of the dais was a stupa made of the seven treasures; furthermore, a casket was fashioned from four kinds of precious gems, and within it was the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, written upon sheets of purple-polished gold. Additionally, banners woven from the seven treasures were interlaced and displayed, their exquisite colors shimmering as they fluttered in the wind.
Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women saw this pavilion made of the seven treasures with latticed windows.

They saw Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with various sons of gods, holding celestial māndārava flowers and celestial sandalwood incense of various colors, which they had ground into a powder as fine as dust; they offered it by scattering it from the midst of the sky upon the pavilion, and further offered worship by playing celestial music.
At that time, Sadāprarudita asked Śakra, Lord of the Devas, from afar:
"For what purpose do you make this offering, scattering flowers upon this terrace?"
Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra replied to Sadāprarudita:
"O son of good family!
Do you not know that this Prajñāpāramitā gives birth to all bodhisattvas?"
"All Bodhisattvas should train in this; they shall accomplish the merits of the various pāramitās, fulfill all Buddha-dharmas, and attain sarvajñatā.
For this reason, we make offerings to it."
When Sadāprarudita heard this, he was doubly joyful.
He then asked Śakra Devānām Indra:
"Where is the Prajñāpāramitā located?"
Śakra-devānām-indra replied:

"It is within a casket of seven treasures at the center of the platform; the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has sealed it with a seal of seven treasures, so that neither you nor I may see it without authorization."

At that time, Sadāprarudita, the daughter of the elder, and the five hundred women each took various famous flowers, renowned incenses, sandalwood, assorted jewels, lapis lazuli, and mani-gems; having made offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā, they set aside a portion for themselves and carried it to the high seat where the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata was.
Furthermore, out of reverence for the Dharma, he made offerings to the Great Master Dharmodgata.
The various flowers he scattered hovered above Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, transforming into a pavilion of the seven treasures that remained suspended in mid-air.

The scattered name-flowers all rained down upon the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata; the various colored precious robes that were scattered remained upon the dais, while emanated devas held celestial banners in their hands and let them hang down.
When Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women saw this transformation, each thought to themselves:
"This is a manifestation produced by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharmodgata; it is truly unprecedented. How much more so will it be when he attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and becomes a Buddha!"

At that time, the daughter of the elder and the five hundred women, seeing Dharmodgata Bodhisattva, leaped for joy and all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Simultaneously, they exclaimed:
"By virtue of these merits, may we also attain the benefits of the Dharma in this very same way."
May we be able to make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā just as the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has;
we too shall extensively proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā to deliver sentient beings, just as the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata has done.

May we attain the Prajñāpāramitā and accomplish upāyakauśalya; may our transformative manifestations reach anuttarasamyaksambodhi, and may we obtain mastery over all dharmas, just like the Great Teacher Dharmodgata.

At that time, Sadāprarudita, along with the daughter of the elder and the five hundred women, having completed their offerings, prostrated themselves with their heads to the ground to pay homage to Dharmodgata. Withdrawing to stand to one side, they joined their palms with a reverent mind and addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, saying:
"In the past, while I was in a place of solitude, I heard a voice in the air say: 'Good son!'"
"By traveling east from here, you will be able to hear the Prajñāpāramitā.
I then departed toward the east, and on the way, I thought:
"From whom shall I hear the Prajñāpāramitā?"
Filled with sorrow and weeping, I remained silent in one place for seven days, not thinking of food or drink, but only wondering when I would obtain the *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, a manifested Buddha appeared standing before me and addressed me, saying:
"O son of good family!..."

Maintaining this diligence and courageous resolve, travel eastward from here for twenty thousand li; there is a land named Gandhavatī where a bodhisattva named Dharmodgata constantly expounds the Prajñāpāramitā. You should go there to hear it from him, for he is your true teacher.

Having heard this instruction from the transformation Buddha, I immediately traveled eastward and saw the Great Master from afar; my heart was filled with joy and exultation, and I felt as secure as a bhikṣu who has attained the fourth dhyāna.
Because of mindfulness of the *prajñāpāramitā*, one immediately attains immeasurable samādhis; then, one sees the Buddhas of the ten directions praising me, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
The samādhis you have attained all arise from the Prajñāpāramitā; when I formerly practiced as a bodhisattva and sought the Prajñāpāramitā, it was also like this.
Having praised me, they vanished from sight.
Upon awakening from my samādhi, I thought to myself:
"From where have these Buddhas come?"
"Where has he gone?
Again, I was filled with great sorrow and anxiety.
I then thought to myself:

“The Great Master Dharmodgata has attained mastery over all dharmas through the *prajñāpāramitā* and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*); I shall go to question the Master as to where the Buddhas of the ten directions come from and where they go.”

"Today, the Great Master has explained for our sake the comings and goings of these Tathāgatas; we wish to know this. Having heard it, we shall constantly behold the Buddhas and never be separated from the World-Honored One."

89. Chapter on Dharmodgata: The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Eighty-Nine, "The Chapter on Dharmodgata. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmodgata replied to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, saying: "Good son!
All Tathāgatas are eternally unmoving; they neither go nor come.
A Tathāgata is suchness (tathatā), which is without arising or ceasing;
that which does not arise neither comes nor goes.
That which is unborn is the Tathāgata. Good son!
The reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) neither knows when it comes nor knows when it goes; that which is the reality-limit is the Tathāgata.
Space neither comes nor goes; that which is empty is the Tathāgata.
Ultimate Truth neither knows when it comes nor knows when it goes; that which is ultimate truth is the Tathāgata.
That which is unconditioned neither comes nor goes; that which is unconditioned is the Tathāgata.
That which is cessation neither comes nor goes; that which is cessation is the Tathāgata.
"Good son! The Tathāgata is not separate from these dharmas; these dharmas are the suchness (tathatā) of the Tathāgata. 'Good son!"
That which is "suchness" (tathatā) is one; it is not two, nor three, nor does it have any numerical plurality, because all phenomena are empty.
Son of good family!

It is like when the spring season has passed and the summer heat is at its peak, with fierce flames of heat; a fool pursues them, thinking they are water, chasing them without ceasing and crying out that he shall obtain water.
What do you think, worthy one?
From where does the water that this man pursues come?
Does it come from the eastern ocean, the western ocean, the southern ocean, or the northern ocean—from which ocean does it come?
Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva replied:
"Even a mirage in the heat is not water; how much less could there be any coming or going from the ocean!"
Dharmodgata spoke again: “Good son!
That ordinary person, driven by the torment of heat and thirst, conceives the notion of water and pursues it until he is exhausted, yet in the end, he does not obtain water.”
Those who give rise to the notion that the Tathāgatas come and go are no different from ordinary worldlings.
Why is this? Do not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the physical body.
The Tathāgata is the dharma-nature; the dharma-nature neither comes nor goes, and all Tathāgatas are likewise without coming or going.
"O son of good family!

For example, it is like a magician who conjures elephants, horses, and chariots; those who claim that these illusions come and go are all fools. Likewise, those who claim that the Tathāgatas come and go are also ordinary worldlings.
"Why is this? Because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) neither comes nor goes.
Sadāprarudita then addressed Dharmodgata, saying:
"What is seen in dreams and illusions is entirely empty and without reality;
it is utterly non-existent. Dharmodgata replied, "O son of good family!..."
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has declared: "All dharmas are like dreams.

Those who perceive a real characteristic within these dream-like and illusory dharmas do not know the Tathāgata; they merely enter into the name and form-body of the Tathāgata, and thus conceive of the Tathāgata as coming and going.

These people are all ignorant ordinary beings; these ordinary beings will have many returns upon the path of birth and death, remaining very far removed from the *prajñāpāramitā* and likewise distant from all Buddha-dharmas.
Regarding all phenomena that are like dreams and illusions, one who knows that all phenomena are like dreams and illusions is to recognize the Tathāgata.

One who does not seek the characteristics of coming or going in any phenomena, nor seeks for any Tathāgatas to have birth or extinction—anyone who knows that the Tathāgata neither comes nor goes and is neither born nor extinguished—is close to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi before long.
This is what it means to practice the Prajñāpāramitā; such a person is a disciple of the Buddha.
These individuals should receive the offerings of the land, for they are fields of merit for the world.
Good son! For example, all the various precious jewels found in the great ocean do not come from the lands of the ten directions;
rather, because of the merit of sentient beings, the ocean produces these jewels, and they do not arise without cause.
This treasure arises due to causes and conditions; at the time of its cessation, it likewise does not go to the ten directions.
It arises from causes and conditions and ceases from causes and conditions, nor does it come or go from the ten directions.

"Good son! The bodies of the Buddhas are formed through the causal conditions of practice; they are brought about by past conduct, yet they do not travel to the ten directions by means of such practice.
If there were no practice and no convergence of causal conditions, and if there were no causal conditions, there would likewise be no body."
Good son! It is like a lute:
due to causes and conditions, there are strings, there are bridges, and when a person strikes it, sounds come and go; yet when the sound ceases, there is likewise no coming or going.
When this sound emerges, it comes from nowhere; when it perishes, it goes nowhere.

If you wish to know that the Buddha-body is likewise so, its immeasurable virtues are not accomplished by a single cause; they are all formed through the convergence of causes and conditions, and do not depart from or arrive at existence apart from causes and conditions.
"Good son! You should know that even the Buddhas have no coming or going; all dharmas are likewise thus, neither arising nor ceasing.
Having realized this, you will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and will surely perfect the Prajñāpāramitā and upāyakauśalya."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra gave heavenly māndārava flowers to Sadāprarudita, saying: "Take these to make an offering to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata;
may you thereby bring me merit."
Why is this? All sentient beings shall receive the grace of the Benevolent One and shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
You, O Superior Being, are rare in this world and extremely difficult to encounter; yet for the sake of sentient beings, you undergo toil, not regarding even incalculable kalpas as labor.
Then, Sadāprarudita accepted the māndārava flowers from Śakra Devānām Indra and scattered them over the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.
Having scattered them, he said:
"From this day forward, I offer my own body to my teacher to provide whatever service is required."
With palms joined, they withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the daughter of the elder and her five hundred attendants said to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:

"We wish to offer our bodies to the Great Master for whatever he may require; by means of this merit, may we attain the benefit of the Dharma just as the Great Master has, and may we always together with the Great Master make offerings to all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."
At that time, Sadāprarudita said to the daughter of the elder and her five hundred female attendants:
"If you will follow my instructions, I shall accept you."
The women replied, "Our lives and bodies belong to you as our teacher; we dare not disobey your instructions.
Then, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita said to the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata:

"We pray that you will take our bodies, as well as these five hundred women, the five hundred chariots, and all that we possess, and offer them to the Great Master; out of compassion for us, we pray that you will accept them!"
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra exclaimed: "Excellent, excellent!
Those who have resolved to attain the mind of a bodhisattva should maintain all they possess just as this worthy one has done."
A bodhisattva who practices giving in this manner will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
one who thus reverently serves their teacher will swiftly be able to hear the Prajñāpāramitā and upāyakauśalya.

All the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past were likewise; by practicing the giving of the mind, they attained the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), and thus realized unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata accepted Sadāprarudita, the merchant’s daughter, the five hundred female attendants, and all the precious treasures from the five hundred chariots; he accepted them all in order to enable Sadāprarudita to fulfill his merit.
Although he accepted them, he then returned them to the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita.
"At that time, as the sun had already set, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata rose from his high seat and returned to his palace.
Then, Sadāprarudita thought to himself: 'I have come for the sake of the Dharma;
it is not fitting for me to sit or lie down. There are two matters for which I must wait for my teacher to emerge:'"
"First, walking meditation; second, standing still.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata entered the palace and sat upright, employing the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the *prajñāpāramitā* to practice innumerable samādhis for seven years.

Sadāprarudita likewise did not sit or lie down for seven years; he constantly practiced walking meditation and remained standing, never giving rise to the three impurities or any taste for sensual desires, but thinking only: "When will the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata emerge to preach the Prajñāpāramitā for me?"
After seven days had passed, Sadāprarudita thought to himself: "I shall prepare a magnificent high seat for my teacher;
with various kinds of famous flowers and by burning renowned incenses, I will await the Dharma Master as he expounds the Prajñāpāramitā for the great assembly."
“Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women each prepared seats, spreading upon them their own fine garments, various famous silks, and soft, delicate fabrics.”
Sadāprarudita then went to seek water, intending to sprinkle it upon the ground, but he was utterly unable to find any.

This was because Māra Pāpīyas had concealed and hidden it so that the water would not appear; his intent was to ruin the Bodhisattva by causing him to give rise to distracted thoughts, rather than allowing him to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Sadāprarudita thought to himself again:
"I shall pierce my own body and shed my blood to sprinkle upon the ground. Why is this?"
Fearing that dust from the ground might come and soil the Master,
I shall not begrudge this fragile and precarious body. Why is this?
"Throughout the countless kalpas from the past until now, we have discarded bodies beyond calculation, yet we had never before encountered this unsurpassed Dharma.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita took a sharp blade, pierced his body until blood flowed out, and used it to sprinkle the ground.
The five hundred women each did likewise.
At that time, Pāpīyān was unable to find any opportunity.
Then, Śakra Devānām Indra thought to himself:

"This Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita and these five hundred women are truly most extraordinary; their craving for virtue is such that they do not begrudge their own bodies or lives in their reverence for the Dharma Master."

Although Māra Pāpīyān seeks to destroy you, he cannot find an opportunity; thus, you remain steadfast in your saṃnāha-vow, not sparing even body or life, as you desire to deliver sentient beings from the boundless suffering of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Śakra praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Your worthy diligence is inconceivable."
"This is the supreme vow; when the Buddhas of the past practiced their original path, their diligence was just like this.
Then Sadāprarudita thought to himself:
"I have now finished preparing the seat for my teacher."
"Where can I obtain fine flowers to scatter over the Dharma Master when he emerges?
At that time, Śakra, knowing his thoughts, gave the Bodhisattva a thousand *droṇas* of celestial *māndārava* flowers and said to him:
"Take these to offer to the Teacher, and also scatter them upon the ground."
He immediately took those flowers, scattered them over the ground, and set aside one portion for himself.

After seven years had passed, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata emerged from his palace and proceeded toward the high seat; Sadāprarudita and the five hundred women then took the celestial flowers and scattered them over Dharmodgata as they met him, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Bodhisattva Dharmodgata addressed the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita:
“O son of good family!
Listen attentively and receive this well; reflect upon it with care.”
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita received the instruction and listened.

"All dharmas are equal to the diamond (vajra); all dharmas are quiescent; because all dharmas are equally quiescent and immovable, the Prajñāpāramitā is also equal to the diamond in its quiescence and immovability."
Because all phenomena are without dependence and all phenomena are without fear, and because all phenomena have a single flavor, the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise without dependence.

Because all phenomena have a single flavor and are without fear, all phenomena are unarisen, all phenomena are unceasing, and all phenomena are like space; therefore, the *prajñāpāramitā* is neither arisen nor ceased, and is also like empty space.
Because the five aggregates are bottomless and boundless, because all phenomena are bottomless, and because the four great elements are bottomless, the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise without bottom.
Because emptiness is without boundary, the great ocean is without limit, and all phenomena are without boundary, the *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise without boundary.
Just as Mount Sumeru is adorned with all manner of excellences, so too is the Prajñāpāramitā.
Because all dharmas are indestructible, all dharmas are unperceivable, all dharmas are without reception, all dharmas are non-existent, and all dharmas are inconceivable;
likewise, the Prajñāpāramitā is indestructible, unobtainable, without reception, non-existent, and inconceivable.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, while seated upon his mat, attained the samādhi of the equality of all dharmas, the samādhi of the tranquility of all dharmas, the samādhi of immovability, the samādhi of non-reliance, the samādhi of fearlessness, the samādhi of one flavor, the samādhi of non-arising, the samādhi of non-cessation, the samādhi of space, the samādhi of the bottomlessness of the five aggregates, the samādhi of the bottomlessness of all dharmas, the samādhi of the boundlessness of the four great elements, the samādhi of the nature of space, the samādhi like the ocean, the samādhi like Mount Sumeru, the vajra-samādhi, the samādhi of indestructibility, the samādhi of non-apprehension, the samādhi of non-reception, the samādhi of non-existence, and the inconceivable samādhi.
"By means of such samādhis as these, he attained sixty thousand gates of samādhi.
Chapter Ninety: Entrustment The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Chapter Ninety: Entrustment. The Buddha addressed Subhūti:

"At that time, after the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita had attained sixty thousand samādhis, he beheld in the ten directions as many trichiliocosm world-systems as there are sands in the Ganges River. In each, he saw Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, surrounded by assemblies of bhikṣu-saṃghas, preaching the Prajñāpāramitā."
Just as I now preach the Prajñāpāramitā for you all, so too do the Buddhas of the ten directions; their names are likewise Śākyamuni.

The Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita is fully endowed with extensive learning, and his wisdom is like the ocean. He never departs from the places where Buddhas are born, remaining before the Buddhas; even in his dreams, he has never been apart from the Buddha. All hardships have been severed, and he has attained mastery.
"Therefore, Subhūti, you should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* brings about the attainment of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

Bodhisattvas who wish to study the six *pāramitās*, and who wish to attain the state of all-knowledge—the realm of all Buddhas—should study and practice the *prajñāpāramitā*; they should receive it, uphold it, recite it, and read it; they should extensively explain its meaning to others, and they should also make offerings with all kinds of famous flowers, famous incenses, silken banners, and flower canopies, employing various skillful means to honor it."
Why is this? Because the Prajñāpāramitā is that which is honored by all Buddhas; it is the charioteer of the honored Path.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What do you think? Do you hold the Tathāgata in high esteem, affection, and reverence? Ānanda replied:
"Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
We love and revere the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata knows this himself.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"You truly love and revere the Tathāgata.
Ānanda! Since you have attended upon me from beginning to end, your body, speech, and mind have always been characterized by goodness and compassion."
"Now that I am old in years, do you think that what a disciple ought to provide in the way of offerings has been completed?
It is not yet complete.
From this day forward, you should reverently serve and attend to the Prajñāpāramitā."
The World-Honored One then repeated this exhortation regarding the Prajñāpāramitā from one to three times.
Why was he so earnest and solemn?
This is because one wishes to prevent its interruption.
If the Prajñāpāramitā were to be interrupted, all sentient beings would be forever left in blindness and darkness.
If the Prajñāpāramitā remains in the world without being cut off, then the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, will likewise never be cut off.
If the Prajñāpāramitā were to be interrupted, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, would likewise be interrupted.

"Ānanda! As long as the Prajñāpāramitā abides in the world, you should know that the Tathāgata is constantly preaching the Dharma, and that all sentient beings do not depart from the Buddha’s assembly nor from the preaching of the Dharma."

Ānanda! If there is one who copies, upholds, recites, contemplates, preserves, practices, explains its meaning, and makes offerings to this Prajñāpāramitā, and furthermore teaches others to copy, uphold, recite, and extensively explain it—know that such a person is always together with the Buddha and is never separated from all Buddhas.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, Maitreya Bodhisattva, the elder Subhūti, the Venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Mahākauṣṭhila, Mahākātyāyana, the Worthy Ānanda, and all those present in the assembly—the devas and asuras—having heard what the Buddha said, were all greatly rejoiced and came forward to pay homage to the Buddha.
The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra of the Radiant Light, Fascicle Twenty.
